title: Decision in the Making
text:
Preface
Five hands rise for one candidate, two for another. A decision is made.
Each member of the hiring committee can explain their vote. They cite the candidates’ qualifications, their interviews, and the needs of the organization. These considerations should guide the choice: what the job requires and which candidate is most likely to meet those requirements.
But their judgments may also reflect influences they have not considered. The order of the interviews may affect how candidates are compared, while the first opinion voiced may guide the discussion. Even how tired or anxious a member feels may influence their judgment without appearing among the reasons they give for their vote. A recent conflict with a colleague, or a successful collaboration many years ago, may shape which qualities they notice and how much weight they give them.
Would the committee have chosen the same person if the interview order had been reversed, or if someone else had spoken first? Explaining why a candidate deserves the job is different from explaining how the committee came to prefer that candidate. To understand the vote, we need to look upstream, at how members interpreted the evidence, formed expectations, and influenced one another before raising their hands.
This is the central question of the book: what shapes a choice before it is made, and how can we use that understanding to choose better?

title: Decision in the Making
text:
Follow the decision upstream
Consider what might lie behind the divided vote. Two members could agree that one candidate is more creative and the other more reliable, yet disagree about which quality matters more. Further evidence could help resolve uncertainty about the candidates’ abilities, but it would not by itself settle a difference in priorities. That requires a conversation about what the team needs.
The available options deserve attention too. A vote between two candidates can obscure a third possibility: reopening the search if neither applicant meets the team’s needs.
The decision map in Figure 1 brings these questions together. It follows how we notice and interpret information, construct options, anticipate consequences, and judge how much those consequences matter. Once we choose and commit, the resulting outcomes give us an opportunity to learn.






Figure 1: A map for following how a choice takes shape. The steps can overlap or repeat; green arrows show how learning can influence later decisions.



Considering another option may reveal information we need, while experience can change what attracts our attention next time.
The decision map makes alternatives, beliefs, and priorities explicit so that we can evaluate a choice. An important gap in evidence calls for investigation; conflicting priorities call for discussion; an inadequate set of options calls for imagination. The map helps us identify the difficulty and choose a response that addresses it.
The early chapters examine how judgments form and how we can check them. A quick impression may draw on useful experience or give too much weight to a vivid story. Taking more time can help us examine the judgment, but it can also help us defend our first answer. The question is what supports that answer and what could change it.

title: Decision in the Making
text:
Decide together
When people decide together, the process must also bring their knowledge into the conversation. A hiring committee can know more than any one of its members, yet fail to use what it knows.
After an influential member endorses a candidate, others may follow because they assume that person has better information. Later endorsements may echo the first judgment without adding independent evidence. Someone with a reservation may stay silent because challenging the emerging agreement feels uncomfortable or disloyal. The group can become more confident while important doubts remain unspoken.
Connection matters because people need to be able to share those doubts. Feeling heard and respected can make it easier to explain a concern, correct a misunderstanding, or consider another perspective. Relationships that allow honest disagreement can therefore support clearer communication, fuller information sharing, and more constructive conflict resolution.
That openness can help the committee understand its disagreement about reliability and creativity. One member may be trying to protect an overloaded team; another may worry that meeting today’s demands leaves no time to develop tomorrow’s ideas. Making these concerns explicit creates room to explore whether redistributing responsibilities could provide reliable coverage while protecting time for new work. If this is impractical, the committee still needs a fair way to weigh those competing needs and decide.
The committee’s decision is only part of the outcome, because the candidate must also decide whether to accept the offer. Each side needs to understand what the other wants and what they can do if no agreement is reached. A candidate may value flexible working hours, while the organization needs reliable coverage at particular times. Agreeing on core hours with flexibility around them could serve both sides better. Listening and sharing priorities can reveal these opportunities to create value. Negotiation then needs to turn them into clear commitments that both parties can fulfill.
These connections explain the book’s movement through choice, influence, and agreement. How we judge affects how we persuade; how we communicate affects what we can learn from one another; and what we learn can change the decisions and agreements available to us.

title: Decision in the Making
section: Ask what makes the choice better
text:
Ask what makes the choice better
Even a welcome agreement can rest on mistaken expectations about life afterward. The committee may expect a successful appointment; the candidate may anticipate meaningful work, financial security, or more time for family. An attractive offer can promise these things while revealing little about an ordinary working day.
The book also follows choices into the lives that result from them. How do we weigh a possible gain against the risk of loss, or a benefit years away against a demand we face today? Why can a sincere plan give way to a familiar habit?
We will also examine how accurately people anticipate what they will enjoy, how experience changes what they value, and how decisions affect relationships and meaning. Better decisions require us to consider whose life is meant to improve and in what way. When we shape choices for others, that responsibility includes asking whether they can understand the arrangement, question it, and choose differently.

title: Decision in the Making
text:
Put understanding to work
The committee can use this understanding to change its next search: agreeing on criteria before meeting candidates, recording individual judgments before discussion, and giving reservations a clear place in the conversation. Each step addresses a different problem and makes the decision easier to examine.
The final part of the book develops this practical approach. It considers how to support useful routines, make choices easier to understand, and improve how organizations gather and evaluate evidence. A proposed change needs a clear purpose, conditions that make it workable, and a way to assess whether it helps.
Assessing a decision requires care, because even the best choice given the information available can have a poor outcome. A route selected after checking traffic can still lead to a delay if an accident occurs after departure. A stock investment can lose value when geopolitical tensions escalate, and a business strategy can lead to losses when an unexpected technological development disrupts the market. To learn from the outcome, we need to consider what information was available when we chose, whether we used it well, and what we have reason to change next time. Recording our expectations before the result gives us something more reliable to consult than hindsight alone.
The same care applies to the evidence behind the book’s recommendations. We will examine what studies actually compared, what they found, and how later research changes the conclusions we can draw. Our recommendations will be based on evidence, with attention to the settings in which they have been tested.
These questions also guide our use of data and AI. A tool may organize information or improve a prediction, while people still need to decide what counts as success and how the prediction should guide action. The final chapter examines how these tools can contribute to decisions we can explain, evaluate, and improve.
This book grew from teaching behavioral economics and decision making, persuasion, and negotiation. Students wanted to understand why sensible recommendations could fail, well-intended conversations could create distance, and useful agreements could remain out of reach. They also wanted to know what they could do differently next time. The activities throughout the book serve that purpose: you will make predictions, examine cases, compare explanations, and try changes whose consequences you can observe.
Think of a decision you are about to make. Before committing, consider how you came to favor one option and whether your reasons deserve the weight you have given them. There may still be time to question an assumption, hear another perspective, or discover a better possibility.
We should pay attention to our decisions while they are still in the making.

title: How to Use This Book
text:
Reading layers
Start with a decision you want to understand, or read the seven parts in order to follow the complete argument. The book is written for advanced undergraduate and master’s students and for professionals who want evidence they can use. Follow the main explanation first, then choose the optional theory, methods, or applications that help with your question.
Each chapter’s opening situation establishes a question that the main argument develops. Follow the explanation in words and the numerical examples first. Mathematical analysis boxes collect equations, model parameters, and derivations; you can skip them without losing the main argument and return when you want to work through a calculation. They can be expanded in the web edition and appear as separate boxes in the EPUB. Appendix A provides the fuller mathematical treatment of decision analysis.
Research Lens boxes and optional research notes examine models, measurement, or debates in greater depth. Occasional applications, including the Applied Module in the strategic-thinking chapter, extend an idea into a particular domain.
A Practice Lab asks you to produce something: a forecast, a question, a decision record, a message, or a proposed change. Choose a manageable example and make the output specific enough to inspect. You can use a fictional case when a personal one would be sensitive.
Footnotes provide methodological details and qualifications that some readers may want to examine more closely. The main text identifies the study’s comparison and outcome as part of explaining its result.

title: How to Use This Book
text:
A recurring chapter rhythm
Chapters introduce a problem, develop an explanation, examine evidence, and give you a way to apply what you have learned. When a Predict first invitation appears, commit to an answer before reading the result. Comparing your expectation with what happened gives you a specific question to investigate: what did your first explanation miss? Afterward, ask what you would now do differently and why.

title: How to Use This Book
text:
Use one recurring ethical audit
When you propose a message, intervention, or agreement, ask whose objective it serves, who benefits, and who bears the cost. Consider whether the people affected can understand the arrangement, refuse it, or seek correction. Unequal power can make apparent consent difficult to interpret.
Finally, decide how you would discover that the proposal is causing harm. Appendix F collects the full ethical audit alongside the practical tools.

title: How to Use This Book
section: Find your place in the book
text:
Find your place in the book
The preface’s decision map helps distinguish questions that need different answers. Uncertainty about an outcome calls for evidence; disagreement about its importance calls for a discussion of priorities. Each part opens with a shorter map of its own questions, while chapter notes locate particular mechanisms in the wider process. These maps organize the inquiry; human thought can move back and forth among the functions. In the preface’s map, green arrows show where learning can prompt revision. The first box identifies the current inputs; action and learning can change what is available for the next decision.
When you use the map, keep the four terms in Table 2 distinct: interpreting what something means, predicting an outcome, forming an expectation, and deciding how much the outcome matters answer different questions.



Table 2: Vocabulary for following the decision process.









Term
Meaning in this book




Interpret
Work out what an observation, action, or message means in context.


Predict
Anticipate the consequences of an option, including uncertainty.


Expectation
A belief about what will happen; in some settings, that belief can also help change the outcome.


Value
Assess how desirable or otherwise important a predicted consequence is.






Chapter 4 also introduces the technical use of prediction in theories of perception and distinguishes it from forecasting future consequences.

title: How to Use This Book
text:
Use the recurring cases cumulatively
Several cases return as the analysis develops. A hiring decision lets us examine evidence, intuition, and group judgment. Supplier, employment, and used-car negotiations show how preparation, offers, useful trades, and implementation create different problems. A difficult workplace conversation connects interpretation to communication and repair.
When a familiar case returns, look for the new question it helps answer. How to Read the Evidence in This Book offers a short guide to evaluating the studies along the way.

title: How to Use This Book
text:
Version and link policy
The version date identifies the current build. Some linked resources and applications change over time; the surrounding text supplies the central explanation so that a broken link need not interrupt your reading. Corrections are most useful when they identify the passage and the evidence that would change it.

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
Begin with the claim
Imagine deciding whether to spend a limited training budget on a programme advertised to “raise productivity by 20%.” The promise sounds large enough to justify the purchase. But if the reported improvement reflects who enrolled or measures a short test rather than work performance, buying the programme may not deliver the benefit you need. The spending decision turns on what the number actually compares.
Did participants improve relative to their own earlier performance, or relative to people who did not receive the training? The answer changes what we can infer about the programme. We also need to know how people entered those groups and whether the outcome measures the benefit the organization wants.
The following questions help turn a memorable result into a claim we can evaluate.
Begin by asking what the training claim promises. Reporting that participants improved is descriptive; using their earlier results to forecast later performance is predictive. Saying that the programme produced the improvement is causal, while explaining how it did so is mechanistic. Extending the conclusion to other people or workplaces adds a claim of generality. These claims require different kinds of evidence.
The training participants might improve because of the programme, because unusually motivated people enrolled, or because a temporary slump ended. An association between attendance and improvement would not separate those explanations. Even a credible causal effect would leave questions about why the programme worked and whether it would work elsewhere.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
Read the comparison and outcome
A useful account of evidence identifies the comparison, the outcome, and the explanation being tested. Methodological details in the footnotes let you examine a result more closely.
For the training example, knowing that the outcome was a short knowledge test directs attention to what participants learned. A follow-up measure of workplace performance would answer a different practical question.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
Separate size from certainty
Ask how large the estimated difference is in meaningful units, how uncertain the estimate is, and whether the range of plausible effects would matter for the decision. Read the result alongside its comparison, including the denominator and study condition when a proportion is reported. A percentage of participants who acted once is different from a percentage of all opportunities to act. In a hypothetical service team, an increase from 10 to 12 completed cases per hour and an increase from 100 to 120 are both 20%, but they add 2 and 20 cases per hour respectively. The starting level and units make the gain interpretable.
A p-value is not an effect size or the probability that a theory is true. A statistically significant result can be too small to matter in practice, while an imprecisely estimated effect may still include important possibilities. Magnitude, uncertainty, and practical relevance need separate attention.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
Ask what was measured
Trust, happiness, attention, and similar constructs are inferred from observations such as answers, choices, response times, or physiological measures. Each measure captures some aspects more directly than others.
For example, a person who rejects an unequal offer might dislike inequality, want to punish the proposer, or be concerned about reputation. The rejection alone does not identify the motive. A convincing explanation needs a comparison that helps distinguish the alternatives, rather than a new label for the same observation.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
Distinguish an illustration from evidence
Fictional cases and classroom demonstrations help make an idea concrete. They show how something could happen. A study investigates a specified comparison; replications examine whether the result survives new samples or implementations. Field studies examine behavior in everyday or organizational settings and may be observational or experimental. Formal models make assumptions and their implications explicit.
A meta-analysis combines studies but inherits difficulties in the available literature, including selective publication and differences in measurement. No source type answers every question. Look for the evidence that bears on the particular claim.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
section: Use replication to update a finding
text:
Use replication to update a finding
A failed replication may weaken confidence in an original finding, reveal a boundary, or expose a difference in measurement or implementation. Comparing the studies helps distinguish these possibilities. A successful replication strengthens support across the conditions tested.
Low precision, flexible analysis, and selective publication can make a literature look more convincing than it is. Preregistration, transparent reporting, accessible data and code, and independent replication help readers examine these problems. Appendix E’s evidence-status map applies this approach to prominent behavioral findings.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
Ask whether the finding travels
Return to the training claim. Results from volunteers may differ from results among employees required to attend; a short course may work differently when instructors, incentives, or opportunities to practise change. The outcome and follow-up period matter too.
Generalization becomes more informative when we specify which differences should matter and test them. “It depends” is the beginning of an explanation only when we can say what it depends on.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
A six-question evidence audit
For any claim you might use, ask:

What exactly is being claimed? Description, prediction, causation, mechanism, or generality?
What is the comparison? Compared with what, for whom, and over what period?
How large and uncertain is the estimate? Consider the units and the range of plausible values.
What else could explain the observation? Identify a competing account.
Where might the finding change? Consider the population, task, and setting.
What evidence would change my confidence? Make the belief open to revision.

You do not need to become a methods specialist before reading the book. Keep these questions nearby, and return to them when a result surprises you or seems useful. Appendix C shows how to use them across a literature, explain what is known, and identify what remains unresolved. Appendix D turns a research question into a study; Appendix E explains how replication and research integrity shape the evidence available to us.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape
text:
Questions to carry forward
A hiring committee is about to vote. Everyone has read the applications, yet the discussion turns on different things: one member remembers an impressive interview, another worries about reliability, and a third keeps returning to the candidate they liked first. They must make one consequential hire, but reading the same applications has not given them a shared basis for choosing. Before asking who should get the job, we need to understand how these judgments took shape.
The route in Figure 1 begins with a standard for a good decision: identify the feasible alternatives, consider their consequences, and clarify what matters. It then follows the actual process, from the evidence that attracts attention to the interpretation, expectations, and values that make one option seem preferable. The hiring case establishes the difference between giving reasons for a choice and explaining how it formed. A choice between job offers then shows how to construct alternatives and investigate an uncertainty that could change the decision. Later chapters examine what we notice, expect, and value before we can explain our preference.
The distinction between predicting an outcome and valuing it will be useful throughout the book. Two people can agree about what is likely to happen and still reasonably prefer different actions.
Once we can see how a judgment forms, we can ask how well it handles uncertainty. Part II follows the shortcuts that help us judge quickly—and the checks that reveal when they mislead.

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
Learning goals
A rational benchmark is not a psychological portrait
Return to the hiring committee in the preface, just before the chair asks for a vote. Two candidates remain, and the committee wants the person who will contribute most to the organization. Its choice will affect both the work the team can do and the opportunities each candidate receives. Before counting the hands, ask:
A defensible process would identify the feasible candidates and any other feasible course of action, such as extending the search, collecting a work sample, redesigning the role, or making a conditional offer. It would predict the consequences of each alternative using job-relevant evidence. It would clarify what the organization values: immediate performance, learning, leadership, reliability, diversity of expertise, retention, or some combination. It would then choose the feasible alternative expected to produce the most valued consequences.
Now ask a different question:
One candidate may have become the early favorite. A vivid story may receive more attention than a reliable but unremarkable indicator. The word fit may mean one thing to the chair and another to the future supervisor. A prestigious employer may be treated as evidence without anyone stating what it predicts. A confident senior colleague may speak first, causing junior members to revise or conceal their judgments. The option of extending the search may never enter the discussion. By the time the vote is called, much of the decision may already have been made.
The committee can agree that it should hire the strongest candidate while allowing prestige, speaking order, or an unexamined idea of fit to determine who looks strongest. A shared intention to decide well has not supplied a reliable process. The first question asks for a standard; the second asks for a causal explanation. The practical challenge is to bring the actual process closer to the standard.
After reading this chapter, you should be able to:

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
Three questions of decision science
The committee needs to improve its hiring process, but it cannot diagnose a failure merely by restating what a good decision would look like. It must identify how the actual judgment departed from that standard and what could change it. The normative, descriptive, and prescriptive perspectives in Table 1.1 separate these tasks and set different standards of success.



Table 1.1: Three questions of decision science










Perspective
Central question
Standard of success




Normative
How should the decision be made under stated assumptions?
Coherence, evidence-responsive beliefs, legitimate objectives, and fit between means and ends.


Descriptive
How are judgments and choices actually formed?
Empirical accuracy about attention, interpretation, option construction, prediction, valuation, action, and learning.


Prescriptive
How can the actual process be improved?
Better calibration, consistency, fairness, implementation, contestability, and learning, given real human capacities and environments.






For the hiring committee, these questions lead to different work. It must agree on relevant evidence and legitimate objectives, investigate how prestige or hierarchy influences the discussion, and design a procedure that makes those influences open to examination. Recording judgments before discussion, for example, could reveal disagreements that an immediate public vote would conceal.
An intervention succeeds only if it improves something worth improving. More agreement or faster voting would not by themselves establish a better hiring decision.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape
1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
section: How a decision should be made
text:
How a decision should be made
If everyone recommends the “best” candidate, apparent agreement can hide disagreement about performance, priorities, or even which options remain open. A rational-choice model makes those ingredients explicit and offers a deliberately thin answer to the normative question. In its most basic form, the decision-maker faces a set of feasible alternatives, ranks them, and chooses a highest-ranked alternative. For decisions whose consequences are uncertain, it is useful to unpack that ranking into three substantive inputs (von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944; Edwards, 1954).

Feasible alternatives: What courses of action can actually be taken?
Beliefs or predictions about consequences: What may follow from each alternative, with what likelihood, timing, and uncertainty?
Values or preferences over consequences: How desirable, undesirable, important, fair, meaningful, or unacceptable would those consequences be?

The beliefs describe what may follow; the values say how much those consequences matter. Together they support a ranking, from which the decision-maker selects a highest-ranked feasible alternative. Figure 1.1 makes these relationships visible: prediction and valuation support choice, while feedback from the outcome can inform later judgment.






Figure 1.1: A normative decision process built around the rational-choice benchmark. Information about alternatives supports prediction; prediction informs valuation; valuation supports choice; and outcomes can provide feedback for later judgment.




Judgment, prediction, valuation, and choice
Judgment includes assessing what may happen (prediction) and how desirable it would be (valuation). Choice selects an alternative, while implementation turns that commitment into action. Implementation connects choice to outcome; review and interpretation turn feedback into learning.
Information also differs from feasibility. The committee may never hear about a candidate it could hire, or may consider someone who cannot accept. Constraints such as budget, law, and time determine what can actually be done; they are already reflected in the feasible set. Chapter 2 shows how to distinguish these limits from assumptions that can be challenged.
The formal conditions for coherent rankings, including transitivity, belong in Appendix A. Risky Decision-Making develops expected utility, one representation of consequence-based choice under risk.
The benchmark is powerful because it separates disagreements that ordinary language often hides. Two colleagues may agree about what matters but disagree about the probability of success. They may agree about the forecast but value the consequences differently. They may agree about both while recognizing different alternatives as feasible. Words such as best, fit, safe, and risky can conceal all three disagreements.
Values may include family welfare, dignity, fairness, environmental consequences, loyalty, moral duties, future generations, or the interests of other affected people. Emotion can provide information about what matters. A choice may consistently advance one person’s objectives while violating another person’s rights. Legitimate objectives, affected parties, and procedural justice therefore cannot simply be hidden inside an unexplained score.
The model is a benchmark, not yet a psychological portrait. It tells us how the ingredients of a coherent consequence-based choice should relate once the alternatives, beliefs, and values have been specified. It does not tell us how alternatives become visible, which evidence receives attention, how that evidence is interpreted, or why beliefs and values change with context. The six examples that follow test those descriptive assumptions.

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
section: From a normative benchmark to descriptive predictions
text:
From a normative benchmark to descriptive predictions
A normative model generates descriptive predictions only after we add assumptions about stability. Suppose that two presentations leave the feasible alternatives, predicted consequences, values, and action costs unchanged. A thin rational-choice account then predicts that the choice should also remain unchanged.
For example, expressing the same outcome as survival or mortality should not reverse preference when the descriptions are understood as equivalent. Adding an inferior option should not improve the attributes of an existing one. Yet a default may change the effort needed to act, and an internal state may change what someone currently values. Those cases require different explanations.
The examples below ask where the model succeeds, where its predictions fail, and where it leaves out part of the decision.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape
1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
Six ways context enters choice

Representation and comparison

1. The same treatment data, framed through survival or mortality
A treatment recommendation should respond to its consequences. Merely switching from the language of survival to the language of mortality leaves those consequences unchanged—yet it may change which treatment people prefer.
McNeil, Pauker, Sox, and Tversky (1982) presented a hypothetical choice between surgery and radiation therapy for lung cancer to ambulatory patients with chronic illnesses, graduate students, and physicians. Different groups received outcome data framed in terms of survival or mortality. The cumulative probabilities and time horizons were complementary, yet surgery was relatively more attractive in the survival frame.
A thin rational model treats the descriptions as different ways of presenting the same consequences. If the event, denominator, horizon, and implications are understood as equivalent, preference should not change merely because one description foregrounds living and another foregrounds dying. The observed shift is therefore a comparatively direct challenge to description invariance.
Complementary descriptions can produce different representations of the same outcome data, and those representations can alter treatment preference. Framing develops the mechanism and the ethical response.


2. The subscription option nobody chose
An option that nobody wants might seem irrelevant to a decision. If removing it changes what people choose, however, the menu is doing more than displaying independently valued products.
A well-known classroom demonstration presented three subscription options: web-only access, print-only access, and print plus web access. The print-only option cost the same as the combined offer and was therefore dominated by it. Ariely (2008) reported that nobody in the classroom group chose the print-only option, yet its presence shifted choices toward the combined offer. When the dominated option was removed, web-only access became much more popular.
The attraction-effect literature supplies the experimental foundation for this pattern. Adding an asymmetrically dominated alternative can increase the share choosing an existing target, contrary to regularity in standard menu-independent models (Huber et al., 1982).
The decoy does not improve the target’s objective attributes. It changes the comparison. Value is not always retrieved from stable preferences and applied to a menu. The menu can help construct the comparison through which value becomes visible. Anchors, Halos, and Decoys develops the evidence and mechanism.



The path from intention to action

3. Organ donation and the consequence of doing nothing
Giving people the same response options seems to preserve the same choice. Yet an unfinished form can have different consequences depending on its design.
An organ-donation form can require people to opt in, presume participation unless they opt out, or require an active choice. Johnson and Goldstein (2003) found large differences in stated agreement across online experimental defaults. Formal freedom to select either response remained, but the consequence of doing nothing did not.
A default can alter effort, perceived recommendation, normality, responsibility, anticipated regret, and the outcome of postponement. These changes affect the decision-relevant environment.
Moving from agreement to transplantation also requires registration, clinical capacity, and successful organ recovery. A longitudinal analysis of five countries that changed from opt-in to opt-out found no average increase in deceased donation after the policy switch, emphasizing the importance of clinical capacity, public trust, family involvement, and implementation (Dallacker et al., 2024). Choice Architecture treats a default as one component of a system.



Two examples from commercial practice
The next two cases suggest useful mechanisms, but their evidence is weaker than the controlled comparisons above. Read them as questions to investigate, not established estimates of what an arrow or a product name will cause.

4. A right-pointing arrow and a more visible action path
In 2012, Google added a clickable right-pointing arrow to text advertisements on its Display Network while also changing typography, spacing, and layout. Google reported higher clicks after the bundled redesign; the report cannot isolate what the arrow contributed (Land & Yuan, 2012).1
The product did not improve, but the route to acting on an interest became more visible. This makes the case useful for examining the path between evaluation and action. Choice Architecture returns to the design and the evidence needed to test it.


5. Mars publicity and Mars-bar accessibility
News reports in 1997 linked rising Mars-bar sales to publicity around NASA’s Pathfinder mission. Repeated references to Mars offer an intuitive hypothesis: the product name may have become easier to retrieve without any change in the chocolate. The available sales account cannot establish that causal connection (Grant, 1997).2
Berger and Fitzsimons (2008) later used the association to motivate experiments on environmental cues and choice. The distinction is worth keeping: a memorable story suggests a mechanism; a suitable comparison tests it. Priming, Fluency, and Familiarity develops the experimentally grounded account.



When an active motive changes the message

6. The same museum, a different active motive
Popularity can promise reassurance or make an experience seem ordinary. An advertiser needs to know which meaning the audience will hear, because the same appeal could support or undermine the message.
Griskevicius and colleagues (2009) independently manipulated an induced state—fear, romantic desire, or a neutral condition—and the appeal used in advertisements for a museum or Las Vegas. Appeals based on behavioral social proof—many people visit—or distinctiveness—stand out from the crowd—changed in effectiveness across the induced states. Fear made behavioral social proof relatively more persuasive and distinctiveness less persuasive; romantic desire produced the opposite pattern in the reported evaluations.
The venue did not change, but students’ persuasion and product-desirability ratings depended on the interaction between the induced motivational state and the appeal.
The experiment illustrates how an option’s appeal can depend on the concerns brought to it. The same venue can promise safety, belonging, novelty, or distinction. A thin model can represent this by changing values, but it does not predict when and how those values will change. Valuation develops state-dependent value.

What the six examples reveal



Table 1.2: Six ways context enters a decision










Example
What changed—and why it matters
Study or observation




Lung-cancer treatment frame
Complementary survival and mortality descriptions shifted treatment preference; representation can alter valuation.
Controlled study of hypothetical treatment preferences.


Subscription decoy
A dominated option shifted choice toward the target; the comparison set can construct relative value.
Classroom demonstration and attraction-effect experiments.


Organ-donation default
Stated agreement changed with the default; inaction, effort, recommendation, and responsibility enter choice.
Online experiment measuring stated agreement; longitudinal research on donation rates.


Advertising redesign
Clicks reportedly increased after a bundled redesign; visibility and affordance affect implementation.
Corporate report of a bundled redesign.


Mars publicity
Sales reportedly rose during Mars publicity; accessibility may influence consideration and evaluation.
News report of a sales association.


Museum message
Message effectiveness changed across induced states; active motives shape interpretation and valuation.
Factorial advertising experiment measuring student ratings.






The contrasts in Table 1.2 distinguish changes to the decision from changes to its representation. A default alters the consequence of inaction, whereas the survival and mortality descriptions present equivalent outcome data. Explaining either requires more than naming the eventual preference.
A model that takes alternatives, beliefs, and values as given can represent a choice once those inputs have been specified. Its harder task is to predict how the inputs will arise. Adding a new preference after every unexpected result may explain the past without predicting the next decision. Bounded-rationality research made this process problem central (Simon, 1955).

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
How decisions are actually made
When people explain a decision, they usually begin near the end: “I chose the consulting job because it had better prospects”; “We hired her because she was the strongest candidate”; “I bought the product because it offered the best value.” These explanations may contain genuine reasons. They are rarely the whole causal story.
Long before the committee votes, members have selected evidence, interpreted it, considered some candidates more seriously than others, and formed expectations about working together. Discussion can change both those expectations and the importance attached to them. Even after a choice, an unavailable candidate or an unclear offer can prevent the intended action.
The next diagram opens the earlier loop to show these influences. It also shows why an outcome must be interpreted before it can inform another decision.






Figure 1.2: How decisions are made. External context shapes presented information and the decision-maker’s internal state and model. Within judgment, selection and interpretation interact with prediction and valuation. Judgment supports choice and action; outcomes provide feedback that may update, reinforce, or fail to correct the internal model.



In Figure 1.2, the functions can overlap, recur, become compressed through practice, or be distributed across people and technologies. The arrows show their dependencies and routes of influence.
The map includes two easily overlooked tasks. People must construct options, because the first visible menu is rarely complete. They must also turn choice into action, which depends on effort, authority, and opportunity. Prediction and valuation can interact throughout: learning what an alternative offers may change its appeal, while recognizing a priority can change what evidence people seek.
Chapter 2 turns this account into practical work: expand the feasible set, identify what commitment would give up, and test the assumptions on which a recommendation depends (Milkman et al., 2009).

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
section: Evaluate decision quality separately from outcomes
text:
Evaluate decision quality separately from outcomes
Once an outcome arrives, judging the decision seems easier: success appears to vindicate the choice and failure to condemn it. But a good decision can produce a bad outcome, and a poor decision can produce a favorable one. Rewarding luck or punishing a defensible risk can teach the wrong lesson. A useful review must separate process quality from result quality.
An investor may buy after one enthusiastic post and make money. Another may diversify on defensible evidence and lose during an unexpected market shock. A surgeon can recommend the treatment best supported at the time and still encounter a rare complication. Outcome bias judges the earlier decision mainly by its result; hindsight bias makes the result seem more predictable after it occurs (Baron & Hershey, 1988; Fischhoff, 1975).
Feedback therefore does not automatically create learning. A useful review reconstructs what was known, which alternatives were considered, what was predicted, what mattered, and what could have changed the decision. A dated record protects the earlier judgment from a narrator who already knows the ending. The Narrator After Choice develops that problem; Decision Hygiene turns it into organizational practice.
The preface’s map sends feedback to five decision functions because a review can change more than a forecast. It may reveal a missed signal, suggest another option, alter the importance attached to a consequence, or change how a choice is carried out. Reconsidering what matters also requires judgment about whose interests count, rather than simply copying whichever action was rewarded.
Learning changes future information as well. An option avoided after a disappointing experience is less likely to be tried again, leaving fewer opportunities to discover that the first result was misleading. Denrell and March (2001) show how adaptive sampling can sustain this kind of error. Current context and information therefore describe the starting point for a particular decision, not conditions that remain fixed across decisions.

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
One architecture across the book
The same questions extend beyond individual choice. Persuasion changes what another person notices or believes; communication makes interpretations open to checking; negotiation lets people construct a path they could not take alone. Throughout, we will ask whose decision is being changed, toward whose objective, and with what opportunity to question or revise it.
The final chapter, Deciding With Data and AI, returns to Figure 1.1 to examine the division of work between AI and people. Better prediction becomes useful when it informs a feasible choice whose consequences matter. The intervening chapters explain why this requires more than a capable model: evidence can be misinterpreted, priorities can remain hidden, authority can silence disagreement, and feedback can fail to correct mistakes. Those lessons provide the basis for designing and evaluating AI-assisted decisions.

Practice Lab
Choose one consequential decision that has not yet been finalized.

Write two short accounts. The first answers How should this decision be made? The second answers How is it actually being made?
Identify one normative, one descriptive, and one prescriptive question.
State the feasible alternatives, beliefs about their consequences, and values over those consequences. Show how constraints determine feasibility rather than listing them as another preference input.

text:
Take it forward
Before calling the vote, the chair could ask: “What are we predicting about each candidate, and where do our judgments differ?” The answer would reveal more than a show of hands. It would expose the assumptions that need attention while there is still time to change the decision.

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
text:
Learning goals
Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness
Two job offers are open on a student’s laptop. The consulting firm promises structured training and a familiar name; the sustainability start-up offers early responsibility and work she cares about. She starts a comparison table, then stops at “work–life balance.” Neither employer has told her what an ordinary week actually looks like.
A comparison table should help her choose the job that best fits her life. But without the missing information, it cannot establish whether the working conditions are sustainable. Its fixed columns may also hide a better possibility: changing an offer before accepting it. Her income, learning, and daily life depend on more than which column wins. What can she negotiate, what would each commitment give up, and what does she need to learn before deciding?
After reading this chapter, you should be able to:
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
text:
Distinguish the feasible set from the smaller set of alternatives that happen to receive serious consideration.
Construct alternatives without treating constraints as a separate item from feasibility.
Identify opportunity cost as the value of the best feasible alternative forgone.
Separate predictions about consequences from values over those consequences.
Assess information by whether plausible results could change action.
Distinguish a robust recommendation from one that depends on fragile assumptions.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
section: A better decision begins before comparison
text:
A better decision begins before comparison
The student may be able to negotiate workload, request another conversation, or agree on a later start date. None of these possibilities appears in a table labeled only “consulting” and “start-up.” Comparison becomes useful after the alternatives have been examined.






Figure 2.1: A practical sequence for better decisions: expand the feasible set, name the best forgone option, ask what information could change the choice, and stress-test the ranking.



The questions in Figure 2.1 can send the student back to an earlier step. A forecast may reveal a new option, and a priority may reveal a term worth negotiating.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
section: Define the decision before solving it
text:
Define the decision before solving it
“Should I accept?” sounds like a clear question. It can nevertheless close off negotiation, further search, and the option to learn before committing. To keep those possibilities available, a useful decision statement specifies the commitment being considered, the decision-maker, the relevant horizon, and the conditions under which the choice can be revised. Compare:

Should I accept the start-up job?

with:

By Friday, should I accept the start-up offer as written, negotiate its terms, request time for one further conversation, continue the search, or decline, given my financial runway, family location, learning goals, and tolerance for employment risk over the next two years?

The second statement makes clear what must be decided now and what can still change. It gives the student a deadline for comparing feasible paths, including a revised offer, against the life she wants those paths to support.
Before analysis, ask:

What commitment is being made now?
Who has authority to make it?
Whose consequences legitimately matter?
What is the relevant time horizon?
Which parts are reversible, and at what cost?
What decision will occur automatically if nobody acts?

These questions prevent a broad life problem from being compressed into a misleading yes-or-no choice.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
text:
Construct the feasible set
A feasible alternative is a course of action that can actually be taken given relevant limits of money, time, law, authority, technology, health, capability, and commitment. Those limits define feasibility; they are not a separate fourth component added after the alternatives have been listed.
For the student, “work anywhere” may be imaginable, a remote role may be feasible, and only the two written offers may receive serious consideration. These are three different sets:

The imaginable set: everything one can describe, including options that are impossible or impermissible.
The feasible set: the alternatives that can genuinely be implemented.
The consideration set: the alternatives noticed, recalled, or taken seriously, some of which may still need a feasibility check.

People commonly consider only part of what is feasible, while also entertaining options that turn out to be unavailable. A consistent ranking cannot recover a good alternative that never entered the comparison.

Distinguish real constraints from assumed constraints
A visa condition may rule out one location; a deadline imposed by an employer may be negotiable. The student needs to find out which kind of limit she faces. Asking for a later start date changes nothing if the employer cannot accommodate it, but the request may reveal flexibility that the original offer concealed.
Ask: What would have to change for this option to become feasible, and who could change it? The answer might identify a negotiation, permission, investment, or redesign. It might also confirm that the boundary is fixed.


Generate alternatives deliberately
When the visible menu is too narrow, use a small set of generative moves:

Maintain: Keep the status quo or continue the current path.
Delay: Preserve the option while waiting for a defined event or date.
Learn: Gather information, run a test, seek a second opinion, or conduct a pilot.
Negotiate: Change price, timing, scope, responsibilities, safeguards, or exit terms.
Combine: Create a package or hybrid from parts of existing alternatives.
Stage: Begin with a limited, reversible commitment and expand only if conditions are met.
Search: Reopen the market or generate alternatives outside the current menu.
Exit: Stop, decline, or abandon the project.

These moves matter because careful comparison cannot recover a better path that never entered the choice. The student need not invent an ideal job; discovering one feasible change to the terms may be enough to improve her options.
A wider menu need not overwhelm the chooser. Early demonstrations of choice overload (Iyengar & Lepper, 2000) were followed by a meta-analysis finding an average effect close to zero across varied settings (Scheibehenne et al., 2010). Later work identifies conditions under which complexity and uncertainty make larger menus harder to use (Chernev et al., 2015). For now, aim for meaningfully different options that can be compared; Chapter 40 examines when and how to simplify a menu.
A useful stopping question is:

Do we have at least one meaningfully different alternative, not merely a slightly altered version of the current favorite?
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
text:
Name the opportunity cost
Each offer makes its own benefits visible: training, responsibility, income, or meaningful work. Accepting those benefits, however, can close off a more valuable path. The student needs to compare what she gains with the best feasible opportunity she gives up. Opportunity cost is the value of the best feasible alternative forgone, including the consequences of that complete path. It is neither just the money paid nor the sum of every benefit in every unchosen life. The same reasoning applies to a meeting that displaces focused work or a project that uses capital needed elsewhere.
Opportunity cost depends on the alternative set. Discovering a better feasible option raises the cost of accepting every proposal already on the table. Conversely, if the apparent alternative is not actually feasible, it should not be used to exaggerate the sacrifice.
Research on opportunity-cost neglect shows that people do not always generate the displaced alternative spontaneously. Frederick et al. (2009) demonstrated this with a minimal change in how a hypothetical purchase was described. One hundred and fifty students imagined deciding whether to buy a desirable DVD for $14.99. When the alternative was simply “not buy,” 75% chose the DVD. When that same alternative added the reminder “Keep the $14.99 for other purchases,” the purchase rate fell to 55%. The objective options had not changed; the reminder made an otherwise implicit use of the money easier to represent.
A later meta-analysis of 39 experiments, mainly involving hypothetical choices, found a robust but considerably smaller average effect than the original studies reported (Maguire et al., 2023). Making a forgone alternative salient can improve awareness of the trade-off and change choice. Decision quality depends on how feasible and valuable that alternative is.
Before commitment, ask:

If I choose this, what is the best feasible path I will no longer be able to take?

Naming that path often clarifies the decision more than adding another score to the favored option.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
text:
Separate predictions from values
Suppose the student and her adviser disagree about the start-up. Another report about the firm might resolve a disagreement about its prospects, but it cannot settle how much autonomy is worth relative to stable income. Before seeking more evidence, they need to identify which kind of disagreement they have. A consequence-based decision combines two distinct judgments:

Prediction: What is likely to happen if this alternative is chosen?
Valuation: How desirable or undesirable would that consequence be?

The distinction sounds obvious but is often lost in ordinary discussion. “The candidate is the best fit” may combine a prediction about performance, a value placed on similarity, a feeling of interpersonal ease, and an unstated view of what the organization should become. “The project is too risky” may combine the probability of failure, the size of the loss, the ability to recover, and the speaker’s tolerance for uncertainty.
For the student and her adviser, the next step is to state their disagreement precisely: do they expect different working conditions, or place different weights on the same conditions? That answer determines whether another conversation with the employer should seek evidence, explore different terms, or both.

Make predictions inspectable
For each alternative, write the consequential forecast, its horizon, a plausible range, and the evidence supporting it. “The start-up will offer faster learning” becomes more useful when the student specifies what she expects to learn in the first year, from whom, and what would make that expectation wrong. Comparable past cases can provide a reference class against which to check the forecast.
The purpose is to make an expectation testable. Confidence and a detailed story cannot substitute for evidence about what usually happens in comparable circumstances.


Make values and trade-offs inspectable
Important decisions usually involve several objectives. A job can affect income, learning, autonomy, health, location, family time, mission, relationships, and future options. A public decision may affect different groups unequally. Some consequences can be traded off; others may be unacceptable even when an aggregate score is high. Multiattribute decision analysis can help make these objectives and trade-offs explicit (Keeney & Raiffa, 1976).
The student should explain what “learning” means before assigning it a weight. Is it valuable in itself, or mainly because it opens future opportunities? Counting both without checking their overlap can exaggerate the advantage. Health may instead be a threshold: an option is unacceptable if its expected demands exceed what she can sustain.
The separate columns in Table 2.1 keep forecasts open to an evidence check and values open to discussion. A weight such as “health: 30 percent” is hard to interpret until the relevant range and trade-off are specified, and uncertainty should remain visible in the entries.



Table 2.1: A prediction–value table for comparing alternatives










Alternative
Prediction: consequences, evidence, and uncertainty
Valuation, thresholds, and safeguards




Option A
What is expected to happen, when, and across what plausible range? What evidence and causal assumption support the forecast?
Which consequences matter, to whom, and why? What must be true before committing?


Option B
What is expected to happen, when, and across what plausible range? What evidence and causal assumption support the forecast?
Which consequences matter, to whom, and why? What must be true before committing?


Status quo or delay
What follows if no new action is taken? Is inaction really neutral?
What is preserved, lost, or postponed? When will the decision be reopened?






The table should preserve uncertainty rather than hiding it. If one option looks best only because every uncertain input has been entered at its most favorable value, the apparent precision is misleading.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
section: Assess the value of further information
text:
Assess the value of further information
When a consequential choice feels uncertain, another question or report can seem like progress. But the offer deadline still approaches, and an answer that leaves every action unchanged may consume time without improving the choice.
Information has instrumental value when it can improve action enough to justify its costs. Those costs include money, delay, attention, privacy, processing, false reassurance, and strategic exposure.
To assess a proposed question or test, list its plausible answers and the action that would follow each. Then compare the expected benefit of acting on the answer with the cost of obtaining and using it. In Table 2.2, the pilot and timing question can redirect action; the diagnostic test, as specified, cannot.
If every plausible result leaves action unchanged, the inquiry may still serve curiosity, reassurance, or documentation. It has little instrumental value for that particular decision.



Table 2.2: A decision-branch test for information










Question or test
Result that could change action
Likely decision value




Reference check on role-critical behavior
Credible evidence changes the ranking, safeguards, or contract terms.
Potentially high when the choice is close and the source is informative.


Small pilot before an irreversible launch
A pre-stated threshold triggers scale-up, revision, delay, or stopping.
Often high when the pilot is cheap, representative, and tied to a decision rule.


Diagnostic test when treatment would be identical either way
No plausible result changes treatment.
Low for this treatment decision.


Negotiation question about timing
A real difference reveals a feasible trade or package.
Potentially high when the answer is credible and contractible.






The technical appendix formalizes the expected value of information. For now, the student can ask the employers about ordinary working hours and decide in advance which answers would change the offer she accepts or the terms she requests.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
text:
Stress-test the recommendation
A comparison table may produce a clear winner even when its most influential entries are uncertain. If a small credible change reverses the ranking, committing on the strength of the final score hides what matters most. The next task is to discover what the recommendation depends on.
A robust recommendation remains preferred across specified, plausible changes in the assumptions. A fragile recommendation reverses when a small credible change is made. Sensitivity analysis examines how the recommendation responds to changes in those assumptions.
Sensitivity analysis asks:

Which assumption contributes most to the recommendation?
How far would that assumption have to move before the preferred option changes?
Is that threshold inside or outside the plausible range?
Are the assumptions correlated?
What happens under a jointly unfavorable scenario?
Can the decision be staged or made reversible if the ranking is fragile?

Suppose the start-up is preferred only if it survives for three years, workload remains below a certain level, and rapid learning receives a very high value. The decision should not be reported simply as “the start-up scores 82 and consulting scores 78.” The useful conclusion is conditional:

The start-up is preferred if its survival probability is above the stated threshold and if early autonomy is valued more than near-term income by at least the specified trade-off. Otherwise, consulting is preferred.

This form of conclusion identifies what should be investigated, negotiated, protected, or monitored.
Fragility does not always justify more analysis. When information is expensive or unavailable, a reversible choice may be better than another forecast. A pilot, probation period, staged investment, contingency clause, or exit option can reduce the cost of being wrong.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
text:
Use proportionate analysis
The preceding tools can improve a decision, but using all of them in depth for every choice would consume the time they are meant to help us use well. The practical problem is deciding how much analysis the decision deserves.
Bounded rationality recognizes that search, attention, time, memory, and computation are scarce (Simon, 1955, 1956). People often satisfice: they search until an alternative meets an aspiration level rather than proving global optimality. That can be procedurally rational when further search costs more than it is likely to improve the decision.
The appropriate depth of analysis depends on the decision.



Table 2.3: When to use more or less decision structure










Decision feature
Usually warrants less structure
Usually warrants more structure




Stakes
Low
High


Familiarity
Repeated and well learned
Novel


Reversibility
Easy and inexpensive to reverse
Irreversible or costly to reverse


Feedback
Fast, clear, and diagnostic
Delayed, noisy, or absent


Interdependence
Mostly individual
Depends strategically on other people


Distributional effects
Limited and private
Affects rights, fairness, or many stakeholders


Uncertainty
Narrow and well understood
Wide, ambiguous, or model-dependent






At the less demanding end of Table 2.3, low-stakes, familiar, reversible choices can rely on routines, trained intuition, or simple rules. High-stakes, novel, irreversible, strategically interdependent, or low-feedback choices deserve more explicit structure. Rationality should guide proportionate deliberation, not turn life into continuous calculation. Intuition and Deliberation asks when compressed judgment is well trained; Risky Decision-Making develops the expected-utility detail needed when uncertain consequences must be combined.

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
section: Turn the comparison into a recommendation
text:
Turn the comparison into a recommendation
By Friday, the student’s recommendation should explain more than which offer scored highest. Suppose the start-up is preferred because she values early responsibility, can absorb a limited period without income, and expects to receive close supervision. The supervision forecast now becomes a question worth checking before commitment. If that support is absent, the recommendation may reverse.
The record should also name the best alternative forgone. If consulting is the next-best feasible path, its complete value is the opportunity cost of accepting the start-up; structured training and income are parts of that value, not separate alternatives to add together.
A short recommendation can therefore state the chosen path, its main reasons, the assumptions that could reverse it, and the safeguards needed to proceed. A workload agreement and a scheduled review may make the choice easier to live with even when uncertainty remains. Use the practice below to create this record for a real decision.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
text:
Practice Lab
Prepare a one-page decision record for a consequential decision.

Rewrite the decision so that the commitment, decision-maker, horizon, and automatic outcome of inaction are explicit.
List the visible alternatives, then add at least one option created through delay, learning, negotiation, combination, staging, search, or exit.
Mark which alternatives are imaginable, feasible, and seriously considered.
State the best feasible alternative forgone by the current favorite.
Separate the three most important predictions from the three most important values.
Identify one piece of information and write the action that would follow each plausible result. If no result changes action, explain any other purpose the inquiry serves before spending time or money on it.
State the assumption most capable of reversing the recommendation and the threshold at which it would do so.
Specify one implementation safeguard and one review point.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: 2  Building a Better Decision
text:
Take it forward
The student began with two offers and a blank comparison table. She can now leave with a decision, a reason to trust it, and a clear account of what might change her mind. For your next consequential choice, start with the same practical test: name one feasible alternative you had overlooked, then identify the uncertainty most capable of changing your recommendation.

title: 3  Limited Attention
text:
Learning goals
What Becomes Evidence?
You are watching players pass a basketball and counting the passes made by the team in white. Keeping count takes effort because players cross paths and the ball keeps moving. While you follow it, how much of the rest of the scene do you expect to remember?
If you have not seen it before, try the attention demonstration before continuing. Follow its counting instructions, then compare what you noticed with what was present. Familiarity with the demonstration changes what you search for, so a second viewing is a different task.
Careful attention should help us make better use of the evidence in front of us. Yet concentrating on the assigned target can leave something else outside awareness. Doing the task well may still leave us unprepared for a decision that depends on an unexpected event. The challenge is to protect useful focus while creating a way for consequential evidence outside that focus to enter judgment.

title: 3  Limited Attention
text:
Explain inattentional blindness and change blindness.
Distinguish top-down selection from bottom-up capture.
Redesign an information environment so that neglected evidence can enter judgment.
