title: 14  Base Rates and Updating
text:
Learning goals
Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating
A candidate passes a screening test that is described as “80 percent accurate.” The committee wants to use the result to reduce hiring mistakes. How confident should it now be that the candidate will meet the performance standard? The number sounds decisive, but it does not yet answer the question. Eighty percent of what? How common are strong performers in the applicant pool? How often does the screen pass a weaker candidate? Was the test validated on a comparable population and outcome?
The committee needs to know how many applicants who pass will perform well. The report may instead say how many strong performers pass. One starts with everyone who passed; the other starts with everyone who meets the performance standard. Confusing the two groups could turn an informative screen into unjustified confidence about whom to hire. We will begin by counting them separately, then use that distinction to interpret the evidence. The optional mathematical analyses express the same reasoning in notation.

title: 14  Base Rates and Updating
text:
Use complement, intersection, union, and conditional probability without changing the event or denominator.
Translate a Bayesian update into natural frequencies and select defensible reference classes.
Diagnose base-rate neglect, reversed conditionals, conjunction errors, and information dilution.

title: 14  Base Rates and Updating
section: Worked update: the same screen in two applicant pools
text:
Worked update: the same screen in two applicant pools
A validated screen may look like a portable measure of candidate quality. Yet the same positive result can mean different things in different applicant pools. To see why, return to the hiring screen.
Suppose that 20% of applicants in a broad pool would meet a clearly defined performance standard, the screen passes 80% of those future strong performers, and it also passes 30% of the others. Among 10,000 applicants:

2,000 would meet the standard; 1,600 pass the screen.
8,000 would not; 2,400 nevertheless pass.
Of 4,000 positive screens, 1,600 are true positives.

Under those assumptions, 1,600 of the 4,000 applicants who pass would perform strongly: 40%. The screen can be meaningfully informative—it raises the probability from 20% to 40%—without making a positive result decisive.
Now place the same screen in a carefully preselected pool where 50% would meet the standard. Assume its sensitivity, the share of strong performers who pass, and its false-positive rate, the share of others who pass, remain unchanged. Among 10,000 applicants it produces 4,000 true positives and 1,500 false positives, so the probability of strong performance after a positive screen is about 72.7%. Interpreting a sensitivity figure requires the starting population and evidence that the test performs similarly in it.

title: 14  Base Rates and Updating
text:
Probability begins with a model
The hiring calculation became useful only after the applicants and possible results were organized into a common population. Without that structure, a percentage can answer a different question from the one the decision requires.
A sample space lists the elementary outcomes allowed by a model. An event collects the outcomes of interest, such as finishing a project by Friday. Probabilities range from zero to one, and the probability of some outcome in the complete sample space is one. Probabilities add when events are mutually exclusive. Calling a coin fair, successive observations independent, or an applicant pool comparable to the validation sample are substantive assumptions.

Complement: preserve the event boundary
An event and its complement cover all possibilities without overlapping. If a project has a 70% probability of finishing by Friday, the remaining 30% is the probability of not finishing by Friday under the same model. “Not finished by Friday” is not the same event as “the project fails.” A complement works only when the time horizon and outcome definition remain fixed.


AND: use the conditional branch
To find the probability that two events both occur, start with the chance of the first and multiply by the chance of the second among cases where the first occurs. If the events are independent, learning that the first occurred does not change the chance of the second.
Independence is not the same as mutual exclusivity. Rain and traffic delay can occur together and may be dependent. Two cards drawn without replacement are dependent because the first draw changes the deck.


OR: restore the overlap
To find the probability that at least one of two events occurs, add their probabilities and subtract the overlap. That last step prevents double counting.
A project can be delayed by a supplier problem, a software problem, or both. Adding the separate probabilities as though the routes were disjoint exaggerates total risk; considering only the most vivid route understates it.

title: 14  Base Rates and Updating
text:
Conditional direction matters
A conditional probability concerns a specified group of cases. In the hiring example, asking what share of strong performers pass starts with the strong performers. The committee instead needs the share of those who pass who are strong performers. Changing the starting group changes the question.
The same reversal appears in court. A one-in-a-million probability of a DNA profile among unrelated people is not a one-in-a-million probability that a matched defendant is innocent. The latter depends on how the suspect was selected, how many people were compared, laboratory error, relatedness, the prior probability of different sources, and the rest of the case (Thompson & Schumann, 1987).
Conditional probability also makes independence explicit. Events are independent when learning one does not change the probability of the other. Zero correlation is not generally equivalent to independence: it rules out one linear relationship, not every probabilistic dependence.







NoteMathematical analysis: probability rules and their notation





Let \(\Omega\) be the sample space, \(A\) and \(B\) events, and \(A^c\) the complement of \(A\). The basic rules are
\[
0\le P(A)\le 1, \qquad P(\Omega)=1,
\]
with additivity for mutually exclusive events. Complement, intersection (AND), and union (OR) are written as
\[
P(A^c)=1-P(A),
\]
\[
P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B\mid A),
\]
\[
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).
\]
Provided \(P(B)>0\), conditional probability is
\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.
\]
Everything after the vertical bar identifies the group being counted within. Thus \(P(\text{positive screen}\mid\text{strong performance})\) and \(P(\text{strong performance}\mid\text{positive screen})\) answer different questions. For independent events, \(P(B\mid A)=P(B)\) when the conditional is defined.

title: 14  Base Rates and Updating
text:
Bayes’ rule restores the alternatives
A positive result supports an explanation when it is more expected under that explanation than under its alternatives. Counting only the cases where the explanation is true leaves out the competing route to the same evidence. Bayes’ rule brings both routes into the comparison.
The prior gives the starting probability, which is the prevalence of strong performance in this screening example. The likelihood asks how probable the evidence would be if the explanation held. The competing likelihood asks how often the same evidence appears without that explanation. The posterior is the probability after incorporating the evidence (Bayes, 1763).
To update, count the cases where the explanation produces the evidence, then compare them with all cases that could produce it. For the hiring screen, both strong and weaker performers can pass.







NoteMathematical analysis: Bayes’ rule





If \(A\) and \(A^c\) partition the cases, total probability rebuilds the denominator:
\[
P(B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)+P(B\mid A^c)P(A^c).
\]
Bayes’ rule then reverses the conditioning without reversing the evidence:
\[
P(A\mid B)=
\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}
{P(B\mid A)P(A)+P(B\mid A^c)P(A^c)}.
\]
Here \(P(A)\) is the prior, \(P(B\mid A)\) is the likelihood under the explanation, and \(P(B\mid A^c)\) is the likelihood under its alternative. The posterior is \(P(A\mid B)\). In the hiring example, this gives \(1{,}600/4{,}000=0.40\).




For the committee, the update is useful only if these inputs describe the applicants and performance standard it actually faces. Selection into the pool, changes in working conditions, and uncertainty about the test’s error rates all affect that judgment.

title: 14  Base Rates and Updating
text:
Natural frequencies make Bayes visible
Knowing the updating rule does not guarantee that the relevant denominator stays visible. Translating percentages into people makes it easier to inspect who could have produced a positive result.
For a second hypothetical example, suppose 1 percent of a population has a disease. A test is positive for 90 percent of people who have it and for 9 percent of people who do not. A person tests positive. The tempting answer is 90 percent, but that describes how often people with the disease test positive. We need to know how often people with a positive test have the disease.
Imagine 10,000 people:

100 have the disease; 90 test positive.
9,900 do not; 891 test positive.
Of 981 positive tests, 90 are true positives.

Of the 981 people who test positive, 90 have the disease: about 9.17%.






Figure 14.1: A positive result can come from either group. In this hypothetical population, the much larger group without disease supplies most of the positive tests.



The two branches in Figure 14.1 answer the crucial question: who could have produced this positive result? Natural frequencies preserve those nested sets, often making Bayesian reasoning more transparent than isolated percentages (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995). They expose the denominator that the 90% sensitivity figure leaves implicit.

title: 14  Base Rates and Updating
text:
Reference classes are judgment calls
The calculation asks for a base rate, but the decision rarely supplies an uncontested comparison group. Should a start-up be compared with all new firms, firms in the same sector, firms at the same funding stage, or firms with similarly experienced founders? A narrow class may be more relevant but noisier. A broad class is more stable but less tailored. Choosing the class is therefore part of the substantive judgment, and it can change the recommendation even when the arithmetic is correct.
Base-rate neglect is more likely when individuating detail feels causal and the statistic feels incidental (Bar-Hillel, 1980). The outside view therefore begins with comparable cases before explaining why the focal case differs (Kahneman & Lovallo, 1993). A defensible analysis reports several nested classes, shows whether the conclusion changes, and identifies which differences are genuinely diagnostic. “This case is unique” is a hypothesis, not a denominator. Chapter 15 examines the sampling uncertainty that remains even after the class is well chosen.
Return to hiring. The base rate should concern future performance under the organization’s role, support, and criterion—not an undefined pool of “talent.” The screen’s sensitivity and false-positive rate must come from a comparable applicant population. If the criterion rewards manager similarity rather than job output, the posterior can be mathematically correct and substantively wrong.







NoteResearch Lens: conjunction, disjunction, and dilution



Chapter 9 showed why a coherent story can feel probable. The set relation is straightforward: requiring two conditions cannot make an event more probable than requiring just one, while allowing either of two routes cannot make it less probable than either route alone.
Adding a condition makes the event a subset. “A bank teller active in a social movement” cannot be more probable than “a bank teller,” however well the detail matches the description (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983). By contrast, adding alternative routes expands a union. The probability that a project is delayed by at least one of several causes cannot be smaller than the probability of any single route, though overlaps must be handled rather than simply added.
More detail is not always more information. Weakly diagnostic detail can dilute attention to stronger evidence. Sivanathan and Kakkar (2017) found that adding minor side effects to serious drug side effects could reduce perceived overall severity. Group evidence by severity, probability, and decision relevance so completeness does not destroy structure.








TipCheck your denominator



For each prompt, write the target conditional before answering.

Seventy percent of successful trainees used a practice platform. What additional quantities are needed to estimate the probability of success among platform users?
Ten percent of projects suffer supplier delay and 12% suffer software delay. What must be known before adding the percentages?
A screen validated in experienced applicants is applied to entry-level applicants. Which part of the Bayesian model may no longer transport?

A complete answer names the conditioning event, denominator, relevant overlap or alternative, and at least one assumption about how the evidence was generated.

title: 14  Base Rates and Updating
text:
Practice Lab
Take one positive test, screening result, warning signal, or performance indicator. Produce a one-page Bayesian audit using a population of 10,000. State the target conditional probability, choose and defend two plausible reference classes, show true positives and false positives under each, and identify one omitted alternative or measurement problem. The observable output is the two natural-frequency trees and a decision rule that states what action changes at which posterior range.

title: 14  Base Rates and Updating
text:
Take it forward
The committee can now replace “the screen is 80 percent accurate” with a meaningful account: who was screened, how often each kind of applicant passed, and what a positive result implies in this pool. Before using a striking percentage, identify its denominator and the alternative route by which the same evidence could appear.

text:

title: 15  Randomness and Overconfidence
text:
Learning goals
Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
A branch manager arrives after the worst quarter in the company’s history. Three months later, sales have recovered and headquarters praises the rescue. Perhaps the manager changed something that mattered. But a branch selected because it had an exceptionally bad quarter may also improve when temporary setbacks pass. How much of the recovery should count as evidence of good management?
Headquarters needs to recognize effective management and decide which practices to repeat. Crediting the entire recovery to the rescue could spread a policy that contributed little; dismissing it as luck could discard a useful change. The same question appears in smaller decisions: whether two successful hires validate an interview method, whether a winning streak reveals skill, or whether a missed deadline was foreseeable. We need to learn what variation alone can produce before deciding what a striking result means.

title: 15  Randomness and Overconfidence
text:
Explain why small samples, streaks, and clusters can look more informative than they are.
Diagnose regression to the mean and distinguish an apparent causal pattern, including superstition, from evidence that an action changes the outcome.
Distinguish three forms of overconfidence, use an outside view to challenge the planning fallacy, and score forecasts for calibration and resolution.

title: 15  Randomness and Overconfidence
text:
Which sequence looks random?
Before explaining the branch’s recovery, consider a simpler problem: recognizing what chance can produce. A fair coin will be tossed six times. Rank these exact sequences from most to least likely:

H H H H H H
H H H T T T
H T H T H T

The first looks designed, while the third looks comfortably random. Yet every specified sequence has the same probability: one in 64.
The intuition answers a different question: Which sequence resembles my prototype of randomness? Alternation looks random; a run looks meaningful. Probability asks which event was specified before the tosses and how many elementary outcomes it contains.
The distinction also explains why “three heads and three tails in any order” is more likely than “all heads or all tails.” The first category contains twenty exact sequences; the second contains two. Each exact outcome remains equally likely. Categories differ because they collect different numbers of outcomes.
Randomness is clumpier than intuition expects. When many sequences, people, schools, funds, products, or locations are observed, some will display striking runs and clusters even when the underlying process is unchanged. A pattern invites explanation; a statistical model asks how surprising that pattern was given all the opportunities for one to appear.







NoteMathematical analysis: counting coin sequences





For six independent fair tosses, each specified sequence has probability
\[
\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^6=\frac{1}{64}.
\]
There are \(\binom{6}{3}=20\) ways to place three heads among six positions. All heads and all tails account for only two sequences.

title: 15  Randomness and Overconfidence
text:
Small samples swing widely
The expectation that a short sequence should look balanced extends to evidence about people and organizations. Tversky and Kahneman (1971) called this belief in the law of small numbers: expecting a small sample to resemble its population too closely. After three successful hires, an interview panel may feel it has found a reliable method. Yet three outcomes can change dramatically with the next appointment, especially if applicants and jobs vary. The question is how much confidence that sample can support.
Small samples produce more extreme proportions because each observation carries more weight. When an outcome has a 50% chance on each independent trial, the standard error, a measure of typical sampling fluctuation, is about 15.8 percentage points with ten observations, compared with 5.0 points with one hundred. The population did not become steadier; the estimate did.







NoteMathematical analysis: sampling uncertainty





For an independent Bernoulli event with probability \(p\), the standard error of the sample proportion is
\[
SE(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}.
\]
When \(p=0.5\), the standard error is about 0.158 for \(n=10\) and 0.050 for \(n=100\).




Selection magnifies the problem. The branch reached headquarters’ agenda because its quarter was unusually bad, just as a fund enters a performance ranking because its returns were unusually good. In both cases, temporary variation has helped select the evidence we are about to explain.
When decisions cannot wait or populations are inherently small, the available sample must still inform action. Report uncertainty and identify which conclusion depends on one or two observations. Where cases are sufficiently comparable, shrinkage methods pull unstable estimates toward the wider average rather than taking each small sample at face value; the regression section below explains that logic.

title: 15  Randomness and Overconfidence
text:
Streaks require a process model
After five reds at roulette, black may feel due. Under independent fair spins, it is not. The wheel has no memory. The gambler’s fallacy treats short-run balancing as a physical correction because the sequence is expected to look representative quickly (Clotfelter & Cook, 1993).
The opposite intuition appears after success: a basketball player who has made several shots seems more likely to make the next. That hot-hand belief could misread random clustering, or it could reflect genuine state dependence through confidence, fatigue, strategy, defense, learning, or shot selection.
Gilovich, Vallone, and Tversky (1985) famously argued that observers saw more hot-hand dependence than basketball data supported. Later work identified a finite-sample bias in common comparisons of success following success and showed that some earlier tests understated streakiness (Miller & Sanjurjo, 2018). Resolving the question requires specifying and testing the process:

What would independent outcomes produce?
Was the streak pattern chosen before or after examining the data?
Did opportunities, difficulty, strategy, or selection change during the run?
Does the pattern replicate with a statistic suited to the sampling process?

title: 15  Randomness and Overconfidence
section: Clusters and the search for causes
text:
Clusters and the search for causes
A cluster of failures deserves attention because it may reveal a preventable cause. Yet searching more units, periods, or subgroups gives chance more opportunities to produce an impressive cluster (Nickerson, 2002). The practical challenge is to investigate a possible hazard without treating the most striking pattern as its own explanation.
A disease cluster may reveal a local exposure; a manufacturing cluster may reveal a faulty machine; a set of related forecast errors may reveal a missing variable. The test needs a denominator that includes the number of units, periods, outcomes, subgroups, and models searched. It also needs a mechanism or independent replication that was not selected by the same extreme pattern.
A useful sequence is:
Describe → compare with chance → specify a mechanism → predict new observations → replicate.
Stopping after description rewards the most surprising pattern. Jumping directly to a favored mechanism invites confirmation. A new prediction forces the proposed cause to do work outside the data that suggested it.

title: 15  Randomness and Overconfidence
text:
Regression to the mean
The branch improved after the manager arrived. To decide how much that timing tells us, we need to separate persistent performance from the temporary variation that helped make the earlier quarter exceptional. An unusually high result can reflect high persistent ability, favorable temporary circumstances, or both. When the next temporary influence is less extreme, performance tends to move toward average even if the underlying ability does not change.
For illustration, suppose two measurements have a correlation of 0.40. A first result two standard deviations above average then predicts a second result only 0.8 standard deviations above average under a simple linear model. The person remains above average; the prediction is less extreme because the first observation was partly unreliable.
The flight-instructor example illustrates the attribution trap. Praise follows unusually good performance and criticism follows unusually poor performance. The next attempt often looks worse after praise and better after criticism. An instructor may conclude that criticism improves performance and praise harms it, although part of both movements reflects regression (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973).
Regression does not show that an intervention had no effect. It shows why before–after change among units selected for extreme outcomes does not identify the effect by itself. Use comparison groups, repeated pre-periods, credible counterfactuals, and uncertainty intervals. A real treatment effect and regression can occur together.






Figure 15.1: A teaching simulation of 50 measurement pairs illustrates regression to the mean. With a correlation near 0.40, an initial result two standard deviations above average predicts a second result only 0.8 standard deviations above average. The optional analysis gives the simulation specification.



Return to the branch manager. If the bad quarter was two standard deviations below average and the same illustrative correlation of 0.40 applied, the model would predict the next quarter at 0.8 standard deviations below average without any managerial change. That is a visible recovery of 1.2 standard deviations. Figure 15.1 shows the corresponding geometry. The recovery can be real while its attribution to the rescue plan remains unproven. Compare the branch with similarly troubled branches, examine several earlier periods, and identify which changes the manager actually introduced. That makes room for a managerial effect while accounting for the recovery that might have happened anyway.







NoteMathematical analysis: regression and the teaching simulation





Suppose observed performance is
\[
Y=\theta+\varepsilon,
\]
where \(\theta\) is a persistent component and \(\varepsilon\) is temporary noise. Selecting an unusually high \(Y\) selects cases with high persistent ability, favorable noise, or both. When the next noise term is less extreme, performance tends to move toward average even if the underlying ability does not change.
For two standardized measures with correlation \(r\), a simple linear prediction is
\[
\widehat z_2=r z_1.
\]
If a measure two standard deviations above average has test–retest correlation \(r=0.40\), the best linear prediction under that model is 0.8 standard deviations above average. The predicted person remains above average; the extreme observation is shrunk because part of it was unreliable.
A fixed-seed teaching simulation draws 50 observations from \(z_1,\varepsilon\sim N(0,1)\) and \(z_2=0.40z_1+\sqrt{0.84}\varepsilon\) (seed 50273; displayed sample \(r\approx0.40\)). The model’s conditional mean is \(E[z_2\mid z_1]=0.40z_1\): \(z_1=+2\) predicts \(z_2=+0.8\).





Superstition: when a coincidence becomes a rule
A basketball player tosses chalk into the air before a game; a golfer wears red on Sunday. LeBron James’s chalk toss and Tiger Woods’s red shirt are familiar sporting rituals (NBA, 2009; PGA TOUR, 2024). In a humorous interview, Woods recalled winning in red, then unsuccessfully trying blue to challenge his mother’s belief that red was his “power color.” The sequence makes a memorable story, but different tournaments also bring different opponents, conditions, and performances. It cannot establish what the shirt contributed.
Superstition attributes influence to an action or sign without adequate evidence of a causal connection. A ritual alone does not establish such a belief: an athlete might use a familiar routine to prepare or concentrate. The question is whether the claimed influence has a plausible pathway and survives a fair comparison.
Skinner’s (1948) pigeon experiment made the apparent connection between action and reward strikingly visible. Food arrived at regular intervals regardless of what the birds did. Six of eight developed recognizable repeated movements, including circling and head motions. Skinner proposed that movements accidentally followed by food had been reinforced, sustaining responses that did not produce the reward.
Staddon and Simmelhag’s (1971) later work found activities organized around the timing of food delivery, challenging the simple account that arbitrary movements had been strengthened by coincidence. Further experiments pointed to species-typical feeding patterns and the arrangement of the feeding environment as influences on the repeated behavior (Timberlake & Lucas, 1985).
For a human causal claim, ask what the ritual is supposed to change. Helping a player settle into a practiced routine is a different claim from changing the odds through an unrelated gesture. Record failures as carefully as successes, compare occasions with and without the action, and consider what else differed. The same discipline applies to the branch manager: a practice that preceded recovery deserves investigation before it becomes a rule for every branch.


Illusion of control: did the action change the odds?
An illusion of control occurs when someone overestimates their causal influence over an outcome. The branch manager may control staffing and training but cannot thereby control every market shock. Naming the controllable action and comparing what would happen without it is more informative than asking whether the manager feels in charge.
Langer’s (1975) classic studies helped establish the topic, but one familiar inference needs care: preferring a lottery ticket one selected does not show a belief that selecting it improved the odds. Preference, ownership, and anticipated regret can also matter. Across 17 experiments with 10,825 participants, Klusowski, Small, and Simmons (2021) found little support for the claim that choice itself creates inflated success expectations when options are functionally identical.
The lesson for the manager is to measure causal beliefs and compare outcomes, rather than treating active involvement—or recovery after a bad quarter—as evidence of effectiveness.

title: 15  Randomness and Overconfidence
text:
Overconfidence: three different errors
The branch manager is now sure the rescue plan will work elsewhere. But what exactly is the claim: a large improvement, better results than other managers, or very little uncertainty? Overconfidence means that confidence exceeds the accuracy or justification it warrants. Moore and Healy (2008) distinguish three forms that should be measured separately:

Overestimation: overestimating one’s performance or ability. Predicting a score of 80 and obtaining 60 is an overestimate on that occasion.
Overplacement: overestimating one’s position relative to a defined comparison group. Someone who expects to rank in the top tenth but ranks near the middle has misplaced their relative standing. Being above average is not itself a bias.
Overprecision: being too certain that a judgment is correct, for example by giving uncertainty intervals that are too narrow.

Each requires a different comparison, as Table 15.1 shows. Asking a confident person to “think harder” supplies none of them.



Table 15.1: Three forms of overconfidence require different comparisons










Form of overconfidence
Comparison required
Useful feedback




Overestimation
Predicted versus measured performance
Record estimates and outcomes on the same scale across comparable tasks.


Overplacement
Predicted versus measured relative standing
Specify the comparison group and criterion, then check the predicted rank.


Overprecision
Stated certainty versus accuracy across comparable judgments
Compare prediction-interval coverage with its stated level, or probability judgments with observed event frequencies.






The forms can move in opposite directions. In Moore and Healy’s experiments, difficult tasks could produce overestimation of one’s score alongside underplacement relative to others; easy tasks could reverse that combination. An error therefore needs a specified task, scale, comparison group, and repeated assessment. A confident manner, an ambitious goal, or one failed prediction cannot establish a general tendency.






TipTest the width of your uncertainty



Before checking results, choose ten comparable quantities whose answers can later be verified, such as completion times for routine tasks. For each, record a central estimate and a 90% subjective prediction interval: a lower and upper bound that you believe together leave a 10% chance outside. A well-calibrated set should contain the answers about 90% of the time across many comparable forecasts, not exactly nine times in every batch of ten.
Afterward, examine both coverage and width. Repeatedly missing many intervals suggests overprecision; making every interval enormous avoids misses but supplies little useful information. Revise the forecasting process, then assess it on new cases. Ten cases start a learning record.


The familiar Dunning–Kruger pattern raises a further measurement question: what explains the relationship between performance and errors in self-assessment? Kruger and Dunning (1999) reported larger self-assessment errors among lower performers in several tasks and proposed that some skills needed for good performance also help people recognize good performance. Measurement error, regression to the mean, scale boundaries, task difficulty, and general self-enhancement can produce part of the pattern; later work suggests that any distinctive metacognitive component may be smaller and more task-specific than the popular slogan implies (Gignac & Zajenkowski, 2020). Measure performance and confidence separately. Do not diagnose a person’s metacognition from one rank comparison.

Planning fallacy: the plan needs an outside view
The planning fallacy illustrates how optimistic forecasts can affect a project: people often construct an inside-view story of the steps that should occur while underweighting delays observed in similar projects (Buehler et al., 1994; Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). Underestimating the time a task needs can express overestimation of what one can accomplish in that time; an unduly narrow completion window also expresses overprecision. Planning fallacy is therefore an application, rather than a fourth form alongside those in Table 15.1. The outside view begins with a reference class and then adjusts only for differences that are genuinely predictive (Kahneman & Lovallo, 1993; Lovallo & Kahneman, 2003).
Suppose a city team proposes an 18-month rail-project schedule. Before hearing why this project is special, obtain the completion-time distribution for comparable projects. Then require each departure from that range to name a causal difference and evidence that the difference changed outcomes elsewhere. The inside view remains useful because it reveals mechanisms and dependencies; the outside view prevents an elegant plan from erasing how projects actually unfold.






NoteResearch Lens: information protocols change probability puzzles





In Monty Hall, seeing two unopened doors can make staying and switching look equally promising. Yet the host’s rule for revealing a goat determines what the reveal tells us: similar-looking endings can carry different evidence. In the standard Monty Hall protocol, a knowledgeable host always reveals a goat behind an unchosen door and always offers a switch; if either goat door could be opened, assume the host chooses between them uniformly at random. Following the unchosen-door branch in Figure 15.2 shows why switching wins with probability \(2/3\), compared with \(1/3\) for staying (Selvin, 1975). If the host instead opens doors or offers a switch selectively, the evidence changes. Likewise, “at least one child is a boy,” “the older child is a boy,” and a parent volunteering “I have a boy” arise from different sampling rules. The transferable question is not the puzzle answer but: How was this information generated?






Figure 15.2: The standard Monty Hall protocol keeps the information-generating rule visible. The initial choice has probability one-third, the two unchosen doors carry two-thirds together, and a knowledgeable host must reveal a goat before offering a switch, using a random tie-break when either goat door is available. The remaining unchosen door retains the two-thirds branch.

title: 15  Randomness and Overconfidence
text:
Calibration makes confidence answerable
A correct prediction can look like evidence of skill, but even a poor forecaster will sometimes be right. To decide whose probabilities deserve weight, we need a record of how stated confidence compares with outcomes across forecasts.
A forecaster is calibrated when events assigned 70 percent occur about 70 percent of the time, events assigned 20 percent occur about 20 percent of the time, and so forth. Calibration is a property of repeated forecasts, not one dramatic success.
Accuracy also requires resolution or discrimination. A forecaster who assigns 50 percent to everything may be calibrated in a balanced environment but contributes little separation. Useful forecasts move away from the base rate when evidence warrants it and remain calibrated across those movements.
The Brier score measures the squared gap between a forecast probability and what happened, coding occurrence as one and nonoccurrence as zero. A lower score is better: a 70% forecast scores 0.09 if the event occurs and 0.49 if it does not. Average the scores across forecasts to evaluate the record rather than its most memorable success (Brier, 1950; Murphy, 1973).







NoteMathematical analysis: scoring a probability forecast





For a binary event with forecast \(p\) and outcome \(o\in\{0,1\}\), the Brier score is
\[
BS=(p-o)^2.
\]
Thus a forecast of \(p=0.70\) scores \((0.70-1)^2=0.09\) if the event occurs and \((0.70-0)^2=0.49\) otherwise.




Research in geopolitical forecasting tournaments suggests that probabilistic forecasting can improve through repeatable practices: define the event precisely, start from reference classes, decompose the problem, update in small increments, seek disconfirming information, aggregate independent views, and obtain feedback (Mellers et al., 2014). Numeric probabilities also reveal false agreement. Two colleagues may both say “likely” while one means 55 percent and the other 90 percent.



Table 15.2: A minimal forecast ledger









Field
Example




Event and resolution rule
“The supplier passes acceptance testing by 30 September, documented by a signed report.”


Probability and date
0.65 on 1 June


Reference classes
Comparable suppliers; this supplier’s last ten deliveries


Main evidence
Prototype passed; staffing remains incomplete


Alternative pathways
Certification, integration, staffing, or scope delay


Update triggers
Test failure, staff appointment, scope change


Outcome and score
Enter after resolution; preserve the original forecast






The dated entries in Table 15.2 matter because memory rounds forecasts toward outcomes. “We knew it might fail” can describe almost any vague prior statement. A dated number, event definition, and update rule allow learning to survive hindsight.
The same discipline is needed when AI supplies the forecast. Chapter 42 carries calibration and sampling into the evaluation of machine predictions: reserve observations that were not used to fit or tune the model, make the test resemble its intended use, and examine whether its probabilities support better actions. This is how the book’s treatment of uncertainty helps distinguish a promising demonstration from evidence that a decision process has improved.

title: 15  Randomness and Overconfidence
section: From a project story to a forecast system
text:
From a project story to a forecast system
Breaking a project into possible failure routes should make its forecast more informative. But combining those routes carelessly can undo the benefit if they share causes or trigger one another.
A project team assigns 15 percent to supplier delay, 10 percent to regulatory delay, and 20 percent to software delay. The probability of at least one of these delays must lie between 20 percent and 45 percent: it cannot be smaller than the largest component, and adding the components would count any overlapping delays more than once. Under an illustrative independence assumption, the chance of at least one delay would be 38.8 percent. But a supplier delay might cause a software delay, so independence needs evidence. An event tree with conditional probabilities can make those dependencies explicit; the probability rules in Chapter 14 provide the first consistency check.







NoteMathematical analysis: combining independent delay risks





Under independence, multiply the probabilities that each delay does not occur, then subtract that joint no-delay probability from one:
\[
1-(1-0.15)(1-0.10)(1-0.20)=0.388.
\]




Missing the final deadline is a separate event. Schedule slack may absorb a component delay, while an omitted failure route may jeopardize completion. Define that final event and model how each route affects it before comparing the forecast with the deadline-miss rate for similar projects. If the estimates differ sharply, investigate the reference class, schedule assumptions, dependencies, and missing routes. The outside view cannot correct the inside view until both refer to the same outcome.
Record one forecast for the final date and separate forecasts for leading mechanisms. Update when relevant evidence arrives, including an unexpected development; record why the new information changes the forecast. After resolution, score the forecasts and examine whether errors came from the base rate, dependence assumptions, missing pathways, or unjustified confidence. Each project adds observations to the calibration ledger.

title: 15  Randomness and Overconfidence
text:
Practice Lab
Choose one event that will resolve within four weeks. Produce a complete forecast ledger: an unambiguous event and resolution source, a numerical probability, two reference classes, an inside-view mechanism, one argument against, and a dated update trigger. For a quantity such as cost or completion time, add the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles and explain every adjustment away from the outside-view distribution. When the date arrives, enter the outcome and score without revising the original entry. Keep the ledger and identify which assumptions the outcome gives you reason to reconsider. One result may reveal a missing pathway, but calibration and systematic overconfidence require a longer record.

title: 15  Randomness and Overconfidence
text:
Take it forward
The next time a spectacular success or failure reaches the meeting agenda, ask what led that case to be selected and what a comparable case would be expected to do next. Then write down the prediction before the next quarter arrives. That simple record gives the organization a chance to learn something more durable than a story about its latest result.

title: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being
text:
Questions to carry forward
Imagine choosing between a secure job and a new venture. The job provides a reliable income; the venture offers independence while putting that income at risk. Even with a clear forecast of success, you must give up something you value. And the option that feels exciting today must eventually fit an ordinary working week. How should a choice account for both the future we imagine and the life we will actually live?
The route in Figure 1 connects uncertain outcomes to the lives in which they occur. It starts with the comparison of risky options and shows why a gain or loss depends partly on the point from which it is judged. It then examines what experience teaches us and leaves unseen, before turning to the mental accounts through which we organize gains, losses, and spending. From there, we ask why choices change as their rewards or costs move closer in time.
Plans also meet familiar routines. A student who intends to write may keep checking his phone, even when checking brings little enjoyment; the habit chapter examines why the response persists. The final chapter asks how choices contribute to daily experience, satisfaction, relationships, and meaning. Together, these chapters help us compare the future we imagine with the behavior and life a choice may actually produce.
Many of those consequences depend on other people. Part IV examines choices whose outcomes are shaped by what others believe, value, and do.

title: 16  Risky Decision Making
text:
Learning goals
A Probability Is Not Yet a Feeling
A small organization receives a quote for cyber insurance. The premium seems expensive beside the average annual loss in its spreadsheet, and the finance team considers declining it. Then someone asks what would happen if an attack arrived next month: could the organization restore its systems, keep paying staff, and continue serving clients? An average loss and an affordable loss are different things.

Compare expected value with expected utility in one consequential insurance decision.
Distinguish known risk, ambiguity, tail exposure, and the limits of risk-preference measures.
Produce an uncertainty-aware recommendation that separates process quality from realized outcome.

title: 16  Risky Decision Making
section: The same expected value, a different choice
text:
The same expected value, a different choice
Choose between:

Option S: €50 for certain.
Option G: a 50% chance of €100 and a 50% chance of €0.

Both have expected monetary value €50. Many people nevertheless choose the sure €50. Now imagine that the gamble determines whether you can pay rent. The sure amount may become much more attractive. Imagine instead that both amounts are entertainment money and the gamble itself is enjoyable. The gamble may become more attractive.
Expected money leaves out what the money would make possible. To evaluate the insurance quote, we need a way to express that difference.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 16  Risky Decision Making
text:
Risk, uncertainty, and ambiguity
In a textbook lottery, outcomes and probabilities are specified: a coin gives a 50% chance of each result. This is risk in the narrow decision-theory sense. In many real decisions, the probabilities are estimated, disputed, or partly unknown. This broader uncertainty includes model error, missing outcomes, changing environments, and ambiguous evidence.
Ambiguity describes uncertainty about the probability model itself. A jar with a known 30 red and 60 black balls is risky; a jar with 30 red and 60 balls of unknown black–yellow composition introduces ambiguity. A precise-looking spreadsheet can still be ambiguous if the probability estimates rest on one historical period or an untested causal model.
For the insurance team, this distinction changes what to investigate. Even a well-estimated frequency of familiar incidents may omit a new kind of attack; a precise average cannot settle whether the model covers the exposure.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 16  Risky Decision Making
text:
Expected value: the monetary benchmark
Expected value is a probability-weighted average. A 1% chance of €10,000 and a 99% chance of zero has expected value €100, although €100 is never paid.
Expected value is powerful when outcomes are repeatable, stakes are small relative to resources, and money is the relevant consequence. A casino can rely on a small expected advantage across millions of plays. One household facing one chance of ruin cannot automatically treat the same average as adequate.
The benchmark also exposes missing costs. A gamble that pays €100 with probability one-half and zero otherwise does not have expected net value €50 if entry costs €60. The expected net value is −€10.







NoteMathematical analysis: expected monetary value





For outcomes \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) with probabilities \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\), expected monetary value is
\[
EV(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i x_i.
\]
Multiply each possible monetary outcome by its probability, then add the weighted outcomes. Subtract any entry cost to obtain expected net value.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 16  Risky Decision Making
section: Expected utility: value over final consequences
text:
Expected utility: value over final consequences
Expected utility theory weights the value of each final consequence by its probability. For monetary choices, that means considering how the outcome changes total wealth and what that wealth is worth to the person. It states conditions under which consistent choices can be represented as if they maximize expected utility (von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944).
The independence axiom is central. If one lottery is preferred to another, mixing both with the same third lottery in the same proportion should preserve the ranking. Common components should cancel. The Allais pattern below shows why this attractive requirement is descriptively fragile.

Curvature and attitudes toward a mean-preserving risk

A linear utility function implies risk neutrality: a sure amount and a lottery with that same average are equally attractive.
A concave utility function implies weak risk aversion: the sure average is at least as attractive as the lottery. Additional wealth brings smaller increments of utility.
A convex utility function implies weak risk seeking over that range: the lottery is at least as attractive as its sure average. Additional wealth brings larger increments of utility.

The preferences become strict when the curve is strictly concave or convex over outcomes that genuinely vary.
Curvature is local. A function can be concave over one wealth range and different elsewhere. Observing one safe choice does not establish a stable trait across stakes, domains, or reference points.







NoteMathematical analysis: expected utility and curvature





Expected utility theory evaluates a lottery over final wealth or consequences:
\[
EU(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i u(W+x_i),
\]
where \(W\) is initial wealth and \(u(\cdot)\) represents preferences over final wealth.
For final wealth \(X\), the curvature comparison is
\[
u(E[X])\geq E[u(X)]
\]
under concavity, with the reverse inequality under convexity and equality under linearity. Strict concavity or convexity gives a strict comparison for a nondegenerate lottery over that range.






Certainty equivalents and risk premia
The certainty-equivalent payoff is the sure payoff that makes the person indifferent to the lottery. The risk premium is the gap between the lottery’s expected payoff and that certainty equivalent.
For illustration, treat the opening lottery’s outcomes of 0 and 100 as final wealth, starting from zero. Under an illustrative square-root utility function, a sure final wealth of 25 is as attractive as this 50–50 lottery. Expected final wealth is 50, so the risk premium is 25. These values follow from the chosen utility function and starting resources.







NoteMathematical analysis: certainty equivalents and risk premia





For payoff changes \(x_i\) around initial wealth \(W\), the certainty-equivalent payoff \(c\) solves
\[
u(W+c)=\sum_i p_i u(W+x_i).
\]
The risk premium is
\[
\pi=E[x]-c.
\]
For the compact opening example, normalize initial wealth to zero and treat 0 and 100 as final-wealth outcomes. Let \(u(w)=\sqrt{w}\). Then
\[
EU=0.5\sqrt{0}+0.5\sqrt{100}=5.
\]
Because \(\sqrt{25}=5\), the certainty-equivalent final wealth is 25. Expected final wealth is 50, so the risk premium is 25. Under this utility function and normalization, the decision-maker is indifferent between the lottery and final wealth of 25 for certain.




Figure 16.1 shows the comparison: the lottery’s average utility lies below the utility of its average wealth.






Figure 16.1: A 50–50 lottery paying 0 or 100 has expected value 50. Under an illustrative square-root utility function, expected utility is 5, the certainty equivalent is 25, and the risk premium is 25. A companion panel separates known risk from ambiguous probabilities and shows why the process should be assessed using information available before the outcome.



If the outcomes are changes around wealth, then wealth must enter the calculation. With €10,000 in initial wealth and the same square-root utility, a 50–50 chance of gaining €0 or €100 has a certainty-equivalent payoff of about €49.94: its risk premium is only about €0.06. The same payoff lottery and utility function look very different when the starting resources change. Prospect Theory asks what happens when people instead evaluate changes around a reference point.


Insurance: expected loss and willingness to pay
Insurance exchanges an uncertain loss for a certain premium. Under concave utility, a person may pay more than the actuarially fair expected loss to remove variability. The difference can reflect a risk premium, but real insurance decisions also include insurer costs, exclusions, deductibles, counterparty risk, liquidity, legal requirements, and protection against ruin.
The key comparison is not “premium versus expected loss” alone. It is final wealth and feasible action in each state. Insurance can be valuable because a rare loss would be unaffordable even when its expected amount is modest.


Why do people buy insurance and lottery tickets?
A globally concave utility function over money cannot explain paying for an unfavorable monetary gamble. Yet a lottery ticket may also buy entertainment and anticipation, while insurance protects against an unaffordable loss. Separate mental accounts, misunderstanding, or extra weight on tiny probabilities offer other explanations. Buying both products challenges a simple account of monetary risk preference without identifying which alternative is right.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 16  Risky Decision Making
section: The Allais paradox: certainty and the independence axiom
text:
The Allais paradox: certainty and the independence axiom
Expected utility gives us a consistent way to compare risky options. The following choices test whether people preserve that consistency when a sure outcome becomes available. Consider two pairs of choices, with monetary units scaled to “millions.”
Pair 1

A: 1 for certain.
B: 89% chance of 1, 10% chance of 5, and 1% chance of 0.

Pair 2

C: 11% chance of 1 and 89% chance of 0.
D: 10% chance of 5 and 90% chance of 0.

Many people prefer A to B but D to C (Allais, 1953). In Pair 1, certainty is attractive. In Pair 2, neither option is certain, so the larger prize becomes attractive.
Under expected utility and independence, the pattern is inconsistent. If A is preferred to B, removing the common 89% chance of receiving 1 implies that C should be preferred to D. Choosing A and D gives special weight to the move from 99% to 100% or to the presentation of certainty.
The Allais pattern identifies a violated axiom. Certainty, regret, misunderstanding, probability weighting, and response noise can contribute. Prospect theory offers one systematic account in the next chapter.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 16  Risky Decision Making
section: The Ellsberg urn: choosing with unknown probabilities
text:
The Ellsberg urn: choosing with unknown probabilities
Certainty about an outcome is one issue; confidence in the probabilities is another. To separate them, consider an urn containing 90 balls:

exactly 30 are red;
the remaining 60 are black or yellow in an unknown proportion.

First choose a bet that pays if red is drawn or a bet that pays if black is drawn. Many choose red because its probability is known to be one-third.
Now choose a bet that pays if red or yellow is drawn or a bet that pays if black or yellow is drawn. Many choose black-or-yellow because its probability is known to be two-thirds.
If the choices reflected only a single probability judgment, preferring red to black would imply that red is more likely. Preferring black-or-yellow to red-or-yellow would imply the opposite: once the common yellow outcome is set aside, black would have to be more likely. No single additive subjective probability can support both comparisons when the payoff is otherwise identical (Ellsberg, 1961).
This pattern is called ambiguity aversion. People may seek ambiguity when they feel competent, suspect favorable hidden information, enjoy exploration, or believe the known option was selected against them. Comparative ignorance matters: an ambiguous option can become less attractive when placed beside a transparent one. The practical response is to separate:

variability given a model;
uncertainty about parameters;
uncertainty about the model and missing outcomes;
the decision-maker’s trust in the source.

Collapsing all four into one probability hides the reason for caution.







NoteResearch Lens: ambiguity and brain signals





Knowing that a gamble pays half the time differs from having too little information to assess its chances. Hsu and colleagues (2005) found that greater ambiguity was associated with stronger fMRI responses in the amygdala and orbitofrontal cortex and weaker responses in the striatum. This shows that missing probability information can change how a choice is processed; it does not directly measure dopamine or establish that ambiguity “switches off” reward signaling.
The uncertain-reward discussion in Chapter 21 concerns a different question: how anticipation and apparent progress can sustain pursuit even when many attempts bring no reward.











TipProcess check: evaluate a risky choice using the evidence available



The distinction between process and outcome matters whenever uncertainty can obscure the quality of a choice (Baron & Hershey, 1988): a well-supported choice can lose, while a reckless choice can be rescued by luck. Preserve the probabilities, alternatives, constraints, and reasons available before the uncertainty resolves; otherwise the result can replace the information that was available when the choice was made.

section: Risk communication: show the denominator and the consequence

title: 16  Risky Decision Making
section: Worked application: should we insure this exposure?
text:
Worked application: should we insure this exposure?
Return to the insurance quote. Declining it saves money the team can use elsewhere, but accepting an unaffordable loss could interrupt the very service that money supports. The team needs to identify which exposure it can carry and which protection the contract actually buys. Four questions organize that comparison:

Exposure: list final consequences—restoration cost, interrupted service, legal liability, reputation, and possible ruin—not only the insurer’s payout.
Probability: use base rates for comparable organizations, internal controls, and uncertainty ranges. Separate known event frequency from model uncertainty.
Contract: read deductibles, exclusions, caps, reporting duties, and insurer credit risk. “Coverage” is not a binary state.
Capacity: compare the uninsured worst credible loss with liquid reserves and the ability to continue operating.

The team may discover that it can absorb minor incidents but cannot finance a major interruption, or that the quoted policy excludes the loss it most needs covered. Either finding changes the decision in a way that the average annual loss alone cannot. Record the recommendation and its assumptions now, so that a quiet year does not automatically make buying insurance look foolish.

For the insurance decision, identify whose losses the policy covers and whose remain exposed. A policy that protects the organization’s balance sheet may leave clients carrying the cost of interrupted service. Those people’s capacity to bear the harm, and their ability to understand and refuse the exposure, belong in the decision alongside the premium.

Extension: one project or a portfolio?
A firm considers ten independent projects. Each costs €40,000 and has a 30% chance of returning €200,000, otherwise zero. The probability-weighted return is €60,000 per project. Subtracting its €40,000 cost leaves an expected net value of €20,000.
Positive expected value does not make one project safe: it still loses the full investment 70% of the time. A diversified portfolio can reduce idiosyncratic variation if the outcomes are genuinely independent, but common market shocks can make the projects move together. The decision therefore needs both project-level EV and a dependence model at portfolio level.
The portfolio comparison must also identify whose returns and losses enter the calculation. A portfolio can be attractive to the firm while exposing employees, customers, or other parties to losses they cannot absorb; expected value does not settle distribution, rights, consent, or ruin.
Mental Accounting examines why people evaluate each gain and loss in isolation. Here the benchmark is already clear: the unit of evaluation changes the risk.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 16  Risky Decision Making
text:
Practice Lab
Build a one-page risk register for a real insurance or project decision. Report final-state consequences, probabilities or ranges, dependencies, affected parties, expected value where meaningful, one capacity-to-bear-loss constraint, and one ambiguity the point estimates hide. Conclude with a recommendation, a review date, and an observable condition that would reverse it. The output is the completed register—not a description of what one might contain.

title: 16  Risky Decision Making
text:
Take it forward
The insurance discussion ends with a more useful comparison: what the organization would be able to do in each plausible state, with and without the contract. The final choice may still be difficult, but the team now knows which losses, assumptions, and obligations drive it.

title: 16  Risky Decision Making
text:
Optional research and application notes






NoteMathematical analysis: the single-period newsvendor





A retailer must commit to stock before learning how much customers will buy. Too little stock loses sales; too much leaves paid-for goods unsold. The decision is how to balance these competing errors. In the single-period model, demand D is uncertain. Each unit sells for \(p\), costs \(c\), and has salvage value \(s\), with \(p>c>s\). Ordering one unit too few sacrifices the margin
\[
C_u=p-c,
\]
whereas ordering one unit too many creates the net overage cost
\[
C_o=c-s.
\]
For risk-neutral expected-profit maximization with a known continuous demand distribution \(F\), the optimal order satisfies the critical-fractile rule
\[
F(Q^*)=\frac{C_u}{C_u+C_o}=\frac{p-c}{p-s}.
\]
For discrete demand, choose the smallest quantity whose cumulative probability reaches the fractile. Shortage penalties, disposal costs, capacity constraints, ambiguity, and risk preferences change the rule.
Experiments often find pull-to-center ordering: too much relative to the optimum when the optimal fractile is low and too little when it is high. Schweitzer and Cachon’s (2000) experiments were consistent with anchoring and insufficient adjustment or a preference to reduce ex post inventory error; their pattern did not uniquely support prospect theory. Demand chasing, asymmetric attention to leftover and missed-sales losses, misunderstanding, and loss aversion in other specifications remain candidate mechanisms.









NoteMathematical analysis: the St Petersburg puzzle





Consider a game in which a fair coin is tossed until the first head. If the first head occurs on toss \(n\), the game pays \(2^n\) monetary units. The probability of that outcome is \(2^{-n}\). Its expected monetary value is
\[
EV=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{-n}2^n
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1
=\infty.
\]
Yet few people would pay an enormous entry price. Bernoulli’s solution was to distinguish money from the utility of money: an additional unit matters less when one already has more (Bernoulli, 1738/1954). If utility grows slowly enough—for example, logarithmically—the expected utility can be finite even when expected money is infinite.
Finite wealth, bounded liability, mistrust, transaction costs, and a limit on tosses can also change willingness to pay. Expected value depends on a realizable contract.









NoteResearch Lens: every elicitation task measures a bundle





A risk-preference measure seems useful because it could help predict choices beyond the task. Yet changing the task can change a person’s classification. Before using that label in another setting, we need to identify what the task measured. Table 16.1 pairs each task with what it can reveal and what complicates the inference. A model maps choices back to a parameter, but comprehension, probability format, reference point, response mode, and noise can also affect the result.



Table 16.1: Common risk-elicitation methods and what travels with them











Method
What the participant does
What it can reveal
Main identification limits




Certainty-equivalent elicitation
States or selects a sure amount equally attractive to a lottery
A point or interval of indifference
Open responses invite rounding, anchoring, strategic answers, and misunderstanding


Multiple price list
Chooses between safer and riskier lotteries as probabilities or payoffs change
A switching interval for curvature under a model
Multiple switching, row-order effects, compound lotteries, and assumed functional form


Ordered lotteries
Chooses one lottery from a menu with changing mean and variance
Coarse ranking of risk taking
Mean and variance change together; few categories; loss and probability weighting remain confounded


Investment task
Allocates an endowment between a safe and risky asset
Continuous risky share
Portfolio framing, endowment, beliefs, and scale affect the share


Bomb risk elicitation task
Chooses how many reward-bearing boxes to collect while one hidden box destroys earnings
A discrete risk-taking threshold: the number of boxes selected
Interface, loss salience, probability knowledge, and task-specific emotion






Holt and Laury’s (2002) multiple-price-list design, Eckel and Grossman’s (2008) ordered gambles, and the bomb task of Crosetto and Filippin (2013) are all useful. They are not interchangeable rulers. Reviews and direct comparisons find that classifications can vary substantially across elicitation methods (Charness et al., 2013; Pedroni et al., 2017).

Identification requires more than a choice
A safe choice might reflect concave utility, distrust of the probabilities, a liquidity constraint, or misunderstanding of the task. Estimating a “risk-aversion coefficient” holds some of these possibilities fixed. Report the task, stakes, probability format, model, error structure, and population so readers can see what the parameter identifies.











NoteMathematical analysis: a positive average can conceal multiplicative collapse





Suppose a deliberately extreme gamble risks all current wealth in every round. It multiplies wealth by 1.8 with probability one half and by 0.4 with probability one half, independently across 52 rounds. The one-round arithmetic mean return is +10%, so expected terminal wealth from €10,000 is
\[
10{,}000[0.5(1.8)+0.5(0.4)]^{52}
=10{,}000(1.10)^{52}
\approx €1{,}420{,}429.
\]
Yet 26 gains and 26 losses—the median and modal number of gains—produce
\[
10{,}000(1.8)^{26}(0.4)^{26}
=10{,}000(0.72)^{26}
\approx €1.95.
\]
The expected terminal value is pulled upward by rare paths with many gains, while the median or typical compounded outcome nearly exhausts the initial wealth; the geometric mean return per round is \(\sqrt{0.72}-1\approx-15.1\%\). Drawdown is different again because it depends on the order of gains and losses. Literal ruin has probability zero in this toy model because neither multiplier is zero, but the probability of crossing a practical solvency threshold can be high and must be defined explicitly. Arithmetic return, expected wealth, median compounded wealth, drawdown, and ruin are therefore different risk questions.

title: 17  Prospect Theory
text:
Learning goals
Gains and Losses Begin at a Reference Point
Recall the outbreak decision in Framing: saving 200 of 600 people and losing 400 describe the same certain outcome, yet the gain wording attracted far more support than the loss wording (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981). The alternatives had stayed the same while the preferred risk changed.
This chapter asks how a model could explain that reversal. If the comparison begins with everyone dying, 200 survivors appear as a gain worth protecting. If it begins with everyone surviving, 400 deaths appear as a loss that a gamble might avoid. Representing the outcome is already part of evaluating it.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 17  Prospect Theory
text:
Use a reference point, value function, and probability weights to explain the fourfold pattern of risky choice.
Test whether a gain–loss effect reflects prospect theory or a competing mechanism such as ownership, attention, inertia, or switching cost.
Translate one choice across frames while preserving final states, probabilities, and meaningful exit.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 17  Prospect Theory
section: The benchmark: final wealth should absorb the frame
text:
The benchmark: final wealth should absorb the frame
For a monetary choice, expected utility evaluates the value of final wealth, weighting each possible outcome by its probability. The mathematical analysis in Chapter 16 sets out this benchmark.
If two descriptions generate the same final outcomes with the same probabilities, a consistent expected-utility chooser should rank them the same. In that monetary model, gains and losses enter through final wealth. For the outbreak problem, the consequences being evaluated are lives and deaths rather than money; equivalent descriptions should still preserve the ranking.
To explain why equivalent descriptions can produce different choices, prospect theory changes three parts of the comparison (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Tversky & Kahneman, 1992):

outcomes are coded relative to a reference point;
value changes nonlinearly over gains and losses;
probabilities become decision weights rather than entering linearly.

Together, these elements let the model explain why a person might protect a likely gain yet gamble to escape a likely loss.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 17  Prospect Theory
text:
The prospect-theory model

Reference dependence: the zero is psychologically constructed
Prospect value depends on how an outcome compares with a reference point, rather than on the outcome alone. The same salary can feel like a gain relative to last year’s pay, a loss relative to an expected promotion, and an insult relative to a colleague’s salary.
A current endowment, expectation, goal, social comparison, or imagined alternative can supply the reference point. These comparisons can conflict, so the active reference must be investigated rather than chosen retrospectively to fit the result.
Counterfactuals make this visible. Olympic bronze medalists can compare their result with no medal, while silver medalists can compare theirs with gold. Medvec, Madey, and Gilovich (1995) found facial and interview evidence consistent with bronze medalists sometimes expressing greater satisfaction than silver medalists. The result suggests that the medal alone cannot explain the reaction: what the athlete compares it with can also matter.
Expectations can also become reference points. A €10,000 bonus may feel like a gain if no bonus was expected and a loss if €15,000 was promised. Models of expectation-based reference dependence make this idea explicit (Kőszegi & Rabin, 2006).


The value function: sensitivity diminishes with distance
The value function describes how the impact of a gain or loss changes with its size. Three features matter:

Reference dependence: the comparison point determines what counts as a gain or loss.
Diminishing sensitivity: the move from no gain to a gain of 100 can matter more than the same increase from 1,000 to 1,100. A similar flattening can occur as losses grow.
Loss aversion: a loss can have greater impact than an equally sized gain. How much greater can depend on the amount and the shape of the value function.

Concavity over gains tends to support risk aversion; convexity over losses tends to support risk seeking. But the value function alone is not the whole theory. Probability weighting can reverse those tendencies, especially for rare events.
Tversky and Kahneman (1992) fitted the model to monetary choices from 25 graduate students at Berkeley and Stanford.







NoteMathematical analysis: the prospect-theory value function





Let \(x\) be the outcome and \(r\) the reference point. A common functional form is
\[
v(z)=
\begin{cases}
z^{\alpha}, & z\ge 0,\\
-\lambda(-z)^{\beta}, & z<0,
\end{cases}
\qquad z=x-r,
\]
with \(0<\alpha,\beta\le 1\) and often \(\lambda>1\).
The parameters represent three ideas:

Reference dependence: \(z=0\) is the reference point.
Diminishing sensitivity: with \(\alpha,\beta<1\), the move from 0 to 100 changes value more than the move from 1,000 to 1,100.
Loss aversion: when \(\alpha=\beta\), \(\lambda>1\) makes a loss carry more value impact than an equally sized gain. If the exponents differ, that comparison also depends on the amount; \(\lambda\) alone no longer settles it.

Tversky and Kahneman (1992) fitted the model to monetary choices from 25 graduate students at Berkeley and Stanford. The median individual estimates were \(\alpha=\beta=0.88\) and \(\lambda=2.25\).






Probability weighting: how chances influence choice
Prospect theory uses decision weights to describe the influence of probabilities on choice. Under commonly fitted models, small probabilities receive disproportionately high weight, while moderate and high probabilities receive less weight than their numerical size would suggest.
A decision weight is not necessarily a judged probability. A person can correctly report a 1% chance while giving that possibility more influence on choice than expected utility would. Vividness, affect, attention, and the possibility of zero can all affect impact without changing stated belief.
For prospects with several outcomes, cumulative prospect theory ranks the outcomes, transforms cumulative probabilities, and assigns decision weights as differences between those transformed cumulative probabilities. With increasing value and weighting functions, this construction respects first-order stochastic dominance: improving an outcome without worsening any other should not make the prospect less attractive.







NoteMathematical analysis: probability weighting





Prospect theory replaces objective probabilities with decision weights. A common one-parameter display is
\[
w(p)=\frac{p^\gamma}
{\left[p^\gamma+(1-p)^\gamma\right]^{1/\gamma}},
\qquad 0<\gamma\le 1.
\]
For commonly fitted parameter values below one, the curve is inverse-S shaped: small probabilities receive disproportionately high weight, while moderate and high probabilities receive lower weight than their numerical size would suggest. Tversky and Kahneman (1992) estimated separate weighting parameters of \(\gamma=0.61\) for gains and \(\delta=0.69\) for losses in their fitted model. The formula requires a parameter range that keeps it increasing: very low positive values can make it nonmonotonic and yield invalid negative cumulative decision weights (Ingersoll, 2008).










Figure 17.1: Schematic curves illustrate prospect theory’s S-shaped value function around a reference point and inverse-S probability-weighting function. Under commonly used parameterizations, they can produce the fourfold pattern: caution for high-probability gains and low-probability losses, but risk seeking for low-probability gains and high-probability losses.



Read Figure 17.1 from the two curves at the top to the risk attitudes below: the value of a gain or loss and the influence of its probability jointly shape the prediction.


Certainty and possibility are psychological boundaries
A probability change from 95% to 100% removes all chance of failure. A change from 45% to 50% does not. Prospect theory captures the special impact of certainty: the final step to 100% can matter more than an equal numerical increase in the middle of the scale. This certainty effect helps explain the sure option in the first Allais pair and risk aversion for high-probability gains.
The move from 0% to a small positive probability creates a possibility that did not exist before. This possibility effect can make a tiny chance of a jackpot compelling and a tiny chance of catastrophe worth insuring.
Very small probabilities may also be ignored, rounded to zero, or never encountered. The next chapter examines how descriptions and experience change their influence.


The fourfold pattern of risk attitudes
We can now combine the two influences. Curvature describes the value of the possible gain or loss; weighting describes the influence of its probability. Crossing the gain–loss domain with the probability range in Table 17.1 gives four recurring patterns under commonly used parameterizations.



Table 17.1: The fourfold pattern predicted by cumulative prospect theory










Domain
High probability
Low probability




Gain
Risk aversion: protect a likely gain; prefer a sure amount to a slightly larger gamble
Risk seeking: pursue a small chance of a large gain; lottery-like choice


Loss
Risk seeking: gamble to avoid a likely loss; escalation or “break even” attempt
Risk aversion: pay to remove a small chance of catastrophe; insurance-like choice






A person can buy insurance and a lottery ticket: the probability range and gain–loss domain differ.


A low-probability gain
Consider a 1% chance of €10,000 and otherwise zero. Its expected monetary value is €100. Under expected utility with linear utility, €100 certain and the lottery are equal.
With the illustrative prospect-theory parameters, a reference point of zero, and no ticket price, this lottery is as attractive as approximately €372 for certain. The small chance receives enough extra weight to outweigh the value function’s diminishing sensitivity to the size of the prize.
That figure is a model prediction, not a measured willingness to pay. Changing probability weighting changes the answer; charging for a ticket requires specifying how its cost is combined with the outcomes and whether it is coded as a loss. The calculation shows how weighting can outweigh diminishing sensitivity without turning the model into advice to buy a lottery ticket.







NoteMathematical analysis: valuing the low-probability gain





The illustrative gain calculation uses \(\alpha=0.88\) and \(\gamma=0.61\). Assume a reference point of zero and no ticket price. Because the alternative outcome is zero, the cumulative-prospect calculation reduces to
\[
w(0.01)\approx0.0553,\qquad
V=w(0.01)\,10{,}000^{0.88}\approx183.0.
\]
A certain €100 has value \(100^{0.88}\approx57.5\). Under these illustrative assumptions, the lottery therefore receives more value than its expected monetary amount. Its certainty equivalent solves \(c^{0.88}=183.0\), giving approximately €372.
