title: 17  Prospect Theory
section: Framing changes the comparison; check equivalence
text:
Framing changes the comparison; check equivalence
The Asian-disease programs are mathematically equivalent under the stated assumptions. A gain frame supports the concave side of the value function; a loss frame supports the convex side. This is risky-choice framing.
The framing chapter’s distinctions separate this change in risky choice from attribute and goal framing. Prospect theory contributes a more specific question: which outcome has become the comparison point, and how are gains, losses, and probabilities being evaluated? A description that omits costs or changes the time horizon may also change the substantive decision, rather than merely its frame.
Before diagnosing bias, verify equivalence. “90% survival after surgery” and “10% mortality during surgery” may differ in time horizon. “Keep €200” and “lose €200” may imply different starting endowments. A preference reversal is normatively troubling only if the options are substantively the same for the decision-maker.
The original Asian-disease results came from separate groups answering hypothetical problems. Later work finds that framing effects vary with wording, numeracy, task structure, and population. In a preregistered multinational replication of the monetary choice problems from Kahneman and Tversky (1979), Ruggeri and colleagues (2020) studied 4,098 participants in 19 countries and 13 languages and replicated 94% of tested items and 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts. That broad support for the tested prospect-theory patterns came with attenuation and meaningful cross-country and within-person variation; it was not a direct replication of the outbreak wording experiment.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 17  Prospect Theory
text:
Measuring loss aversion
Loss aversion means that, around a reference point, a loss changes value more than a comparable gain. It is not the same as risk aversion. A person can be loss averse yet risk seeking over losses, and risk averse without coding an outcome as a loss.
The familiar statement “losses loom about twice as large as gains” turns a model estimate into a law. The estimated loss-aversion parameter depends on the assumed reference point, outcome range, weighting and value functions, response noise, and institutional setting. It can also change when the task involves certain exchanges rather than risky choices.
Gal and Rucker (2018) argue that evidence does not justify loss aversion as a context-free general principle. Other work supports loss aversion in particular tasks and populations. To compare estimates, specify the domain, measurement model, and reference point.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 17  Prospect Theory
section: One applied audit across three settings
text:
One applied audit across three settings
In each setting below, identify the reference point, reconstruct the future consequences, and ask what else could explain the choice.

Investment: look beyond the purchase price
An investor bought a share at €100. It now trades at €70. “I will not sell until I break even” treats 100 as a reference point and converts selling into a sure loss. But the prospective decision is whether €70 should remain in this asset or move to the best alternative.
Ask what the investor would buy today with €70 cash, allowing for taxes, transaction costs, liquidity, and the rest of the portfolio. That comparison tests whether the purchase price contributes useful information or merely marks the loss. Prospect theory can explain the pain of selling without recommending that the investor hold.


Organizational change: make the sacrifice legible
A manager says, “If we do not adopt the system, each team will lose €200,000.” A loss frame may create urgency, but it can also encourage risk seeking, conceal uncertainty, and make dissent look irresponsible.

Show the expected consequences of adoption and non-adoption on the same scale, including transition costs, uncertainty, reversibility, and who bears the loss. State the objective behind the recommendation and keep feasible alternatives visible. Readers can then translate between gain and loss language, question the recommendation, and revise their choice without losing a material fact.


Defaults: separate reference dependence from switching cost
An employer automatically enrolls workers in a retirement plan. Staying may reflect loss aversion, recommendation, inertia, trust, or a considered choice. A defensible default keeps fees, contribution rate, investment risk, and exit visible; allows easy adjustment; and tests outcomes across employees with different liquidity needs.
Higher enrollment alone does not show that the default serves the worker. The employer must be able to justify the implied recommendation for the people receiving it, while preserving the usable exit and adjustment options.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 17  Prospect Theory
text:
Practice Lab
Take one live purchase, policy, investment, or negotiation. Produce a three-column comparison showing the choice as final states, gains, and losses while preserving probabilities and time horizons. Mark the reference point, locate the case in the fourfold pattern, and specify one competing mechanism and one observation that would distinguish it. Finish with a transparent redesign and a meaningful exit route.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 17  Prospect Theory
text:
Take it forward
Look again at the outbreak programs. Translate each into the final number of survivors and deaths before choosing. You may still find one description more compelling, but now you can see what it emphasizes—and check whether the recommendation survives the complementary description.






NoteResearch Lens: related phenomena require separate diagnoses





Endowment effects, effort-based valuation, status quo bias, and narrow framing are often placed under the prospect-theory umbrella. The following cases show how to distinguish those explanations.

Endowment effects: how ownership changes valuation
A mug can serve the same purpose before and after it becomes yours. Yet ownership may change the price you require to give it up, making an otherwise attractive trade harder to complete. An endowment effect occurs when ownership changes valuation or willingness to trade. In classic experiments, randomly endowed participants were often less willing to exchange an object, and sellers demanded more than buyers offered for similar goods (Kahneman et al., 1990). What has ownership added to the comparison?
Loss aversion offers one explanation: giving up an owned mug is coded as a loss. But a willingness-to-accept/willingness-to-pay gap can also reflect transaction costs, income effects, misunderstanding, strategic answers, attachment, or different information and attention among buyers and sellers. The gap is not a direct measure of the loss-aversion parameter.
Plott and Zeiler (2005) found no WTA–WTP gap in their mug and lottery experiments when they used extensive training, incentive-compatible procedures, anonymity, and controls aimed at misconceptions. List (2003) found that the anomaly diminished with market experience in field and experimental evidence. Morewedge and Giblin (2015) review evidence for several cognitive and strategic accounts.


A practical ownership test
When an owner refuses to sell, ask:

Would the owner buy one more at the stated selling price?
What replacement cost, search cost, tax, or uncertainty is being omitted?
Does the object carry identity, memory, or relationship value absent from the market price?
Would the choice change if the initial allocation were randomized and the mechanism practiced?
Which attributes are buyers and sellers considering?

“Loss aversion” should begin the investigation, not end it.


The IKEA effect: labor can create value
Assembling a product costs time and effort that a finished purchase would save. Yet doing that work can make the result more valuable to its maker. The IKEA effect is this increased valuation of something one has helped create. To understand when effort becomes a source of value, Norton, Mochon, and Ariely (2012) studied assembled boxes, origami, and Lego creations. Valuation increased after successful completion, but the effect weakened when participants failed to complete or had to destroy their work.
Successful creation may change value through competence, authorship, customization, or familiarity; effort justification and anticipated loss are further possibilities.
The mechanism matters for design. Inviting customers or employees to co-create can build agency and knowledge. It can also exploit sunk effort to keep them in a poor product or project. Successful labor may add real experiential value.


Status quo bias: staying can be rational, psychological, or designed
Keeping a familiar option can avoid disruption; its status can also make an otherwise comparable alternative feel like a loss. A useful choice process must distinguish what staying protects from what the designation itself changes. Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988) documented disproportionate selection of an option designated as the status quo. Loss aversion can contribute: changing makes possible losses salient, while foregone gains from staying are less visible.
Staying can also reflect switching costs, uncertainty, an inferred recommendation, inattention, anticipated regret, or a valued commitment. The default may be substantively best.
A diagnostic intervention varies one mechanism at a time: make switching costs explicit, provide a neutral recommendation, simplify comparison, add a reversible trial, or randomize the initial allocation where ethical. If the effect remains, the evidence for deeper preference construction becomes stronger.


Narrow and broad framing: what counts as one prospect?
Suppose you reject a 50–50 gamble to lose €100 or gain €200. Would you accept 100 independent repetitions? The repeated portfolio has positive expected value and a much smaller probability of an overall loss. Evaluating each gamble separately can produce a different choice from evaluating the distribution of total outcomes.
Narrow framing evaluates one transaction, account, day, or outcome in isolation. Broad framing evaluates its contribution to total wealth, a portfolio, or a longer time horizon. Neither bracket is always correct. A single catastrophic exposure should not disappear inside an average, and legal or moral constraints may be transaction-specific. The right bracket follows the decision objective and dependence structure.
Mental Accounting develops how people create and label these brackets. Prospect theory supplies a value function over gains and losses; mental accounting helps determine which outcomes are grouped and which reference point each account uses.

title: 18  Decisions From Experience
text:
Learning goals
When Rare Events Are Not Encountered
Option A always pays €3. Option B pays €32 with probability 10% and €0 otherwise. You may sample either option as often as you wish before making one consequential choice.
The description gives everything required to calculate expected value: A is worth €3; B is worth €3.20. Experience creates another problem. A learner who samples B five times has a probability of about 59% of seeing no €32 outcome at all. For that learner, B has so far looked like a machine that pays zero. Another learner may encounter €32 on the first draw and see B as extraordinarily attractive. Although both learners face the same distribution, they have encountered very different evidence.
The two learners must infer what each option can deliver from the outcomes they happened to see. A team deciding whether to add a second supplier after eight years of reliable deliveries faces a similar problem. Its experience is reassuring, but did those years include the kinds of disruption it needs to prepare for? We will return to that decision after examining what experience reveals and conceals.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 18  Decisions From Experience
text:
Distinguish a described distribution from the selective path a decision-maker actually experiences.
Diagnose sampling, stopping, recency, avoidance, and feedback mechanisms in one supplier-risk case.
Design a learning system that combines calibrated description with representative experience.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 18  Decisions From Experience
section: Description and experience are different information conditions
text:
Description and experience are different information conditions
A decision from description states the possible outcomes and their probabilities. A weather forecast gives a probability of rain. A medicine fact box reports estimated benefits and harms. An insurer may provide estimated claim frequencies and loss amounts. The decision-maker may misunderstand, neglect, or transform these numbers, but the distribution is externally represented.
A decision from experience requires the distribution to be learned from observations. A driver infers how dangerous a familiar road is from previous journeys. A manager estimates supplier reliability from deliveries that happened to be observed. A person decides whether to back up a computer after years without a disk failure. Outcomes and probabilities are not fully listed; the person samples, remembers, and updates.
Many consequential decisions contain both. A physician can read trial evidence and also remember patients. A resident can see a flood map and also remember years without flooding. An investor can study a long return series and still give special weight to the market experienced during early adulthood. The independent dimensions in Figure 18.1 make room for all four combinations, including having neither source. When both are present, disagreement calls for investigation; neither is automatically superior.






Figure 18.1: Four information states created by the presence or absence of statistical description and personal experience.




Four sources-of-information situations
Hertwig and Wulff (2022) organize risk situations by asking whether description and experience are present or absent. The responses in Table 18.1 follow from what is missing: a selective history calls for broader evidence, while a described distribution may need a clearer, more usable presentation.



Table 18.1: Four information states require different diagnoses











Information state
What the chooser has
Central danger
Useful response




Neither
No credible description and little relevant personal experience
Missing information can be mistaken for zero risk
Seek information, use scenarios, preserve reversibility, and state what is unknown


Description only
Outcomes and probabilities, but no lived feedback
Rare outcomes can be unusually salient, misunderstood, or detached from action
Use natural frequencies, absolute risks, denominators, and comparisons


Experience only
A sequence of observed outcomes, but no explicit distribution
Small or selective samples can miss rare events and conceal the generating process
Enlarge the sample, examine selection, and add base rates


Both
Statistical description and personal or simulated experience
Vivid experience can contradict representative evidence, or abstract numbers can fail to become usable
Reconcile the sources; explain why they differ and what each can identify






Having neither source leaves the chooser information-poor. This becomes deep uncertainty when no credible model can yet specify the relevant outcomes and probabilities. With a new technology or an unprecedented disruption, scenarios and reversible trials may be more useful than an unjustifiably precise estimate (Hertwig & Wulff, 2022).
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 18  Decisions From Experience
text:
The description–experience gap
Early experiments found that choices based on sampled outcomes often differ from choices based on explicitly described lotteries (Barron & Erev, 2003; Hertwig et al., 2004). In many description tasks, small-probability outcomes receive more decision weight than their objective probability. An unlikely gain can make a lottery attractive; an unlikely loss can make insurance attractive. This is one part of the fourfold pattern in Prospect Theory.
In many experience tasks, rare outcomes have less impact. If the rare outcome is not sampled—or appears less often than its population probability—it cannot strongly affect choice. A person may therefore select the option with an unlikely severe loss more often after sampling than after reading the same loss probability.
Hertwig and Erev (2009) summarize the resulting description–experience gap as a contrast between information conditions:

description: rare events tend to receive relatively high decision weight;
experience: rare events often receive relatively low decision weight.

Wulff, Mergenthaler-Canseco, and Hertwig’s (2018) meta-analysis found a robust aggregate description–experience gap whose size and behavioral expression depended on the structure of the problem and the learning procedure. Sometimes the sample is unrepresentative; sometimes memory or learning changes the use of observed outcomes; sometimes a single severe event produces lasting avoidance.

Learning the probabilities before valuing the options
Prospect theory begins with represented outcomes and probabilities, then explains how reference dependence, diminishing sensitivity, loss aversion, and probability weighting shape valuation. A decision-from-experience task adds an upstream stage: the path sampled from the environment shapes what the person learns, which then informs valuation and choice.
The chooser helps create this evidence by deciding where to look, how long to sample, whether to stop after a striking result, and which feedback to revisit. Two people can therefore apply the same valuation process to different learned representations of the same environment.
That distinction prevents a common conceptual mistake. Underweighting a rare event in experience need not mean that a person observed the true probability and assigned it a low weight. The event may simply be absent from the person’s evidence.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 18  Decisions From Experience
text:
Why the gap emerges

Small samples can erase rare events
In Hertwig and colleagues’ (2004) experiment, participants made a median of only fifteen draws per problem across the two options before choosing. A sample of that size can easily omit a 1% or 5% event. It can also overrepresent it. Sampling error therefore creates heterogeneity across learners before psychological weighting begins.






Figure 18.2: An independently occurring rare event can remain absent from a small experience sample. With 15 observations, a 1% event remains unseen about 86% of the time and a 5% event about 46% of the time. The highlighted band shows a small sample of 11–19 observations for comparison.



The slowly falling one-percent curve in Figure 18.2 shows why an uneventful sample can coexist with a real rare-event risk. The following sections examine how selective exposure, stopping, and memory shape the experienced record.
Larger forced samples reduce this source of the gap, but do not always eliminate the gap (Hau et al., 2008, 2010; Wulff et al., 2018). That residual matters. If exposure were the entire explanation, choices should converge once experienced frequencies are controlled. Remaining differences direct attention to memory, recency, learning, format, and choice rules.







NoteMathematical analysis: the chance of never encountering a rare event





If an event occurs independently with probability \(p\) on each observation, its chance of being absent from all \(n\) observations is
\[
P(\text{unseen in }n\text{ observations})=(1-p)^n.
\]
With fifteen observations, \((1-0.01)^{15}\approx0.86\) for a 1% event and \((1-0.05)^{15}\approx0.46\) for a 5% event.






Stopping is part of the evidence
Sampling is rarely neutral. People may stop when one option looks sufficiently good, when uncertainty feels tolerable, or immediately after a striking outcome. Optional stopping changes the sample that reaches the final choice. In autonomous-sampling tasks, apparent recency can partly reflect the fact that the last observations help determine when sampling ends.
The practical question is not only “How many cases did we see?” It is also:

Why were those cases observed?
What made observation stop?
Were failures more likely to be documented than uneventful cases?
Did the decision rule remove an option before it could reveal its long-run distribution?

A ten-year record for retained suppliers describes performance under the firm’s screening and replacement policy. If vulnerable suppliers were dropped after early problems, the successful survivors cannot by themselves tell us how well an untested supplier would perform.


Recent and memorable outcomes receive more influence
Learning models often fit experienced choice better when recent observations receive more weight. Recency can be adaptive when an environment changes: yesterday’s defect rate may predict tomorrow better than the rate from five years ago. But recency can be misleading in a stationary environment, especially when the recent run is unrepresentative.
Memory adds another selection layer. Frequent ordinary outcomes blur together; a vivid loss remains retrievable. Frequency in memory is therefore not identical to frequency in the world. Ask whether there is evidence that the environment has changed, and whether the memorable event helps identify that change. A recent failure deserves more weight if it reveals a new vulnerability than if it is ordinary variation in a stable process.


Contingent sampling retrieves “similar” histories
Managers tend to recall projects from a similar market rather than draw randomly from every project they have known. This contingent sampling can extract relevant structure, but it can also create a small, biased reference class.
Similarity needs an explicit test. Which features made the prior case comparable? Which disconfirming cases were excluded? A compelling analogy is not yet a representative sample.


Format changes what can be understood
Descriptions often use percentages or one-event probabilities. Experience naturally produces counts: three failures in one hundred trials. Natural frequencies can support better Bayesian reasoning than normalized probabilities in some tasks (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995). But format and experience should not be conflated. A description can also be written as frequencies, and a simulation can obscure denominators.
The useful comparison holds the information constant. Show absolute risks with the same denominator, state the reference class and time horizon, and make both benefits and harms visible. Then ask whether sequential experience adds learning beyond a clear description.

title: 18  Decisions From Experience
section: Experience can hide a rare event—or make one event dominate
text:
Experience can hide a rare event—or make one event dominate

The hot-stove effect
After one painful encounter with a hot stove, avoiding it is sensible. The same learning rule can mislead a team that abandons a promising but variable strategy after one unlucky trial. Denrell and March (2001) show why adaptive sampling can create this pattern: actions with uncertain outcomes are sampled less after bad experiences, so the learner receives fewer opportunities to discover their higher mean.
This is “as-if” overweighting of a rare adverse outcome. It does not require a stable probability-weighting preference. Because the bad outcome reduces future exposure, the learner may never encounter the evidence that would correct the initial impression.
Exploration therefore has value. But exploration is not automatically wise. A hospital should not repeatedly sample a treatment suspected of severe harm merely to learn its distribution. The value of information must be weighed against the cost and reversibility of experimentation.


Personal history becomes a reference class
An investor can consult the long market record and still find their own lifetime more convincing. If that personal history supplies the reference class, advice built on the same published probabilities may lead different investors to different choices. Malmendier and Nagel (2011) studied U.S. household data from 1960–2007 and found that people whose lifetimes included lower stock-market returns reported less willingness to take financial risk, participated less in the stock market, invested a smaller share in stocks when participating, and expected lower returns. More recent lifetime experiences received more weight, especially among younger people.
This link between lifetime macroeconomic experience and later financial beliefs and behavior is sometimes called the Depression Baby hypothesis.
Lejarraga, Woike, and Hertwig (2016) created experimental investment environments with booms and busts. Whether people learned through descriptions or sequential experience changed their stock allocations and responses to market regimes. The teaching point is broader than one graph: investors do not encounter a timeless return distribution. They observe a path, and the path teaches them which world they think they inhabit.


Locals and visitors can encounter different risk signals
Yechiam, Barron, and Erev (2005) reported that residents of areas exposed to repeated terrorist attacks appeared less behaviorally sensitive to the risk than international tourists, with sensitivity among residents diminishing over time even while attacks continued. Their laboratory task produced a related description–experience contrast.
Repeated ordinary days coexist with rare attacks for residents, while media descriptions can make the rare event central for visitors.1


Normalcy bias: when surviving becomes evidence of safety
“Nothing bad happened last time” can be useful evidence, but it does not establish that the next exposure is safe. Normalcy bias is a broad label for interpreting a warning through an expectation that familiar conditions will continue. One specific pattern was documented after the Loma Prieta earthquake: households without mainshock damage perceived less aftershock risk and responded less to warnings, a pattern Mileti and O’Brien (1992) called normalization bias. Their household study was observational.
A warning may also be unclear, distrusted, or impossible to act on. Diagnose those barriers before attributing the response to bias. For a supplier or safety review, compare the uneventful record with the exposure it actually tested, then specify which new signal requires action. Chapter 8 examines decisions under time pressure; preparation must make the response usable before the warning arrives.

title: 18  Decisions From Experience
section: Learning from outcomes without being fooled by luck
text:
Learning from outcomes without being fooled by luck
An outcome teaches us something, but it does not reveal all the paths a choice could have taken. The process–outcome distinction therefore matters especially when learning from a selective record: a lucky success can reinforce an unreliable rule, while a rare harm remains unseen.



Table 18.2: Process quality and outcome quality must be reviewed separately











Good outcome
Bad outcome




Good process
Preserve the process; do not assume success proves every assumption
Preserve what was sound; identify which uncertainty realized


Bad process
Treat success as a warning: luck can reinforce a fragile rule
Diagnose the process without pretending the bad outcome was inevitable






Reviewing the four cells in Table 18.2 prevents a successful result from excusing a poor process or a bad result from condemning a sound one. Hindsight, self-serving attribution, and rationalization make this separation difficult. People can sincerely explain choices whose causes they did not notice (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977; Johansson et al., 2005), so a retrospective account needs something firmer than memory to compare with.

A decision record for experiential learning
Before choosing, preserve the alternatives, evidence, predictions, trade-offs, unknowns, and review rule. Afterward, compare the outcome with those predictions and identify which assumption gained or lost support. Add the question distinctive to learning from experience: Did our choice determine what we could observe? A successful supplier audit is less reassuring if it never tests the conditions most likely to cause failure.

title: 18  Decisions From Experience

title: 18  Decisions From Experience
section: Communicating risk: combine numbers and experience
text:
Communicating risk: combine numbers and experience
A clear risk table can state every outcome while leaving a reader unable to imagine the variability. A simulation makes a sequence tangible, but the particular draws may leave a rare loss unseen. Risk communication needs to make the distribution both understandable and available for judgment. The studies below examine what each presentation contributes.
Kaufmann, Weber, and Haisley (2013) compared investment-risk presentations, including experience-sampling displays of return distributions. Experience-like tools increased risky allocation in their setting and helped participants recall features such as expected return and loss probability. The tool changed what participants could encounter and retrieve.
Wegwarth and colleagues (2022) randomly assigned 300 German patients with chronic noncancer pain to a descriptive fact box or an interactive simulated-experience format about long-term strong-opioid use. Both formats improved objective risk perception. The fact box produced more accurate estimates for some outcomes, while the simulation group showed a larger reduction or termination of opioid use and greater uptake of alternative therapies.2
A strong risk display therefore combines:

Calibrated description: absolute risks and benefits, common denominators, time horizon, reference class, and uncertainty.
Representative experience: enough simulated draws to reveal ordinary variability and rare tails without allowing selective stopping to manufacture a story.
Comparison: the same scale for every option, including no action.
Reflection: a prompt to state what was learned and which outcomes were not encountered.
Agency: time to decide, access to advice, and freedom to refuse.

In medicine, these displays support deliberation with current clinical evidence and professional guidance. A calm personal history or dramatic side-effect story cannot supply the missing comparison on its own.

A display can defeat these aims by curating favorable testimonials, showing only winning outcomes, stopping an animation before losses appear, or presenting one victim’s story without a denominator. The opposite error is to dismiss lived experience merely because it conflicts with an aggregate average.
Representative statistics may miss subgroup harm, implementation failure, or unmeasured outcomes; personal experience can reveal a mechanism without estimating its prevalence. Keep both sources open to scrutiny. Show who is absent from each record, provide a way to report rare harms, and preserve disagreements between evidence sources until they can be investigated.

title: 18  Decisions From Experience
section: Worked application: a supplier has never failed us
text:
Worked application: a supplier has never failed us
A team rejects dual sourcing because its supplier has delivered reliably for eight years. Paying to qualify another supplier seems to buy protection against a problem the team has never faced. Yet relying on the existing supplier leaves the team exposed if those years omitted the disruption that would stop production. The decision turns on what the record actually covers:
Experience audit. How many relevant disruptions occurred in the wider industry? Did the eight years include the geopolitical, climate, logistics, and financial states that matter now? Did earlier screening remove fragile suppliers, making the observed history conditional on a successful policy?
Description audit. What do base rates, financial indicators, network dependencies, and scenario models imply? Are reported probabilities traceable, or are they precise-looking guesses?
Choice audit. Dual sourcing has a visible current cost; disruption has an uncertain tail cost. What resilience threshold would justify a pilot rather than a full switch?
Learning design. Run a limited second-source qualification, stress-test a delay, record predicted recovery times, and review near misses. The pilot generates information while preserving production.
The pilot and stress test address a gap the eight-year record cannot fill. They let the team investigate resilience without assuming that failure is imminent.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 18  Decisions From Experience
text:
Practice Lab
Audit a supplier judged “reliable because it has never failed us.” Produce a sampling map with the observation window, number of exposures, near misses, avoided situations, unreported failures, relevant base rate, and stopping rule. Add one controlled stress test or simulation, then state what finding would change the sourcing decision. Show which conditions the record covers and which remain untested, then explain how that gap affects your recommendation.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 18  Decisions From Experience
text:
Take it forward
Eight reliable years count as evidence. The supplier team’s task is to find out what those years cover, add evidence about conditions they did not include, and choose a proportionate way to test resilience. Confidence then rests on a record whose limits are visible.
Experience shapes which outcomes enter a decision. The next chapter, Mental Accounting, asks how we group and label those outcomes—and why the same saving can seem worth more in one purchase than another.






NoteResearch Lens: transporting the sampling diagnosis





The sampling problem also matters in disaster preparedness and other settings, where opportunities to learn come with constraints that laboratory draws do not reproduce.

Disasters and the experience trap
Mount Vesuvius, the 2021 eruption on La Palma, and floods in Passau provide vivid teaching cases. A city can go decades without a catastrophic event. Everyday experience then supplies thousands of “safe” observations, while historical and scientific description carries the tail risk. The absence of a recent disaster is evidence about frequency—but not evidence that the hazard is zero.
Location reflects family, employment, housing prices, insurance, identity, public protection, and the feasibility of moving. The decision requires at least four layers:

Hazard: What is the best available estimate of event frequency and severity?
Exposure: Who and what would be in harm’s way?
Vulnerability: How much damage would follow, given infrastructure and preparation?
Agency: Which protections, insurance, evacuation plans, or relocation options are feasible?

Long calm periods can produce underpreparedness. A recent disaster can produce excessive avoidance after conditions have changed. Good design keeps historical evidence available between events and updates it after each event without letting one experience stand for the whole distribution.


Beyond rare-event lotteries
The description–experience framework also helps organize other choices:

Ambiguity: Sampling can make an unknown probability feel learnable, yet the sample may create false precision.
Intertemporal choice: Waiting through a delay can feel different from reading a date; experienced delay includes boredom, uncertainty, anticipation, and changing states.
Adolescence: Age differences in risky choice can depend on whether risks are described or learned through feedback; “adolescents are risk seeking” is too coarse.
Generalization: Experience can teach frequent local regularities while a description supplies an abstract rule that transfers to new cases.
Reinforcement learning: Outcomes update expected values through prediction errors; partial feedback teaches only about chosen options, whereas full feedback also reveals forgone outcomes.
Operations: Inventory, maintenance, and quality decisions are learned from demand and failure histories whose samples may be censored by earlier policy.

Specify what description and experience contain: simulated outcomes, personal consequences, or a numerical history of other people’s experience.

title: 19  Mental Accounting
text:
Learning goals
Money Is Fungible; Minds Label It
Imagine that another shop is twenty minutes away. It sells the product you want for €6 less.
The trip, time, and saving are identical. Would the cheaper product nevertheless make the trip feel more worthwhile? Assuming the twenty-minute journey must be made each way, the economic benchmark asks whether €6 is worth forty minutes of travel and any inconvenience. The product’s original price should not change that comparison.
The example adapts Tversky and Kahneman’s (1981) calculator-and-jacket problem. Respondents imagined buying both items, with a combined price of $140. A twenty-minute drive would save $5 on the calculator: 68% would make the trip when its price fell from $15 to $10, compared with 29% when it fell from $125 to $120. The jacket’s price changed in the opposite direction, keeping the original total constant. These were hypothetical choices by separate groups of 93 and 88 respondents, respectively.
The saving appears to have been evaluated inside the calculator purchase rather than against the whole shopping bill. The same money bought a more satisfying “deal” when it was a larger fraction of the item’s price (Thaler, 1985). Waiting-time research shows a related pattern: people may pay more to avoid the same wait when the underlying purchase is more expensive (Leclerc et al., 1995).

title: 19  Mental Accounting
text:
Diagnose how labels, brackets, payment coupling, and account-closing rules change economic choice.
Separate sunk-cost escalation from forward-looking value while preserving valid informational and implementation reasons to continue.
Redesign one budget or project account so it protects a goal without hiding substitution, total cost, or exit.

title: 19  Mental Accounting
section: The benchmark: fungibility and total wealth
text:
The benchmark: fungibility and total wealth
Money is fungible when one unrestricted unit can substitute for another otherwise-equivalent unit of equal value. A €20 note received as salary can buy the same groceries as €20 won in a raffle. Taxes, withdrawal penalties, timing, or other constraints can make nominally equal amounts economically different; the source label alone cannot change their purchasing power.
Mental accounting describes how people organize financial activities into accounts, code entries as gains or losses, and decide what to evaluate together (Thaler, 1985, 1999). Figure 19.1 follows these operations into valuation, where the same boundary can support a goal or hide a valuable alternative.






Figure 19.1: Mental accounting can label, code, bracket, couple, or close outcomes before valuation. The resulting boundaries may support an endorsed goal or distort substitution across otherwise-equivalent resources.



Borrowing while saving might reflect a psychological boundary or an actual withdrawal penalty. Establish which constraint is operating before prescribing greater flexibility.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 19  Mental Accounting
section: Four operations: label, bracket, couple, and close
text:
Four operations: label, bracket, couple, and close
The shopping example shows one account boundary: the saving belongs to a particular purchase. Other boundaries concern where money came from, which outcomes are considered together, and when a past payment feels settled. Following these operations shows both what mental accounts make easier and what they can hide.

Label: acquisition utility and transaction utility
Suppose you want a cold beer on a hot beach. A companion can buy the same beer either from an expensive resort or from a run-down grocery shop. People commonly state a higher maximum price when the seller is the resort, even though the beer and the pleasure from drinking it are unchanged. Thaler’s (1985) hypothetical demonstration found a higher median stated willingness to pay in the resort version.
The distinction is between two evaluations:

Acquisition utility is the value of the item minus the money given up. It resembles consumer surplus: is the beer worth at least its price to me?
Transaction utility is the pleasure or pain of the deal relative to a reference price: am I paying less or more than I expected to pay here?

A price below the reference can create a satisfying “deal” even when the item is not valuable enough to justify buying. Conversely, a price that feels unfair can block a purchase whose total benefit exceeds its total cost. “€45 plus €5 shipping” may feel worse than “€50 with free shipping” because the fee is posted as a separate loss, although total expenditure is identical. Separating a price from unavoidable fees can also hide the total when those fees are disclosed late; the comparison then lacks information rather than merely changing its label.
The reference price is not always mistaken. A high resort price may signal scarcity, service, or future replacement cost. But transaction utility becomes dangerous when “how good is this deal?” silently replaces “is this worth buying?” The two questions need separate answers.


Close: sunk costs and the pain of closing an account
Sunk costs are one route into escalation of commitment: continuing a course after unfavorable evidence because prior money, effort, identity, or responsibility makes stopping feel like admitting a loss. Mental accounting supplies one mechanism. Abandoning an activity can feel like closing its account in the red even when the past payment cannot alter any future consequence.
Vince prepays for a tennis season and later develops a painful elbow. He continues playing because stopping would “waste” the membership. Yet if a friend offered the same painful game for free, he would refuse.
The payment is unrecoverable. Under a forward-looking benchmark, the choice should compare the future benefits and costs of playing: enjoyment, exercise, time, and injury. Paying in the past does not make playing now healthier. But mental accounting opens the tennis account with a negative balance. Attendance appears to repay the payment; quitting closes the account with an explicit loss (Arkes & Blumer, 1985).
The project team saying “we have already spent too much to stop” faces Vince’s problem at a larger scale. More investment cannot undo the earlier spending; it needs to earn its place through what it makes possible from today onward.
Escalation can also involve self-justification, public commitment, accountability for the initial choice, competition, and a hope that one more tranche will vindicate the decision (Staw, 1976, 1981).
Prior investment can create reusable assets or information; continuation may preserve reputation, learning, option value, or avoid switching costs. Those are future consequences, not reasons to recover an irrecoverable past. The diagnostic is narrower:

If the past payment disappeared from memory but every future consequence remained, would the best next action change?

If yes, ask what legitimate future consequence carries the effect. If none can be named, the account may be keeping an irrelevant cost alive.


Couple: when consumption repays a purchase
The tennis example concerns a payment that keeps influencing whether to play. How long does that influence last? A gym membership buys access throughout the paid period, yet a fresh bill can make going feel more urgent, as if each visit repays the purchase. Researchers describe this link between payment and consumption as coupling.
Gourville and Soman (1998) found gym attendance rose after periodic payments and then declined as the payment became less salient. In a field experiment with theatre season tickets, randomly assigned discounts reduced attendance relative to full-price tickets during the first part of the season; the difference faded over time (Arkes & Blumer, 1985). Sunk costs can motivate consumption, but their salience decays.
A visible per-use charge keeps a “running meter” in mind; delayed billing or a flat rate can weaken that connection. Weak coupling may make an experience easier to enjoy, but it can also obscure cumulative spending. The design should leave total cost recoverable even when each use carries no immediate reminder.


Label and bracket: useful budgets that can become walls
People commonly organize expenditures into food, housing, entertainment, education, and holiday budgets; wealth into cash, investments, and retirement savings; and income into salary, bonus, refund, or windfall. These categories reduce computational burden and can protect long-run goals. “The retirement account is not for ordinary spending” is a self-control rule before it is a financial calculation.
But a notional budget can become nonfungible. Someone may reject a worthwhile theatre ticket because the entertainment budget was used on a sports event, yet buy it after an equally costly medical expense or after receiving the sports ticket as a gift. Heath and Soll (1996) used such comparisons to show category-sensitive spending. Table 19.1 reports the study’s $50 prior-expense condition. Each entry is the percentage showing the predicted “no after a prior purchase, yes after receiving that item as a gift, yes after an unrelated expense” pattern, averaged across four unrelated-expense controls.

A later Registered Report found mixed results. Li and Feldman’s (2025) adapted replication recovered the predicted dinner-versus-sports-ticket contrast, but not the flu-vaccination-versus-sports-ticket contrast: the flu-vaccination responses resembled the supposedly related sports-ticket condition.
Field evidence can make nonfungibility more consequential. When gasoline prices fell sharply in 2008, consumers shifted toward higher grades. In the paper’s baseline model, marginal utility responded about fifteen times as strongly to a gasoline-price increase as to an equivalent income reduction; comparable quality shifts did not appear for milk or orange juice (Hastings & Shapiro, 2013). A plausible interpretation is that consumers kept part of the saving inside a gasoline account rather than reallocating it across the household budget.
A budget boundary can preserve money for an important goal. It becomes costly when a person saves at a low return while carrying avoidable high-interest debt, refuses a necessary substitution, or spends a windfall on something they would reject if it were called salary.


Lost ticket, lost cash
Before entering a theatre, one person loses a €20 ticket. Another loses €20 in cash before buying the ticket. Should either person spend €20 now to attend?
If preferences, remaining wealth, and all future consequences are the same, the two losses leave total wealth in the same place. Yet replacing the lost ticket often feels like spending €40 on theatre, whereas buying after lost cash feels like a separate decision. The first loss is posted to the entertainment account; the second may be posted to general wealth (Thaler, 1985).
A strong budgeting rule does two things at once: it protects goals before temptation, and it allows deliberate exceptions when the original categories no longer serve the whole plan.


Close and reopen: house money, break-even, and realization
The current gamble is not always evaluated alone. A recent gain or loss can determine which account is open.
In stylized experiments, a prior gain sometimes increases subsequent risk taking: the house-money effect. A loss feels less painful when it can be coded as giving back part of a recent gain. A prior loss can also increase attraction to a gamble that offers a salient chance to recover it: the break-even effect. The pattern depends on whether the outcomes are integrated, how large they are, and whether the new gamble can plausibly close the account near zero (Thaler & Johnson, 1990).
The same logic helps organize the disposition effect: investors are often more willing to sell assets trading above their purchase price than assets trading below it. Selling a winner closes an account with a gain; selling a loser realizes an explicit loss (Shefrin & Statman, 1985). In Odean’s (1998) brokerage data, investors displayed a stronger propensity to realize gains than losses. The winners sold subsequently outperformed the losing positions retained by about 3.41 percentage points in market-adjusted return over the following year, which is inconsistent with the simple claim that retained losers had better prospects.
Taxes, rebalancing, information, liquidity, transaction costs, and differing expectations can all affect which positions are sold. Experimental markets provide more control and have also produced disposition-like behavior (Weber & Camerer, 1998). The practical decision remains forward-looking:

If I did not already own this asset, would I buy this amount today at its current price, given my portfolio, taxes, costs, information, and alternatives?

The purchase price matters for taxes and learning. It should not become a forecast.


Bracket: one decision or a portfolio?
Narrow bracketing evaluates each choice in isolation. Broad bracketing evaluates related choices jointly across time, states, or a portfolio (Read et al., 1999).
Consider a 50–50 gamble that gains €20 or loses €10. Many people reject one play because the possible loss is salient. Now consider one hundred independent repetitions. Expected value accumulates, while diversification makes a loss on the full sequence much less likely. Treating each trial as a separate account can reject every component of an attractive portfolio.
Broad bracketing still requires defensible probabilities, affordable losses, and a realistic account of dependence, leverage, and transaction costs. Repetition cannot make an unaffordable worst case disappear, particularly when exposures share a common shock or funding source.
Evaluation frequency can itself create myopia. Investors who see frequent returns encounter many visible losses even when long-horizon performance is favorable. In Study 3 of Benartzi and Thaler (1999), the median hypothetical allocation to stocks was 40% among staff shown one-year return distributions and 90% among those shown 30-year distributions, with 25 participants in each group. The result illustrates myopic loss aversion: loss aversion combined with narrow, frequent evaluation can make long-run risk look worse.






Figure 19.2: Two studies offer different kinds of evidence about investment decisions. In Odean’s (1998) brokerage sample, winners sold outperformed losing positions retained by about 3.41 percentage points in market-adjusted return over the following year. In Study 3 of Benartzi and Thaler (1999), median hypothetical stock allocations were 40% when staff saw one-year return distributions and 90% when they saw 30-year distributions (25 participants per group).



The two panels of Figure 19.2 separate when an investor closes an account from the horizon over which returns are evaluated. Choose an evaluation horizon that matches the decision horizon and still permits disciplined review.


Bracket for experience: hedonic editing
Reference-dependent value is typically concave for gains and convex for losses. That shape produces hypotheses about how separate outcomes will feel (Thaler, 1999):

Segregate gains. Two positive surprises may feel better when experienced separately than when integrated into one total.
Integrate losses. Combining two losses can hurt less than experiencing each as a separate negative event.
Integrate a small loss with a larger gain. A fee can feel less painful when absorbed into a larger positive outcome—the cancellation effect.
Segregate a small gain from a larger loss. A rebate, reward point, or “silver lining” can preserve a visible positive entry.

Releasing bad news as one opaque bundle may hide material information. Separating trivial positive features can distract from a large loss. Ethical presentation keeps the total recoverable even when experience is staged.
Mental accounting also explains why a gift may be appreciated precisely because the recipient would not buy it from an ordinary budget, and why consumers may pay a per-unit premium for small packages of tempting goods as a self-control device. The category creates permission or restraint. The value is partly in crossing—or protecting—the boundary.


Diversification: when the menu becomes the portfolio
When people allocate across several options at once, they may use a simple 1/n heuristic, also called naive diversification: divide resources approximately equally among the available categories. If a retirement menu offers one stock fund and one bond fund, equal division implies 50% stocks. Adding a second stock fund can shift the same rule to two-thirds stocks even though the investor’s goals and risk tolerance have not changed (Benartzi & Thaler, 2001).
Equal allocation becomes a problem when the architecture of the menu, rather than underlying exposure, determines the portfolio. Company stock is especially easy to misclassify as a separate account even though employment income and investment value may already depend on the same firm.
Ask about underlying risks, not the number of labels. Ten funds can still hold the same assets.
Choice bracketing also affects variety outside finance. Choosing next week’s snacks all at once can yield more variety than choosing a snack separately before each occasion. Read and Loewenstein (1995) examined this diversification bias in consumption choices: a combined decision can make repeated favorites look excessively repetitive, even when time between consumption would restore their appeal. This differs from splitting money equally across funds. One concerns predicted variety needs over time; the other concerns allocation across a menu. Variety and equal allocation can both be reasonable, so compare the resulting pattern with actual enjoyment or underlying exposure before calling it an error.


Daily income targets
A high-wage day makes each extra hour more rewarding, but it also brings a daily earnings target within reach sooner. Those comparisons can point toward different stopping times. The driver needs to decide whether another hour’s income is worth the leisure it displaces.
New York taxi-driver data produced a famous claim: drivers appeared to stop sooner on high-wage days and work longer on low-wage days, as if a daily income target defined the account (Camerer et al., 1997). Later analyses found that conclusions depend on reference-point specification, changing opportunities, driver experience, and empirical method (Farber, 2005, 2008; Crawford & Meng, 2011).
This debate makes daily income targets a useful test case for distinguishing reference dependence from responses to changing work opportunities.

title: 19  Mental Accounting
text:
A mental-accounting audit

A budget helps protect money for a purpose, yet the same boundary can make a worthwhile purchase seem unaffordable while funds sit elsewhere. The audit needs to preserve the useful protection and expose the costly restriction. Check whose goal the boundary serves, whether total cost and alternatives remain visible, and whether the chooser can revise it. A saving rule should protect a goal the household endorses; a seller benefits from a misleading boundary when it hides a cost or a feasible substitute. Use Table 19.2 to reconstruct the decision twice, comparing the existing account with the alternatives and future costs that its boundary may hide:



Table 19.2: A two-representation audit for mental accounts










Audit step
Narrow representation
Broader test




Label
What is this money called?
Would another source label change the choice?


Reference
Compared with what does it feel like a gain or loss?
Is that comparison relevant to future value?


Boundary
Which budget or transaction contains it?
What substitutes and opportunity costs sit outside?


Time
When did the account open, and when will it close?
Which costs are sunk; which consequences remain?


Portfolio
Is this one gamble, purchase, or asset?
What is the combined exposure across choices?


Function
What goal does the boundary protect?
Could a more flexible rule protect it at lower cost?






Worked application: savings beside expensive debt.
A household keeps €30,000 in a “do not touch” savings account while revolving €20,000 on a high-interest credit card. The narrow labels are safety and ordinary spending. The broad balance sheet reveals simultaneous lending at a low rate and borrowing at a high rate.
But simply ordering the household to use all savings may destroy the emergency buffer that prevents future expensive borrowing. A better redesign protects the function rather than the rigid label: define a minimum emergency reserve, use excess cash against high-cost debt, automate repayment, and set a rule for rebuilding the buffer. The goal is not perfect fungibility. It is an account system whose boundaries serve the household rather than the reverse.
Worked application: a project in the red.
A team has spent two years on a product that has missed its adoption targets. Ask whether the team would acquire the project today, in its current state, for the remaining budget. Retain reusable assets and future learning in that comparison; remove spending that cannot be recovered. Then name the adoption milestone that would justify the next tranche and the finding that would stop it.

title: 19  Mental Accounting
text:
Practice Lab
Choose a subscription, retirement contribution, household budget, or project that is currently “in the red.” Produce two decision sheets: one using the existing account boundaries and one using total future consequences across the relevant portfolio. On the second sheet, remove unrecoverable expenditure, retain information or switching costs that still affect the future, state the best feasible alternative, and define the milestone that would continue or close the account.

title: 19  Mental Accounting
text:
Take it forward
Would you still make the twenty-minute trip if the €6 saving came from a different purchase? Asking that question reveals the account boundary without forcing you to abandon every budget. Keep the boundaries that protect a worthwhile goal, and reopen those that make the same resources seem unavailable for a better use.
Keeping money in a savings account can protect a future goal, but spending it today may become more attractive when an immediate need or temptation appears. Intertemporal Decision Making examines how timing changes that comparison and why a plan made in advance may be revised when action is due.

title: 20  Intertemporal Decision Making
text:
Learning goals
Why Later Loses to Now
Choose between €100 today and €120 in one month. Now choose between €100 in twelve months and €120 in thirteen months.
Many people are more willing to wait in the second choice than in the first. Yet both require waiting one additional month for the same additional €20. If the distant choice later reverses when the smaller reward becomes immediate, the person has changed a plan as the dates approached.1
Consider a manager who decides on Friday to discuss a recurring problem with a colleague on Monday. On Monday, the discomfort is immediate and the improvement in their working relationship remains uncertain. Postponing until Tuesday feels reasonable, just as it did the week before. What would help the manager carry out the conversation—and how would the answer differ if waiting really allowed better information or a calmer setting?

title: 20  Intertemporal Decision Making
text:
Use discounted utility and present bias to diagnose preference reversal without reducing it to weak willpower.
Separate time preference from liquidity, trust, uncertainty, utility curvature, and task representation.
Build a credible bridge from a present action to a delayed benefit using the MOST audit.

title: 20  Intertemporal Decision Making
text:
The benchmark: value across time
The discounted-utility model represents a stream of outcomes by reducing the present weight of outcomes that arrive later (Samuelson, 1937). In its simple exponential form, each additional period of delay reduces the weight by the same proportion.
With preferences and relevant circumstances held fixed, exponential discounting preserves the relative ranking of two future outcomes as time passes. If €120 in thirteen months is preferred to €100 in twelve months, moving both rewards eleven months closer should not reverse the preference.
The benchmark is useful even when it is not descriptively accurate. It forces a decision-maker to state the outcome stream, time horizon, assumptions, and trade-off between present and future. It also separates two ideas that ordinary language blends:

Utility curvature: an additional €100 may matter less to a wealthy person than to someone who cannot pay rent.
Time weighting: the same valued outcome may receive less weight because it arrives later.

Observed choices usually identify neither component cleanly. A person choosing money today may be impatient, cash-constrained, worried that the promise will not be honored, or facing an urgent need whose marginal value is high. Frederick, Loewenstein, and O’Donoghue (2002) therefore warn against treating every implied discount rate as pure time preference.
crumbs: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being

title: 20  Intertemporal Decision Making
section: Why delay changes more than mathematical value
text:
Why delay changes more than mathematical value

Present bias and preference reversal
Exponential discounting treats each added period proportionally. Human choices often display declining impatience: the difference between now and soon feels larger than an equal difference between two distant dates. Hyperbolic models capture this pattern by making the implied discount rate fall with delay (Ainslie, 1975). Quasi-hyperbolic models simplify it into a special penalty for anything not immediate, followed by more regular discounting across later periods (Laibson, 1997).






Figure 20.1: Three discount models illustrate different implications. With linear utility, the quasi-hyperbolic example prefers €120 in thirteen months when viewed today but reverses to €100 when that reward becomes immediate; exponential discounting keeps the relative ranking stable. The optional analysis specifies the plotted functions and parameters.



The worked example in Figure 20.1 shows dynamic inconsistency: a plan that looks best from a distance can lose when temptation or effort becomes immediate. O’Donoghue and Rabin (1999) show how present bias can produce two familiar failures:

procrastination: an action has an immediate cost and delayed benefit, so the person repeatedly postpones it;
premature indulgence: an action has an immediate reward and delayed cost, so the person repeatedly brings it forward.

The manager’s postponed conversation contains both sides: delaying avoids discomfort now while moving the unresolved problem into the future.







NoteMathematical analysis: discounted utility and the plotted models





The discounted-utility model represents a stream of outcomes by reducing the present weight of outcomes that arrive later (Samuelson, 1937). In a simple exponential form,
\[
U = \sum_{t=0}^{T} \delta^t u(c_t), \qquad 0 < \delta \leq 1.
\]
Here, \(u(c_t)\) is the utility of consumption or another outcome at time \(t\), and \(\delta\) is the weight placed on each additional period of delay.
Three discount functions illustrate different implications: exponential \(D(t)=0.95^t\), hyperbolic \(D(t)=1/(1+0.15t)\), and quasi-hyperbolic \(D(0)=1\) and \(D(t>0)=0.70(0.95^t)\). With linear utility, the quasi-hyperbolic example prefers €120 in thirteen months when viewed today but reverses to €100 when that reward becomes immediate; exponential discounting keeps the relative ranking stable.
These are illustrative functions.




A person can also differ in awareness. A sophisticated present-biased chooser anticipates future reversal and seeks a commitment device. A naïve chooser expects future intentions to survive unchanged. A partly sophisticated chooser knows there is a problem but underestimates its size.
Commitment devices alter future options or make deviation costly before the tempting state arrives. A voluntary deposit contract is one example; its benefits and limits are examined below.


Credibility, attention, and imagination






Figure 20.2: Intertemporal choice can be shaped by immediate salience, uncertainty, weak future imagery, friction, and changing states.



Waiting is rarely just empty time. Figure 20.2 traces how uncertainty, weak future imagery, and friction can obstruct the path to a delayed benefit. The distinctions in Table 20.1 broaden the diagnosis to include urgent needs, subjective time, and the emotions experienced while waiting:



Table 20.1: Delay enters the decision through several mechanisms










Mechanism
Diagnostic question
Example




Immediate salience
Which outcome can be felt or imagined now?
The taste of dessert competes with an abstract health benefit.


Uncertainty
Will the later outcome arrive, and can the promise be trusted?
An unstable employer promises a future bonus.


Liquidity and need
What urgent constraint changes marginal value today?
Cash now prevents a late fee or missed meal.


Subjective time
How long does the interval feel?
“In six months” feels different from a calendar date.


Future-self continuity
Does the later beneficiary feel like me?
Retirement saving can feel like giving money to a stranger.


Anticipatory emotion
Is waiting filled with savoring, dread, anxiety, or relief?
Delaying a holiday can create pleasure; delaying a medical result can create dread.






The diagnosis changes the intervention. A future-self exercise cannot repair an institution’s broken promises, and advice about patience cannot pay an overdue bill.


Amount, sign, wording, search, and domain
There is no single discount rate that travels unchanged across every choice. Several recurring patterns show that time preferences are partly constructed.
Before trying to make someone more patient, check whether the way the options are described changes the comparison. The classroom mnemonic MOST in Table 20.2 keeps four option attributes visible, so that a change in wording or scale is not mistaken for a change in patience:



Table 20.2: MOST: four attributes that shift apparent discounting











Letter
Attribute
Recurring pattern
Diagnostic




M
Magnitude
Larger outcomes are often discounted less steeply
Does a fixed cost of waiting matter more for a small reward?


O
Opportunity cost
A choice hides what is received at the other date
Are both outcome streams, including zeros, visible?


S
Sign
Delayed gains and losses are not mirror images
Do dread, savoring, or a reference point change the comparison?


T
Time frame
Dates and delays create different representations
Does the wording make waiting or the future event salient?






Larger outcomes often receive more patience.
People commonly discount small rewards more steeply than large rewards—the magnitude effect (Thaler, 1981). Someone who refuses to wait for €10 may wait for €10,000 even when the proportional return is the same. Larger stakes can justify fixed waiting costs, attract more attention, or invite more deliberate comparison.
Gains and losses are not temporal mirror images.
Delayed gains are often discounted differently from delayed losses. People may be impatient to receive a gain yet willing to postpone a payment. But waiting for a negative outcome can also generate dread, making sooner resolution preferable. The sign effect therefore depends on framing, anticipation, and domain (Loewenstein & Prelec, 1992; Weber et al., 2007).
Dates and delays create different representations.
“In six months” emphasizes waiting. “On February 12” locates an event in a calendar and may make it more concrete. Read and colleagues (2005) found lower discounting when outcomes were described with dates rather than delays. A calendar date can make the future event easier to imagine.
The invisible zero can be made visible.
The choice “€100 today or €120 in a month” hides two complete outcome streams. The fuller representation in Figure 20.3 makes the forgone payment at each date explicit:

€100 today and €0 in one month, or
€0 today and €120 in one month.

Making both zeros explicit increased selection of delayed rewards in the hidden-zero studies (Magen et al., 2008). The mechanism connects directly to opportunity-cost neglect: the immediate reward is not free; it replaces a later reward.






Figure 20.3: The abbreviated and complete-stream displays contain the same payoffs. Writing the otherwise hidden zeros makes the forgone outcome at each date explicit and can redirect attention to opportunity cost.



The search path can construct patience.
An intertemporal option has at least two attributes: amount and time. A person can search within an option, integrating “€100 now” before considering “€120 later.” Or the person can search across an attribute, comparing €100 with €120 and then now with one month. These paths make different contrasts salient.
Reeck, Wall, and Johnson (2017) traced information search and identified substantial heterogeneity in these strategies. Comparative searchers—who moved across amounts or across times—made more patient choices than integrative searchers. In a second experiment, the researchers made one search path slightly harder, causally shifting both search and choice. Most participants reported no awareness that the manipulation had changed their behavior.
The finding shows that a measured “discount rate” can partly reflect how information was searched. Inspect both the complete packages and the separate amount and time differences; disagreement between them is a reason to examine the representation.
Money, health, environment, effort, and relationships differ.
Money is tradable and often measurable. Health, pain, environmental quality, effort, and social trust are not interchangeable bank balances. People may discount across domains differently because uncertainty, irreversibility, emotion, identity, and moral meaning differ (Chapman, 1996; Hardisty & Weber, 2009).
A decision about a delayed health benefit may involve side effects now, uncertain benefit later, caregiving burden, trust in the institution, or values the experiment did not measure.


What did the patience task identify?
A multiple price list seems to turn patience into a number: at which row does a person switch from a smaller-sooner to a larger-later amount? But choosing the earlier payment could also keep an urgent bill paid or avoid a promise the person distrusts. Treating either constraint as impatience would point to the wrong remedy. The design responses in Table 20.3 show what must be measured or held comparable before attributing the observed choice to time preference.



Table 20.3: A discount-rate estimate combines preferences, beliefs, constraints, and task design










Possible component
How it can resemble impatience
Design response




Utility curvature
€200 may be worth less than twice €100
Jointly estimate or independently measure curvature


Payment risk
A later promise may be less credible
Equalize and verify payment reliability


Liquidity
Immediate cash may prevent a costly shortfall
Measure constraints; do not call urgent need a preference


Transaction costs
Waiting may require effort, return visits, or account access
Match procedures and delivery costs


Inflation and beliefs
The later amount may buy less
Elicit expected purchasing power and macro conditions


Task representation
Defaults, dates, search order, and hidden zeros change attention
Vary representation and report sensitivity






Incentive-compatible payment can improve a task, but it does not solve every identification problem. Cross-domain comparisons require matched procedures and explicit assumptions. A reported association between patience and education, saving, or health is not by itself evidence that changing one stable discount parameter will change those outcomes.
