title: 23  Strategic Interdependence
text:
Learning goals
The Best Move Depends on Other Minds
You start chatting with someone in the queue at a concert and find that the two of you really click. You decide to watch the performance together. Once inside, you lose each other in the crowd before you have exchanged phone numbers.
You could head toward the stage, return to the entrance, or wait where you last saw them. A good spot near the stage would let you enjoy the music, but it will not help you find each other if they have gone back to the entrance.
The other person faces the same problem. Where you should go depends on where you expect them to go—and on where they expect to find you.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 23  Strategic Interdependence
text:
Explain strategic interdependence through three situations in which the outcome depends on other people’s choices.
Distinguish personal preferences from expectations about others, including what they expect you to do.
Use equilibrium to describe choices that fit together, while recognizing why it may not predict actual play.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 23  Strategic Interdependence
text:
Finding each other
Returning to the main entrance might seem promising because you both came through it. You know the other person has seen it, and they know you have too. That shared experience gives you a reason to expect the same destination, even though you know little about each other’s habits or preferences.
But the stage may seem more obvious to them: that is where you intended to watch the performance together. A place can make sense to each of you for different reasons without bringing you together. Waiting matters as well. If one person arrives just after the other leaves to search elsewhere, choosing the same destination will still fail.
The other person is also trying to work out what you will do. They might return to the entrance because they expect you to see it as an obvious place to wait. Your uncertainty concerns someone who is responding to their own uncertainty about you. The next chapter examines how a shared experience, a landmark, or a convention can help people settle on the same answer.
Game theory calls the value of an outcome to a player a payoff. Here, the value of choosing a place depends partly on whether the other person goes there too. The next exercise separates personal preference from this dependence on another person’s choice more sharply.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 23  Strategic Interdependence
section: Choosing a face: preference or prediction?
text:
Choosing a face: preference or prediction?
Imagine a classroom exercise in which everyone receives the same set of labeled portraits. First, each participant selects the face they personally find most attractive. There is no correct answer and no reward for matching anyone else.
Now the instructor changes the rule. Participants are paired, and both receive a reward if they select the same face. Different selections earn nothing. Each chooses again without seeing the partner’s answer. How would this rule change what you consider when choosing?
Nothing about the faces has changed, but a different feature of them now matters: which one the other participant is likely to select. You might keep your original choice because you expect them to share your preference. You might instead choose a face you like less because it seems more widely appealing or distinctive. Either decision can be sensible under the new rule.
If matching earns 15 units, a face’s expected reward depends on how likely the partner is to select it. For a player concerned only with that reward, the best response is to choose a face with the highest chance of a match. Your own ranking supplies possible evidence about their choice, but it no longer directly determines the monetary payoff.
The two tasks separate what I prefer from what I expect someone else to choose. A change of answer need not mean your taste changed or that you gave in to social pressure. The incentive changed. Equally, an unchanged answer does not establish that you ignored the incentive: preference and prediction may happen to point to the same face.







NoteMathematical analysis: the expected reward from matching





If your reward is 15 units, its expected value from selecting face \(j\) is
\[
15\times\Pr(\text{the other person selects face }j).
\]
Because every successful match pays the same amount, maximizing the expected reward means maximizing the chance of a match.





The other person is predicting too
The second participant is also paid to match. They may choose what they think you expect them to select. This makes a face that is commonly recognized as striking potentially useful even when neither person ranks it first privately. Shared expectations can converge on a choice that would not win a private-preference poll.
Keynes (1936, Chapter 12) used a newspaper beauty contest to illustrate a related difficulty in investing: anticipating others’ judgments can matter alongside judging an asset’s underlying value. His contest had different rules from this pair-matching exercise, but the distinction transfers. A trader expecting to resell soon must consider what the next buyer will pay, as Markets, Mispricing, and Bubbles examines. That concern can influence trading without proving that every price movement reflects imitation or that fundamentals have ceased to matter.
To investigate a change of answer in the face task, record both the person’s private ranking and their prediction of the other participant’s selection. Observing the final choice alone cannot tell us whether they anticipated shared tastes, a salient face, or a convention learned from an earlier round.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 23  Strategic Interdependence
section: The guessing game: how far will others reason?
text:
The guessing game: how far will others reason?
In a group of at least three people, everyone chooses a real number from 0 to 100. The person closest to two-thirds of the group’s mean wins a fixed prize, shared equally in a tie. Choose your number before continuing.
The face task rewarded matching another person’s answer. Here the target itself depends on everyone’s answers, including yours. If the mean were 45, the target would be 30; if it were 30, the target would be 20. A number becomes a good choice through its relation to what the group chooses.
One starting guess is that people will choose roughly at random across the range, giving an expected mean of 50. Two-thirds of that is about 33. But the other players can see the same rule. If you expect them to take that step, a number around 22 becomes attractive. If you expect them to anticipate that step too, you may aim near 15.
These numbers approximate where a player might aim. Your own number influences the mean, and winning depends on how close the other numbers are to the target. Reasoning from an expected average becomes more useful in a large group, where your own effect on that average is small.

Does thinking further always help?
Suppose most of the others stop around 33. A choice near 22 may beat them, while taking several more steps toward zero could leave you far from the target. Understanding the rule is useful, but winning also requires judging how the other people will use it.
Nagel’s (1995) guessing-game experiments found behavior consistent with limited steps of reasoning, rather than everyone following the argument all the way down to zero. Level-k models describe such steps (Nagel, 1995; Stahl & Wilson, 1995). Level 0 supplies a starting rule, such as random choice; level 1 responds to that rule; level 2 responds to level 1. The familiar 50-to-33-to-22 sequence illustrates the idea.
The starting assumption matters as much as the number of steps. A sophisticated player may choose a relatively high number because they expect others to reason little. A low number is therefore not a direct measure of intelligence or strategic competence.
The poisoned-goblet scene from The Princess Bride makes this vulnerability memorable: each additional “I think that you think” rests on assumptions about the opponent. More reasoning cannot rescue a mistaken premise merely by extending it.


Different reasoning can produce the same choice
A choice of 22 could reflect two steps from a random anchor. It could also come from remembering a previous classroom game, predicting a mean of 33 for another reason, or copying a familiar answer. Behavioral game theory compares such explanations rather than assigning a reasoning type from one number (Camerer, 2003; Crawford et al., 2013).
A further possibility is that players expect different people to reason differently. Cognitive hierarchy models allow a mixture of reasoning depths rather than assuming everyone is exactly one level below the player (Camerer et al., 2004). The Research Lens at the end of the chapter develops this model and the evidence across participant groups.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 23  Strategic Interdependence
text:
What changes with experience?
After several rounds, guessing-game choices often move downward. A player who saw a low group mean may revise their expectation; another may repeat a number that nearly won. Someone else may finally understand the rule. These routes can produce similar movement while implying different lessons about the next group.
Belief learning updates expectations about others. Reinforcement learning increases the tendency to repeat an action after a favorable outcome. Imitation copies another player’s action. To distinguish them, vary the feedback: show the distribution of choices, show only the player’s own earnings, or show which action won. Record expectations before each round as well as choices afterward.
A useful account should explain why the specified feedback changes behavior. Simply describing a falling mean as “greater rationality” leaves that explanation unfinished. Change in the prevalence of strategies across a population is a further question, developed in Chapter 25’s research lens.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 23  Strategic Interdependence
text:
When do choices fit together?
The three situations have raised the same difficulty in different forms: you are deciding while other people are deciding too. Is there a combination of choices at which nobody would gain by changing their own choice alone?
A Nash equilibrium is such a combination: each player’s strategy is a best response to the others (Nash, 1950). A best response gives the highest payoff against the other players’ specified strategies. Equilibrium describes how the choices fit together; it does not require that the players reached them through a particular thought process.
In the meeting problem, suppose both people choose an accessible place and time where they can meet. Switching elsewhere alone would defeat their purpose. Many meeting arrangements could have this property, so identifying an equilibrium does not yet explain which one you and your new acquaintance will select. Likewise, several matching faces could satisfy the reward rule in the second exercise.
The guessing game has a different endpoint. Under its specified rules, the unique Nash equilibrium is for everyone to choose zero (Nagel, 1995). If everyone else chooses zero, choosing zero shares the prize. Choosing a positive number raises the mean, but in a group of at least three it leaves the zero-choosers closer to the resulting target, so the deviation loses.
The ladder in Figure 23.1 connects a few steps of reasoning with that endpoint. It separates where the argument can lead from where a particular group is likely to stop.






Figure 23.1: An illustrative level-k ladder for the two-thirds guessing game starts from a random-choice anchor with mean 50, then aims near 33, 22, and 15. These are large-group approximations; the game’s equilibrium is 0.



Choosing zero by yourself does not put the group in equilibrium. If others choose positive numbers, zero can lose. Your decision still depends on what you have reason to expect from these players. Coordination and Focal Points introduces payoff matrices and develops equilibrium analysis from this starting point.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 23  Strategic Interdependence
section: Application: anticipate the response before committing
text:
Application: anticipate the response before committing
A manager may propose a new reporting system because it improves their team’s work. Other departments may delay adoption because the system is useful only if everyone joins, because they bear more of the transition cost, or because they prefer to keep information private. The manager’s own benefits cannot establish how those departments will respond.
Start by identifying what each person can do and how combinations of actions affect their payoffs. Separate your own preference from your prediction of theirs. Then ask what they know about your plan and what response they expect if they hesitate. A useful prediction identifies what could change another person’s choice.

Include the people affected by the arrangement, even if they cannot choose within it. An agreement between competitors can harm customers; a shared convention can exclude newcomers. A successful strategy for the people at the table may impose costs on others whose interests the model leaves out.
For an exercise in model construction, watch the strategic-interdependence scene from A Beautiful Mind. List the participants’ options, including those of the people the characters discuss, and check whether anyone could gain by departing from the proposed arrangement.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 23  Strategic Interdependence
text:
Practice Lab
Revisit the three examples in order. For the meeting problem, pair people who know little about one another and ask them to imagine being separated at a crowded event. Have each choose a place to wait independently, then compare the cues each expected the other to recognize. For the face task, give everyone the same set of labeled portraits, then compare private rankings with rewarded matching choices. For the guessing game, record an initial choice and prediction of the mean, then play five rounds with feedback.
Before revealing each result, ask participants what they expect others to do and why. Afterward, identify one change in behavior and develop two possible explanations. Propose a change in information or incentives that would make those explanations predict different choices. Knowing an equilibrium answer is less informative than being able to explain when it would help predict the people actually playing.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 23  Strategic Interdependence
text:
Take it forward
The meeting problem required anticipating where your new acquaintance would go to look for you. The face task separated private taste from rewarded prediction, and the guessing game made you examine where other people’s reasoning might stop. In each case, evaluating your own choice required a view of someone else’s action.
Before committing to a plan, identify the response you are counting on and what gives you reason to expect it. The next chapter makes that dependence visible in payoff matrices, then asks why people can struggle to coordinate even when they understand what would work.







NoteResearch Lens: cognitive hierarchy and the evidence





In cognitive hierarchy, a step-\(k\) thinker best responds to a distribution of steps \(0\) through \(k-1\). Camerer, Ho, and Chong (2004) model the population frequency of step \(h\) with a Poisson distribution,
\[
f(h)=\frac{e^{-\tau}\tau^h}{h!},
\]
and renormalize the distribution over the lower steps the player believes exist. The parameter \(\tau\) controls the average number of steps. The authors report that a value around 1.5 fits behavior across many games, although fitted values differ by task and participant pool.
Table 23.1 reproduces selected guessing-game results from their Table II. The sample sizes count participants across the reported groups. The fitted \(\tau\) values in this table were chosen to match the observed mean.

The mean was 37.9 among the chief executives and 19.1 among the game theorists, but these are comparisons across settings and selected participant pools. Substantial variation remains within pools, and alternative beliefs can produce the same number. Model evaluation should compare predictions against new choices or against experimental changes on which rival explanations disagree.
The zero endpoint in the guessing game can also be approached through iterated elimination of weakly dominated high choices. The target cannot exceed \(66\frac{2}{3}\); after excluding choices above that bound, the next upper bound is \(44\frac{4}{9}\), then \(29\frac{17}{27}\), and so on toward zero (Nagel, 1995). A weakly dominated choice never yields more than an alternative against the others’ possible choices and yields less in at least some cases. This is a stronger assumption about what players rule out than simply saying that they want to win. Chapter 24 develops the comparison of strategies.
Coricelli and Nagel (2009) compared play against human and computer opponents using behavioral and neural measures. Their findings associate strategic reasoning with differences in processing when the opponent changes. Such evidence can help discriminate between accounts.










NoteResearch Lens: the €50 auction and competitive escalation





In Shubik’s dollar-auction game, the highest bidder wins the prize, but the second-highest bidder must also pay their final bid (Shubik, 1971). Early entry looks attractive. Once two people are competing, another small bid can appear cheaper than accepting a certain loss. Each expects that the next bid may make the rival quit. If both reason this way, bids can exceed the prize.
The game makes it possible to examine competition neglect, when bidders enter without accounting for rivals’ persistence, and escalation of commitment, when earlier choices make stopping difficult (Staw, 1976). A further bid can also be a forward-looking response to a belief that the rival will stop. Bidding beyond the prize therefore does not by itself identify either psychological failure.
Competitive acquisition creates a related trap. When bidders have noisy estimates of a common value, winning can be bad news: the winner may simply be the most optimistic bidder (Bazerman & Samuelson, 1983). This winner’s-curse problem concerns what winning reveals about the estimate, whereas the dollar auction concerns a rule requiring the runner-up to pay. Before entering, examine the rules and likely competitors, separate private synergies from common value, and set a reservation price based on future benefits and costs.









NoteApplied module: market rules change the strategic game





Buyers and sellers can stand to gain from trade yet fail to find acceptable terms. Compare Table 23.2: each rule changes who can act, what they observe, and how a price forms.



Table 23.2: Market institutions alter information, timing, and bargaining power










Institution
Basic rule
Strategic consequence to inspect




Continuous double auction
Buyers and sellers submit and accept bids and asks during the trading period.
Rapid feedback can aid price discovery; timing and order visibility affect bargaining.


Posted-offer market
Sellers post take-it-or-leave-it prices and buyers choose among them.
Search and substitutability affect sellers’ pricing power.


Call market
Orders are pooled and matched at a scheduled clearing time.
Pooling reduces continuous speed competition; clearing and rationing rules determine trades.






A fish-market activity can assign private buyer values and seller costs, then vary supply across rounds, extending the experimental-market tradition of Smith (1962). Run the same underlying values under different trading rules. Compare prices, quantity, total surplus, and its division between buyers and sellers. Hold the economic environment as constant as possible so that differences can be traced to the rules under study.

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
text:
Learning goals
Finding a Way to Act Together
Two departments need to exchange reports. Each has tested a different system, and each can explain why its preferred system works better. Department A values integration with its existing software; Department B values flexibility. Both agree that adopting incompatible systems would waste time and create errors.
The deadline approaches, but neither commits. A manager calls the delay resistance to change. Yet accepting the other department’s preferred system would solve only part of the problem: someone must still arrange training, move the records, and ensure that both departments switch at the same time. A department can reasonably support the shared plan while hesitating to act first.
The disagreement contains several questions. Which standard should they use? Can each rely on the other to adopt it? Who should bear the transition costs? These questions require different answers, even though all three can look like a failure to cooperate.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
text:
Construct and read a payoff matrix, then identify best responses and pure- and mixed-strategy equilibria.
Distinguish focality, payoff dominance, and risk dominance as explanations for which coordinated outcome people pursue.
Diagnose whether a coordination problem requires a focal point, common knowledge, credible assurance, or an agreed division of benefits and responsibilities.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
text:
Representing the interaction
The departments’ arguments mix the quality of a system with the benefits of compatibility and the costs of changing. A game-theoretic model separates these features so that we can inspect how each department’s choice depends on the other’s. Begin with a simpler version of the meeting problem, where the shared objective is easier to represent.
A game is a model that specifies the players, their possible actions, and how their choices jointly determine payoffs. Five features make the meeting model explicit:

Players: the two people trying to meet.
Actions: the places and times each can choose.
Payoffs: how each person values meeting or failing to meet.
Information: what each knows about the venue, the other person, and the situation.
Timing: each chooses where to go before learning the other’s destination.

An action is a particular move. A strategy is a complete plan for what to do at every point where a player might have to choose. In a one-move meeting game, choosing a place and time specifies the whole strategy. If messages or later decisions were allowed, a strategy would also specify how to respond to them.
Safety, time, fairness, and the relationship can all affect how someone values an outcome. Allowing communication or letting one person observe the other’s choice changes the game even if the possible destinations stay the same.

Reading a payoff matrix
To isolate the choice of destination, suppose each of you goes to either the main entrance or the information desk and waits there. Assume that you find each other if you choose the same place, and set aside differences in walking distance or the view of the performance. Represent a successful meeting with 50 illustrative payoff units for each person and a failed meeting with zero. The payoff matrix in Table 24.1 records what each receives under every combination of choices.



Table 24.1: A simplified meeting game; your payoff appears first





Your choice \ Other person’s choice
Entrance
Information desk




Entrance
50, 50
0, 0


Information desk
0, 0
50, 50






Read the rows as your actions and the columns as the other person’s actions. Within each cell, your payoff comes first and theirs second. If you choose the entrance and they choose the information desk, the relevant cell is the top-right one: both receive zero. The two diagonal cells show the successful meetings.


Best responses and beliefs
A best response gives a player the highest payoff against specified choices by the others. If the other person chooses the entrance, compare your first payoff in that column: choosing the entrance gives 50, while the information desk gives zero. Your best response is the entrance. If they choose the information desk, your best response changes to the information desk.
Of course, you cannot see which column will apply when you make your choice. Suppose you assign a 70% chance to the other person choosing the entrance. Weighting the reward of 50 by each matching probability gives an expected payoff of 35 at the entrance, compared with 15 at the information desk. Choosing the entrance is then the best response to that belief, provided you maximize the expected value of the displayed payoffs.


Mutual best responses: checking equilibrium
To check a Nash equilibrium, examine a whole combination of strategies and ask whether anyone would gain by changing their own strategy alone (Nash, 1950). Both choosing the entrance passes this test: neither person gains by going alone to the information desk. Both choosing the information desk passes it too. Choosing different places fails because either person could improve their payoff by joining the other.
These choices are pure strategies, which specify a definite action at each decision point. A mixed strategy assigns probabilities to pure strategies. In this one-move game, that means randomizing between destinations. Independent 50–50 randomization by both players is also an equilibrium in this particular symmetric matrix: either destination offers an expected payoff of 25 against the other’s randomization, so neither player can improve it by changing their own mix. Yet they meet only half the time on average.
The meeting game therefore has two pure-strategy equilibria and a mixed-strategy equilibrium. Finding them does not tell the people where to go, and the mixed equilibrium does not deliver the highest available joint payoff. We still need to explain which expectations can bring their actions together.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
text:
Coordination depends on shared expectations

The departments face the same selection problem. Suppose either common standard is preferable to incompatible systems, even though each department has a favorite. Both adopting A and both adopting B are then Nash equilibria: at either matched outcome, one department would lose by switching alone. The meeting matrix’s two successful destinations become two compatible standards.
If A expects B to adopt standard A, choosing A makes sense. If both expect standard B, their choices can sustain that outcome instead. Everyone can respond sensibly to what they expect and still end up at a convention that nobody selected through a joint comparison of the alternatives.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
section: When everyone knows—but no one knows that everyone knows
text:
When everyone knows—but no one knows that everyone knows
Knowing which outcome would be good is only the beginning. In a coordination problem, what matters is also what you know about what other people know.
In The Emperor’s New Clothes, the emperor walks before a crowd wearing nothing. Read as a parable about coordination, each observer can see what is happening, yet sees everyone else behaving as if the magnificent clothes were real. Speaking up is risky: perhaps others will defend the emperor, leaving the person who objects exposed as the fool.
Then a child says aloud what people could already see: the emperor is wearing no clothes.
The announcement adds little information about the emperor. It changes what observers can infer about one another. Each hears the statement in front of the crowd and can recognize that others heard it too. What had been privately perceived becomes publicly acknowledged. Pinker, Nowak, and Lee (2008) use the story to illustrate common knowledge: communication can change what people know about one another’s knowledge even when it adds little to their knowledge of the world.
The distinction builds through the levels in Table 24.2. Here X stands for a fact.



Table 24.2: Knowing a fact and knowing that others know it are different informational conditions










State of knowledge
What it means
What remains uncertain about others’ knowledge of X?




Private knowledge
I know X.
Do you know X?


Mutual knowledge1
Everyone knows X.
Does everyone know that everyone knows X?


Common knowledge
Everyone knows X, everyone knows that everyone knows X, and so on through every higher level.
No further uncertainty within this hierarchy.






This hierarchy is central to the accounts of convention and common knowledge developed by Lewis (1969) and Aumann (1976). In ordinary conversation, information known by many people is sometimes called public knowledge. For strategic reasoning, distinguish that wide distribution from a genuinely public signal: its reception and meaning are themselves commonly recognized. Under those idealized conditions, a truthful public announcement can generate common knowledge. Giving everyone the same information separately need not.
Consider two ways to change the departments’ reporting system. The manager could email each department separately: We will switch to System A on Monday. Both may read exactly the same plan. Yet Department A may wonder whether B received it, whether B understood the date in the same way, or whether B knows that A has received it.
Alternatively, the manager could announce the decision in a joint meeting, display the migration schedule, and have both teams visibly acknowledge their roles. The plan is identical. What changes is each side’s evidence about what the other has heard and expects. Similarly, seeing smoke provides information about a possible fire; a recognizable building-wide alarm also gives occupants reason to believe that others have been alerted. Neither example guarantees that everybody understands or acts as intended.






NoteThe information may be old; the social knowledge is new



The child does not make the emperor naked. The joint meeting does not make System A technically better. What changes is what each person can infer about other people’s knowledge and expectations.
Communication can therefore do two jobs: tell us something about the world and tell us what others know about the world.


These higher-order beliefs matter because my best action depends on yours, while your action may depend on what you expect me to do. Predicting your choice can therefore require reasoning about your prediction of mine. Common knowledge specifies an idealized information structure in which the chain of Does she know that I know that she knows? is settled for a particular fact. It does not by itself select an equilibrium or ensure that people keep an agreement.

Unreliable communication and the electronic-mail game
Rubinstein’s (1989) electronic-mail game shows why unreliable communication complicates coordination. One player learns that circumstances have changed and sends a message to the other. Receipt triggers an automatic confirmation, which triggers another confirmation, and so on. Each message has a small chance of failing, ending the exchange.
Many successful messages establish many levels of I know that you know that I know. Yet no finite chain makes the changed circumstances common knowledge: the sender cannot know whether the last message arrived. Under the model’s payoff and communication assumptions, even a long exchange fails to recover the coordinated switch supported when the changed circumstances are common knowledge.
This is a result about a particular game, not a claim that people must complete infinite reasoning before acting. People routinely coordinate through conventions, trust, and imperfect signals. The lesson is that uncertainty about what others know can matter greatly when acting together is valuable and acting alone is costly. For the departments, learning that System A is good differs from learning that the other team knows the plan and expects a joint switch.


Why public events can have disproportionate effects
Chwe (2001) argues that one function of public rituals, ceremonies, and broadcasts is to generate common knowledge. Their strategic importance can come from people recognizing that others are attending to the same message. The same words delivered privately to a thousand people and before a thousand mutually visible participants can therefore have different consequences.
An all-hands meeting can serve this function inside an organization. Employees hear the new standard and see colleagues acknowledge it. But audience size alone does not establish common knowledge. People may miss the message, interpret it differently, or doubt whether others understood it. Even common knowledge of the announcement leaves open whether colleagues will follow it.
The diagnostic question is practical: Do people merely know the plan, or do they have reason to believe that others know it and expect a joint response? Sending another explanation may leave this gap untouched. A shared occasion can help make expectations visible.
This also prepares the logic of focal points. A salient answer helps when I expect it to attract your attention and expect you to recognize its salience to me. Shared history and conventions can align these expectations even without a new announcement.

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
section: What makes an answer stand out?
text:
What makes an answer stand out?
A focal point is a solution that stands out in a way that helps people coordinate their expectations (Schelling, 1960). The main entrance might serve this role at the concert because both people remember arriving there together and expect the other to see it as a natural place to return. Being memorable to one person is insufficient; the crucial link is the expectation that it will also stand out to the other.
A familiar file format, an established deadline, or an equal split can provide the same service. Shared history makes a choice easier to anticipate without requiring a long chain of guesses. But what seems obvious depends on whose history is shared. A newcomer may not know which entrance colleagues mean, while two departments may each regard their own reporting convention as the natural default.
Focality also differs from payoff dominance. An equilibrium is payoff dominant if it gives every player a higher payoff than the other equilibrium being compared. A salient outcome need not have that advantage. Nor does the existence of a better common outcome ensure that people will select it.

A ten-cent difference can disrupt a common answer
Crawford, Gneezy, and Rottenstreich (2008) studied matching games in which two players independently chose X or Y and earned nothing if they failed to match. With matching payoffs of $5 each, the observed choice frequencies implied a 64% coordination rate. In another condition, matching on X paid $5 to one player and $5.10 to the other, while matching on Y reversed those payoffs. The implied coordination rate fell to 38%.2
Only ten cents separated the preferred coordinated outcomes, while a mismatch cost each player at least $5. Nevertheless, a shared label became less effective when payoffs pulled expectations in different directions. People also had to anticipate what the difference would mean to their partner.
The practical implication is precise. Naming an obvious option may help when interests align closely. Once people prefer different coordinated outcomes, they may need an agreed selection rule as well as a salient answer.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
section: When the better outcome feels too risky
text:
When the better outcome feels too risky
Now suppose both departments agree that a new common system would be better than keeping the old one. The conflict over which system to choose has disappeared, but the danger of switching alone remains. Each may wait for evidence that the other will follow, leaving both with the old system.
The stag hunt isolates this problem (Skyrms, 2004). Two hunters can secure the larger return only by hunting stag together. Each can instead hunt hare independently. In the illustrative payoff matrix in Table 24.3, the first number belongs to Player 1.



Table 24.3: Stag hunt: mutual commitment offers more, but acting alone is costly





Player 1 \ Player 2
Stag
Hare




Stag
15, 15
2, 10


Hare
10, 2
10, 10






Stag–stag and hare–hare are both Nash equilibria. Stag–stag is payoff dominant, giving each player 15 rather than 10. Hare guarantees 10 regardless of the partner’s action, whereas choosing Stag leaves a player with 2 if the partner chooses Hare.
How much confidence is enough? With these numbers treated as utility payoffs, Stag is strictly better when the player believes the partner’s chance of choosing Stag exceeds about 61.5%. At the exact threshold, both actions are best responses. Below it, choosing Hare is a sensible response to uncertainty about the partner, even for someone who prefers mutual stag hunting. This threshold follows from the illustrative payoffs; it is not a measured level of trust that people universally require.
Under a fifty–fifty belief about the partner, Stag yields 8.5 while Hare yields 10. In this symmetric two-action game, hare–hare is therefore the risk-dominant equilibrium: Hare is preferable over a larger range of beliefs about the partner, whereas stag–stag is payoff dominant. This comparison concerns uncertainty about another player; it requires no additional assumption that the person is risk averse.







NoteMathematical analysis: the stag-hunt confidence threshold





Suppose the displayed numbers are utility payoffs and Player 1 assigns probability \(p\) to Player 2 choosing Stag. The expected payoff from Stag is
\[
15p+2(1-p)=2+13p,
\]
while Hare yields 10. Stag is strictly better when
\[
p>\frac{8}{13}\approx0.615.
\]
At \(p=8/13\), the player is indifferent; below that threshold, Hare gives the higher expected payoff.




This is strategic uncertainty: uncertainty about what others will do. A pilot, staged adoption, or compatibility guarantee could make the departmental switch more attractive by increasing confidence in the partner’s action or reducing the loss from being left alone. Improving the promised system matters less if the unresolved obstacle is whether anybody else will use it.
Van Huyck, Battalio, and Beil (1990) tested a related problem with groups choosing effort levels from 1 to 7. Each person’s payoff increased with the group’s lowest effort, but choosing more effort than the minimum incurred an extra cost. Everyone would earn more if everyone chose the highest level. Yet in seven large-group experiments, the minimum effort reached 1 within four rounds.
The design made higher effort attractive only when others also supplied it. Seeing a low minimum could therefore make reducing one’s own effort a sensible response, while helping the group remain at the lower outcome. Learning from experience can reinforce a disappointing convention as well as improve coordination.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
section: How a convention becomes difficult to leave
text:
How a convention becomes difficult to leave
Once a common standard is established, using it can become valuable precisely because others already do. Colleagues know the file format, support staff know how to repair failures, and suppliers build compatible products. These network benefits reinforce the initial choice. Training and conversion costs add further reasons to stay.
The resulting path dependence means that earlier events can influence which outcome persists. It does not mean the outcome must be inefficient. The relevant comparison includes the benefits of compatibility and the costs of a coordinated transition, not just the technical features of two isolated products.
David (1985) used the history of QWERTY to develop the path-dependence argument. Liebowitz and Margolis (1990) challenged the evidence that the keyboard persisted despite a demonstrably superior alternative. The familiar story that QWERTY was designed to slow typists should therefore not carry the explanation. Installed bases, learned skills, and compatibility provide mechanisms worth investigating without treating a contested historical verdict as established fact.
For the departments, this suggests a useful distinction: evidence that a new system is better in isolation differs from evidence that changing together is worthwhile. A credible transition plan addresses the second question by making costs, timing, and support explicit.

A familiar convention can make work easier for insiders while leaving newcomers unable to anticipate what is expected. Compatibility alone does not settle whether a standard is fair: the people bearing its training and conversion costs also need a voice in choosing it.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
text:
Coordinating when interests differ
Return to the original disagreement: Department A prefers integration; Department B prefers flexibility. Both want compatibility, but each coordinated outcome distributes benefits differently. This structure is conventionally called the Battle of the Sexes, named after an older example in which two people want to spend an evening together but prefer different activities. Finding a common choice and deciding whose preference prevails are separate problems.
A lottery, rotation, or neutral tie-breaker can provide an answer both sides anticipate. The appropriate rule depends on the activity. Taking turns may work for recurring meeting times but waste resources if it requires replacing the reporting system every month. For a durable standard, compensating concentrated training costs or sharing implementation work may produce a more acceptable agreement.

Compatible bargaining claims
A simple bargaining game makes the distribution problem explicit. Two players simultaneously claim shares of a total of 4. If their claims sum to at most 4, each receives the amount claimed; if they exceed 4, both receive 0.
The claims 2 and 2 fit together, as do 3 and 1. In either of those pairs, raising one’s claim would destroy the agreement, while lowering it would reduce one’s payoff. Both are Nash equilibria. Equilibrium alone does not decide which division should prevail. Equal shares may be focal, but contribution, alternatives, past agreements, and power can support other expectations.
The example fixes the total at 4. Real negotiation can also discover trades that create more value before deciding how to divide it. Negotiation as Joint Decision Design develops that task. Even an agreement that improves both parties’ outcomes can preserve an unequal division; mutual gain does not settle whether the allocation or procedure is fair.






NoteResearch Lens: coordination can require different actions





Matching is only one form of coordination. In chicken, two drivers approach a one-lane bridge. Each would rather proceed while the other yields, but both prefer avoiding a collision. The desirable actions are complementary. A right-of-way rule can select who yields; commitments by both drivers to keep going can instead make the worst outcome more likely.
In a volunteer’s dilemma, everyone benefits if someone acts, and each values getting the task done more than the personal cost of volunteering, but prefers someone else to bear that cost. A team may need one person to report a software failure, but an open request can leave everyone waiting. Assigning the task or rotating responsibility addresses who acts. Shared Responsibility examines the psychological evidence and distinguishes this incentive problem from uncertainty about whether help is needed.
These cases extend the chapter’s question: which combination of actions is needed, and what rule makes each person’s role predictable? Coordination does not always mean doing the same thing.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
text:
Making an agreement credible
The earlier distinction between mutual and common knowledge explains why a joint announcement can help. Both departments may know the Monday migration plan and know that the other knows it. They can still hesitate if they doubt the other’s readiness or expect a last-minute withdrawal.
Communication can identify a common option, reveal transition costs, make expectations more public, and specify who will do what. In the stag hunt, confidence that the partner will hunt Stag can make Stag attractive. But common knowledge of a promise does not establish that fulfilling it will be feasible or worthwhile when the moment arrives.
Words can matter even without a binding commitment. In a stag-hunt experiment, Charness (2000) found much more efficient coordination when a player could send a costless, nonbinding message before choosing an action than when communication was unavailable. Reversing the order of message and action changed behavior. Communication can therefore coordinate expectations without mechanically enforcing behavior.
A credible commitment goes further by changing the cost or feasibility of departing from a future action. Booking shared training, allocating an implementation budget, making an irreversible investment, or signing an enforceable contract can strengthen a plan when it makes withdrawal harder and the other party understands that consequence. Schelling (1960) emphasized the strategic value of limiting one’s future freedom: the restriction can change someone else’s response.
The practical sequence is to make the desired outcome identifiable, make the shared expectation visible, and make the promised action credible. A failure can arise at any stage. More explanation of the plan’s merits may leave uncertainty about others’ knowledge unresolved; a public promise may leave the incentive to withdraw unchanged.
The same mechanism can serve competitive purposes. In 1999, Ford promised UK buyers a refund if it cut prices before the end of the year (Motor Trader, 1999b). The strategic logic is that a later reduction would then cost Ford money on qualifying earlier sales as well as on new ones. Yet a contemporary report described buyers postponing purchases until January, when they expected the guarantee to expire and prices to fall (Motor Trader, 1999a). The report illustrates how a commitment might shift expectations in an unintended direction, without isolating its causal effect on purchases.
Commitment has a cost: the flexibility surrendered. A public promise to use one system may persuade the other department to invest, but it can also make managers defend that system after serious defects emerge. A useful commitment specifies the response it is intended to change and preserves a clear review condition. If persistence mainly protects an earlier decision rather than a worthwhile future arrangement, the escalation problem discussed in Strategic Interdependence deserves attention.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
section: Application: diagnose the obstacle before choosing the tool
text:
Application: diagnose the obstacle before choosing the tool
The reporting dispute can now be separated into actionable problems. The rows of Table 24.4 identify obstacles that can coexist; each suggests a different first intervention.



Table 24.4: Different coordination obstacles call for different responses










Obstacle
Evidence to look for
Possible response




Different expectations about the common choice
Each department assumes its own standard is the obvious answer.
Choose one standard explicitly and confirm that both understand the choice.


Uncertainty about what others know
Both have received the plan, but neither knows whether the other received and understood it.
Review the plan together and make each team’s acknowledgement visible to the other.


Fear of acting alone
Both prefer the joint switch but doubt the other’s readiness.
Set a shared launch condition or reduce the cost of a failed transition.


Disagreement over benefits and burdens
Both want compatibility, but one bears more training or conversion costs.
Compare total gains and agree how to share transition costs.


Unassigned or conflicting roles
Each waits for the other to act, or both claim the same decision right.
Name responsibilities and agree on a tie-breaker.






Begin with a joint pilot that uses the same evaluation criteria and records costs for both departments. Agree on the decision rule before results are available, then specify who transfers the records, who trains staff, and what must be ready before launch. A review date creates a way to respond to evidence without making every temporary difficulty a reason to abandon the common plan. The rule should also remain understandable and open to challenge by the people expected to follow it.
The diagnostic also marks a boundary. If one department benefits from abandoning the agreement even when the other fulfills it, reassurance alone will not solve the problem. The incentives or the agreement itself need to change.
After specifying the game, keep the answers supplied by equilibrium analysis separate from questions that require evidence about the people involved. Table 24.5 collects that distinction: identifying a stable combination is one step in evaluating a joint decision.



Table 24.5: Questions answered by equilibrium analysis and questions requiring further evidence









Equilibrium can clarify
Equilibrium alone cannot establish




Whether each strategy is a best response to the others.
Whether players understand the game or hold those expectations.


Whether anyone gains by changing their strategy alone.
Whether the outcome is fair or best for the people affected.


Which strategy combinations remain stable under specified rules.
Which equilibrium people select when several exist.


How changing incentives alters that stability.
Whether the proposed payoffs capture actual motives.

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
text:
Practice Lab
Choose a real situation in which two people or groups must adopt compatible actions. Specify their options and construct a payoff matrix, stating the assumptions behind the numbers. Mark each player’s best responses and identify any pure-strategy equilibria. If more than one coordinated outcome could work, explain why the people have not settled on one: different expectations, uncertainty about what others know, fear of acting alone, conflicting benefits, or an unassigned role.
Propose one change that addresses the identified obstacle. State whose expectation or incentive should change and what behavior would count as evidence that the diagnosis was useful. If you propose communication, explain how participants will know that others received and understood it, and whether it changes any incentive to act. If you propose a guarantee, calculate what it protects against; if you propose a rule, explain how the people bearing its costs can take part in choosing it.
crumbs: Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
text:
Take it forward
At the next stalled meeting, separate three questions: “Which plan would work?”, “What does each person know about the others’ understanding?”, and “What makes each person willing to act?” Look for the missing shared expectation, assurance, decision rule, or allocation of responsibility before treating hesitation as unwillingness.
Cooperation and Social Preferences takes the next step: what if a person gains by departing from the common plan even when everyone else keeps it? Future relationships, institutions, and concern for others can change that decision in different ways.







NoteResearch Lens: dependence without a changing best response





In the meeting game, your best response changes with the other person’s choice. Strategic dependence can also exist when one action is best regardless of what the other player does. A strictly dominant strategy yields a higher payoff than every alternative against every strategy combination of the others.
The illustrative price-war matrix in Table 24.6 shows the distinction. Its numbers represent profit units and omit many features of an actual market. Rao and colleagues (2000) examine how responses to price competition depend on such details of the competitive setting.



Table 24.6: Illustrative price-war payoff matrix; Firm 1’s payoff appears first





Firm 1 \ Firm 2
High price
Low price




High price
10, 10
2, 15


Low price
15, 2
5, 5






Against a high price, Firm 1 earns 15 by choosing low rather than 10 by choosing high. Against a low price, it earns 5 rather than 2. Low strictly dominates high for both firms. Low–low is the unique Nash equilibrium, even though each firm’s profit remains affected by its rival’s action.
Both firms would earn more at high–high, but an agreement to charge high prices would harm customers and may be unlawful. The firms’ joint profit is not a measure of social welfare. Chapter 25 develops the incentive conflict in a Prisoner’s Dilemma and examines what can sustain cooperation.

title: 24  Coordination and Focal Points
text:
Terminology varies across fields. Here, mutual knowledge means that every member of a specified group knows X; statements about what others know add higher-order levels. Shared knowledge sometimes names the same first-order condition (Herzig & Perrotin, 2020), but psychological research also uses it for a finite number of higher-order levels that fall short of common knowledge (De Freitas et al., 2019). Public knowledge often means that information is widely known or publicly available. Availability alone does not establish that everyone knows it. In formal models, a truthful public announcement can generate common knowledge when its reception and meaning are themselves commonly recognized. These terms should therefore be read according to the author’s definitions, rather than treated as interchangeable labels.↩︎
Table 2 reports rates implied by choices, not observed pair-success rates. There were 50 participants in the symmetric condition and 23 and 25 in the asymmetric roles.↩︎

title: 25  Cooperation and Social Preferences
text:
Learning goals
Self-Interest Is Not the Only Payoff
Two colleagues need each other’s working notes to finish a joint report. Preparing clear notes takes time away from work assessed individually. Each would welcome the other’s help while skipping their own contribution. If both withhold their notes, both lose useful input.
They agree on what working together would require. Their difficulty is that each can gain by letting the other do the work. In the stag hunt in Coordination and Focal Points, confidence that the other person would join made joining worthwhile. Here, confidence that the colleague will help still leaves a reason to withhold one’s own contribution.
Yet people often share the notes, return a favor, or refuse an unfair advantage. Some expect a later benefit; others care about the colleague or believe that helping is the right thing to do. Those differences matter when we try to make cooperation last.

title: 25  Cooperation and Social Preferences
text:
Distinguish a coordination problem from a conflict between individual incentives and collective gains.
Explain how continued interaction, reputation, and institutions can support cooperation, including the need for repair after mistakes.
Use differences between games to separate strategic incentives, social preferences, and expectations about appropriate behavior.
Explain how ingroup favoritism can restrict cooperation and how shared goals and a more inclusive identity can help rebuild it.

title: 25  Cooperation and Social Preferences
text:
When cooperation invites exploitation
The colleagues choose simultaneously whether to share their notes. Table 25.1 represents sharing as Cooperate and withholding as Defect. Its illustrative payoffs combine the benefit of receiving useful input and the cost of providing it.



Table 25.1: One-shot Prisoner’s Dilemma; Player 1’s payoff appears first





Player 1 \ Player 2
Cooperate
Defect




Cooperate
4, 4
0, 6


Defect
6, 0
2, 2






Defecting raises Player 1’s payoff from 4 to 6 if Player 2 cooperates, and from 0 to 2 if Player 2 defects. It does the same for Player 2. Defection is therefore a strictly dominant strategy for each: it pays more regardless of the other’s choice. The unique Nash equilibrium is Defect–Defect, giving each 2 instead of the 4 each could receive through mutual cooperation.
This is the Prisoner’s Dilemma: individually attractive departures undermine a mutually beneficial outcome. Unlike the stag hunt, no greater confidence in the partner’s cooperation makes cooperating a best response in this one-shot calculation. Something beyond reassurance must change.

Is the scene really a Prisoner’s Dilemma?
Watch the ferry dilemma from The Dark Knight and reconstruct each group’s options and payoff ranking. Does defection dominate, who can communicate, and can the threat be trusted? The fictional scene tests the model’s assumptions.
The opening matrix also leaves out future encounters and concerns beyond the stated rewards. Adding either can change the choice. The branches in Figure 25.1 distinguish these routes: repeated interaction and reputation attach later consequences to today’s act, rules alter the conditions of the interaction, and social preferences change what a player values. The optional evolutionary lens examines how the structure of a population can support cooperation over time.






Figure 25.1: Cooperation can be supported by repeated interaction, reputation, social preferences, norms and institutions, and network structure. These supports work through different processes; their effects also depend on mistakes, exclusion, enforcement, and the ability to leave.

title: 25  Cooperation and Social Preferences
section: How a future relationship supports cooperation
text:
How a future relationship supports cooperation

The future can outweigh today’s temptation
Suppose the colleagues will work together again. Withholding notes may save effort today but cost access to useful notes later. Cooperation can now serve each person’s own interests, provided the future relationship is valuable enough and the response to defection is credible.
Consider an indefinitely repeated version of the opening game. Under a grim-trigger strategy, each player cooperates until someone defects, then defects forever. Defecting brings a larger reward today but replaces future mutual cooperation with mutual defection.
Whether that trade is worthwhile depends on how strongly the future relationship counts, allowing for both the chance of another encounter and the discounting of later payoffs. With the opening payoffs, cooperation can remain a best response when each next round carries at least half the weight of the current round. The optional analysis derives that threshold. The practical point is that a short-term gain can be outweighed by losing a sufficiently valuable stream of future cooperation.
This identifies when cooperation can be sustained by these strategies, not that players will necessarily reach it. The comparison assumes reliable observation and the specified response to defection. Misobserved actions can trigger punishment after an innocent error. A known final round can also unravel cooperation by backward induction when the stage-game incentives and rationality assumptions apply throughout. Experimental evidence reviewed by Dal Bó and Fréchette (2018) makes continuation and incentives central to understanding when repeated cooperation emerges. Reputational links or further relationships can preserve future consequences after one particular project ends.







NoteMathematical analysis: when future cooperation outweighs defection





Consider an indefinitely repeated version of the opening game. Under a grim-trigger strategy, each player cooperates until someone defects, then defects forever. Let \(T\) be the temptation payoff from defecting against a cooperator, \(R\) the reward from mutual cooperation, and \(P\) the payoff from mutual defection. The continuation weight \(\delta\), between 0 and 1, captures how strongly the next round counts, allowing for both the chance of another encounter and discounting of future payoffs.
Continued cooperation yields
\[
\frac{R}{1-\delta},
\]
whereas a one-time defection followed by permanent punishment yields
\[
T+\frac{\delta P}{1-\delta}.
\]
For cooperation to remain a best response to the other player’s grim-trigger strategy,
\[
\frac{R}{1-\delta}\geq T+\frac{\delta P}{1-\delta},
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\delta\geq\frac{T-R}{T-P}.
\]
With \(T=6\), \(R=4\), and \(P=2\), the threshold is \(\delta\geq0.5\). At \(\delta=0.5\), continued cooperation is worth \(4/(1-0.5)=8\); defecting is worth \(6+0.5\times2/(1-0.5)=8\) as well. At \(\delta=0.75\), cooperation is worth 16 and defection followed by punishment only 12. The current gain of 2 is outweighed by the loss of future cooperation.






Reciprocity needs a way to repair mistakes
Permanent punishment illustrates an incentive; it is a severe policy for working with fallible people. A colleague may fail to send notes because a file was lost, not because they intended to exploit anyone. A useful response needs to deter deliberate withholding while allowing cooperation to recover from error.
Tit-for-tat begins by cooperating and then copies the partner’s previous move. Axelrod’s tournaments made four properties memorable: be nice, be provocable, be forgiving, and be clear (Axelrod, 1984). Here, forgiving means returning to cooperation after the partner does. These properties help explain its success in those tournaments.
An accidental defection can nevertheless send two tit-for-tat players into alternating retaliation. Generous tit-for-tat sometimes cooperates after a defection, while win-stay, lose-shift repeats an action after satisfactory outcomes and switches after unsatisfactory ones. Imhof, Fudenberg, and Nowak (2007), for example, find win-stay, lose-shift rather than tit-for-tat selected above a cooperation-benefit threshold in their particular finite-population evolutionary process. Which strategy succeeds depends on mistakes, the alternatives present, and how success changes future play or population composition.
The “live-and-let-live” system that emerged in parts of the Western Front during the First World War illustrates reciprocal restraint outside a laboratory: units facing one another repeatedly could respond to local restraint and punish violations (Axelrod, 1984). The possibility of a continuing response helped sustain restraint even between enemies.


Reputation extends the relationship
Future consequences need not come from the person we help today. A colleague who shares useful work may later be invited onto another team because others have learned that they can rely on them. Indirect reciprocity operates through that wider reputation, while direct reciprocity operates through another encounter with the same partner (Nowak, 2006).
For a reputation to affect incentives, an action must leave a record that reaches someone who can respond. A rating system, a reference, or informal information sharing can provide that link. The link can also fail: records can be mistaken, selective, or manipulated, and a permanent bad label can block recovery. The design of the record and the possibility of correcting it are part of the cooperation problem.



A social cue can also suggest an audience without creating one. Burnham and Hare (2007) displayed images of Kismet, a robot with humanlike eyes, during a public-goods game. Participants seeing Kismet contributed an average of 5.39 of 10 tokens across six rounds, compared with 4.17 without it—about 29% more.
The comparison did not isolate the eyes from the rest of the robot image. Later meta-analyses, which included this study, found no reliable overall increase in generosity from artificial surveillance cues (Northover et al., 2017). A reputation system still needs consequences that other people can actually impose.


Rules can change the temptation
An organization need not wait for colleagues to punish one another. It can recognize useful contributions, make responsibility visible, or require a shared handover before a project is accepted. Contracts and enforcement can similarly change the expected return from keeping an agreement. A penalty for withholding notes, however, needs a clear definition of the required contribution, a proportionate response, and a way to correct a mistaken record. Otherwise the rule can punish a technical failure or a justified refusal to disclose sensitive information.
Rules also communicate what the relationship means. Paying people for helping, fining them for withholding, and recognizing a shared obligation can produce different responses even when the monetary changes seem small. We will return to this issue after considering what people value beyond their own rewards.


Cooperation for large prizes on Golden Balls
The television game Golden Balls ended with contestants choosing Split or Steal for large and widely varying prizes. Stealing could secure the whole prize against a partner who split; splitting exposed a contestant to leaving with nothing. Before reading the evidence, watch one Split-or-Steal round and an unusual communication strategy. Record the promises, threats, and choices that remain credible.
Van den Assem, van Dolder, and Thaler (2012) report stakes averaging more than $20,000. Many contestants chose Split even though Steal weakly dominated it in immediate monetary payoffs: Steal did better against Split and equally well against Steal. The authors find evidence consistent with reciprocal preferences from earlier interaction, little support in their sample for conditional cooperation based on an opponent’s expected action, and an age-dependent gender pattern.
The choices show cooperation at high stakes in a setting where contestants interacted before choosing and faced a television audience.1

title: 25  Cooperation and Social Preferences
section: What people value beyond their own payoff
text:
What people value beyond their own payoff
Future consequences explain why helping can serve a player’s own material interests. They do not exhaust the possibilities: a person may share even when doing so brings no later return. A social preference means that utility depends on more than one’s own material payoff. People may care about another person’s welfare, inequality, total surplus, the worst-off person’s outcome, intentions, or obligations to a group.
Two important forms can predict different choices. Altruism, in an outcome-based preference model, gives positive weight to another person’s welfare. Inequity aversion places a cost on unequal outcomes, often distinguishing being behind from being ahead. Helping someone already better off can improve their welfare while widening the gap. Allocation experiments vary such trade-offs to distinguish motives; the optional research track develops the models (Andreoni & Miller, 2002; Fehr & Schmidt, 1999).

Ultimatum game: fairness has strategic force
In the ultimatum game, a proposer divides a sum. A responder accepts, implementing the division, or rejects, giving both zero. A responder concerned only with their own money prefers accepting any positive offer to rejecting it. With a smallest positive monetary unit, and if the responder rejects zero, backward reasoning predicts that smallest positive offer. If zero is accepted, a zero offer can be optimal instead; continuously divisible money has no smallest positive amount.
Classic experiments instead commonly find modal offers around 40–50% and mean offers around 30–40%; offers below 20% are often rejected roughly half the time in multi-study summaries (Camerer, 2003; Oosterbeek, Sloof, & van de Kuilen, 2004).
Rejecting a positive offer costs the responder money. That sacrifice changes the proposer’s calculation: an offer that leaves little for the responder may also leave nothing for the proposer. Fairness can therefore affect the bargain even when the proposer cares only about their own return.
An offer can still mix motives. A proposer may value fairness, fear rejection, follow a norm, or misunderstand responders. A responder may dislike inequality, punish an insulting intention, preserve self-respect, or enforce a norm. Rejection reveals a willingness to sacrifice money, without uniquely identifying the reason.
The linked ultimatum scene provides a communication exercise. Identify the demand, the threatened consequence, and the recipient’s outside options. Then consider whether posing the ultimatum changes only the material menu or also respect, identity, and the perceived intention behind the offer.


Dictator game: remove strategic rejection
A generous ultimatum offer can express care or simply buy acceptance. To test how much acceptance matters, remove the recipient’s power to reject. In the dictator game, the allocator can keep the money without risking that punishment. Removing rejection usually reduces transfers. In classic comparable treatments, average giving is around 20% in Forsythe and colleagues (1994) and closer to 10% under the double-blind procedures of Hoffman and colleagues (1994).
Removing rejection does not remove the rest of the setting. Anonymity, earned entitlement, experimenter observation, and whether the menu allows taking as well as giving can change the meaning of the action. The progression across Figure 25.2 shows which rights and options change between games.






Figure 25.2: The comparison covers the ultimatum, dictator, and take-or-menu-variant games. Removing the responder’s rejection option separates strategic rejection from giving; changing the allocator’s ability to give, take, or leave the study changes property rights and the meaning of the observed allocation. Reported patterns come from Forsythe et al. (1994), Hoffman et al. (1994), Camerer (2003), and Oosterbeek et al. (2004).





Mutual cooperation can be rewarding
Sharing notes may matter because the other person responds in kind. In two fMRI experiments involving 36 women, Rilling and colleagues (2002) found that mutual cooperation with a presumed human partner was associated with stronger responses in parts of the ventral striatum and orbitofrontal cortex than the average of the other three Prisoner’s Dilemma outcomes. Mutual cooperation paid less than exploiting a cooperating partner.
Reciprocated help may acquire value through social connection and expectations of continued cooperation. The repeated-game design leaves both in play. For the colleagues, a reliable exchange can make contributing valuable because of the relationship it sustains as well as the notes it delivers.
The measurement was blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) activity, an indirect indicator of neural activity. It did not measure dopamine release. The findings support a role for reward processing in mutual cooperation. This is the same distinction between brain activity and neurotransmitter release discussed in Chapter 21.


Why punishment can feel rewarding
Social preferences can also make another person’s loss attractive. Someone who has been deliberately betrayed may be willing to pay to punish the offender, even when doing so cannot recover the lost money. The prospect of seeing a wrong answered may itself enter the payoff.
De Quervain and colleagues (2004) studied this possibility using positron emission tomography (PET) during a trust game. After a partner kept money instead of returning a share, participants could assign punishment points. Effective punishment reduced the partner’s earnings; symbolic punishment did not. While participants considered their response, effective punishment produced greater activity in the dorsal striatum, a region involved in reward processing and goal-directed action. Stronger activation was also associated with willingness to spend more of one’s own money to punish.
The authors interpreted this pattern as evidence of anticipated satisfaction from punishment. A monetary sacrifice can therefore be consistent with pursuing something the person values. The term altruistic punishment does not establish a selfless psychological motive: enforcing a cooperative norm and expecting personal satisfaction can coexist.
How literally should we take the idea that “revenge is sweet”? Reward-related brain activity is not a direct measure of experienced pleasure, and the study did not establish that striatal activation caused punishment. Its analysis included 14 men who had trusted their partners. As Chapter 6 explains, a brain region’s involvement cannot uniquely identify a mental experience.
Anticipation can also differ from the emotional aftermath. In separate behavioral experiments, Carlsmith, Wilson, and Gilbert (2008) found that participants expected punishment to improve their mood. Yet participants given the opportunity to punish, most of whom used it, reported worse mood than those without it. Continued rumination about the offender helped explain the pattern.
For the colleagues sharing notes, this creates a practical tension. Wanting an exploiter to face consequences can motivate enforcement, but the appeal of retaliation does not establish that it will repair the relationship. A useful sanction needs to be judged by what happens to cooperation as well as by how satisfying it seems to impose.
