title: 29  Culture and Identity
section: Worked application: redesign the silent meeting
text:
Worked application: redesign the silent meeting
Return to the opening puzzle. The manager can redesign the process without pretending to know why everyone was silent.
Step 1: Separate observation from interpretation. Observation: nobody responded to a public yes-or-no question after the senior person presented.
Step 2: Generate meanings. Agreement, uncertainty, deference, fear, processing time, language difficulty, private-disagreement norm.
Step 3: Inspect power and process. Who spoke first? Was independent thinking possible? Can a junior person disagree publicly without cost?
Step 4: Ask locally. In one-to-one conversations or an anonymous channel, ask how concerns are normally raised and what would make disagreement usable.
Step 5: Change the architecture. Distribute the proposal in advance. Ask everyone to record risks independently. Invite the most junior or relevant expert before senior commentary. Use “What concern would we regret not discussing?” rather than “Does everyone agree?” Provide a private escalation path.
Step 6: Learn. Compare the number, novelty, and usefulness of concerns before and after the redesign. Check whether some members still carry disproportionate social cost.
The redesigned meeting gives concerns several routes into the decision. Check which routes people use and ask what made a concern easier to raise; changing several features together will not identify their separate effects. Later chapters use this habit of inquiry in persuasion, communication, and negotiation. Before trying to change another person’s response, establish what the situation means to them.

title: 29  Culture and Identity
text:
The culture-and-identity meaning audit
Before a consequential decision or design, ask:



Table 29.4: A culture-and-identity meaning audit









Audit question
Decision risk it exposes




Which identities are active?
Treating a person as an abstract chooser


What does each option symbolize?
Missing status, loyalty, care, or belonging


What norms determine what can be said?
Mistaking silence for preference


Who can disagree with whom?
Information filtered by hierarchy


What do acceptance and refusal communicate?
Material offer interpreted as social act


Whose script is treated as normal?
Dominant-culture design hidden as neutrality


Could an incentive change the meaning of the action?
Crowding out or distrust


What local evidence could correct our interpretation?
Stereotype replacing inquiry


Who bears the cost of adaptation?
Power and unequal cultural labor


Would affected people endorse the design and its identity message?
Efficient influence that reduces dignity or agency






Use Table 29.4 to identify how the same material option could carry different meanings for different people, then seek local evidence that could correct your interpretation.

title: 29  Culture and Identity
text:
Practice Lab
Choose one ambiguous action: silence, a direct refusal, a gift, an apology, public praise, a concession, or asking for help. Produce a Meaning Audit with four rows: salient self or identity; sanction strength; hierarchy and face; local relational or institutional meaning. For each row, state a rival interpretation, evidence that would distinguish it, and one perspective-getting question. Finish with a process redesign that prevents interpretation from silently becoming judgment.

title: 29  Culture and Identity
text:
Take it forward
Before attributing a colleague’s silence to personality or culture, ask what speaking would mean in that particular relationship. The answer may change both your interpretation and the way you invite disagreement.
Once the same action can mean different things across audiences and relationships, influence cannot begin with the message alone. It must begin with the model through which the audience interprets it. Part V takes up that deliberate task through persuasion, communication, and repair.

title: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
text:
Questions to carry forward
A manager explains why a new system will save time. The team hears a different message: their existing work is being dismissed, and another disruption is coming. The manager expects evidence of efficiency to win support; the team is judging what the change says about their contribution and control over their work. Repeating the time-saving argument leaves the source of their resistance unanswered.
The route in Figure 1 begins with what the team is being asked to reconsider and ends with checking whether the message has been understood. The persuasion chapters examine the audience’s beliefs, concerns, and reasons to trust a speaker. Stories can make consequences easier to imagine, but their wider significance still needs evidence. We then use workplace examples to build messages whose proposed action follows from a problem the audience recognizes.
Communication gives the audience an opportunity to answer and correct the speaker. Questions and paraphrasing let both sides test what they think the other means. Connection helps make that exchange possible when a concern is difficult to voice. The final chapter follows a workplace conversation through honest disagreement and repair, showing why being understood and reaching agreement are different achievements.
Negotiation adds a shared decision to the conversation. Each side can accept, propose a different arrangement, or walk away; Part VI examines how to use those possibilities well.

title: 30  Persuasion
text:
Learning goals
Changing Minds Means Updating Models
Imagine that a company plans to replace its familiar project system with a shared digital platform. Leaders present figures showing time lost to duplicate files. Employees ask who will see their activity data and when they will have time to learn the system. The next presentation contains more efficiency statistics, and the objections remain.
The leaders are answering Will this improve coordination? Their audience is also asking Will this cost me autonomy, and will the promised support arrive? A correct answer to the first question cannot settle the others. To make progress, the proposal itself may need to change.
Persuasion begins by finding the question that stands between the audience and a possible change of mind. We will follow this platform proposal from an argument people resist to a decision they can examine.

title: 30  Persuasion
text:
Diagnose the main barrier preventing a particular audience from revising its model.
Design an evidence-aligned message that integrates source, argument, emotion, and feasible action.
Produce and ethically audit a persuasive proposal that preserves the audience’s agency.

title: 30  Persuasion
section: From information transfer to model updating
text:
From information transfer to model updating
The culture chapter showed why the same action can carry different meanings. The platform proposal reveals the consequence for persuasion: leaders see coordination, while employees also see possible surveillance. Each side is using a different model, or working explanation of how the system will affect their work. More facts help when they answer a question within that explanation or give a reason to revise it. They help less when the speaker keeps answering a question the audience has already set aside.
Evidence constrains the models that deserve belief. But a visible pattern may fit several accounts: steady growth, acceleration, or an approaching plateau. In Figure 30.1, all three curves fit the observations so far, but a later observation of 44 favors the plateau. These are synthetic data: the point is to identify an observation that could distinguish the accounts before deciding which story to tell.






Figure 30.1: Three candidate curves match the synthetic values 12, 18, 24, 30, and 36 in periods 1–5, then extrapolate as steady growth, acceleration, or a plateau. A new observation of 44 at period 8 favors the plateau.



A useful starting point is therefore to identify what the audience expects and what evidence could change that expectation. Predictive processing offers a theoretical analogy, especially from perception and action: incoming information is compared with predictions, and discrepancies can lead to revision (Clark, 2013). The sequence in Table 30.1 turns that idea into practical questions for a message:



Table 30.1: A practical model-updating sequence










Stage
Diagnostic question
Design move




Current model
What does this audience expect, and why is that expectation intelligible?
Begin inside shared reality.


Meaningful mismatch
What relevant observation can the old model not explain?
Surface one real, consequential gap.


Candidate model
What better explanation resolves the gap?
State the mechanism, not merely a preferred conclusion.


Evidence
Why should the new account receive more weight?
Match source, comparison, test, and uncertainty to the claim.


Action
What feasible next step follows if the update is accepted?
Name who does what, by when, while preserving refusal.






For the platform proposal, ask employees what makes adoption unattractive or difficult. Their answers might reveal several barriers requiring different responses:



Table 30.2: A barrier matrix for persuasive design










Barrier
What the audience may be thinking
Appropriate design response




Attention
“This is one more announcement.”
Lead with the consequential mismatch, not background.


Trust
“Management will use the data against us.”
Use a credible messenger, disclose governance, and make commitments verifiable.


Comprehension
“I cannot see how this changes my work.”
Demonstrate the workflow with concrete before-and-after tasks.


Identity and values
“This treats professional judgment as a defect.”
Protect valued competence and explain what remains under local control.


Feasibility
“Even if it helps, I have no time to learn it.”
Provide time, training, support, and a reversible pilot.


Belief
“The promised benefit is only a projection.”
State the mechanism, uncertainty, comparison, and success test.






Table 30.2 separates objections that another statistic can address from concerns requiring a change in governance, training, or workload. Listening may reveal a defect in the proposal rather than in its presentation.






TipBring one message to redesign



Choose a product, policy, behavior-change request, difficult conversation, or research claim. In six lines, write: audience; desired response; current model; main barrier; credible evidence; constraint. Then write one observation that would genuinely discriminate the old model from your proposed one. If you cannot state that test, you may have a preference rather than a persuasive explanation.

title: 30  Persuasion
text:
Source, evidence, and stakes
The platform’s efficiency evidence may be sound while employees still have good reasons to resist. They must judge both whether the system works and whether those controlling it will protect their interests. A proposal that answers only the technical question leaves the decision unresolved. Aristotle’s ethos, logos, and pathos help distinguish the questions a message must address. Ethos asks whether the source is competent, trustworthy, and accountable. Logos asks whether evidence and causal reasoning support the claim. Pathos asks whether the emotional meaning fits what is genuinely at stake. These are not competing recipes. A warranted update may require all three.
Source credibility depends especially on perceived expertise and trustworthiness, although goodwill, similarity, status, confidence, and intent can also affect reception (Hovland & Weiss, 1951; Pornpitakpan, 2004). Credentials do not settle trust. A technically expert manager may still be an unsuitable messenger when earlier promises were broken or when the proposal benefits management at employees’ expense. A different, conditional pattern is the sleeper effect: a message initially discounted because of a credibility warning can become more persuasive later. Kumkale and Albarracín’s (2004) meta-analysis found this delayed effect under particular message and discounting-cue conditions.
For the platform proposal, a respected project leader who tested the system may be a more credible messenger than the chief technology officer alone. Yet a better messenger cannot substitute for verifiable governance. Employees need to know which data are recorded, who can see them, how the data may be used, and what recourse exists if the commitment is violated.
Evidence must answer the audience’s actual question and match the claim being made. A demonstration can show that a workflow is possible; comparison data can estimate an effect; a case can illustrate a mechanism. Two-sided refutational messages can be especially useful for informed or skeptical audiences because they acknowledge consequential objections and answer them rather than pretending they do not exist (Hovland et al., 1949; O’Keefe, 1999). The test is not whether an objection was mentioned, but whether a reasonable skeptic can inspect the comparison, assumptions, uncertainty, and conditions under which the proposal would be withdrawn.
Emotion gives those consequences value. Different emotions orient attention and action differently, so “make it emotional” is not a scientific prescription (Lerner et al., 2015). Fear appeals are most defensible when the threat is real and the recommended response is both effective and feasible; fear without efficacy can produce avoidance or defensive control rather than protective action (Rogers, 1975, 1983; Witte, 1992). Hope, pride, compassion, anger, or humor may also affect motivation, but the relevant question is whether the feeling is proportionate to the evidence and points toward a feasible action.
Three diagnostic questions keep the modes aligned:

Source: Why should this audience trust this messenger on this claim?
Evidence: What would a reasonable skeptic need to know, and what result would count against the proposal?
Stakes: What should the audience feel if it understood the consequences accurately?

For the platform, that means showing where duplication occurs, how the proposed workflow is expected to reduce it, what comparison produced the estimate, and which costs were included. The message can make avoidable frustration and pride in competent work salient. It should not manufacture fear of dismissal unless employment risk is real and openly addressed.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 30  Persuasion
text:
Two routes through a message






Figure 30.2: Message design can address obstacles involving attention, evidence, meaning, or efficacy, with belief revision, intention, and action as distinct outcomes.



The separate outcomes in Figure 30.2 keep three tests distinct: whether employees accept the claim, intend to act, and actually act. A detailed workflow comparison gives them material to inspect, but only if they have the time and motivation to use it. Others may initially rely on a colleague’s recommendation. The same presentation must therefore make careful scrutiny possible while giving a hurried reader a trustworthy entry point. Two influential theories explain how motivation and available attention affect this balance.
The elaboration likelihood model, developed by Petty and Cacioppo, uses central and peripheral routes as shorthand for the high- and low-elaboration ends of a continuum (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986; Petty & Briñol, 2012). Toward the high-elaboration end, people devote more thought to issue-relevant information. Toward the low-elaboration end, attitudes depend more on processes requiring little issue-relevant thought, such as familiarity, affect, or a simple source cue. Mixed processing is common.
What encourages this thought? Motivation rises when the issue is relevant to a person’s goals; ability depends on knowledge, clear presentation, available time, and freedom from distraction. When both are high, argument quality generally matters more. When either is low, simple cues tend to carry more weight. More thought still does not guarantee a fair assessment: people can devote considerable effort to defending an identity or their initial position.
Petty, Cacioppo, and Goldman (1981) demonstrated this with a study about comprehensive exams. When the issue was highly relevant to students, strong arguments produced more persuasion than weak arguments. When relevance was low, source expertise mattered more. More generally, the same variable can play different roles: source expertise can operate as a simple cue, be treated as evidence relevant to the merits, change the motivation to think, bias the thoughts generated, or change confidence in those thoughts. Its role must be identified rather than inferred from the label central or peripheral.
The heuristic-systematic model, developed by Chaiken, makes a related distinction between systematic processing and heuristic processing (Chaiken, 1980; Chaiken et al., 1989). Systematic processing involves comparatively careful evaluation of message content. Heuristic processing relies on simple rules such as “experts can be trusted,” “longer messages are stronger,” “consensus implies correctness,” or “likable people are credible.” The processes can co-occur rather than forcing an either–or classification.
One useful idea from this model is the sufficiency principle: people exert enough effort to reach a desired level of confidence, but not more. If a low-effort heuristic gives enough confidence, they may stop. If the decision is important or uncertainty remains, they may process more systematically.
These models connect persuasion to the rest of the book. Heuristics, fluency, authority, social proof, and affect can influence attitudes under lower elaboration, but they can also alter what people think about, how they interpret evidence, and how confident they are under higher elaboration. The scientific question is therefore not simply “Which route?” It is “How much issue-relevant thinking occurred, what did this variable do within that processing, and what changed—belief, evaluation, intention, or action?”
Attitudes formed or changed through greater elaboration tend, under appropriate conditions, to be more persistent, resistant to counterpersuasion, and predictive of behavior because they are connected to a more developed structure of supporting thoughts. Lower-elaboration change may be more fragile, though repetition, identity, learning, and later experience can stabilize it.
In the platform meeting, a dense technical report may help an interested specialist while overwhelming a colleague who has ten minutes between tasks. Use Table 30.3 to match the presentation to people’s motivation and ability to inspect it:



Table 30.3: Audience conditions and elaboration










Audience condition
Likely elaboration pattern
Design implication




High motivation and ability
Higher elaboration is likely; cues may still shape direction or confidence.
Use strong evidence, causal logic, uncertainty, and counterarguments.


High motivation, low ability
Elaboration is desired but constrained by comprehension, time, or load.
Reduce jargon, scaffold concepts, and show concrete mechanisms.


Low motivation, high ability
Lower elaboration is likely unless relevance increases; mixed processing remains possible.
Establish genuine relevance before adding detail.


Low motivation and ability
Lower-elaboration processes and simple cues are more influential.
Use transparent cues, one clear action, and avoid exploiting inattention.







How credibility, reciprocity, and other influence cues work
A colleague’s recommendation can help a busy employee decide whether the platform deserves a closer look. Yet visible approval may reflect independent experience or merely repeated endorsement of the same claim. Treating the two alike gives the proposal more support than the evidence warrants. The cues in Table 30.4 may provide information, alter attention or motivation, create obligation, or change behavior without changing belief. Judge each cue by whether it reliably tracks what it appears to signal.



Table 30.4: Influence cues should be audited for cue validity, independence, transparency, and agency





Cue
Legitimate information
Counterfeit form
Pause question




Reason-giving
The request has a relevant justification.
A reason-shaped phrase supplies no decision-relevant information.
Would this reason change my judgment if the word because disappeared?


Social proof
Independent others have relevant experience or information.
Purchased approval or correlated copying appears to be independent evidence.
How independent and relevant are these observations? See social norms and conformity.


Commitment
A freely chosen promise expresses an endorsed value or plan.
A small early commitment is used after important costs have been concealed.
Was the later cost visible, and is revision or exit still meaningful?


Reciprocity
Help or a genuine concession signals goodwill and supports cooperation.
An unwanted gift or inflated first request manufactures obligation.
Am I evaluating the proposal, or merely repaying a feeling of debt?


Authority
Accountable, domain-relevant expertise improves the evidence.
A title, uniform, confidence, or logo substitutes for reasons.
What does this source know, how do they know it, and who can check them? See authority and responsibility.


Scarcity
A real capacity or timing constraint changes the feasible choice set.
A fake countdown or artificial shortage creates urgency.
Is the constraint genuine, and does it change the option’s underlying value?


Liking
Rapport or similarity may convey shared context and cooperative intent.
Manufactured affinity spills into judgments of truth or competence.
Would the claim survive if I did not like the messenger?


Unity
Shared identity can imply mutual obligation and a longer relationship.
Belonging is made conditional on compliance, or outsiders bear hidden costs.
Who is excluded, who pays, and can a member disagree without losing belonging?






Classic experiments show why the pause matters. In a low-cost photocopier request, reason-giving increased compliance compared with asking without a reason, even when the stated reason added little information, but the pattern weakened when the request imposed a larger cost (Langer et al., 1978).


Small commitments, concessions, and self-persuasion
Consider two invitations to employees. One asks them to test the platform for ten minutes before considering a six-week pilot. Another begins with a large rollout request and, after resistance, retreats to the pilot. The final request may be identical, but the preceding interaction gives it a different meaning.
The foot-in-the-door technique starts with a small request before a larger related one. Freedman and Fraser (1966) found that agreement to an initial request could increase later compliance. The door-in-the-face technique begins with a larger request that is rejected, followed by a smaller one; Cialdini and colleagues (1975) studied how this apparent concession can encourage reciprocal compliance. Accepting a request does not establish that someone now believes the proposal is good. Chapter 36 applies the distinction between concessions and independent value to bargaining.
Self-persuasion concerns reasons people generate themselves. Ask employees what a worthwhile pilot would need to demonstrate, and let them propose the conditions under which they would support it. Their answers can make the decision intelligible and reveal defects in the proposal. They can also make a position easier to defend: Chapter 7 distinguishes dissonance reduction from self-perception, two accounts of how our actions can influence our attitudes. These are possible mechanisms, not interchangeable explanations for every commitment effect.
A useful invitation leaves room to reject the pilot or change one’s mind. A small initial “yes” should not hide later costs, manufacture obligation, or be treated as consent to a larger commitment.

title: 30  Persuasion
section: Diagnose the audience before designing the message
text:
Diagnose the audience before designing the message
The barrier matrix becomes useful when the audience can correct it. Ask a few employees to explain the proposed change in their own words, identify their strongest objection, and describe what would make a trial worthwhile. An efficiency argument may miss a concern about professional judgment; moral reframing studies show that the values used to justify a proposal can affect its reception (Feinberg & Willer, 2015). Adapting the explanation should make the real reasons accessible, without concealing the speaker’s aims or the proposal’s costs.
Then distinguish agreement from action. Employees may accept the case for coordination yet lack training time. “Support innovation” leaves that obstacle untouched; “test this workflow for six weeks with two hours of training provided” creates a decision they can evaluate. Chapter 32 develops the message-building routine.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 30  Persuasion
text:
Resistance and reactance
Employees who hear “Only people afraid of accountability oppose this system” now have a further reason to object. Their freedom to disagree has become part of the dispute.
Reactance is motivation to restore a freedom perceived as threatened (Brehm, 1966; Brehm & Brehm, 1981). It is one explanation for resistance, alongside reasonable disagreement, distrust, competing priorities, and practical constraints. Calling every objection reactance would simply repeat the original mistake of ignoring its content.
An autonomy-supportive message can explain a strong recommendation while acknowledging concerns and identifying real choices. Self-determination theory connects the quality of motivation with experiences of autonomy, competence, and relatedness (Deci & Ryan, 2000). That framework offers reasons to provide choice and support. Where a decision is mandatory, communicate that limit honestly and specify what remains open to input.
Respecting the audience’s judgment also means helping it evaluate arguments encountered later. Employees may understand the present proposal yet subsequently hear a misleading claim about what the pilot can establish. Repeating the original presentation may leave them unprepared to assess that claim. Inoculation theory asks whether preparing people to recognize and answer such arguments can protect their judgment. McGuire (1964) proposed that people can be made more resistant to persuasion by exposing them to weakened counterarguments and refutations, much like a vaccine exposes the body to a weakened threat. Inoculation messages warn people that they may encounter persuasion attempts, present common misleading arguments, and refute them. Meta-analyses suggest that inoculation can build resistance across domains (Banas & Rains, 2010).
One application is to explain a misleading technique before people encounter it: show how a graph can exaggerate a change, then let the audience inspect another example. Test whether the exercise improves later judgment.
Corrections also deserve a realistic expectation. A broad effect in which corrections routinely strengthen false beliefs has proved elusive (Wood & Porter, 2019), although a corrected claim can continue to influence reasoning. Clear corrections that offer an alternative explanation can help people replace the account they previously used (Lewandowsky et al., 2012).
When a person is weighing reasons both for and against change, a conversation may be more useful than another rebuttal. Clinical motivational interviewing offers an example of eliciting those reasons while respecting autonomy (Miller & Rollnick, 2013). Its conversational stance can inform workplace discussions without making a management meeting equivalent to a clinical intervention.
The platform pilot should preserve meaningful choice where possible: teams can compare two workflows, propose safeguards, and examine results before scale-up. Participation makes concerns testable inputs.

Calling the pilot “voluntary” is insufficient if refusing the manager’s request could affect promotion. Specify what saying no would mean, as well as the proposal’s costs, uncertainty, and purpose. The actual freedom to decline must support the reassuring phrase in the presentation.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 30  Persuasion
text:
The platform proposal, redesigned
The original message said, in effect, “The evidence shows that this platform is efficient; therefore use it.” The redesigned proposal follows the audience’s model instead of ignoring it.
First, it begins in shared reality: teams are losing time to duplicate files, conflicting versions, and invisible handoffs. Second, it names the concern fairly: a shared system can improve coordination and create surveillance if access rules are vague. Third, it offers evidence matched to the claims: workflow data for duplication, a live demonstration for usability, written governance for data use, and a limited pilot for predicted time savings. Fourth, it makes identity and value explicit: the aim is to protect professional time and judgment, not replace them. Finally, it proposes an actionable and revisable step: two volunteer teams test the system for six weeks against predeclared measures, with training time, an independent feedback channel, and a decision rule for stopping, revising, or scaling.
The account of wasted time should illuminate an observed problem; invented threats of dismissal would distort the choice. Check the messenger, example, evidence, and requested action against the proposal’s stated purpose. If their effectiveness depends on hiding a cost or manufacturing an obligation, revise them.
Ethos, logos, and pathos now support the same update. A trusted project leader and a technical specialist share the message. The causal argument is inspectable. The emotional stakes—avoidable frustration, competent work, and fear of misuse—fit the situation. Motivation and ability are supported by relevance, demonstration, training, and time. Resistance is not treated as a defect; it helps specify the test.
Successful persuasion gives a defensible model appropriate weight while preserving the audience’s capacity to judge and refuse. The pilot gives both sides evidence for accepting, revising, or rejecting the proposal. Building an Evidence-Aligned Message turns this diagnosis into a usable draft.

title: 30  Persuasion
text:
Practice Lab
Choose one organizational change that has met resistance. Produce a one-page persuasion brief containing: the desired response; the audience’s current model; a completed barrier matrix; one claim-evidence-warrant chain; the messenger and why that source deserves weight; the appropriate emotional stake; a feasible next action; and one observation that would make you revise or withdraw the proposal. End with the transparency test: would you still use this design if the audience could see the brief?
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 30  Persuasion
text:
Take it forward
Return to the platform proposal. More efficiency statistics will help only if uncertainty about efficiency is what holds the audience back. A useful proposal lets employees examine the consequences they care about and gives leaders a reason to revise their plan when the objections are sound. The next chapter asks when a story can make those consequences easier to understand, and when it makes the proposal feel better supported than it is.

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Learning goals
Narrative turns information into simulated meaning
Sara, a fictional team leader, reads an anonymous comment about her meetings: “We wish we could tell you bad news before it becomes an emergency.” She had thought solving problems quietly protected her team. Now she wonders whether her habit of arriving with an answer has made people reluctant to bring her a question.
Compare that scene with the statement “Leaders should encourage upward feedback.” The statement is clear, but the scene gives us something to investigate: why might a capable, well-intentioned leader make it difficult to speak? Following Sara can make the problem easier to imagine. It can also make her explanation feel true before we have tested it.
This chapter asks what a story adds to a message, and when the addition helps people judge well.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Distinguish a story from information, an example, and a vivid anecdote.
Explain how stories influence attention, simulation, identity, emotion, memory, and resistance.
Diagnose when a story adds decision-relevant meaning, when it adds distortion, and what evidence must accompany it.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
What is a story?
For this chapter, a story follows someone pursuing a goal through events that have consequences. Look for a protagonist, goal, obstacle, stakes, choice, and change. Sara wants to protect her team; a comment raises doubts about how she has tried to do it.
An example can clarify a concept without developing an unfolding situation: asking each team member for a concern illustrates upward feedback. An anecdote is a particular case, which may or may not develop into a story.
Bruner (1986, 1990) distinguished narrative thinking, organized around agents and consequences, from reasoning through categories and general principles. Both can help us understand a problem. Fisher (1984, 1987) likewise distinguished a story’s coherence from its fit with an audience’s experiences and values. These accounts explain why a story may feel meaningful; neither coherence nor familiarity establishes that its causal account is correct.
Practitioner writers such as Lisa Cron and Will Storr offer useful craft questions: What does the protagonist want? What changes? Which belief becomes less workable?

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
section: How a story connects events, choices, and consequences
text:
How a story connects events, choices, and consequences
A report might say, “The team introduced anonymous feedback and monthly check-ins.” To turn that information into a story, we need a person with a reason to care and events that alter the situation.
In our fictional continuation, Sara initially dismisses the comment as unfair. Then she rereads the last month’s meeting notes and finds that nearly every proposed solution was her own. At the next meeting, she waits for colleagues to describe the problem before offering an answer. One raises a delivery risk that has not appeared on the dashboard.
The story makes the tension between helping and taking over visible. It also embeds a hypothesis: Sara’s meeting style discouraged useful information. The scene makes that hypothesis easy to examine.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Story as model updating






Figure 31.1: A narrative-design template begins with the audience’s current model, introduces meaningful trouble, and offers a candidate new model, supporting evidence, and a possible action.



The previous chapter treated a model as an explanation of what is happening and what to expect. A story can make a change in that explanation visible: Sara begins by equating quick solutions with helpful leadership, encounters information that troubles this view, and tries another way of running a meeting.
The five-part route in Figure 31.1 turns this change of explanation into a writing template. Ask what the protagonist believed, what challenged that belief, and what further evidence would justify changing it. Sara’s discovery of a previously unreported risk gives her a reason to investigate the meeting process.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Why facts alone can fail
“Invite more participation” gives Sara a clear instruction. Yet it leaves out the difficulty that made the instruction necessary: her effort to protect the team by supplying answers may be keeping problems out of view. Unless that conflict becomes visible, readers can agree with the rule without recognizing the behavior it needs to change.
Following Sara’s hesitation lets readers examine why a choice is difficult, whom it affects, and how its consequences could unfold. A story earns its place when it supplies this missing understanding; a direct factual statement serves the reader when the decision is already clear.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Four mechanisms of narrative persuasion
A reader may follow Sara closely and still leave without understanding how to change a meeting. Another may remember her embarrassment while forgetting the information that challenged her belief. Holding attention, making a choice understandable, and leaving a useful lesson are different jobs. To design the story, identify which job the message needs. Research and theory suggest several overlapping ways stories can affect readers, including absorption in the narrative, identification with a character, and imagining consequences (Green & Brock, 2000; Cohen, 2001; van Laer et al., 2014). The four families in Table 31.1 connect these mechanisms to a writing decision and a risk: earning attention, for example, is useful only if the suspense serves a relevant question.



Table 31.1: Narrative mechanisms, design questions, and risks










Mechanism family
Design question
Risk




Attention and curiosity
What unresolved question earns attention?
Manufactured suspense can hide weak relevance.


Identity and self-reference
Whose goals and constraints can the audience understand?
A single perspective can erase affected others.


Emotion, memory, and reduced resistance
What should matter and remain retrievable?
Feeling can exceed the evidence and bypass scrutiny.


Simulation and causal understanding
What mechanism links choice to consequence?
Coherence can be mistaken for causal proof.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
1. Attention and curiosity
The comment Sara receives creates an unresolved question: could the effort she regards as helpful be making the team less able to ask for help? Readers have a reason to continue because the answer matters to what she should do next. That is the useful role of curiosity in a story opening.
Background earns attention when it helps resolve such a question. “Our organization was founded in 1986 and has always valued innovation” gives a reader little to investigate. “The new system solved the problem in every demonstration, yet no one used it” presents a discrepancy worth explaining. The opening needs enough context to make the difficulty intelligible, rather than a long history before the difficulty appears.

Transportation
Narrative transportation refers to mental absorption into a story world. When transported, people devote attention, imagery, and emotion to the unfolding narrative. They are not merely evaluating claims from the outside; they are experiencing a situation from within. Green and Brock’s work made transportation a central concept in narrative persuasion, and later research, including meta-analytic work by van Laer and colleagues, supports its importance.
While absorbed, readers can imagine choices within the situation as well as assess claims about it. In teaching, this provides a reason to introduce a problem before its definition: the term answers a question the learner now understands. It also creates an obligation to return from the imagined situation to an examination of the evidence.
Transportation also creates risk. A compelling story can smuggle assumptions into experience. A political film can make a misleading causal story feel true. A corporate change story can make a strategy feel inevitable while hiding alternatives. Ethical storytellers must ask: What world am I inviting the audience to enter? What assumptions does that world make? Whose perspective is centered? Whose perspective is missing? What will feel true after the story ends?
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
2. Identity and self-reference

Identification
From outside the meeting, it is easy to tell Sara to stop supplying every answer. From her position, holding back means changing the very behavior she has regarded as helpful leadership. Readers need access to that tension to understand what the proposed change asks of her. Identification occurs when audience members imaginatively take the perspective of a character, share goals or emotions, and experience events partly from inside the character’s situation. Identification differs from liking. You may identify with a character you do not entirely like because you understand their motives or feel their struggle from within.
Following a character can shift the question from “What do I think of this person?” toward “What would this situation be like from their position?” Sara need not be wholly admirable for readers to understand her wish to appear competent.
A useful character has intelligible reasons and meaningful constraints. Showing why speaking up risks embarrassment, for example, gives an audience more to consider than labeling a colleague timid. Another character may experience the same meeting differently.


Self-reference
A reader may connect Sara’s predicament to a meeting they have led or attended. That connection gives the abstract issue a personal reference point. It can also narrow interpretation: a leader who recognizes only their own good intentions may miss how the meeting feels to a junior colleague.
Use identification to expand the perspectives available for judgment. After following Sara, ask what the quiet team member wanted, what made speaking costly, and how the same exchange looked from that seat.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
3. Emotion, memory, and reduced resistance
Stories persuade because they connect information to value. Emotion is not merely decoration added to cognition. It helps prioritize attention, encode memory, guide action, and signal what matters. In a story, emotion arises from stakes: someone wants something, something could be lost, and the outcome is uncertain. Without stakes, there is little reason to care.
A common mistake in academic and managerial communication is to remove all emotion in the name of objectivity. Objectivity is important for evidence, but persuasion requires significance. A story can preserve accuracy while making significance visible. “The project was delayed by six months” is information. The meaning becomes clearer when we understand who was affected: a small supplier that invested in new equipment, expected a contract, lost revenue, laid off workers, and became reluctant to join future innovation partnerships.
Stories can also improve retrieval when their causal and emotional structure organizes otherwise disconnected details. People may remember what someone wanted, what blocked them, what they chose, and what happened. The story can provide a retrieval path for the principle, although vividness may also preserve an unrepresentative case better than the qualifying evidence.

Reduced resistance
A teacher may use a story to help students enter a difficult choice before defending a position. The same absorption that makes the choice accessible can leave less attention for questioning its assumptions. The teaching task is therefore to invite participation and then reopen the account to examination. Green and Brock (2000) linked transportation with story-consistent beliefs and evaluations across their experiments.
After the story, ask students which assumptions made its ending seem reasonable and what would happen if those assumptions were wrong. This turns absorption into an opportunity to examine the account.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
4. Simulation and causal understanding
Students may readily endorse “report unfavorable results” or “look for shared interests” without seeing why either becomes difficult in practice. A favor can create felt obligation; an urgent demand can hide the interest that would make a trade possible. If teaching stops at the rule, the obstacle remains unexamined. Stories let students rehearse the decision before facing its consequences: What do we know? What is uncertain? What are the options? What are the risks? What would I do?
Such rehearsal can help people trace a proposed causal sequence: a favor creates an obligation, the obligation makes disclosure uncomfortable, and withholding information changes the eventual decision. The value lies in exposing those steps for examination, including where the imagined sequence could unfold differently.
An ethics lecture that says, “Conflicts of interest are dangerous” may be less effective than a story in which a researcher accepts a small favor, then a larger favor, and gradually finds it harder to report unfavorable results. The story simulates moral drift. A negotiation lecture that says, “Positions hide interests” may be less effective than a story in which two teams fight over a deadline until they discover that one side needs symbolic reassurance and the other needs operational flexibility.

Causal stories and causal evidence
Stories persuade because they organize causality. They show how one thing led to another: because the protagonist believed X, they did Y; because they did Y, consequence Z followed; because Z happened, the old belief had to be revised. A coherent sequence can help a reader organize scattered evidence, while also making a missing link easy to overlook.
Organizations do something similar after success or failure. They construct stories: the market changed, leadership failed, customers were not ready, the technology was immature, incentives were wrong, or the team lacked discipline. The story determines what the organization learns. If the story is wrong, the organization learns the wrong lesson.
This creates a discipline: distinguish causal story from causal evidence. What mechanism does the story imply? What evidence supports that mechanism? What alternative story could explain the same events? What base rates or comparison cases are missing? What role did luck play? What structural factors are hidden by focusing on one character?






NoteResearch Lens: following the same story



Naturalistic neuroscience has found time-locked similarities in brain activity when people encounter the same films or stories, and speaker–listener coupling has been associated with comprehension (Hasson et al., 2004, 2008; Stephens et al., 2010). Selection and sequence can guide audience attention.1
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
The power—and danger—of one
Imagine receiving five one-dollar bills for completing a survey, then opening a request to donate some of them to charity. One letter introduces an individual child; another describes the scale of the food crisis; a third combines the child with those statistics. Would the combination preserve the child’s emotional force while adding a sense of proportion?
Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic (2007, Study 3) tested these three appeals with 159 people recruited on a university campus, who could donate from a small payment. Average donations were $2.38 for the identifiable child alone, $1.14 for statistics alone, and $1.43 for the combined appeal. Adding the statistics reduced giving relative to the child alone. The result makes the design problem harder: information about scale can weaken the response that a personal account first creates.
A compelling case still needs a denominator. One vivid victim can dominate attention while many unseen victims receive little; a striking customer complaint can similarly outweigh a much larger service record. The availability problem returns here through a narrative we can readily imagine and recall.
The ethical task is to help people care and judge proportionately, even when those goals pull in different directions. State what the individual case illustrates, how representative it is, and what different uses of help could achieve. Presenting the story and the wider evidence in separate stages is one possible design to test, not a remedy established by this experiment. Evaluate comprehension and the quality of the resulting decision alongside immediate donations.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Practice Lab
Select one existing message that uses a story—or one abstract claim for which a story has been proposed. Complete a one-page narrative diagnosis:

Decision: What belief or choice should the message help the audience examine?
Narrative job: Which one function is most needed—attention, simulation, identity and self-reference, or emotion and memory?
Form: Is a story necessary, or would a direct statement, example, comparison, or case make the point with less distortion?
Evidence companion: If a story is retained, name the denominator or scale estimate, relevant comparison, evidence for the proposed mechanism, strongest alternative account, and one affected perspective the story leaves out.
Verdict: Retain, replace, or omit the story, and give the reason in one sentence.

Chapter 32 provides the construction workflow if your diagnosis gives the story a clear job.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Take it forward
A story can make an unfamiliar problem worth attending to, but its vividness cannot tell us how common the problem is. When you retell a case, carry that distinction with it: explain what the story illustrates and which broader claim still needs evidence.

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Learning goals
Use narrative to carry evidence, not to replace it
A restaurant owner receives a pitch for a forecasting assistant. The first slide lists algorithms; the second celebrates the development team. By the third, the owner still cannot tell whether the tool will help decide how much food to prepare tomorrow.
Imagine rebuilding the pitch around that decision. Too much preparation wastes ingredients; too little loses sales. The proposed tool might help, but the owner needs to see how it uses the restaurant’s records, what evidence supports its forecasts, and what trying it would cost.
We will use this fictional pitch to build a message that earns attention and gives the audience enough information to decide. A story is optional; a defensible claim and a clear request are essential.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Build one message with STORY as the primary workflow; use AND–BUT–THEREFORE only as an optional compression test.
Match the strength of each claim to appropriate evidence, comparison, and uncertainty.
Produce and audit a message that remains accurate, dignified, and genuinely rejectable.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Design the change

Begin with the audience’s current story
Ask the owner how preparation decisions are currently made and where mistakes become costly. An experienced owner may already forecast informally using bookings, weather, and local events. Beginning with “Restaurants need data-driven decisions” would overlook that knowledge and give the owner a reason to distrust the rest of the pitch.


Hidden resistance and protected identity
Find out what makes trying the tool unattractive. The owner may doubt its accuracy, lack clean records, or worry that staff will treat recommendations as orders. Identity can also make a popular choice unattractive: Berger and Heath (2007) found more divergence from others in product domains that participants regarded as identity-signaling. For this owner, adoption might imply surrendering a valued skill. Ask whether that concern is present before treating it as the explanation. Once the concern is clear, choose a response that addresses it. A demonstration can address usability; a pilot may test forecasts; explicit override rules address control. If the product cannot meet an important constraint, the proposal needs work before the message does.


Protagonist, goal, and stakes
If a story would help, follow a person facing the decision. Picture the owner checking yesterday’s waste against today’s bookings, knowing that a cautious preparation plan could leave popular dishes unavailable. This scene gives the audience a goal and a trade-off. It does not need an invented crisis or a heroic founder.


Conflict, obstacle, and misbelief
The obstacle should make the proposed response worth considering. Perhaps the owner has sales records but cannot readily combine them into a daily forecast. That problem suggests a role for the tool. If the real problem is unreliable deliveries, better demand forecasts may help little.
Do not assume the audience’s current belief is a “misbelief” simply because it conflicts with the proposal. The pitch should reveal a limitation that can be investigated, with room for the investigation to vindicate the current practice.


Turning point, evidence, and change
A useful turning point changes what the audience can see. Comparing a forecast with the owner’s existing estimate may reveal a promising improvement, or it may reveal that the tool adds little. Either result should change what the speaker claims.
In a fictional story, label the episode as imagined. In a factual case, report what was actually observed and what alternatives remain. An illustrative ending cannot establish demand, effectiveness, or savings; those claims need their own evidence.






NoteOptional research note: give curiosity a question





Imagine showing the restaurant owner two days with similar bookings but very different amounts of leftover food. Before presenting the software, ask what might explain the difference. The owner now has something specific to investigate: what did the booking count miss, and could that information improve tomorrow’s preparation?
Loewenstein’s (1994) information-gap account of curiosity explains why a partly understood situation can invite further attention. Curiosity arises when people become aware of a gap between what they know and what they want to know. Simply presenting an unfamiliar subject may leave them without enough understanding to notice a particular gap. A recognizable starting point and an answerable question can give the missing information a place to fit.
For this pitch, use the owner’s experience to make the question meaningful, then show how it could be answered. A comparison of forecasts with actual demand might reveal useful information, or show that the owner’s existing judgment performs just as well. Either result resolves something worth knowing. Curiosity helps invite the investigation. Disclose costs and limitations when they become relevant to the decision, even if withholding them would make the presentation more suspenseful.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
section: Build the message with one primary workflow
text:
Build the message with one primary workflow






Figure 32.1: An ethical communication framework braids human meaning with base rates, mechanisms, comparisons, and uncertainty.



A pitch can make the owner care about wasted food and still leave tomorrow’s preparation decision unanswered. The two strands in Figure 32.1 show what must fit together: the story makes the owner’s stakes understandable, while evidence lets the owner judge how common the problem is and whether the proposed explanation holds. The following five prompts keep that decision visible throughout the draft, with as much narrative as the message needs.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
The STORY framework
STORY is this book’s practical mnemonic: Shared reality, Trouble, Opportunity, Reasons, and Yes. “Yes” names the decision being requested; a well-informed “no” remains a legitimate outcome. The tests in Table 32.1 keep each part tied to that decision, from a recognizable opening to a request the audience can evaluate and decline.



Table 32.1: STORY as an operational model-update sequence










Letter
Function
Test




S · Shared reality
Start with an accepted goal, behavior, change, or constraint.
Is the opening recognizable without jargon or a claim the audience already rejects?


T · Trouble
Identify a consequential difficulty the current approach leaves unresolved.
Is the difficulty real, and does the proposed response address it?


O · Opportunity
Explain the better model or mechanism of progress.
Does it resolve this trouble, rather than merely advertise a feature?


R · Reasons
Supply the evidence needed for the pivotal claim, including a relevant comparison and uncertainty.
Can the audience inspect the support, and does it match the claim?


Y · Yes
Ask for a specific decision or next step.
Who does what, by when, at what cost—and can the audience genuinely decline?






For a brief version, try AND–BUT–THEREFORE (ABT): the shared situation, the consequential difficulty, and the proposed response. Use it as a compression test. A narrative index based on counts of connecting words can flag a draft that keeps adding information without establishing a difficulty or consequence. Such a writing heuristic does not measure whether the causal argument is valid or whether an audience understands it. Inspect what the connections actually mean.
Here is an imagined pitch built from those moves. Its numbers illustrate the owner’s decision; they are not findings about a real restaurant or product.

Shared reality: You already plan tomorrow’s preparation using bookings and experience, and you need enough food without tying money up in leftovers.
Trouble: Suppose you prepare 100 portions and sell 82. The 18 left over reveal a forecasting error, but preparing only 82 tomorrow could create a shortage if demand changes.
Opportunity: We propose comparing your estimate with a forecast built from sales history, bookings, and local events. The useful question is whether it adds information your current approach misses.
Reasons: A working prototype would establish that a forecast can be produced. It would not establish that following it reduces waste. We need forecasts recorded before demand is known and a comparison with your existing estimates.
Yes: Would you consider a four-week trial in which both estimates are recorded, while you keep control of preparation? We would agree on the data, staff time, costs, and criteria for continuing before the trial begins; either side could decide the evidence does not justify adoption.

The ending requests a test proportionate to the evidence.
After drafting, read the message from the owner’s position. Is tomorrow’s preparation decision still visible, or has the pitch drifted back to celebrating the software? Keep a statistic when it helps evaluate the proposal, and remove it when it merely makes the slide look authoritative.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Match evidence to the claim
The owner needs to know whether using the software improves preparation enough to justify its cost. A demonstration that the software runs leaves that question open, just as observed adoption would not by itself show that users benefit. Even an established benefit may cost more to deliver than it is worth. Start by identifying the claim on which the decision depends, then use Table 32.2 to ask what evidence could test it and what that evidence would leave unestablished.



Table 32.2: Match the pivotal claim to evidence that can test it











Claim to be tested
Decision question
Evidence that can address it
What that evidence alone does not establish




Need or problem
Does the problem exist, for whom, how often, and with what consequence?
Representative surveys, administrative or behavioral records, systematic observation, interviews with a clear sampling purpose, prevalence and distribution data
That the proposed solution works or that every affected group experiences the same problem


Mechanism
Why should the proposed change produce the predicted result?
Discriminating process measures, mechanism-specific predictions, experiments or comparisons that vary the proposed pathway, triangulated qualitative process evidence
Population-scale effectiveness, durability, or affordability


Feasibility
Can the intervention or product be delivered reliably under the relevant constraints?
Working prototypes, technical tests, operational pilots, failure logs, capacity and safety checks
Demand, beneficial impact, or viable economics


Adoption or behavior
Will eligible users choose, use, return to, pay for, or comply with it under realistic conditions?
Observed uptake, use, retention, purchase, referral, or completion with a stated denominator and comparison period
Why behavior changed or whether use improves welfare


Causal impact
Does the intervention change the intended outcome relative to a credible counterfactual?
Randomized experiments or defensible quasi-experimental and comparative designs, with outcome definitions, uncertainty, attrition, and relevant follow-up
Generalization to every setting, implementation capacity, or net value


Economics
Can the model create and sustain value after relevant costs, risks, and alternatives?
Transparent cost and revenue data, unit economics, sensitivity analysis, opportunity costs, and distribution of gains and losses
Causal or social benefit merely because the activity is financially viable






Not every message needs all six claim types. A policy recommendation may hinge on need, causal impact, distribution, and cost; an early prototype may appropriately make only a feasibility claim. For the Reasons row of STORY, record the pivotal claim, its type, the strongest available evidence, the relevant source or comparison, and what remains unestablished. If the available evidence cannot support the necessary claim, weaken the claim, change the requested action, or collect better evidence.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Fluency: power and danger
A clear layout and familiar language help the owner inspect the evidence. They can also make a weak claim feel comfortable: repetition increases familiarity, which can increase perceived truth (Hasher et al., 1977; Fazio et al., 2015). The distinction from Chapter 13 therefore matters when editing: make the comparison easier to check, rather than merely making the conclusion easier to repeat.
For the restaurant owner, show waste in units they can reconstruct—portions or ingredient costs over a stated period—and identify the comparison. Resolve the question that earned attention rather than using suspense to delay an inconvenient limitation.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
The story-evidence braid
Return to the owner preparing food for tomorrow. The scene makes a cost understandable, but only data can show how common that cost is or whether the proposed tool reduces it. The aim is informed judgment: retain the human stakes while making the denominator and comparison inspectable (Slovic, 2007; Dahlstrom, 2014). As the donation experiment in Chapter 31 showed, adding statistics can reduce a story’s immediate motivational effect (Small et al., 2007). The braid is an ethical design principle, not a demonstrated recipe for maximizing persuasion.
A useful draft can move from the scene to evidence, explain the proposed mechanism, and then return to the decision. If there are no pilot results yet, say so and request a trial. If there are results, show who participated, what was compared, and what remains uncertain. The ending should reflect the evidence available, even when that makes the story less tidy.

Check the selected details for an omitted affected group, a rare event made to seem common, or one person’s success presented as something everyone can achieve. The ethical audit below can then locate such omissions in actual sentences.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
section: Adapt the message without changing its discipline
text:
Adapt the message without changing its discipline
A message built for the restaurant owner cannot simply be relabeled for a student, patient, or negotiating partner. Each faces a different decision and needs different evidence before acting; carrying over the scene while losing that decision turns adaptation into decoration. STORY travels across teaching, leadership, health, policy, entrepreneurship, and negotiation by preserving the questions that organize the message: start from the stakeholder’s consequential decision, make the trouble specific, state the proposed mechanism, match reasons to claims, and end with an action that can be refused.
In teaching, a case should create the need for a concept and then yield to analysis. In leadership, a change story should acknowledge loss and protect valued identity rather than invent a “burning platform.” In health and policy, a patient or citizen story should be paired with prevalence, effects, alternatives, and uncertainty. In entrepreneurship, the stakeholder—not the product or founder—is usually the protagonist. In negotiation, a short story can explain why an interest matters without pretending that one side’s account is the whole situation.
Across these settings, the important adaptation is to the audience’s decision and available evidence. A compelling scene is useful only if it helps that audience evaluate the proposal.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Common mistakes

Speaker-first opening: beginning with the organization, product, or research team before establishing the audience’s decision. Start with shared reality and a consequential stake.
Decorative trouble: adding a dramatic but that changes the subject without exposing why the current model fails. The trouble must make the proposed explanation necessary to consider.
Anecdote as denominator: allowing one vivid case to imply frequency, representativeness, or causal force. Pair the case with the comparison or distribution needed to judge scale.
Evidence dump: presenting impressive numbers that do not test the pivotal claim. State what each item of evidence should change and what it cannot establish.
Inevitable yes: ending as though understanding obliges agreement. Name the decision, costs, alternatives, uncertainty, and a meaningful way to decline, revise, or stop.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Worked transformations

Worked example: structured hiring
Persuasive goal: convince managers to use structured hiring interviews.
Information-only version: “Structured interviews have higher validity than unstructured interviews. Comparable questions and job-relevant criteria can reduce inconsistent judgment.”
Fictional story version: Maria had hired dozens of people and believed she was good at reading candidates. In one interview, a candidate from a familiar university spoke confidently about teamwork and leadership. Maria felt an immediate connection. Another candidate was quieter, less polished, and from an institution Maria did not know well. The team hired the first candidate. Six months later, performance problems appeared: missed deadlines, poor collaboration, and resistance to feedback. During a later review, Maria reread the interview notes and realized there were almost none. She had recorded impressions, not evidence. When the company introduced structured interviews, she resisted at first. They felt mechanical. But after using the same job-relevant questions and scoring evidence separately, she noticed something uncomfortable: her “intuition” had often been confidence responding to confidence. The structure did not replace her judgment. It gave her judgment something better to work with.
This story begins inside the manager’s existing belief: “I can read people.” It introduces a problem: a confident choice is followed by poor performance. It creates a turning point: rereading the notes reveals the absence of evidence. It offers a new model: structure improves judgment rather than replacing it. The example makes the reason for structure understandable; Chapter 41 examines the comparative evidence on structured judgment. The missing job-relevant records are the reason she cannot evaluate that process reliably afterward.


Worked example: negotiation deadline
Persuasive goal: explain why a delivery deadline matters without making it sound like an arbitrary demand.
Information-only version: “We need delivery by June 1.”
Fictional story version: Last year, a component arrived four days late. The delay looked small on paper. But the production line had been scheduled tightly, customers had already booked installation dates, and workers were assigned to shifts that depended on the component arriving. By June 5, the line was stopped, customer orders were rescheduled, and the team had to explain a preventable delay. This year, the June 1 date is not a preference; it is the point that keeps the rest of the system from failing. We are willing to discuss price, batch size, or earlier partial delivery, but we need a plan that protects that date.
This story explains an interest without revealing a reservation value. It humanizes the constraint and opens problem-solving rather than simply asserting a position.

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
section: Edit for clarity without confusing fluency with truth
text:
Edit for clarity without confusing fluency with truth
Once the message is evidence-aligned, make it easier to process: use concrete verbs, legible comparisons, one governing tension, and a visible denominator. Familiar language can provide an entry point and one meaningful surprise can create attention. These are editing choices, not reasons to believe the claim.
Numbers, images, and metaphors should make magnitude or mechanism inspectable. Ask what each representation reveals, what it hides, and whether the audience could reconstruct the underlying quantity. A memorable metaphor may help organize a claim, but its average persuasive advantage is small and context-dependent (Sopory & Dillard, 2002).
A message worth sharing is not necessarily worth believing. People may pass content on because it expresses identity, creates connection, signals competence, helps someone, or supports collective action (Berger & Milkman, 2012; Falk et al., 2013; Baek et al., 2017). Optimize first for accuracy and inspectability, then for transmission.
An anecdote may illustrate a concept, and a case may contain a story. Use Table 32.3 to choose the form by the communication task; the labels describe overlapping uses rather than exclusive categories.



Table 32.3: Choose the form that supplies what the audience needs to understand











Communication task
Form and function
Example
Limitation




Report facts
A factual summary states events, features, dates, or numbers.
“The team introduced monthly check-ins.”
May not show why the change was difficult or meaningful.


Clarify a concept
An example illustrates the concept.
“Asking each colleague for a risk illustrates upward feedback.”
May not create tension, cause, stakes, or transformation.


Make an individual experience concrete
An anecdote provides a vivid individual case.
“One customer waited three hours and gave up.”
Can be unrepresentative and can overpower base rates.


Support analysis
A case describes a real or hypothetical situation to examine.
A company adopts a feedback system and engagement rises.
A useful case can remain descriptive; it need not contain an inner transformation.


Show action and its consequences
A story follows motivated action under constraint and change through cause and consequence.
Sara resists anonymous feedback, sees that her competence has become a bottleneck, changes her meeting ritual, and creates a habit of honesty.
Can mislead if causality, evidence, or representativeness is distorted.









Table 32.4: An ethical story audit










Principle
Guiding question
Warning sign




Truthfulness
Is the story factual, composite, or fictional, and is that clear?
Invented realism or altered key facts.


Representativeness
Does the case reflect a broader pattern supported by evidence?
Anecdote pretending to be a base rate.


Dignity
Are people more than props, victims, villains, or stereotypes?
Humans reduced to symbols or emotional instruments.


Complexity
Is causality simplified without becoming false?
One villain explains everything.


Transparency
Does the audience know what kind of story this is?
Composite or illustrative stories presented as single real cases.


Evidence alignment
Does the story illuminate evidence rather than replace it?
The story is used to hide weak or missing evidence.


Agency
Does the story expand action possibilities?
Fear, shame, or identity threat without a path forward.


Plurality
Are important missing perspectives acknowledged?
The story prevents the audience from seeing anything else.


Proportion
Does emotional force match the real significance of the issue?
Rare cases presented as common without scale.


Actionability
Does the story point toward a meaningful response?
Distress without a credible path.






Before sharing the draft, use Table 32.4 to check whether its emotional force, treatment of people, and requested action remain proportionate to the evidence. A vivid case needs revision if it leaves the audience with a mistaken impression of how common the problem is.

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Practice Lab
Build a one-page STORY brief for one research claim, policy, product, leadership request, or negotiation proposal. The single brief contains five rows: Shared reality, Trouble, Opportunity, Reasons, and Yes. In the Reasons row, identify the pivotal claim, classify it using Table 32.2, give the strongest available evidence and comparison, state the uncertainty, and name what the evidence does not establish. At the bottom, answer three audit questions: Is any case presented as representative without a denominator? Can the audience meaningfully decline or revise the requested action? Which one sentence should be weakened or removed if the evidence is insufficient? Use the completed brief to deliver a 90-second message. Peer feedback identifies one unsupported inferential jump and one concrete repair. Working alone, mark every claim that needs outside evidence, check the pivotal one against its source, and revise the brief before delivering it again.

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Take it forward
Read your draft from the audience’s position. Can a reader identify the problem, inspect the evidence behind the pivotal claim, and understand the next decision? Revise any sentence whose force depends on hiding a material fact.
Even a carefully drafted message leaves some meaning for the audience to infer. Chapter 33 follows what happens when another person interprets the message and gives the speaker a chance to correct a misunderstanding.

title: 33  Communication
text:
Learning goals
Language Is Not a File Transfer
After a project deadline slips, a manager writes: “We need to discuss accountability. Please come prepared tomorrow.” The manager intends urgency and clearer ownership. One employee reads blame. Another expects layoffs. A third assumes the sentence targets someone else. The next meeting begins defensively before anyone has spoken.
Every reader received the same words, yet each prepared for a different conversation. The manager knew the intended purpose; employees had to infer it from an ambiguous instruction and their previous experience. Before the meeting can clarify responsibility, someone needs to discover that this misunderstanding has already occurred.
The manager and employees need to establish what problem they are meeting to solve. The feeling that they understand or attach similar meaning to the same event is one example of shared reality (Echterhoff et al., 2009). That perceived commonality does not require agreement on every issue, and it does not establish truth. Both sides could agree that someone ignored a deadline when the records show that the new date never reached them. Communication must make interpretations clear enough to examine, while evidence tests whether those interpretations fit what happened.

title: 33  Communication
text:
Map how the same utterance can produce different interpretations.
Use grounding and perspective-getting to test a social inference.
Redesign a high-stakes message so its intent, context, action, and repair path are recoverable.
