title: 33  Communication
section: Meaning is inferred, tested, and repaired
text:
Meaning is inferred, tested, and repaired






Figure 33.1: An utterance permits several interpretations. Context supplies evidence, while grounding and repair make those interpretations mutually testable. Grounding theory explains this process of testing and repair.



The two interpretations in Figure 33.1 show how “discuss accountability” could mean clarifying responsibilities or assigning blame. Employees use the words alongside what they know about the manager and earlier meetings to decide which interpretation fits. If someone asks whether the meeting concerns performance, the manager can discover the ambiguity and explain the purpose. This exchange makes meaning partly jointly constructed: each person’s response gives the other evidence about what still needs clarification.
A useful design goal is recoverability: give the listener enough information to reconstruct the intended meaning and a way to correct an error. For example, a terse “Fine. Let’s discuss this tomorrow” leaves its tone and purpose uncertain. A fuller message explains the delay and invites a response: “I am too tired to give this a fair hearing tonight. I am not dismissing the concern. Could we discuss it at 09:00 tomorrow? If I have misunderstood what is urgent, tell me now.” The message cannot eliminate ambiguity, but it gives the other person a path to repair it.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 33  Communication
text:
Communication is coordination and repair






Figure 33.2: Grounding gives participants ways to check and repair interpretations, seeking enough shared understanding for the purpose of the exchange.



If the email had been corrupted or lost, restoring the signal would solve a transmission problem. Here every word arrived, yet the employees prepared for different conversations. Sending the same words again gives them no new basis for checking those interpretations. The feedback loop in Figure 33.2 gives the manager a way to discover and repair those interpretations before acting on them: invite a response, check its meaning, and clarify what remains uncertain.
The transmission model associated with Shannon and Weaver’s mathematical theory of communication (Shannon & Weaver, 1949) explains how a sender transmits a signal through a channel to a receiver and how noise can interfere. Human coordination adds a further task: checking what the receiver understood the signal to mean.
Herbert Clark’s work emphasizes common ground: the shared knowledge, assumptions, and context that speakers use to understand one another (Clark, 1996). Communication requires people to coordinate on what they both know, what they assume, and what has already been established. Clark and Brennan (1991) describe grounding as the process of establishing that people have understood each other well enough for the current purpose.
Grounding is why conversation includes signals such as “yes,” “I see,” “wait,” “what do you mean?,” “so you are saying…,” nods, pauses, repetition, examples, and repair. These are not meaningless fillers. They are coordination devices. They help participants check whether meaning is shared.
Grice’s cooperative principle also helps explain communication. Grice (1975) argued that conversation is guided by expectations that speakers provide information that is relevant, truthful, sufficiently informative, and clear. Much meaning comes from these expectations. If someone says, “Some of the students passed,” listeners may infer that not all passed, even though the sentence does not logically say that. If someone asks, “Can you pass the salt?” the literal answer may be “yes,” but the intended meaning is a request.
Such pragmatic inference goes beyond the literal sentence to infer what a speaker means in context. People often say less than they mean because they expect listeners to make that inference. This makes communication efficient, but also fragile. Misunderstanding happens when people do not share the same assumptions.
This is especially clear in email and text communication. Kruger and colleagues (2005) found that people overestimate how well they can communicate tone over email. In Study 2, participants sent statements intended to be either sarcastic or serious. For email, senders expected about 78% correct interpretation and receivers judged themselves about 89% accurate, while actual accuracy was about 56%—not statistically distinguishable from the 50% chance benchmark. Voice raised accuracy to about 73%. The striking result is the gap: both sides can feel confident while reconstructing different tones. The sender thinks, “How could they not understand?” The receiver thinks, “How could they write such a thing?”






Figure 33.3: In a task involving 29 dyads, senders predicted high decoding accuracy and receivers judged themselves highly accurate; actual accuracy was lower, especially in email (Kruger et al., 2005, Study 2). Plotted percentages are approximate. The companion schematic contrasts private perspective-taking with perspective-getting through questions and verification (Eyal et al., 2018).



The left panel of Figure 33.3 makes the gap between confidence and accuracy visible in the tone-decoding task. The right panel shows a practical response: use richer evidence when stakes rise, and let the other person correct the model you have formed (Eyal et al., 2018).



Table 33.1: Designing a message for recoverability









If a message is easy to misread, add…
Example




Context
“I am writing after today’s deadline changed.”


Intent
“My aim is to clarify ownership, not assign blame.”


Relational stance
“I value the work and want us to solve this together.”


Next action
“Please mark the two dates you can meet.”


Repair invitation
“If this lands differently from how I intend, call me.”






The manager can use the context, intent, and repair prompts in Table 33.1 to rewrite the email: “Yesterday’s delay exposed two handoffs without clear owners. My aim is to repair the workflow, not assign blame. Before tomorrow’s meeting, please mark where you believed ownership changed and one constraint I may not see. We will compare the maps, agree on the next handoff, and record unresolved concerns. If you read this as a performance warning, please tell me; that is not the purpose of this meeting.” The revision makes the intended model, evidence request, next action, and correction path visible.
At the meeting, “Which handoff did you think you owned?” will reveal more than “Everyone understands now?” A concrete example lets each person check whether the same words imply the same action. The repairs in Table 33.2 address different sources of misunderstanding: a misunderstood term needs an example, while an untested inference about intent needs a question.



Table 33.2: Grounding failures and repair moves





Failure
Hidden source
Repair move




Same word, different meaning
Different assumptions or professional models.
Ask for an example and define the term in use.


Tone is misread
Text removes vocal and contextual cues.
State intent explicitly and check interpretation.


Mind-reading hardens
An inference is treated as fact.
Name it as a hypothesis and ask the person.


Agreement is assumed
Silence is interpreted as consent; local conventions are overlooked.
Invite a summary, private response, or explicit concern.


Perspective-taking projects the self
We imagine what we would feel.
Use perspective-getting: ask, listen, and verify.

title: 33  Communication
text:
Mind-reading is a hypothesis
A curt reply seems to tell us how a colleague feels: “She is angry with me.” Responding to that anger may seem sensible, yet the reply could reflect an urgent task we cannot see. Defending ourselves before checking can introduce a dispute where there was only a hurried message. Inferring another person’s beliefs or intentions is often called mentalizing or theory of mind. We need it to cooperate and coordinate; the task is to keep the interpretation open to correction before acting on it.
One mismatch concerns the level of detail. We can judge ourselves through the fine-grained circumstances of an action while other people form a broader impression. Eyal and Epley (2010) found that matching these levels of construal could improve judgments of how one was seen. The practical question is what evidence the other person had: the manager remembers the pressures behind the email, while the employee sees a brief, ominous instruction.

When your own view becomes the default
One major error is egocentric projection: anchoring on one’s own perspective and insufficiently adjusting to another person’s perspective (Epley et al., 2004). We assume that our model of the world is closer to theirs than it really is. “I would not be offended by this feedback, so she should not be offended.” “I understood the email, so they should understand it.” “I enjoy this kind of small talk, so they must too.” “I would want direct advice, so they must want it.”
The communication task is to notice when your own reaction is doing more work than evidence about the other person. Ask what they understood before defending what you intended.
A related error is the false consensus effect: people overestimate how common their own beliefs, preferences, choices, and behaviors are (Ross et al., 1977). If I think an action is ethical, I may assume most reasonable people agree. If I dislike a policy, I may assume most people secretly dislike it too. If I would accept a risk, I may assume others would. Here the estimate concerns how widely a view is shared, rather than what one colleague thinks.
The distinction matters for checking the judgment. Ask the colleague to correct an inference about their view; use evidence from the relevant population to assess a claim about what most people believe. In either case, your own reaction is a starting point that needs checking.
People can also misjudge how self-serving others’ accounts will be. Kruger and Gilovich (1999) studied such “naïve cynicism” in responsibility judgments. Expecting a colleague to claim all the credit can make their explanation sound strategic before we have examined it.


When intention feels visible
Another error is the illusion of transparency: people overestimate how visible their internal states are to others (Gilovich et al., 1998). We think our anxiety, gratitude, embarrassment, confusion, or affection is obvious. A manager may therefore leave appreciation unspoken, believing the team already knows, while an employee waits for an acknowledgment that never comes. Connection and Repair develops the relational consequences of making that meaning explicit.
The same problem appears when we assume that readers recovered context we never stated. Looking for certainty in a face or gesture does not solve it: faces, bodies, and brief behavioral samples can contain information without becoming reliable dictionaries of a person’s exact emotion, motive, or truthfulness (Ambady & Rosenthal, 1993; Barrett et al., 2019; DePaulo et al., 2003). Verbal information and direct questions are often more diagnostic than confident interpretation of isolated expressions (Gesn & Ickes, 1999; Hall & Schmid Mast, 2007). If something is important, do not rely on hints, microexpressions, or silence. State it, ask, and verify.
In the deadline case, the employee’s defensiveness may reflect guilt, but it may also reflect an innocent misunderstanding or a history of blame. Treat the inference as a hypothesis that the next exchange can revise.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 33  Communication
text:
Ask rather than merely imagine
The manager wants to respond fairly and tries to imagine why a colleague missed the deadline. But imagining the colleague’s position while assuming they knew the new date preserves the very mistake that needs correcting. Before judging responsibility, the manager needs information only the colleague can supply. Perspective-taking means imagining how a situation looks to another person. Perspective-getting means asking them and listening to the answer. Imagination can generate the question; listening can revise its premise.
Across 25 experiments, Eyal, Steffel, and Epley (2018) found no overall accuracy improvement from instructions to take another person’s perspective. In their final experiment, direct conversation improved accuracy where imagining the other person’s perspective did not. Asking supplies information that imagination alone cannot, although its usefulness still depends on what the person knows and is willing to disclose.
For the manager, a useful question is: “When did you learn that the deadline had changed?” That may uncover a missing message rather than reluctance to accept responsibility. Follow with a paraphrase the colleague can correct: “So you were still working toward Friday because the new date was only discussed with the client team?”
Use ask–listen–reflect–verify as a practical routine: ask a specific question, listen without completing the answer, reflect what you understood, and invite correction or check the consequential fact. The name is this book’s shorthand for applying grounding and perspective-getting, not a separately validated four-step intervention.
Direct answers can also be incomplete, especially when honesty carries a cost. Perspective-getting works best when the question is specific and the response can be given without avoidable pressure; consequential factual claims may still need independent checking.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 33  Communication
section: Close the loop: utterance to shared-enough meaning
text:
Close the loop: utterance to shared-enough meaning
The manager’s first email treated understanding as private: the sender knew the intended meaning and assumed everyone else would recover it. The revised email treats understanding as a sequence:
Utterance → interpretation → test → correction → shared-enough meaning.
At the meeting, each person first maps where they believed ownership changed. The manager asks for examples rather than motives. Participants reflect what they heard before defending a view. Differences become visible: one handoff was never defined, one deadline changed without reaching operations, and one employee interpreted an ambiguous sentence through a previous experience of blame. Those differences explain why the same instruction produced different responses. With the missing deadline message and unclear handoff identified, the group can assign the next action while keeping unresolved questions visible.
This is the boundary between communication and persuasion. Persuasion seeks a warranted change in another person’s model. Communication makes the models mutually testable. Either can support the other, but a communicator has not established shared meaning merely because the other person complied.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

Take it forward
Choose one interpretation you have been treating as settled in a conversation. Turn it into a question, listen to the answer, and offer a summary the other person can correct. The useful outcome is an understanding both people can work with, even when they still disagree.

title: 34  Connection and Repair
text:
Learning goals
Warm Honesty Makes Truth Usable
A project manager receives a colleague’s section after the client deadline and writes, “This is unacceptable. We need to discuss your reliability.” The colleague replies, “You never told me the client changed the date.”
The manager checks the email thread. The new date was discussed with the client, but the colleague was never copied in. There is still a delivery problem to solve, and now there is an unfair accusation to repair. Explaining the original intention will not do both jobs.
We will follow this fictional exchange through listening, a more accurate account of what happened, and a response that accepts responsibility without losing sight of the work.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 34  Connection and Repair
text:
Diagnose whether a difficult conversation calls for practical help, emotional recognition, or identity repair.
Produce a warm-honesty opening that separates observable behavior, experienced impact, inferred intent, and a testable request.
Complete a repair sequence that acknowledges harm, accepts responsibility, and specifies changed behavior.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection

title: 34  Connection and Repair
text:
1. Understand accurately

Diagnose the conversation before answering it
The manager still needs a delivery plan, while the colleague needs the accusation about reliability corrected. Moving straight to scheduling may look efficient to the manager and dismissive to the colleague; discussing only the hurt leaves the work unresolved. The first task is to identify what kind of response the conversation needs at this moment. The same sentence can carry at least three kinds of need. A practical conversation asks what to do. An emotional conversation asks for recognition, regulation, or company. A social or identity conversation asks what the event says about respect, belonging, competence, fairness, or the relationship (Duhigg, 2024; Stone et al., 2010). The three layers in Table 34.1 connect possible needs to opening questions and the mismatches to avoid. Advice fails when the speaker is asking to be understood; validation frustrates when an urgent plan is needed.



Table 34.1: Three conversations can occupy the same words











Conversation layer
What the speaker may need
A useful opening question
Common mismatch




Practical
Options, information, decision, next step.
“Would it help to think through what to do?”
Solving before the problem is understood.


Emotional
Validation, containment, companionship.
“Do you want me to listen, or help you think?”
Advice that implies the feeling is a defect.


Social or identity
Dignity, respect, belonging, role clarity.
“What did this seem to say about you or the relationship?”
Debating facts while the person experiences disrespect.












Figure 34.1: A sentence may raise practical, emotional, or social and identity concerns.



The same sentence in Figure 34.1 permits all three readings, so ask what kind of help is useful now rather than choosing a response from the words alone. A conversation may move between layers as the answer changes.






NoteWatch for the mismatch



Predict first
It’s Not About the Nail is a comic illustration of this mismatch. Before watching, predict what kind of help each person thinks the conversation requires. While watching, note the sentence where practical problem-solving and emotional recognition diverge. Afterward, write a response that both validates and asks permission before solving.


The manager cannot identify the colleague’s immediate need by deciding privately which conversation to have. A question gives the colleague a voice in that decision. Research on ordinary conversations suggests another benefit: Huang and colleagues (2017) found that people who ask more questions, especially follow-up questions, are better liked by their partners. Building on an answer can show that it received attention.
Use the answer to decide what to ask next. The ladder in Table 34.2 moves from what happened to why it mattered:



Table 34.2: A question ladder





Level
Example question




Facts or events
What happened?


Experience
Which moment stays with you?


Meaning
What did that mean to you?


Emotion
What did you feel then?


Values or needs
What mattered, or what did you need?






Depth does not mean forcing intimacy. It means allowing the conversation to move beyond labels into experience, meaning, emotion, values, needs, or identity when appropriate. Follow the last answer rather than reciting a prepared list. Ask for specificity, label emotion tentatively, invite correction, and move only one level deeper at a time.
In the project exchange, “What happened?” opens the sequence of events; “What did my message imply to you?” opens its meaning. The second question is useful only if the manager is prepared to hear an answer that changes the account.
Sensitive questions often go better than askers predict, and deeper conversations can create more connection than expected (Kardas et al., 2022). Preface a personal question with control: “May I ask something a little more personal? It is completely fine to pass.” A deep question is an invitation, not a demand.
Closeness depends on more than question depth. In a structured experiment, gradually escalating reciprocal self-disclosure produced greater immediate feelings of closeness between strangers than comparable small-talk tasks (Aron et al., 1997). In ongoing relationships, disclosure was more closely connected to intimacy when the partner was experienced as understanding, validating, and caring (Laurenceau et al., 1998). The lesson is not to reveal as much as possible. It is to disclose at an appropriate pace, notice whether the other person reciprocates voluntarily, and respond to what was entrusted rather than treating vulnerability as a technique.


Test the social forecast
The obstacle to connection can arise before a conversation begins. Epley and Schroeder (2014) randomly assigned commuters to connect with a stranger, remain disconnected, or commute as usual. People expected more enjoyment from solitude, but participants assigned to connect reported a more positive experience, without the predicted loss of productivity. Boothby and colleagues (2018) documented a related liking gap: after conversations, people tended to underestimate how much their partners liked them. Anxiety is therefore a forecast, not a verdict. When the situation is appropriate, test a small prediction—say hello, ask one genuine follow-up question, or invite later contact—and compare the anticipated with the experienced result.
When contact is safe and welcome, do not let an untested pessimistic forecast make the decision by itself. Leave the other person an easy way to decline.
The patterns in Table 34.3 adapt Brooks’s (2025) practitioner framework to distinguish questions that invite an answer from those that corner the listener or ignore what they have said:



Table 34.3: Questions should make updating possible










Pattern
What goes wrong
Better move




Boomerasking
Ask, then immediately answer your own question; the interest appears performative.
Disclose directly, then ask a real follow-up.


Gotcha question
The question is designed to expose or corner.
State the concern and invite an explanation.


Repeated question
Re-asking signals disbelief or ignores the answer.
Paraphrase the answer and identify what remains unclear.


Agenda-laden question
Only one acceptable answer is implied.
Use neutral wording and acknowledge your own interest.






Follow a point the other person has made rather than searching for the next question on a list. If the colleague says, “I felt you had already decided I was unreliable,” ask what in the message conveyed that verdict.


Put the partner at the center of attention
Partner-centered attention means deliberately tracking the other person’s goals, interpretations, constraints, and dignity while still pursuing your own purpose. Egocentrism makes our own goal and discomfort more accessible, so a behavior intended as efficient may land as dismissive or unsafe. When context is uncertain, state the observation, offer a plausible benefit of the doubt, and ask before attributing motive: “The draft arrived after review time. I may be missing a constraint—what happened from your side?” The question allows the colleague to correct the account before a judgment about character hardens (Epley et al., 2004; Laurenceau et al., 1998).
Benefit of the doubt is a starting hypothesis, not a requirement to ignore repeated harm. Where conduct is unsafe, the appropriate move may be a boundary, documentation, representation, or a formal channel.


Replace mind-reading with verified understanding
Use the ask–listen–reflect–verify routine to give the other person an account they can recognize or correct. Its relational value comes from showing what you have understood: “You thought the original date still applied because the client’s message never reached you.” That response gives the colleague something to check and shows that the explanation affected your judgment. Nods, eye contact, generic agreement, and silence are too ambiguous to do this on their own (Laurenceau et al., 1998).


Listen for the layer beneath the words
The manager sees a late section and wants to prevent another missed deadline. The colleague hears a judgment about reliability and wants the accusation corrected. Treating either account as the whole problem would leave the other concern unanswered. Start by separating the event, your own felt impact, and your interpretation. Table 34.4 is a self-check before listening: it helps identify which parts of your account the other person needs an opportunity to correct.



Table 34.4: Separate your reaction before checking the other person’s experience










Layer
Meaning
Question




What
Perceived situation, event, issue, task, or context
What is happening?


How
Bodily feeling, emotion, affect, impulse, anticipated feeling
How does it land in me?


Why
Interpretation, appraisal, attribution, perceived intent, prediction
Why did I feel that way?


Who
Value, need, identity, dignity, status, belonging, competence, autonomy
What self-relevant concern is touched?


When
History, habit, culture, prior experience, learned expectation
Where did I learn to see or feel it this way?


Action
Automatic reaction or mindful response
What do I do next?






In the project case, the event is a late section, the manager’s feeling is exposure to the client, and the first interpretation is unreliability. The colleague’s concern is being judged for information they never received. Separating these elements makes two corrections possible: revise the attribution and repair the handoff process.
Choose the prompts that expose an uncertainty in your account, rather than asking the colleague to work through every category.


Building connection through validation and shared experiences
Validation shows that a partner’s meaning was noticed, understood, and incorporated. It may be as small as a precise “That makes sense because…” or “I see why that mattered.” It does not require endorsing every conclusion or action. Repeated, diagnostic signals—paraphrase, follow-up, acknowledgment, and specific appreciation—help build shared reality (Laurenceau et al., 1998; Rossignac-Milon et al., 2021).
Once the colleague’s experience has been acknowledged, a shared task can give both people an opportunity to work differently together. Redesigning the handoff becomes such a task when the manager invites the colleague’s expertise and follows through on the agreed change.






TipTwo small practices that strengthen connection



People often underestimate the value of a sincere appreciation and others’ willingness to help (Bohns, 2016; Kumar & Epley, 2018; Zhao & Epley, 2021, 2022). Experiments on small acts of kindness likewise found that givers underestimated recipients’ positive responses (Kumar & Epley, 2023). Make appreciation specific—name the action and its effect. Make a request specific—say why you ask this person, make refusal safe, receive the help without minimizing it, and close the loop by saying what changed.




When asking for help can build liking
The Ben Franklin effect names the possibility that doing someone a favor increases liking for that person. It is often explained through dissonance reduction or self-perception, but the request can also communicate a wish for connection.
Niiya (2016) tested a direct request for help with a puzzle in Japanese and American student samples. Liking increased relative to baseline when the recipient personally asked for help, but not when participants helped at the experimenter’s instruction. Participants already had the ability and time to help, so this was a favorable setting for a modest request. The study suggests that the interpersonal meaning of asking matters.
For the colleagues repairing a difficult handoff, a sincere request for advice may acknowledge competence and invite cooperation. It should follow acknowledgment of the problem, preserve a comfortable refusal, and serve a real need. Chapter 30 separates this relational possibility from attempts to secure escalating compliance.

title: 34  Connection and Repair
text:
2. Speak with warm honesty

Truth, vulnerability, and feedback
After an unfair accusation, it can be tempting to protect the relationship by avoiding another uncomfortable subject. Yet the delivery problem remains, and silence gives neither person the information needed to prevent a repeat. The challenge is to make truth usable without turning it into another attack.
Speaking honestly also requires deciding what private information the conversation needs. Relevant disclosure can help another person understand a concern, but disclosure for its own sake can burden the listener. Research on secrecy shows why keeping information private can be costly too: secrets can create psychological burden and isolation. Slepian and colleagues have shown that the burden of secrecy often comes not only from hiding in social interaction but from mind-wandering back to the secret (Slepian et al., 2017). Sharing a secret with a trusted person can sometimes reduce isolation and increase connection, though disclosure must be safe and appropriate.
Honesty is complicated because people often use kindness as a reason to avoid truth. White lies can protect feelings, but they can also be paternalistic or prevent learning. People often underestimate others’ desire for honest feedback and overpredict how badly honest conversations will go (Levine & Cohen, 2018; Levine et al., 2020). In professional contexts, avoiding necessary feedback may feel kind in the moment but unfair in the long run.
Useful feedback identifies behavior the recipient can examine and change. Instead of “You are unreliable,” the manager can begin, “The section arrived after the client deadline; I had not checked whether you received the revised date.” This makes the event discussable without turning it into a character judgment.
A specific observation can still contain an inference. “You interrupted Anna twice” is easier to verify than “You made her feel unimportant.” If the impact on Anna matters, ask her rather than presenting your interpretation as her experience.
Admitting uncertainty or a mistake can make this exchange more credible when it is relevant and followed by action. Disclosure should serve the conversation, not make the other person responsible for reassuring the speaker.


Cross the net carefully
Warm honesty differs from nice silence, protective distortion, and “brutal honesty.” It combines care with information the other person can examine. Conflict is an interpersonal cycle: private intent becomes observable behavior, that behavior has an impact, and the response becomes observable behavior in the next turn. Good intent does not erase impact, and impact does not prove intent. Stay on your own side of the net: describe the observable behavior, own its impact on you or the work, name the relevant need, and make a testable request. Then ask across the net about the other person’s intent, constraints, and experience instead of declaring them.






Figure 34.2: Private intent becomes observable behavior, experienced impact, and a next response that feeds the interpersonal cycle. Warm honesty separates observation, impact, inquiry, and request.



The cycle in Figure 34.2 shows why repair requires two kinds of evidence at once: describe the observable behavior and its impact, and ask about what remained private. The paired statements and questions in Table 34.5 keep impact discussable without turning it into a verdict about motive.



Table 34.5: Warm honesty separates observable impact from inferred motive









Stay on your side
Ask across the net




“The revised file arrived after the client deadline.”
“What happened from your side?”


“I felt exposed because I had promised delivery.”
“What constraints did I not see?”


“I need earlier warning when timing changes.”
“What warning process would work for you?”


“Could you message me by 14:00 if the date is at risk?”
“What would make that request unrealistic?”






A useful practice metaphor is pinch → story → avoidance → crunch, which names one possible escalation pattern. A small disappointment creates a private story about motive. Avoidance prevents correction. The accumulating pattern later erupts as a large conflict. Raise the pinch while it is still observable: “When the agenda changed without notice, I felt unprepared. What happened?” In unsafe settings or strong power asymmetries, direct conversation may not be prudent; documentation, a representative, or formal support may be necessary.
Had the manager used this approach before sending the accusation, the opening could have been: “The section arrived after the client deadline, and I felt exposed because I had promised delivery. I may be missing information—when did you hear about the revised date?” Once the missing message became clear, both could discuss how deadline changes should be recorded and acknowledged. Inquiry belongs before the judgment about reliability; a request for earlier warning cannot repair a date the colleague was never given.

title: 34  Connection and Repair
text:
3. Repair meaning and relationship
Figure 34.3 brings the conversation back to three tasks: describe the event, check what it meant, and agree on the next action. Each needs an answer from both people.






Figure 34.3: A repair procedure moves from the event and private interpretation toward perspective-getting and a shared next action.




Support without trapping attention
Repeated discussion can provide closeness while keeping attention fixed on a problem. Rose (2002) called extensive revisiting of problems and negative feelings co-rumination; in a questionnaire study of children and adolescents, it was associated with both closer friendships and symptoms of anxiety or depression. For an everyday conversation, the practical question is whether talking is producing understanding, perspective, or a useful next step.
Ask what kind of support is wanted: listening, problem-solving, distraction, or company. First make the feeling intelligible; then, with permission, ask what else might be true, what remains controllable, or how the event may look from a more distant standpoint (Kross & Ayduk, 2011). Support that rushes to optimism feels dismissive. Support that never releases attention from the injury can maintain distress.


Constructive disagreement
The manager and colleague may agree that the accusation was unfair while still disagreeing about how the next handoff should work. Suppressing that disagreement could preserve a calm meeting and an unreliable process. Pursuing it as another contest over competence could undo the repair. They need a way to test competing accounts while keeping each other able to contribute.
Disagreement becomes destructive when people feel unheard, disrespected, or existentially isolated: “How can you not see what is obvious?” When people disagree about seemingly self-evident truths, they may feel that the other person inhabits a different reality. That feeling can push people toward groups that validate them and away from dialogue.
Civility matters because contempt closes minds and damages the conditions for thought. Civility makes room for firm disagreement and careful comparison of evidence.
Moral reframing is also useful. A review by Feinberg and Willer (2019) describes evidence that political arguments can be more persuasive when framed in terms of the audience’s moral values rather than only the speaker’s. If someone values loyalty, authority, liberty, care, fairness, or purity differently than you do, repeating only your own moral language may fail. Translation is not manipulation when it remains truthful; it is respect for the listener’s moral world.
Personal experience can also preserve respect across moral disagreement. Kubin and colleagues (2021) found that experiences of harm were judged as more rational and increased respect more than factual claims in several political disagreements. Such stories help make the personal stakes understandable.
Before answering an argument, reflect it in terms the other person recognizes. In the project case: “You want the correction recorded because the original accusation could affect how others judge your work.” This identifies a concern that another explanation of the deadline would miss.
Then examine the evidence together and state what remains in disagreement. Respect makes the discussion possible; it does not require equal weight for claims with unequal support.


Apology and repair
Explaining “I only wanted to protect the deadline” leaves the colleague’s damaged standing untouched. The manager’s intention and the harm require different responses: the colleague needs the false accusation corrected and a reason to expect a different process next time. An apology should identify the harm, accept appropriate responsibility, and make a credible offer of repair. Studies of apology components find that responsibility and repair can be particularly influential in how apologies are evaluated (Fehr & Gelfand, 2010; Lewicki et al., 2016).
“I’m sorry if you were offended” leaves the disputed action and responsibility unclear. The manager’s apology can instead identify the actual mistake: “I called your reliability into question before checking whether I had sent you the revised date. I had not, and the accusation was unfair. I am sorry. I will correct that account with the client team, and from now on we will record deadline changes in the shared plan and confirm who has received them.”
The colleague may still want time, an explanation, or a stronger safeguard. Forgiveness and reconciliation are separate decisions; an apology does not entitle the speaker to either. What can be checked is the promised correction and whether the next deadline change reaches the people responsible for it.






NoteOptional research note: forgiveness without surrendering judgment





Suppose the manager corrects the accusation, but the colleague still replays it after work. Whether to forgive now concerns how the colleague wants to relate to that hurt. In Worthington’s (2006) account, emotional forgiveness involves a movement away from resentment and ill will toward more benevolent feelings. It can develop gradually, even after someone has decided not to retaliate.
Forgiveness does not establish that the accusation was acceptable or that the manager has become reliable. Reconciliation concerns rebuilding the relationship; trust concerns what the colleague is prepared to rely on in future. The colleague might choose to forgive while insisting on written deadline changes and waiting for a record of fair conduct before trusting again. The manager can offer repair, but cannot demand an internal change from the person harmed.
Worthington’s REACH approach offers a structure for someone who wants to work toward forgiveness: recall the hurt; try to empathize with the other person’s perspective without excusing the act; consider forgiveness as an altruistic gift, freely chosen; commit to the forgiveness one has reached; and hold on to that commitment when painful memories return. These prompts provide a way to revisit the experience, without requiring emotions to change on command.
What does the evidence show? Toussaint et al. (2015) collect research and theory on forgiveness and health. More directly, a randomized trial involving 4,598 adults found that a self-directed REACH workbook reduced self-reported unforgiveness and, to a smaller extent, depression and anxiety symptoms at two weeks relative to a waitlist (Ho et al., 2024). The workbook produced short-term benefits.1 The colleague’s decision about reconciliation depends on what the manager does next.

title: 34  Connection and Repair
text:
Connection as decision infrastructure
At the next project meeting, the important difference is observable: the deadline is written in a shared place, the colleague can raise a concern before committing, and the manager corrects a mistaken account instead of defending it. Trust, if it improves, will have something to rest on.
Connection can help information reach a decision, but friendliness alone is insufficient. People also need accurate records, clear responsibilities, and ways to challenge a claim without depending on the goodwill of one person.
When apparent agreement could reflect authority, suppressed dissent, unshared information, pluralistic ignorance, or diffused responsibility, use the mechanism-specific diagnosis in Authority, Groupthink, and Shared Responsibility.
These practices become especially consequential in negotiation. Parties need enough confidence in the conversation to disclose a priority or correct an assumption, while retaining the freedom to reject an unsuitable deal. The next part asks how that information can produce agreements worth making.

title: 34  Connection and Repair
text:
Practice Lab
Use the late-project case or a genuinely low-stakes issue. Produce three artifacts: (1) a verified-understanding transcript containing one ask, one paraphrase, and one accepted correction; (2) a warm-honesty opening that names observable behavior, impact, inquiry, and a reviewable request; and (3) a repair statement containing acknowledgment, responsibility, remorse, repair, and changed behavior. An observer marks any sentence that crosses from evidence about behavior into an unsupported claim about motive.

title: 34  Connection and Repair
text:
Take it forward
The next conversation need not resolve the whole relationship. Start with one specific moment, explain its effect without claiming access to the other person’s motives, and make room for their account. What happens afterward will matter more than a perfectly worded apology.

title: Part VI. Negotiating Joint Decisions
text:
Questions to carry forward
A supplier wants a higher price, while the buyer insists on a lower one. Both want a workable deal, but bargaining over that single number can leave them deadlocked even when delivery timing, payment terms, volume, or reliability would permit a useful trade. They risk losing an agreement each would prefer to walking away. What do they need to learn about one another’s priorities to find it?
The route in Figure 1 follows negotiation from preparation to implementation; supplier relationships, employment packages, and a used-car sale reveal different problems along the way. We begin with preparation: what each side can do without an agreement, what an acceptable agreement must provide, and what remains uncertain. Offers and concessions determine how value is divided. Discovering differences in priorities can also create value: a change that costs one side little may matter greatly to the other. The chapters develop both tasks and show how listening and preparation help keep them connected.
Finally, we ask what happens after agreement. A promise needs clear terms, a way to check performance, and a response to foreseeable disagreement. Reaching a deal is useful only when the deal is worth making and can be carried out.
The final part carries this concern with implementation into everyday behavior, the design of choices, and the way organizations make and review decisions.

title: Part VI. Negotiating Joint Decisions
text:
What can each side do if we do not agree?
Which differences could support a useful trade?
How will we know whether the agreement is working?

title: 35  Negotiation as Joint Decision Design
text:
Learning goals
Interdependence turns choice into a shared search
A manufacturer asks a long-standing supplier to accept a large order at the current unit price and deliver it before a fixed production date. The supplier refuses. The buyer hears, “You do not value the relationship.” The supplier means, “At that date and batch size, accepting would displace higher-margin work and expose us to a penalty we cannot control.”
Pressing harder on price would leave the supplier’s capacity problem unresolved. Even a compromise price could produce an agreement the supplier cannot carry out on time. Before making another offer, the buyer needs to learn which parts of the request can change. Could a different batch size or delivery schedule give both sides a better outcome than walking away?
The buyer cannot solve this decision alone. An offer proposes a course of action for both organizations, and the supplier’s response can reveal a constraint the buyer had missed. Questions therefore do more than improve the presentation: they can uncover another option.
This is where communication and persuasion enter a joint decision. Clear communication makes interests and constraints discussable; persuasion helps the other side examine the reasons for a proposal. Each exchange also changes what the parties believe about their alternatives and about one another. Learning, proposing, and protecting one’s interests must work together (Thompson et al., 2010).
The rest of this part develops the details. This gateway chapter supplies one map: prepare the joint decision, interact to learn and propose, then implement and review.

title: 35  Negotiation as Joint Decision Design

Map a negotiation as parties, alternatives, positions, interests, issues, options, and implementation conditions.
Distinguish value claiming from value creation while managing information deliberately.

title: 35  Negotiation as Joint Decision Design
text:
1. Prepare the joint decision

Replace performance myths with design questions






Figure 35.1: Negotiation links each party’s alternatives and priorities to a jointly designed agreement space.



The buyer’s first demand treated price and date as fixed. The two-sided map in Figure 35.1 asks what else could change and what each party would do without agreement (Raiffa, 1982; Lax & Sebenius, 1986; Thompson, 2015). The habits in Table 35.1 can obscure that search; its replacement questions shift attention from appearing tough or securing a signature to protecting interests and implementation:



Table 35.1: Negotiation myths and replacement questions










Myth
Hidden cost
Replacement question




“Good negotiators are tough.”
Toughness can destroy information and value.
What process protects interests and learning?


“Success means reaching agreement.”
A deal can be worse than walking away.
Is this agreement better than our best alternative?


“Compromise is the ideal.”
Splitting positions can miss compatible interests.
What do the parties value differently?


“Negotiation begins at the table.”
Alternatives, stakeholders, and standards are left undeveloped.
What can be improved before the conversation?


“Signing ends the negotiation.”
Implementation and adaptation are ignored.
How will the agreement be governed, reviewed, and repaired?








What skilled practice looks like
If the buyer answers refusal with a longer argument, the supplier’s capacity problem remains. Useful skill must uncover terms that can change the decision, as well as explain why the buyer cares. Rackham and Carlisle’s (1978) field study selected negotiators using reputations for effectiveness, a record of success, and successful implementation. The author’s report describes 48 such negotiators observed across 102 sessions. During planning, 38% of their comments concerned anticipated agreement or common ground, compared with 11% in the comparison group. During negotiation, questions accounted for 21.3% of their coded behavior, compared with 9.6% (Rackham, 1980).
These are observational contrasts, not the effects of assigning people a questioning strategy. The comparison group included negotiators who did not meet the selection criteria or whose record was unknown. The practical lesson is a hypothesis worth testing: prepare possible overlap and ask a question that could reveal it before lengthening your argument.


Positions, interests, and issues
The buyer’s deadline and the supplier’s refusal look incompatible while each is treated as a complete demand. To search for a workable package, the parties must distinguish what was requested from what it protects and which terms could change. A position is what a party says it wants; an interest is the reason the demand matters; an issue is a dimension the parties can negotiate. “Deliver by June 1” is a position. Protecting a production schedule is an interest. Delivery date, batch size, price, penalty allocation, and review are issues. Positions can conflict while interests remain compatible, especially when several issues are available (Fisher et al., 2011).
This approach is often called principled negotiation: separate the people from the problem, explore interests beneath positions, develop options for mutual gain, and evaluate proposals against defensible criteria (Fisher et al., 2011).
Use Table 35.2 to turn preparation into decisions about what can be varied, which standards apply, and who can commit and implement the agreement:



Table 35.2: The gateway map for a negotiation









Element
Supplier question




Alternatives
What will each party do without agreement?


Interests
Why do price, date, capacity, and certainty matter?


Issues
What can be varied, added, staged, or made contingent?


Standards
Which market, cost, quality, or fairness criteria are relevant?


Authority
Who can commit each organization?


Implementation
What must happen after signature for value to exist?
crumbs: 35  Negotiation as Joint Decision Design

title: 35  Negotiation as Joint Decision Design
text:
2. Interact: learn, propose, and protect

Claiming and creating value
Suppose the buyer can accept half the order later, freeing the supplier from the costly rush. That change may improve the deal for both sides. Creating value means finding such changes by using differences in priorities, timing, forecasts, risk tolerance, or capabilities. The parties must still decide who receives the gains; claiming value concerns that division. The two tasks create a difficulty: disclosing that an early batch is essential could reveal a useful trade, but also invite a higher price. Lax and Sebenius (1986) call this the negotiator’s dilemma.
Do not solve that dilemma by revealing everything or nothing. Prepare alternatives and limits, then share interests and priorities reciprocally, in stages, and at the level needed to test a trade. Distributive Negotiation develops alternatives and limits; Integrative Negotiation develops discovery and package construction; Designing Better Agreements turns the package into operating terms.


Information is currency and risk
Without information, parties cannot identify interests, estimate the agreement range, or construct trades. Yet exact limits, desperation, and internal division can be exploited. Begin with diagnostic questions about priorities, constraints, stakeholders, standards, and implementation. Reveal interests before walk-away points: “Delivery timing matters because the production schedule depends on it” creates more search value than disclosing the exact maximum price. Treat every interpretation as a hypothesis and material claims as candidates for verification.

Negotiation does not require revealing a reservation value or every private preference. It does require care with material facts, authority, promises, deadlines, and terms the other side reasonably relies on. Strategic privacy is different from manufacturing a false belief. Truthfulness affects the information the parties can exchange, the promises they can implement, and their ability to repair a later failure.


Fairness and objective standards
A buyer with a strong alternative may be able to press for a lower price, but the supplier still needs a reason to regard the terms as acceptable and to work within them. Power alone leaves that problem unresolved. Alternatives create power; standards help create legitimacy. Market data, cost indices, law, precedent, quality benchmarks, and internal equity can discipline a proposal, although parties may reasonably disagree about which standard applies (Fisher et al., 2011). Procedure matters as well: voice, neutrality, respect, and transparent reasoning can affect whether an outcome is accepted as legitimate (Lind & Tyler, 1988; Tyler, 1990). Ask which standard each side would defend to a reasonable outsider and how competing standards should be reconciled.
Pressure, complexity, and information asymmetry can undermine consent when a party is vulnerable or cannot leave. Before using a tactic, consider whether its justification would survive disclosure to the counterpart—and whether the same tactic from a stronger party would be acceptable to you.


Emotion, face, and relationship
A buyer may expect a forceful demand to produce a concession. If the supplier hears contempt for its competence, defending its standing can take priority over explaining the capacity constraint. Pressure then costs the buyer information needed for a workable deal. In computer-mediated negotiations, participants made larger concessions to an angry than a happy opponent, partly because the emotion informed their estimate of the opponent’s limit (Van Kleef et al., 2004). This supports a specific inference mechanism, not a prescription to display anger. In the supplier case, a concession gained by intimidation may still leave damaged trust or an unworkable promise. Ask what the agreement will do to the relationship that must implement it, and design a path that lets both sides explain acceptance to their constituencies without humiliation.


Culture and meaning: learn how the counterpart negotiates
The buyer may treat the supplier’s silence as refusal and improve the offer, while the supplier is still consulting someone who must approve it. The same pause can then trigger an unnecessary concession. Negotiation is culturally embedded: directness, silence, fairness, face, authority, contract, and trust can carry different meanings. Culture and Identity provided a Meaning Audit. Use it here to establish how this negotiation works: Who must be consulted? How should concerns be signaled? What does “yes” commit us to? How will changes be handled after signing? National, professional, organizational, and relational averages cannot diagnose an individual counterpart. A question about who must approve this offer is therefore more useful than an assumption based on where the counterpart comes from.
Questions about culture, truthfulness, and verification return in Chapter 38, where they can be connected to disclosure rules and agreement safeguards rather than treated as personality diagnosis.


Design for your own predictable errors
Preparation should help the buyer recognize an acceptable package. Yet if every supplier proposal is read as a threat, even a useful trade may be rejected because of who offered it. Anchoring, overconfidence, self-serving interpretation, reactive devaluation, and fixed-pie assumptions can turn compatible differences into presumed conflict (Ross, 1995; Thompson & Hastie, 1990). Before the meeting, record likely triggers, a pause or consultation rule, and the evidence that would revise your fairness judgment.

title: 35  Negotiation as Joint Decision Design
text:
3. Implement and learn
Suppose the supplier can meet the production date by delivering half the order first, while the buyer can postpone the remainder. A higher price for the urgent batch may now be affordable because it avoids a production shutdown. This gives the parties a possible trade to investigate.
Even if both sides like the package, several decisions remain: who confirms capacity, what quality check permits payment, and what happens if the first batch is late? These operating rules are governance—the arrangements for monitoring, adjusting, and resolving disagreement after signature.
The next three chapters develop this sequence. Preparation establishes what you can accept; searching across differences improves the available packages; agreement design makes the chosen package workable.

title: 35  Negotiation as Joint Decision Design
text:
Practice Lab
Prepare a one-page joint-decision map for the supplier case. List both parties, stated positions, plausible interests, negotiable issues, alternatives, standards, decision authority, information to ask for, information safe to reveal, possible value-creating differences, and implementation risks. Produce one opening question for each missing element and one condition under which walking away is better than agreement.

title: 35  Negotiation as Joint Decision Design
text:
Take it forward
Before making an offer, make the joint decision visible: what could each side do without agreement, and what could they achieve together? That map helps distinguish a term that must be divided from a problem whose solution is still open to design.

title: 36  Distributive Negotiation
text:
Learning goals
Preparing and Claiming Value
Imagine that you are selling a used car and already hold a firm offer of €8,000. A second buyer wants to negotiate but has not named a price. You hope for more, while knowing that you can return to the first offer.
Once bargaining starts, that comparison can become surprisingly easy to lose. A low opening makes each increase feel like progress, even if the eventual price remains below €8,000. Refusing anything below your hoped-for price creates the opposite risk: losing a deal that improves on your alternative. Before the conversation begins, separate what you need to protect from what you hope to achieve. Write down:

title: 36  Distributive Negotiation
text:
Produce a preparation sheet containing BATNA, reservation value, target, estimated ZOPA, standards, and learning questions.
Make or answer a first offer using independent analysis and a defensible rationale.
Conduct and audit a concession sequence from opening through close.

title: 36  Distributive Negotiation
section: 1. Prepare: the case before the vocabulary
text:
1. Prepare: the case before the vocabulary
The five answers describe different parts of preparation. Start with the firm €8,000 offer: if this negotiation fails, you can accept it instead. That course of action is your BATNA, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement (Fisher et al., 2011).
Your reservation value is the point at which a deal is as good as that alternative. With identical payment, timing, risk, and selling costs, it is €8,000. If the competing offer involves travel, uncertain payment, or other costs, account for those differences before comparing prices. A BATNA is an available course of action; its value in this negotiation must be assessed.
Your target, or aspiration, is what you hope to obtain. It might be €9,800 if comparable sales and the car’s condition support that amount. The target guides your requests; the reservation value guards against accepting less than the alternative is worth.
The buyer has an alternative and a reservation value too, although you may know little about them. When acceptable prices overlap, there is a zone of possible agreement, or ZOPA. We will calculate it below. In a negotiation involving several issues, that zone is a set of packages rather than a single price interval.
A credible alternative is an important source of bargaining power because it makes refusal possible. It is not the only source: information, timing, authority, resources, and the rules of the negotiation also shape what each party can do.

The negotiation before the negotiation
Before meeting the buyer, confirm that the competing offer is still available and on what terms. Gather comparable sales, inspect any condition differences, and decide which facts you need to learn. Preparing this evidence gives your target a basis and helps you recognize when an attractive price comes with an unattractive condition.
Preparation also includes authority and process. If someone else must approve the sale, agree on the limit before the conversation. If an inspection could change the price, decide how that information will be handled rather than discovering the rule under pressure.


A complete preparation test
Before entering the room, use Table 36.1 to identify both sides’ alternatives, possible trades, and unresolved questions. Each answer should inform a decision about how to bargain:



Table 36.1: Preparation as a set of decisions rather than a list of wishes









Domain
Decision to make before bargaining




Alternatives
What are each side’s BATNA and current reservation value? How could ours improve, and how might theirs change over time?


Surplus
Is a positive ZOPA plausible? What facts support that estimate, and what would falsify it?


Aspiration
What is our ambitious but defensible target? What objective standard supports it?


Unknowns
Which facts, constraints, stakeholders, and approvals do we need to learn? What question could reveal each one?


Issues and priorities
Which issues matter to each side, how strongly, and where might priorities differ?


Trades and forecasts
What can be exchanged across issues? Where do predictions differ enough for a contingent term?


Process
Who decides, in what sequence, by what deadline, and how will agreement be documented and implemented?






Prepare at least one tough question you would prefer not to hear, then answer it truthfully without surrendering private information. Also prepare one question whose answer could make you abandon your favored strategy. That second question protects preparation from becoming confirmation bias.


Map the bargaining zone






Figure 36.1: A positive zone of possible agreement (ZOPA) exists when the buyer’s maximum exceeds the seller’s minimum; the overlap is the bargaining surplus. If the buyer’s maximum were below the seller’s minimum, tactics alone could not create agreement: the parties would need to add issues or walk away.



A distributive negotiation occurs when parties divide a resource and their interests are directly opposed on at least one issue. The clearest example is a single-issue price negotiation.
Figure 36.1 shows the bargaining zone in the used-car case, assuming all non-price terms are equivalent. The seller’s competing offer makes the reservation value €8,000. Suppose the buyer’s reservation value is €10,000: above that, the buyer prefers another option.
The bargaining zone, also called the zone of possible agreement or ZOPA, lies between €8,000 and €10,000. Prices strictly inside that interval are better than the alternatives for both sides; an endpoint leaves one party indifferent. At €8,000, the seller is just indifferent between selling and walking away, while the buyer gets a very favorable deal. At €10,000, the buyer is just indifferent between buying and walking away, while the seller gets a very favorable deal. At €9,000, the surplus is split evenly.
The bargaining surplus is the overlap between the parties’ reservation values: €2,000 in this case. Changing the price reallocates that surplus. At a settlement of €9,200, the seller receives €1,200 above the competing offer, while the buyer pays €800 less than its maximum. The negotiated gain is different from the final price.







NoteMathematical analysis: dividing the bargaining surplus





The total surplus is the buyer’s reservation value minus the seller’s:
\[
€10{,}000-€8{,}000=€2{,}000.
\]
At a settlement of €9,200, the buyer’s surplus is its reservation value minus the price:
\[
€10{,}000-€9{,}200=€800.
\]
The seller’s surplus is the price minus its reservation value:
\[
€9{,}200-€8{,}000=€1{,}200.
\]
The two shares add to the total bargaining surplus. These comparisons assume the non-price terms are equivalent.




A positive surplus means mutually beneficial prices exist. If the seller instead requires €12,000 and the buyer will pay at most €10,000, there is no acceptable price overlap. Another issue might change that calculation, but pressure alone cannot make an inferior deal worthwhile.


BATNA, aspiration, and bargaining power
Keep the reservation value, target, and opening offer separate. In our example, €8,000 protects the seller’s alternative, while a €9,800 target directs the effort to claim part of the €2,000 surplus. Research on aspirations supports the importance of targets (White & Neale, 1994).
An opening offer should have a defensible relationship to that target and the available evidence. Asking too little can leave value unclaimed; asking an implausible amount can undermine credibility or end the discussion. Fast acceptance can prompt regret and a review of your preparation.
A quick “yes” can make you wonder whether a higher request would also have been accepted. Negotiation advice sometimes calls this regret a “winner’s curse,” but the classic auction concept is different: winning a common-value asset can be bad news because the winning bid may reflect the most optimistic valuation error. Keeping the concepts separate prevents a moment of bargaining regret from becoming a claim about auction theory.


Estimate the other side
Your alternative tells you when to walk away, but it does not tell you how much the buyer would pay. Guess too low and you may offer away value; guess too high and you may mistake a binding limit for a bargaining move. The buyer’s maximum is therefore a question to investigate. Comparable cars, urgency, inspection results, and stated constraints can support a range; record why you consider that range plausible.
Ask questions whose answers could change the range: “Which alternatives are you comparing?” or “How did you arrive at that price?” The buyer may decline to answer, and an answer may require verification. Hesitation, confidence, or irritation is especially ambiguous; it should not become a price detector.
Update when the content warrants it. A documented repair requirement changes the package; a small concession may reflect a limit or simply a bargaining strategy. Recording what would change your estimate helps prevent every response from confirming the number you guessed first.


When to disclose a reservation value
Revealing an exact reservation value usually weakens value claiming because it tells the other side how far it can push. Yet secrecy is not an absolute rule. A credible disclosure can sometimes correct a mistaken estimate, prevent an avoidable impasse, satisfy a transparency obligation, or make a multi-issue agreement possible. The decision is not “honest or secretive”; it is whether this particular disclosure improves the chance of an informed agreement without unnecessarily surrendering value.
If disclosure is useful, explain the underlying constraint and evidence before giving a naked number. “Our board-approved ceiling is €10,000 and we cannot exceed it” is more informative than “€10,000 is my bottom line,” but it should be said only if it is true and if the strategic and relational benefits exceed the cost. Never fabricate a reservation value or alternative.

title: 36  Distributive Negotiation
section: 2. Open: anchor only when you can defend the frame
text:
2. Open: anchor only when you can defend the frame
The anchoring mechanism from Chapter 11 now has direct consequences for who receives the surplus. A first offer supplies a reference point before the other side has necessarily settled on its own.
Suppose the buyer begins at €6,500. Even knowing your €8,000 alternative, you may now feel pulled toward explaining why the car is worth more than €6,500. The proposed number has become the reference point for discussion.
Experiments show that first offers can anchor settlements (Galinsky & Mussweiler, 2001), extending anchoring research on numerical judgment (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). A number can direct attention and also signal what the speaker expects. The effect is not solely a failure to adjust: an offer carries strategic information, too.
That creates a trade-off. An informed opening can shape the discussion, while a poorly informed one may reveal that you would accept far less than the counterpart was prepared to offer. Before choosing to open, consider how much you know and what your number would disclose.






Figure 36.2: A first-offer information matrix treats opening as a joint decision about anchoring and disclosure.



The four cells in Figure 36.2 show why “always make the first offer” is too crude: opening can create leverage, but it also discloses the quality and limits of your preparation.
Use Table 36.2 to pair each possible opening strategy with the risk you need to test. These are conservative preparation heuristics:



Table 36.2: A first-offer decision heuristic when each side’s information can be assessed











Your information
Counterpart’s information
Default move
Main risk to test




Good
Good
Consider opening first.
Credibility or chilling from an extreme offer.


Weak
Good
Invite or learn before opening.
Revealing ignorance and anchoring below a defensible target.


Good
Weak
A first offer can anchor, but use a defensible standard.
Exploitation, relationship cost, or an uninformed impasse.


Weak
Weak
Research first; if forced, use a provisional, justified range.
An arbitrary number becoming the conversation’s center.






If you cannot assess your information or the counterpart’s, ask and investigate before committing.
A rationale gives the counterpart something to examine. “Comparable sales, adjusted for the recent service, put my asking price at €9,800” is more informative than a bare demand. Use accurate comparisons that the counterpart can check. Keep the distinctions in Table 36.3 explicit: an opening offer aims to shape the discussion, while the reservation value determines when agreement is no better than walking away.



Table 36.3: The alternatives, thresholds, and offers to prepare before bargaining









Concept
Question




BATNA
What will I actually do if no agreement is reached?


Reservation value
At what point is an agreement as good as the BATNA?


Target
What ambitious but defensible outcome am I pursuing?


Opening offer
What anchor can I justify with standards and information?


Estimated ZOPA
Where might both parties prefer agreement to their alternatives?

title: 36  Distributive Negotiation
text:
3. Respond: return to independent analysis
Return to the buyer’s €6,500 opening. If the seller starts from that number and argues for a modest increase, the discussion can drift below the firm €8,000 alternative. Pause to compare the offer with that alternative, the €9,800 target, and the market evidence. Ask what supports the buyer’s number if the answer could change your estimate. Otherwise, explain the gap and give an independently supported counteroffer:
“€6,500 is outside the comparable range and below a firm alternative I already have. Based on the car’s condition and recent listings, €9,800 is the appropriate starting point.”
A strong response does four jobs: it refuses the anchor, supplies an independent standard, places a new reference point, and gives the other side a face-saving explanation for moving. Precise offers can signal informed calculation (Mason et al., 2013), but extra digits need a defensible basis. Loschelder and colleagues (2016) found that excessive precision could backfire with expert negotiators, who inferred lower competence; a rationale for the precision could reduce that problem. A narrow range may combine ambition with flexibility, but both endpoints anchor. If €9,800 is the target, “€9,800 to €10,200 depending on timing and payment” is safer than a range whose lower endpoint concedes the target (Ames & Mason, 2015).
If the first offer is unexpectedly attractive, do not invent conflict. Pause long enough to inspect hidden conditions, other issues, and implementation. Immediate acceptance can create regret on the other side or leave important terms undefined. A considered acceptance is still acceptance.

title: 36  Distributive Negotiation
text:
4. Move: make concessions carry information
A concession is meant to bring agreement closer. It also teaches the counterpart how to bargain with you: a large immediate move can imply that the opening lacked legitimacy, while two unreciprocated moves can teach that waiting produces value. The seller may give up money without gaining a commitment or learning anything new. Make each move communicate what changed and what reciprocal response would justify it.
Use four disciplines:

Make movement reciprocal. Do not negotiate against yourself.
Label what you give. Make the cost and significance visible without exaggeration.
Make movement conditional. “If payment is completed this week, I can move to €9,500.”
Connect movement to information or value. A concession should respond to a changed term, verified constraint, or reciprocal move—not discomfort alone.

Shrinking concessions can signal an approaching limit. Across seven studies, recipients of decreasing concessions made less ambitious counteroffers than recipients of constant concessions or a single large concession. In one interactive study, they also reached worse deals than recipients of a single concession; the disadvantage fell on the recipient, not the sender, and a pre-set target was protective (Tey et al., 2021). Treat the pattern as communication and ask whether each move is deliberate, credible, and connected to exchange.
Silence can create time for deliberation and sometimes improve value creation, but it can also signal disrespect, anxiety, or disengagement (Curhan et al., 2022). Make the pause recoverable: “I want a moment to compare that with the full package.” Deadlines require the same discipline. Ask what changes at the deadline and for whom. Time pressure can accelerate agreement, but delay costs are rarely symmetric (Stuhlmacher et al., 1998).

title: 36  Distributive Negotiation
section: 5. Close: check the terms before accepting
text:
5. Close: check the terms before accepting
Suppose the buyer offers €9,400 with payment this week. The seller should compare the whole agreement with the €8,000 alternative, not compare €9,400 with the emotionally salient €9,800 target. Before closing, confirm the condition of the car, payment method, transfer date, documents, and whether either side has added a new term. A midpoint is not fair merely because it is a midpoint; inspect the legitimacy of the endpoints.
A late request for an extra benefit changes the package you have just evaluated. Compare the revised terms with your alternative and, where appropriate, ask for a reciprocal adjustment. If no available package beats that alternative, walking away is a successful use of the preparation.

title: 36  Distributive Negotiation
text:
Practice Lab
Run the used-car negotiation in pairs. Before speaking, each side submits a preparation sheet with BATNA, reservation value, target, estimated counterpart limit, evidence, opening decision, and planned questions. Record every offer, concession, condition, pause, and justification. Afterward, calculate each party’s surplus; mark where an anchor changed an estimate; and evaluate economic outcome, information quality, relationship, ethics, and implementation separately.

title: 36  Distributive Negotiation
text:
Take it forward
A persuasive first number can make the rest of a negotiation revolve around it. Prepare your alternative and reservation value before that number arrives, then judge each package against what you could actually do without agreement. An accepted offer still needs to earn its place in that comparison. The next chapter asks whether a better package becomes available when the negotiation includes more than one issue.
