title: 37  Integrative Negotiation
text:
Learning goals
Creating Value Across Differences
In a reported negotiation case, a large buyer and a small European supplier have agreed on $18 per pound for one million pounds of an ingredient each year. The buyer will invest in a new product only if competitors cannot obtain the ingredient, yet the supplier refuses exclusivity—even after the buyer offers minimum orders and more money. The commercial opportunity is substantial, but the condition that makes the investment worthwhile is the very condition the supplier rejects. Raising the price again may simply make an unworkable proposal more expensive. What would the buyer need to learn before deciding whether this agreement is possible?
Write one sentence you would say at the table. Before offering another concession, try asking, “Help me understand what selling outside this agreement protects for you.” In the teaching case, the supplier’s objection concerned an existing promise to sell only 250 pounds a year to a cousin. A narrowly tailored exception could protect that relationship while giving the buyer commercial exclusivity. Malhotra and Bazerman (2007) report the case with identifying details changed. Its practical lesson is to diagnose the interest before paying to move the position.
The refusal looked puzzling because the buyer had not understood what exclusivity would cost the supplier. We will use that gap to examine how questions reveal priorities, how differences support trades, and how to check whether the resulting package improves on each side’s alternative.
The buyer still wants a good price, and the supplier still wants a margin. Discovering a useful exception does not end that conflict; it gives the parties a better package within which to bargain. Value creation changes what is available, while value claiming determines how the benefits are divided.
The same distinction matters when the stakes extend far beyond a commercial contract. The Camp David negotiations illustrate why separating issues can open possibilities that a single disputed demand conceals. In the Egypt–Israel strand of the Camp David process, an official U.S. account describes Egypt pressing for Israeli withdrawal from the Sinai in exchange for security arrangements; the negotiations also addressed settlements, airbases, timing, implementation, and Palestinian questions. The issue split in Figure 37.1 shows how separating territorial sovereignty from security arrangements made a multi-issue package conceivable (U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian, n.d.).
This creates a central tension. To create value, negotiators must often share information about their interests, priorities, constraints, and preferences. But sharing information can make them vulnerable when value is later claimed. If I tell you that delivery speed matters more to me than price, you may use that information to demand a higher price. If you tell me that you have no strong alternative, I may push harder. If I reveal that one issue is easy for me to concede, you may ask for it without giving anything back.
Lax and Sebenius (1986) call this the negotiator’s dilemma: the tension between cooperative moves that create value and competitive moves that claim value. Too little openness prevents value creation. Too much openness can lead to exploitation.
Manage this tension through staged, reciprocal disclosure. Explaining why a delivery date matters may reveal a possible trade without disclosing the highest price you would pay. A conditional offer—“If we guarantee volume, can you reserve capacity?”—then tests the trade.
Keep the preparation from Chapter 36: your alternative, walk-away point, and target. Creating more value does not ensure that you receive an acceptable share.

title: 37  Integrative Negotiation
text:
Diagnose the interests and constraints hidden beneath a stated position.
Build a priority map that identifies differences capable of creating joint value.
Produce and evaluate a package trade that improves both parties without surrendering distributive discipline.







TipWatch and diagnose: position versus interest



Predict first
Watch “Focus on interests, not positions”. Pause before the explanation and write (1) the visible positions, (2) at least two possible interests behind each, and (3) the question that would distinguish those hypotheses.










Figure 37.1: Separating territorial sovereignty from security arrangements creates options that a single territorial line conceals.

title: 37  Integrative Negotiation
section: Creating value beyond splitting the difference
text:
Creating value beyond splitting the difference
Splitting the difference can be a reasonable way to settle a distributive issue, but it may conceal a better trade. Before choosing a midpoint, check whether the parties need different things from the disputed term.
In the supplier case, offering more money for complete exclusivity is positional compromise: the buyer moves on price and expects the supplier to move on exclusivity. It still treats “exclusive or not” as one line. Interest discovery changes the option. The buyer needs commercial protection for a major investment; the supplier needs to honor a small family commitment. A carve-out for the existing 250-pound sale can protect both. No one split exclusivity in half. The parties changed its scope.
The exception works only if the buyer’s commercial protection is preserved and the family commitment can be defined and verified. Integration changes the option being considered.

title: 37  Integrative Negotiation
text:
Barriers to value creation
A useful trade depends on discovering how the parties differ, yet the conversation can make those differences hard to reveal. A negotiator may treat every gain for the other side as a loss, hide a priority that could support a trade, or read a firm position as the whole interest. The result can be an avoidable impasse—or an agreement that costs both sides more than necessary. The barriers below identify what blocks the search.
A fixed-pie belief treats the available value as fixed, so one side’s gain must be the other’s loss. Such beliefs and inaccurate judgments about the counterpart can hide compatible interests and differences in priorities (Thompson & Hastie, 1990). The diagnosis in Table 37.1 separates this problem from missing information and an unhelpful bargaining process:



Table 37.1: Three families of barriers to value creation










Barrier family
Typical failure
Corrective move




Beliefs
Fixed-pie assumptions, illusory conflict, overconfidence, self-serving fairness, or reactive devaluation make compatibility invisible (Ross, 1995; Thompson & Hastie, 1990).
State the competing hypothesis, evaluate proposals independently of their source, and identify what evidence would revise the forecast.


Information
Mistrust, weak listening, and fear of appearing vulnerable prevent priorities and constraints from becoming recoverable.
Ask diagnostic questions, disclose interests progressively, and reciprocate useful information without revealing exact limits automatically.


Process
Positional or single-issue bargaining converts every term into a separate fight.
Expand the issue set, compare packages, and defer final commitment until trade-offs can be evaluated together.






Use the diagnosis to decide what to try next. A question can test an assumed conflict; a package comparison can test whether different priorities support a trade. If those tests reveal no acceptable package, insisting that “there must be a win-win” would replace inquiry with pressure to agree.

title: 37  Integrative Negotiation
text:
Interests behind positions
Chapter 35 distinguished a position from the interest it protects. Here that distinction becomes a search procedure. Galinsky and colleagues (2008) found that instructed perspective-taking could improve outcomes in negotiation tasks. That does not establish that imagining a counterpart’s priorities makes those inferences accurate. The communication research supplies a complementary discipline: get new information through questions and let the counterpart correct the account (Eyal et al., 2018). The same demand for exclusivity might protect investment, quality control, brand consistency, or an internal promise. Each diagnosis implies different packages.
The question “What is this term meant to protect?” is a useful opening. Follow the answer with a concrete test: “Would a named exception meet that concern, or is a wider freedom to sell important?” Also ask who must approve the deal. A term may protect an obligation to someone outside the room.

title: 37  Integrative Negotiation
text:
Preparing across issues
List the negotiable issues and distinguish your priorities from guesses about theirs. The supplier case includes exclusivity, volume, timing, investment, price, and quality. Which of these can move, and what would each movement cost?
The hypotheses in Table 37.2 identify possible differences that could support a trade. Priorities, costs, risk attitudes, and time horizons are distinct sources of difference; each row names the comparison being proposed. Update the hypotheses as the counterpart explains or chooses between packages.



Table 37.2: Illustrative hypotheses about differences to test, not facts about a counterpart










Issue
Possible difference to investigate
Potential trade




Price / salary
Both sides may give the material term high priority.
Use standards; do not expect easy integration.


Timing
One side may value speed strongly while the other has more flexibility.
Trade speed, start date, or staging for value elsewhere.


Risk allocation
The sides may differ in willingness to bear risk or forecasts of the outcome; check which difference is present.
Use warranties, insurance, or contingent terms.


Recognition / title
Recognition may cost one side little while carrying high symbolic value for the other.
Trade status or visibility for a material term.


Future relationship
The sides may value short-term and longer-term outcomes differently.
Use volume, renewal, review, or option clauses.







Discover priorities rather than guessing them
The phrase “Which issues matter most?” is a start, not a complete diagnosis. Use several low-risk tests:

Quick rank: Ask each side to order the issues from most to least important.
Label and confirm: Offer a tentative inference—“It sounds as if delivery reliability matters more than customization; have I understood that correctly?”
Allocate 100 points: Spread 100 points across issues to force explicit trade-offs. Do this separately before sharing, then compare patterns rather than exact scores.
Ask thresholds: “What is a must-have, what is a preference, and what is flexible?” A threshold is different from a ranking.
Run a small reaction test: Offer two safe packages that differ on one trade and observe which direction is preferred.

As packages become concrete, priorities may change and a “deal-breaker” may reveal a previously unexamined interest. Mirror the answer back, ask what evidence supports it, and update throughout the conversation.

title: 37  Integrative Negotiation
text:
Logrolling
Suppose a supplier wants a longer contract for predictable revenue, while the buyer wants delivery flexibility because demand is uncertain. Bargaining over each demand in isolation makes the requested concession look like a cost with nothing in return. Considering them together creates another possibility: the buyer offers a longer commitment in exchange for flexible quantities.
Logrolling means trading across issues based on differences in priorities. Each side gives way on issues it values less in exchange for gains on issues it values more. The question is which linked concessions improve the whole package for both sides.
Test the relative priorities through a conditional package: “If we commit for longer, could you allow more flexible quantities?” This reveals a possible trade without disclosing either reservation value. The counterpart may accept the logic, reject the assumed cost, or propose another exchange. Each response improves the map.
Settling price, delivery, warranty, and timing one at a time can use up those opportunities before their connections become visible. Keep the linked concessions conditional until the whole package can be assessed.

An information strategy for creating and claiming value
Not every piece of information does the same work. Some information mostly affects value claiming; other information is needed to create value. The separate columns in Table 37.3 make this trade-off explicit (Fisher et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2010).



Table 37.3: What different kinds of information do in negotiation











Information
Effect on claiming value
Effect on creating value
Sensible default




BATNA and reservation value
Exact disclosure often weakens leverage; credible constraint disclosure can prevent impasse.
Usually not needed to discover trades.
Protect exact limits; disclose only for a clear process or agreement benefit.


Position or opening demand
Opacity and an ambitious opening can help claim value.
A position alone reveals little about how to enlarge the pie.
State it with a legitimate reason, then move to interests.


Interests
Disclosure can expose where pressure would hurt.
Essential for inventing alternative ways to solve the problem.
Share progressively and reward reciprocity.


Priorities
May reveal which concessions are cheap or costly.
Essential for logrolling and claiming a share of the enlarged surplus.
Reveal relative priorities through questions, packages, and conditional trades.


Key facts
Information asymmetry can create bargaining power, but concealment may be unlawful or unethical.
Accurate material facts improve agreement quality and implementation.
Verify and disclose facts required for informed consent or performance.


Substantiation
Reasons and evidence strengthen a claim.
Shared standards can reduce conflict and support joint search.
Use real evidence; avoid ploys that damage trust.






Handle material facts according to disclosure duties, safety, and informed consent.

title: 37  Integrative Negotiation
text:
Differences are opportunities
Even after priorities are clear, the parties may disagree about what will happen or what it will cost to deliver. Trying to settle those differences by winning the argument can leave a useful trade unexplored. One party may have spare capacity, another may need earlier delivery, or one may bear a particular risk more cheaply. Different forecasts can also motivate a contingent term: payment varies with a later outcome rather than requiring agreement about it now. Chapter 38 explains the conditions that make such terms workable.
Treat a difference as a question about the package. “If you value reliable volume more than a fixed monthly schedule, could we combine an annual commitment with flexible call-offs?” This searches for value without requiring either party to adopt the other’s preferences.

title: 37  Integrative Negotiation
text:
Pareto efficiency






Figure 37.2: A discrete menu of feasible packages for two parties. The highlighted packages are nondominated; dashed lines connect them for visibility.



Both parties can prefer a deal to walking away and still leave gains undiscovered. Agreement answers whether the package is acceptable; it does not tell them whether another package could improve one side’s outcome without costing the other. To judge how well the negotiation used the available value, they need a second benchmark.
An agreement is Pareto efficient relative to a specified feasible set if there is no feasible alternative that at least one specified party prefers while no specified party is worse off. The parties may still argue about distribution, rights, or implementation, but no Pareto improvement remains within the parties, issues, constraints, and value measures included in that comparison.
A Pareto frontier is the set of Pareto-efficient agreements under those specifications. The feasible set may be discrete, nonconvex, or only partly known. The two axes in Figure 37.2 represent each party’s own value measure. Each axis is interpreted in that party’s own units.1
For a separate four-package example, assign hypothetical, party-specific scores to the contract-length and delivery trade.



Table 37.4: A trade across differently valued issues





Package
Buyer’s score
Supplier’s score




Short contract, fixed quantities
30
30


Short contract, flexible quantities
100
0


Long contract, fixed quantities
0
100


Long contract, flexible quantities
70
70






In Table 37.4, moving from short/fixed to long/flexible raises both scores from 30 to 70. Within this four-package menu, every package except short/fixed is nondominated: improving one party beyond its score in any of them would hurt the other. The scores need not be comparable across parties, so adding the columns would not measure social welfare.
Pareto efficiency does not mean fairness. One efficient package can favor one party relative to another efficient package. Efficiency asks whether a specified feasible mutual improvement remains; fairness asks whether the rights, process, risks, and division are defensible. A complete negotiation must consider both, and must also ask whether important parties or issues were excluded from the map.
Suppose walking away scores 40 for the buyer and 45 for the supplier. Only the long/flexible package in this menu beats both alternatives. Efficiency and acceptability therefore answer different questions; neither can be inferred merely from a signature.

title: 37  Integrative Negotiation
text:
Build the supplier package
The buyer and supplier can now replace isolated demands with linked terms. The exclusivity exception in Table 37.5 follows the reported teaching case; the remaining rows are proposed extensions for exploring a fuller agreement, rather than reported terms from that case:



Table 37.5: Turning differences into a supplier package











Issue
Buyer values
Supplier values
Package move




Exclusivity
Protection of the product investment
Honoring the existing family commitment
Commercial exclusivity with a named 250-pound legacy exception.


Volume
Reliable capacity
Predictable revenue
Annual minimum volume with quarterly call-off forecasts.


Timing
Delivery before production milestones
Protection from uncontrollable schedule risk
Staged delivery and jointly defined dependency dates.


Price and investment
Competitive unit economics
Recovery of dedicated-capacity cost
Volume tiers plus a contribution to verifiable capacity investment.


Quality
Reliable inputs
Clear acceptance criteria
Shared specifications, inspection, cure periods, and review.






The proposed links give the parties something concrete to evaluate. They still need to check whether the trades create gains, decide how to divide any gains, and compare the result with their alternatives. A package worth accepting also needs promises that can be measured and fulfilled, which is the task of the next chapter.

title: 37  Integrative Negotiation
text:
Practice Lab
Begin with Table 37.4: identify the dominated package and compare each remaining package with the stated walk-away scores. Then use the opening supplier case to draft three more realistic packages. The reported case does not supply complete valuations or BATNAs, so label any scoring assumptions you introduce and identify the information needed to replace them. In pairs, assign roles and exchange rankings or conditional package preferences before revealing exact limits. Working alone, write two plausible priority maps and the question that would distinguish them. Revise one package after that check.

title: 37  Integrative Negotiation
text:
Take it forward
When a term seems immovable, ask what it is protecting. A delivery date, a price, or a quantity may stand for a concern that another package could satisfy. Finding that difference creates a possible trade; deciding whether the trade is fair and workable remains part of the negotiation.

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
text:
Learning goals
Make the promise clear enough to carry out and check
The buyer and supplier agree on a promising package: a volume commitment, flexible call-offs, shared capacity investment, and a defined exception to exclusivity. Then the buyer asks for an urgent extra batch. The supplier says the forecast came too late; the buyer says flexibility was the point of the agreement.
Both may remember the deal accurately while assuming different operating rules. The package promises flexibility, yet it leaves the urgent batch uncertain and the parties arguing over who failed. Before signing, they need to decide what counts as an accepted order, who confirms capacity, and what happens when a commitment is missed. This chapter turns a package both sides value into a promise they can carry out and check, adding complexity only when it solves a specific problem.

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
text:
Produce a minimum viable agreement covering ownership, measurement, verification, review, failure, and exit.
Diagnose whether unclear priorities, forecast disagreement, sensitive claims, or process failure warrants an optional agreement-design module.
Add an advanced term only when its measurement, incentives, authority, and implementation burden are defensible.

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
section: Start with a minimum viable agreement
text:
Start with a minimum viable agreement
Begin with the urgent batch. Someone must be able to tell whether the supplier accepted the order, which date now applies, and what each side should do if capacity is unavailable. The six fields in Table 38.1 organize the information needed to answer those questions:



Table 38.1: Six fields that turn a package into a minimum viable agreement









Required field
Agreement-design purpose




Owner
Assign the promise to a named role with authority and resources.


Measure
Define the observable event, metric, threshold, and deadline.


Verification source
Name the record, data source, inspection right, and challenge process.


Review date
State when the responsible parties will examine performance and who may approve a revision.


Failure rule
Define cure, escalation, consequence, and treatment of relevant external shocks.


Exit
Define termination rights, transition, surviving duties, and any appeal.






For the supplier’s forecast-and-capacity obligation, the minimum record could look like this:



Table 38.2: A minimum viable agreement for one supplier obligation









Field
Illustrative operating term




Owner
The buyer’s demand-planning lead submits the rolling forecast; the supplier’s account lead confirms available capacity.


Measure
Submission is time-stamped; capacity inside the agreed band is confirmed within two working days.


Verification source
Both parties can inspect the shared forecast, order, and confirmation log.


Review date
Operational leads review the record monthly; designated commercial sponsors approve any change to the band.


Failure rule
A buyer-caused late forecast moves the delivery clock; a supplier-controlled miss after confirmed capacity activates the stated cure and service-credit rule.


Exit
Repeated uncured failure activates the agreed termination and transition process, including treatment of dedicated tooling and surviving duties.






The named roles, shared log, and response rules in Table 38.2 make the operational promise testable before complexity accumulates.1






TipAdd an advanced module only for a diagnosed problem






Table 38.3: Route a diagnosed agreement problem to an optional module










Diagnosed problem
Optional module
Use only if…




The parties do not know which issues the other side values most
Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers (MESOs)
The packages are sincere, understandable, and approximately equivalent to the offer-maker


The parties make materially different forecasts
Contingent term
The outcome is measurable, verifiable, sufficiently controllable, and worth the contracting burden


Important information is sensitive or a claim is consequential
Staged disclosure and claim verification
Disclosure is reciprocal or protected and a credible verification path exists


Agenda, authority, communication, or impasse blocks progress
Process or third-party rule
Decision rights, confidentiality, timing, and transfer of control can be specified


A signed agreement may leave mutually beneficial trades unexplored
Protected post-settlement search
The signed agreement remains the fallback and either party may stop without penalty






Use Table 38.3 to check both the problem a module addresses and the conditions it needs. If no diagnosed problem fits, do not add a module. Complexity creates interpretation, monitoring, gaming, and enforcement costs of its own.

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
section: Optional module 1: Reveal priorities through packages
text:
Optional module 1: Reveal priorities through packages
The supplier can ask whether the buyer values capacity or flexibility more, but a general answer may conceal how much of one the buyer would exchange for the other. Committing to a single offer too early can close off that discovery. Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers, or MESOs, let the parties learn from a choice among workable packages before settling on one.
A MESO is a set of two or more offers made at the same time, each designed to be roughly equal in value to the offer-maker but different in how value is allocated across issues. The other side’s reaction can provide clues to its priorities.
The supplier might offer three packages it has privately valued as roughly equivalent:

Capacity package: lower unit price, firm annual minimum, narrow monthly call-off band.
Flexibility package: higher unit price, wider call-off band, quarterly forecast commitment.
Investment package: middle unit price, buyer contribution to dedicated tooling, longer term, and an exit schedule for unrecovered investment.

The buyer can compare these trade-offs without disclosing its reservation value, and its response gives the supplier a reason to ask which terms mattered. Research comparing MESOs with single-package offers has found economic and relational benefits from offering a choice of packages (Leonardelli et al., 2019). The useful information comes from examining the preference, rather than assuming the first choice reveals a complete ranking of priorities.
Prepare the packages carefully. Approximate equivalence is from the offer-maker’s perspective, not an assurance that the counterpart will regard them as equally attractive. Each must be sincere and understandable; a deliberately unavailable decoy would undermine the exchange.

Turn a package into a diagnostic question
Return to the supplier’s capacity and flexibility packages. Ask which is closer to the buyer’s needs, then ask why. A preference for flexibility might reflect expected demand variation, reluctance to commit cash, or a hidden approval constraint.
A useful next question isolates one trade: “If we widened the call-off band, could you accept a longer forecast commitment?” The answer gives more information than simply treating the first package choice as a stable priority ranking.

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
section: Optional module 2: Use contingent terms when forecasts differ
text:
Optional module 2: Use contingent terms when forecasts differ






Figure 38.1: Four agreement-design tools and the conditions that make each useful.



Use Figure 38.1 to check package sincerity, measurement and incentives, protection of the signed agreement, and governance. These conditions determine which tool fits the negotiation.
Suppose a builder expects early completion while a buyer fears delay. A fixed payment asks them to settle the price of that uncertain performance now, when their forecasts differ. Repeating the forecasts need not bring them closer to agreement. A contingent contract makes a term depend on the future outcome: a bonus for finishing early and compensation for specified delays may offer each something it values, provided the possible payments, risks, and incentives are acceptable.
The main questions concern measurement and control. Define completion so that speed cannot be achieved by omitting quality checks. Specify which delays the builder controls, how external disruptions are treated, who verifies the date, and how a disputed finding can be challenged. A payment tied to a vague “successful launch” simply moves the disagreement into the future.
Contingent terms also create new incentives. A party that controls the measurement or part of the outcome may be able to influence the payment in ways the other did not intend. The contracting and verification burden must be worthwhile relative to a simpler fixed term (Bazerman & Gillespie, 1999).

Apply the logic to supplier capacity
The buyer expects monthly demand to remain within a narrow band. The supplier expects volatile peaks that would require overtime and displaced orders. Arguing about whose forecast is right will not create capacity. A contingent term can allocate the consequence:

The buyer supplies a rolling twelve-week forecast and commits only to the first four weeks.
Volume inside the agreed band receives the base price.
Volume above the band is accepted only when capacity is confirmed and carries a predeclared surge price.
If the buyer’s committed forecast arrives late, the delivery clock moves by the same number of days.
If the supplier confirms capacity and then misses a dependency it controls, service credits apply; repeated failure activates cure and exit rights.

This term turns forecast disagreement into a measurable allocation of responsibility. It still needs definitions: what counts as a forecast, confirmation, surge volume, supplier-controlled delay, external shock, and cure? The agreement should avoid cliffs that reward strategic reporting just above or below a threshold. When parties disagree about the future, let future evidence affect terms only when measurement, control, incentives, and enforcement are credible (Bazerman & Gillespie, 1999).

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
section: Optional module 3: Stage disclosure and verification
text:
Optional module 3: Stage disclosure and verification
To specify a meaningful delivery commitment, the supplier needs to know why timing matters. The buyer might explain, “Our customer contract contains penalties,” without immediately disclosing its maximum acceptable loss or price. Begin with information that helps define the problem and invite comparable information in return. More sensitive details can follow when they serve a clear purpose and have appropriate protection. Exact reservation values and confidential alternatives may remain private unless disclosure produces a process, legal, or agreement benefit.
How the supplier responds will affect what the buyer is willing to share next. Using the concern to propose a workable delivery safeguard gives openness a purpose; using it solely to intensify pressure gives the buyer a reason to withhold more. Each exchange should therefore supply information needed to design or check a term, without assuming that willingness to talk makes every claim reliable.

Ask before inferring
Chapter 33 distinguished perspective-taking from perspective-getting. Imagination can reduce egocentrism and improve strategic thinking, but it can also project one’s own priorities onto the counterpart; direct questions provide new, correctable evidence (Eyal et al., 2018; Galinsky et al., 2008). Ask what a term protects, who must approve it, what risk worries the other side, and what implementation success would look like. Partial or strategic answers remain possible, so verify consequential claims and reward useful disclosure with reciprocity rather than immediate exploitation.


Culture changes the meaning of a move
A buyer may leave the meeting treating “yes” as a capacity commitment while the supplier intended only to acknowledge the request. The apparent agreement then conceals an order neither side knows how to implement. Culture, profession, organization, and law can change what a move means. Directness can signal efficiency or disrespect; silence can mean refusal, consultation, deference, or thought; a concession can invite reciprocity or threaten face. Cross-cultural negotiation studies document this variation, including differences across settings in how common measures predict joint gains (Brett & Okumura, 1998; Brett et al., 2021).
Return to the Meaning Audit in Culture and Identity. Treat cultural knowledge as a hypothesis and ask how this interaction works:

How is disagreement expressed safely here?
Who must be consulted before a proposal can become a commitment?
Does “yes” mean agreement, acknowledgment, or willingness to continue?
Which terms need explicit definition rather than assumed shared meaning?
Would a public concession, correction, or apology impose an avoidable face cost?

These questions turn broad cultural knowledge into checks of meaning, authority, and consent in this interaction (Gunia et al., 2016).


Replace lie detection with claim verification
Negotiation creates incentives to manage information. A person may lie by commission, omit a material fact, answer a different question, or use literally true statements to create a false impression—the practice called paltering (Rogers et al., 2017). But privacy is not automatically deception. A negotiator may decline to reveal a reservation value, private preference, or confidential alternative without making a false claim.
The dangerous response is to become a human lie detector. A meta-analysis of 206 documents involving 24,483 judges found average unaided truth–lie classification of 54 percent, compared with a 50 percent chance benchmark: 47 percent of lies were identified as deceptive and 61 percent of truths as truthful (Bond & DePaulo, 2006). Reviews conclude that nonverbal cues to deception are faint and unreliable (Vrij et al., 2019). A pause, gaze shift, nervous movement, polished delivery, or confident tone does not reliably diagnose deceit. Such behavior can also reflect stress, memory search, language, status, culture, or fear of being disbelieved.






Figure 38.2: Beliefs about behavioral “tells” exceed the observed associations for several behaviors. Positive values indicate more of a behavior during deception, observed or believed according to the series. Across nine observed correlations, the largest absolute value is .19; several estimates are heterogeneous. Seven pairs of belief estimates are available, with none reported for nodding or hand movements. Sporer and Schwandt (2007, Figure 1) report the observed associations; their belief estimates came from Zuckerman et al. (1981) and Köhnken (1988).



In Figure 38.2, the observed associations are much smaller than many of the belief estimates: expecting a behavior to reveal deception does not make it diagnostic. This is the same inference problem developed in The Predictive Mind, Confirmation Bias and Motivated Reasoning, and Communication. Suspicion supplies a prior; ambiguous behavior then appears to confirm it. Instead of treating the pause as an answer, identify what evidence would establish whether the claim is accurate.
For every material claim, ask:

What exactly has been asserted, and what has merely been implied?
What record, date, document, authority, reference, test, or independent source could verify it?
Can the claim become a representation, warranty, milestone, inspection right, or contingent term?
What happens if the claim is mistaken rather than deceptive?

Schweitzer and Croson (1999) found that direct questions reduced deception overall in their first study; in their second, direct questions particularly reduced omission but could increase lies of commission. Therefore ask a precise question and verify the answer when it matters. Good agreement design makes important claims testable.

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
text:
Optional module 4: Negotiate the process
A promising package can fail because the wrong people are in the room or because tentative suggestions are treated as commitments. Agree early on who can approve terms, which information is confidential, and when a proposal becomes binding.
For the supplier discussion, the buyer might say: “Could we first list the issues and compare two complete packages? Our planning leads can test capacity, while the commercial sponsors approve any price or volume commitment.” This allows operational knowledge into the search without confusing expertise with authority.
Record how an impasse will be handled as well. A pause for data, an internal approval, or an outside facilitator solves a different problem from another price concession. Revisit earlier assumptions when new information changes the package’s value.







NoteResearch Lens: when direct negotiation needs a third party



When direct bargaining stalls, bringing in a third party can seem like the obvious next step. Yet the parties may want help finding their own agreement or need a final decision they cannot reach together. Choosing a process without resolving that difference can surrender control when assistance was intended, or prolong the dispute when finality was needed. A third party can repair a process or replace it. The mediation–arbitration distinction in Table 38.4 follows the allocation of authority used in the UNCITRAL frameworks (UNCITRAL, 2022).



Table 38.4: Mediation assists party choice; arbitration transfers decision authority












Process
Third party’s primary role
Who controls the outcome?
Best fit
Central risk




Mediation
Structure communication, clarify issues, test assumptions, and help the parties search for settlement
The parties: the mediator does not ordinarily impose a settlement
The parties still need a negotiated solution, especially when communication, trust, emotion, or option search has stalled
Power imbalance, strategic delay, pressure to settle, or no agreement


Arbitration
Hear the parties’ submissions and decide the dispute under agreed rules
The arbitrator or tribunal, to the extent specified by the agreement, rules, and governing law
The parties need finality, authoritative interpretation, or a decision after bargaining has failed
Loss of outcome control, cost, adversarial escalation, and a result neither party would have designed






Mediation is therefore not “soft arbitration,” and arbitration is not “strong mediation.” A mediator can reframe, carry proposals, surface interests, manage difficult interaction, and reality-test a package while leaving acceptance to the parties. An arbitrator receives authority to decide.
A 2012 review of the preceding decade found diverse goals, settings, mediator strategies, and outcomes, but relatively few controlled studies comparing specific strategies or observing actual mediation behavior (Wall & Dunne, 2012). Choose the process by its task: Do the parties need help making a joint decision, or do they need someone else to make a decision?
A staged commercial clause might move from operational leads, to executive sponsors, to mediation, and finally to arbitration or litigation. It should specify the triggering dispute, decision authority, time limits, interim obligations, applicable rules, and how urgent action can be taken. Make the transfer of control explicit.
Hybrid procedures such as mediation–arbitration offer a settlement opportunity plus finality and may produce perceived time or cost savings in some disputes. They also create a predictable problem when one person performs both roles: information disclosed to a mediator in confidence may appear relevant when that person later becomes the decision-maker. Parties may become less candid or doubt impartiality. Barsky (2013) analyzes these risks in family-law disputes; recent American Arbitration Association commercial-practice guidance identifies the same concerns about candor, ex parte information, informed consent, and the integrity of an eventual award (American Arbitration Association, 2025). If a hybrid is used, the parties should decide in advance whether separate neutrals will serve, what information can cross stages, and whether renewed consent is required before the role changes. Potential speed should not hide a change in authority or confidentiality.

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
section: Optional module 5: search safely after agreement
text:
Optional module 5: search safely after agreement
Once a deal is secure, both sides may see a further gain. Yet reopening the discussion can threaten concessions they thought were settled. A post-settlement settlement makes that search possible by looking for a mutually preferred replacement while protecting the initial agreement. The essential condition is explicit: the existing agreement remains in force unless every required party voluntarily accepts the replacement, and either party can stop the search without penalty.
The buyer and supplier might discover that a different payment schedule releases cash or reduces risk for both. They can investigate that trade without surrendering the terms already secured. If one side uses the search to reopen settled concessions under pressure, the protection has failed.
Use the procedure only when the original agreement is secure, participants have authority, and the possible gain justifies further effort.

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
section: Complete the minimum agreement: implementation and review
text:
Complete the minimum agreement: implementation and review

Turn the supplier package into operating rules
Return to the opening disagreement about the urgent batch. “Flexible call-offs” becomes usable when the agreement specifies the permitted volume band, forecast deadline, confirmation procedure, and surge price. A shared record then shows whether the buyer requested capacity, whether the supplier accepted it, and which clock started.

Use the priority map from Chapter 37 to distinguish needs from assumptions. Later payment may protect the buyer’s cash flow, a longer term may support the supplier’s planning, and a service guarantee may protect reliability. Confirm those interests before turning them into contractual obligations.
In this illustrative design, the buyer submits the rolling forecast and the supplier confirms capacity within two working days. Their shared record distinguishes requested volume from accepted orders, so an urgent request cannot silently become a commitment. A monthly operating review examines forecasts, quality, and delays; designated sponsors can revise the agreed bands and investment milestones at a quarterly review.
The parties also specify opportunities to correct a failure, exceptions requiring urgent action, and the route from operational leads to commercial sponsors and any formal dispute process. If the relationship ends, the record must still explain which duties continue and how dedicated-tooling value is recovered. These terms need to fit the parties’ circumstances and governing law, rather than being copied as a complete contract.

Before relying on the signature, ask each side to explain these operating terms and failure rules in its own words. Resolve discrepancies, make material costs visible, and confirm that responsibilities sit with people able to carry them. A contingent bonus must not reward gaming, and a package menu must not hide an unattractive common term; either party still needs a meaningful opportunity to refuse the proposed agreement.
Test the six fields against the opening event: the buyer asks for an urgent batch, capacity is uncertain, and production is approaching. Can both parties identify the next action, who must take it, and which commitment follows? A clear answer shows what the added terms contribute; an unanswered question shows where the agreement still needs work.

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
text:
Practice Lab
Produce a one-page minimum viable agreement for the supplier obligation most likely to fail. Complete its six fields: owner, measure, verification source, review date, failure rule, and exit. Then stress-test the record against one plausible failure and revise whichever field did not provide a clear response.
Choose no more than one optional module from Table 38.3. State the diagnosed problem that justifies it and add only the information that module requires—for example, two or three sincere packages for unclear priorities, one measurable contingent term for forecast disagreement, or one explicit escalation rule for process failure. If no module is justified, record “none.” Multiple packages, full contingent-contract drafting, independent audits, detailed mediation or arbitration clauses, and multi-shock testing belong in an advanced agreement-design file, not in the minimum exercise.

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
text:
Take it forward
Return to the term in your agreement most likely to become disputed. Can both sides tell what was promised, how fulfillment will be checked, and what happens if circumstances change? Add the provisions needed to answer those questions, then check that the extra complexity has not made the agreement harder to carry out.

title: Part VII. Designing Better Decisions
text:
Questions to carry forward
The committee knows it should hear independent judgments, yet the most senior member still speaks first. A student plans to study, yet the phone remains beside the keyboard. Knowing the problem has not changed the situation that keeps producing it: reservations go unspoken and study time slips away. What could change in the meeting or at the desk to make the intended action easier?
The route in Figure 1 turns an explanation of the problem into a proposed change and a test of its effects. Behavior design asks what would make a useful action easier to repeat. Choice architecture examines how options are presented and how people move from intention to action. Decision hygiene considers the procedures through which a group gathers evidence, compares judgments, and learns from results.
The final chapter, Deciding With Data and AI, brings that work back to the distinction between prediction, valuation, and choice introduced in Chapter 1. An improved prediction still leaves people to decide what matters and which action to take. The earlier questions about evidence, values, and disagreement therefore remain necessary when AI enters the process. Chapter 41 builds a procedure that can be examined and revised; Chapter 42 asks how a tool can improve that procedure and how we would know whether it has.
Each intervention is a proposal to test. We need to identify whose goal it serves, what outcome would count as improvement, and how affected people can question or leave the arrangement.
We return to the hiring committee with a more useful question than whether its members are rational. How could its next decision be made easier to examine, challenge, and improve?

title: Part VII. Designing Better Decisions
text:
Where does the intended action break down?
What small change to the conditions addresses that obstacle?
What evidence will show improvement, failure, or harm?

title: 39  Behavior Design
text:
Learning goals
Make the Better Action Easier
A student intends to work on a term paper before opening email, but the laptop opens onto the inbox each morning. Replies offer small tasks with clear endings; the paper offers a vague instruction: “Work on the literature review.” By the time the student opens the draft, much of the available writing time has gone.
One possible change is to leave the draft open the evening before, beside notes on two studies and a precise next step: “Write one sentence explaining how their findings agree or differ.” The next morning begins with a visible action instead of a decision about where to start. That could help if the vague starting point was the main obstacle. If the student cannot yet interpret the studies, needs guidance on academic writing, or has no time available that morning, a clearer prompt will accomplish little.
The useful change depends on why the intention fails. Behavior design starts with that explanation, then changes a specific condition and tests whether the intended action becomes easier to carry out.
The habit chapter used bedtime scrolling to distinguish familiar cues, wanting, and enjoyment (Wood & Rünger, 2016). Term-paper writing is a useful transfer case because several other obstacles can produce a similar detour. Opening email may be habitual, but it can also avoid an unclear or uncomfortable task, meet a real coordination need, or fill time too short for the planned work. This chapter turns that diagnosis into a plan for change, whether the aim is to alter an established routine or begin something new.

title: 39  Behavior Design
text:
Apply one five-step workflow: define the behavior, diagnose the bottleneck, redesign the decisive point, measure, and review.
Match a practical change to the obstacle it addresses.
Distinguish follow-through from the outcome it is meant to improve, and plan how to resume after a lapse.

title: 39  Behavior Design
section: From intention to a testable change
text:
From intention to a testable change
“Work on my paper” gives the student a direction, but it does not specify what should happen differently tomorrow. “Draft one comparison of the two selected studies before opening email” identifies an action, a competing response, and an occasion to observe. Now the student can ask why email comes first and choose a change that addresses that obstacle.

Relying on willpower alone would mean resisting the inbox afresh whenever writing feels difficult. That can work on a particular morning, but it leaves success dependent on repeatedly winning the same conflict. A more reliable plan prepares the conditions under which the desired action starts and continues (Duckworth et al., 2016).






CautionSelf-control effort and the debate over ego depletion



The ego-depletion account pictures willpower as a fuel supply that each act of self-control uses up. Large preregistered tests have challenged that account (Hagger et al., 2016; Vohs et al., 2021). In a 36-laboratory study with 3,531 participants, the planned analysis found a near-zero effect of prior self-control effort on subsequent performance. Another multilab study found a small effect (Dang et al., 2021), but a performance cost does not establish that a fuel has been consumed. Willpower should not be treated as a fixed, depletable supply; effort and fatigue can matter without that explanation. Appendix E examines the disputed evidence.


Two tasks clarify what self-control evidence can establish. The Stroop demonstration in Chapter 8 shows interference from a practiced response. The marshmallow studies in Chapter 20 separate the effect of a reliable promise from the association between childhood waiting and later achievement. Neither task is a direct gauge of a person’s fixed supply of willpower.
Use the CIAO habit loop to organize that preparation: choose a reliable cue, anticipate the impulse that competes with the goal, make the intended action easy enough to begin, and arrange an outcome that makes progress visible. For the student, this means returning to the prepared draft after breakfast, marking an uncertainty instead of escaping into email, and completing one useful comparison. Repeating that start in a familiar setting can build a cue–action association; deliberate effort helps establish and adjust the arrangement.
The return arrow in Figure 39.1 matters: an unsuccessful attempt can reveal that the obstacle was misidentified. Making the next writing step visible tests a different explanation from obtaining missing studies, learning how to evaluate their methods, or finding a feasible period to work.






Figure 39.1: A practical workflow defines an action, finds an obstacle, changes one condition, and tests the result. Review can change the diagnosis; after a lapse or harm, recovery or support may also change the goal or design.



Table 39.1 turns the figure into a short record. Write down the prediction before trying the change, so that the result can challenge the explanation that seemed plausible at the start.



Table 39.1: A minimum behavior-design record










Step
Required output
Governing question




1. Define the behavior
One observable target action, the competing action, and the situation in which one displaces the other
What would a camera or reliable record show?


2. Diagnose the bottleneck
The cue, immediate function or consequence, and the main constraint on the target action
Why does the current response win at this moment?


3. Redesign the decisive point
One change to the cue, action size, friction, prompt, support, or immediate feedback
What is the smallest change that directly addresses the diagnosed bottleneck?


4. Measure
What happens before the change, a prediction, measures of follow-through and outcome, and a test period
What observable pattern would show that the diagnosis was useful?


5. Review
A review date and a keep, revise, or stop rule, including recovery after a lapse or harm
What will change next if the prediction succeeds or fails?






For the student, the prediction might be: leaving the draft open with a specific comparison to make will make writing more likely to begin before email. Starting is the first thing to observe; whether the paragraph offers an accurate, useful comparison is a separate question to return to when evaluating the change.

title: 39  Behavior Design
text:
Diagnose the moment with B=MAP
The student wants to advance the paper, yet willingness alone has not settled what happens when the laptop opens. The Fogg Behavior Model, B=MAP, describes behavior as occurring when motivation, ability, and a prompt converge (Fogg, 2009, 2020). Here ability means how easy the action is to perform at that moment; a prompt calls for it to happen.
This distinction gives the student three questions to answer. Is this writing step worth doing now, or does fear of producing a poor paragraph make email more attractive? Can the student carry it out with the writing skills, understanding, materials, and time available? What will bring it to attention before the inbox does? A reminder addresses the last question, but cannot supply missing understanding or protected time. Calling every detour a habit or “low motivation” would obscure the diagnosis.
Opportunity can also influence motivation. The smoking studies in Chapter 21 show that expecting access can strengthen craving itself. Changing access may therefore affect the impulse before action, as well as make the action easier or harder to carry out.
When motivation fluctuates, preparing an easier first action and a timely prompt may offer a more workable plan than expecting the same enthusiasm every morning.
Look for mornings when writing already begins before email. Such bright spots can suggest conditions worth reproducing and testing, such as a clearer first task or a quieter setting (Heath & Heath, 2010).

title: 39  Behavior Design
text:
Make the first action small
The inbox offers an easy response with a quick sense of completion. To give the paper a feasible starting point, the student could draft one rough comparison using the two studies already selected. The small action provides an entry into the work; its value depends on what follows, including whether the comparison is accurate and helps answer the research question.
Fogg’s practical recipe connects that small start to an existing routine: After I [reliable anchor], I will [tiny behavior]. Then I will [authentically acknowledge completion]. The anchor supplies a prompt, the small action reduces the effort needed to begin, and acknowledgment marks progress. For the student, the anchor might be sitting down with breakfast finished, and the action might be drafting the first comparison sentence.
An inspiring class or approaching deadline may make an ambitious plan feel easy. Use that motivation to prepare for a tired Wednesday: obtain the studies, identify the next comparison, and arrange a workable time. The arrangement still has to be tried when the initial enthusiasm fades.

title: 39  Behavior Design
text:
Implementation intentions
A feasible action can still be forgotten at the moment it matters. Implementation intentions connect an anticipated situation to a specified response: If this happens, then I will do that. The plan helps bring a goal to mind and guide action when the situation occurs (Gollwitzer, 1999).
The student can turn “I will work on my paper” into “If I finish breakfast on a weekday, then I will sit at my desk and draft the selected comparison before opening email.” Twenty-five minutes of writing might remain the session goal, while drafting the comparison specifies how to begin. The same structure works beyond writing: a manager might plan to ask one clarifying question when receiving criticism, or a saver to transfer 10 percent of each salary payment immediately. Each plan identifies an occasion and an action concrete enough to carry out.
Milkman and colleagues (2011) randomly assigned employees to three flu-clinic reminders: basic information, information plus a field for a planned date, or fields for both date and time. Vaccination rates were 33.1% in the basic-reminder group and 37.1% in the date-and-time group—a 4.0-percentage-point difference. The covariate-adjusted estimate was 4.2 points (95% confidence interval: 0.5–7.8); the date-only prompt did not reliably outperform the basic reminder. A concrete plan helped translate an available opportunity into action.
Sometimes the difficulty is choosing a realistic response to an obstacle. WOOP (Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan) adds that preparation: identify a meaningful, feasible wish, imagine the valued outcome, consider what could obstruct it, and form an if-then plan. For the student, “I want to explain what these studies tell us” becomes more actionable after identifying the vague starting point that sends them toward email. Imagining success alone would leave that obstacle unchanged. Evidence on mental contrasting with implementation intentions supports modest average gains in goal attainment compared with control conditions without the combined exercise, with variation across goals and settings (Oettingen, 2012; Wang et al., 2021). The WOOP research lens explains what that evidence establishes.

title: 39  Behavior Design
text:
Friction, rewards, and commitment
A plan specifies what to do, but the effort and immediate appeal of competing actions still matter. Friction includes the steps, time, and effort needed to act. Leaving the draft and source notes open reduces friction for writing; putting the phone in another room adds friction to checking it. The same principle can guide other changes, such as removing saved payment details before an impulsive purchase or simplifying a form that people repeatedly abandon.
Changing the default also changes what happens without an active choice. Chapter 40 develops this approach across a whole choice process, including its boundary conditions and ethics. Here the student can begin with the narrower question of which action the current arrangement makes easiest. Defaults change the starting point; the home-energy-report experiments in Chapter 40 instead test repeated feedback and whether its effects persist after messages stop. These are different interventions, even when both support follow-through.
When effort is immediate and the benefit delayed, temptation bundling pairs a beneficial activity with something enjoyable now. Milkman and colleagues (2014) randomly assigned participants to gym-only access to tempting audiobooks, encouragement to restrict audiobook listening to the gym themselves, or a comparison condition. Initially, gym visits were 51% higher with restricted access and 29% higher with encouragement than in the comparison group. These are relative differences in visits, not percentage-point changes in attendance rates. The effects weakened over time, especially after the Thanksgiving break.
A person might similarly reserve a favorite podcast for walking. The experiment suggests that linking an immediate attraction to an effortful activity can help people begin, while the fading effect makes recovery after disruption part of the design.
If the problem is a predictable future temptation, precommitment can constrain the later choice (Thaler & Shefrin, 1981). App blockers, cancellation penalties, and restricted-access accounts do this in different ways, with different costs and possibilities for reversal. Assess whether the constraint supports the person’s goal and remains acceptable when circumstances change. The intertemporal-choice chapter reviews commitment evidence, including the retracted deadline study; a plausible device still needs evidence that it helps.

title: 39  Behavior Design
text:
Design an attention boundary
For the student, beginning the comparison will accomplish little if every new message interrupts it. In Indistractable, Eyal (2019) distinguishes traction, which serves an intended activity, from distraction, which takes us away from it. Email can support a planned correspondence period and interrupt a writing period; chosen rest also deserves protected time.
Checking can begin with an external trigger, such as an alert, or an internal trigger, such as boredom or uncertainty. An attention boundary therefore needs more than silenced notifications: notice what prompts the detour, reserve realistic time for the intended activity, and adjust interrupting cues. If uncertainty about a study repeatedly precedes checking, mark the unresolved issue or seek the needed explanation. If a rough sentence feels unacceptable, try drafting it before editing. The precommitment tools above can help protect a feasible plan when temptation is predictable; they cannot teach writing skills or create unavailable time.
These changes should address an observed problem. Ward and colleagues (2017) reported lower cognitive performance when participants’ own phones were nearby, but a later meta-analysis found a narrower pattern: pooled impairment appeared for working memory, while other cognitive outcomes showed no significant effect (Parry, 2024). Phone presence and an actual notification are different conditions; Limited Attention discusses interruption. Switching away from an unfinished task also creates a distinct difficulty: part of the previous task can remain mentally active—attention residue—and reduce performance on the next task (Leroy, 2009).
Digital services can also encourage the repetitions through which habits develop. Eyal’s (2014) Hook Model describes a product-design sequence: Trigger → Action → Variable reward → Investment. The last two elements help explain why someone might return after the first visit.
A variable reward concerns the outcome: opening a course forum may reveal useful feedback, a routine reply, or nothing new. In four experiments with real consequences, Shen and colleagues (2019) found that uncertain incentives could encourage repetition even when financially inferior to certain incentives. The advantage appeared after people experienced the activity and when uncertainty was resolved immediately; delaying resolution removed it. This supports an explanation in which finding out the outcome can itself reward participation.
Compare that with Shen and colleagues’ (2015) pursuit experiments in Chapter 21: uncertainty can make working toward a reward more engaging, whereas the 2019 studies examine repeating an activity after experiencing its outcome. Neither finding establishes that repetition has become automatic or that uncertainty always helps.
An investment is effort that makes a later visit more valuable or sets up another cue. Saving an explanation creates useful material to return to; posting a follow-up question may generate the next reply alert (Eyal, 2014). In the student’s writing routine, leaving notes and a selected comparison prepares the next start. Variable rewards and investment can thus support repetition, but neither is required for every habit: reliable, satisfying progress can also encourage return. Table 39.2 examines when these features support the user’s goal and when they make disengagement difficult.



Table 39.2: Applying the Hook Model: useful return, capture risks, and safeguards











Hook stage
Helpful use
Capture risk
Agency safeguard




Trigger
A chosen reminder or relevant reply
Continuous interruption or anxiety-driven checking
User-controlled timing and batching


Action
Easy access to the intended task
One-tap entry into an endless feed
A visible stopping point and deliberate continuation


Variable reward

Repeated searching for the next uncertain payoff

Investment
