title: 42  Deciding With Data and AI
section: Choose tools by the work they must do
text:
Choose tools by the work they must do
Suppose the city asks a team to “use AI” to improve pipe replacement. One member proposes a risk model, another a chatbot to answer residents’ questions, and a third a scheduling tool for crews. Each addresses a different obstacle. The four analytical purposes help the team identify which obstacle matters before choosing a tool. The workbench in Table 42.4 includes ordinary reporting and causal analysis alongside predictive models, language models, retrieval systems, and optimizers. A workflow can combine them, with a different check for each output.



Table 42.4: Select methods for the work a decision needs; their uses overlap











Work inside the decision
Possible tool
Output to request
Human check that matters




Describe outcomes and coverage
Spreadsheet, database query, statistical summary, chart
Counts, rates, distributions, and missing cases
Are units, denominators, definitions, and coverage correct?


Estimate a quantity or probability
Regression, tree ensembles, neural networks
Demand range, failure risk, or class probability
Is it validated for these cases and this time horizon?


Find structure or unusual cases
Clustering or anomaly detection
Groups or flagged deviations
Does the pattern have a useful interpretation, and could the flag be harmless?


Estimate what an action changes
Randomized comparison or a credible observational causal design, with suitable estimation
Expected difference under alternative actions
Does the design support that causal comparison, and for whom?


Find and organize evidence
Search, retrieval, document extraction, assisted summarization
Relevant passages with traceable sources
Does the source actually support the claim, and what was omitted?


Generate and compare language
A large language model
Drafts, alternative explanations, questions, or a comparison table
Are facts, calculations, implications, and the option set sound?


Allocate resources under explicit rules
Optimization, possibly using model estimates
A feasible schedule or allocation
Are the objective, constraints, and uncertainty acceptable?






A central training task for many LLMs is predicting subsequent tokens—pieces of text—given a context. Additional training and connected tools can support instruction following, retrieval, coding, and other tasks. A fluent answer is therefore not equivalent to a calibrated forecast about the external world. Generated facts and references can be false; asking the model to sound more certain does not validate them (Ji et al., 2023).
The optional Research Lens in Chapter 4 explains how prompts guide generation through context, why this offers a limited analogy with human perception, and why plausible content still needs external evidence. Much organizational work consists of turning scattered information into something another person can understand and use. A useful LLM can lower that cost, provided the workflow preserves the evidence and gives someone the means to check it.

Customer support: help at the moment of action
A support worker needs a useful answer while the customer is still waiting. Searching a long manual costs time, but an immediate answer that is wrong leaves the problem unresolved. An assistant that brings relevant guidance into the live conversation could change that trade-off. Brynjolfsson and colleagues studied a staggered rollout of a generative-AI assistant among 5,172 customer-support agents. Compared with working without the assistant, access increased issues resolved per hour by 15 percent on average, with substantial differences across workers (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025).
The assistant’s value was connected to an immediate task: helping a worker respond to a customer. Translating that idea elsewhere requires identifying what the worker needs at the moment of action. A draft that arrives too late, cannot be checked, or contradicts the organization’s obligations may save writing time while worsening the service.


Screening: change the workflow, then test it
Screening programmes need to find cancers while managing the work of reading large numbers of examinations. Reducing the number of human readings would save effort, but missed cancers could make that saving costly. The Swedish MASAI trial tested an AI-supported mammography workflow in which scores helped route examinations to one or two radiologists and supported detection. In the 2023 interim analysis of about 80,000 women, screen-reading workload fell by 44.3 percent relative to standard double reading (Lång et al., 2023).
The later randomized analysis examined interval cancers: cancers diagnosed between scheduled screening rounds. Rates were 1.55 per 1,000 women with AI-supported screening versus 1.76 with standard double reading, meeting the trial’s non-inferiority criterion: ruling out worsening beyond a prespecified margin. The rate ratio was 0.88, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.65–1.18. The AI-supported workflow detected 80.5 percent of cancers, compared with 73.8 percent under standard double reading (sensitivity). Both workflows correctly cleared 98.5 percent of women without cancer (specificity) (Gommers et al., 2026).
The lesson is practical: the intervention included a division of work, a comparison condition, and patient-relevant evaluation. It was more specific than making an algorithm available and hoping it helped.


A capable assistant can still fail to improve the user
Strong performance on a clinical case gives a reason to test a model as a physician’s assistant. The physician must still know when to consult it, recognize a useful answer, and change the relevant judgment. A study can therefore find capable model output without finding better performance by people given access to it. In a randomized study, 50 physicians solved clinical vignettes using conventional resources, with half also given access to an LLM. Their median diagnostic-reasoning scores per case were 76 percent with LLM access and 74 percent without it. The adjusted difference was 2 percentage points, with a 95 percent confidence interval from −4 to 8. Yet in a separate assessment using a standardized prompt, the LLM alone achieved a median score of 92 percent on the same scoring rubric. A strong standalone result had not translated into a significant improvement for physicians given access to the tool (Goh et al., 2024).
A tool’s standalone performance and its effect on a person using it are different quantities. The user must recognize when to consult it, interpret its output, detect errors, and change an appropriate action. Interface design, training, time pressure, and incentives can all become part of the intervention. Their contribution has to be tested rather than assumed.
The cases differ in setting and research design, but each directs attention to the arrangement around the tool. The useful comparison concerns the work and its consequences under that arrangement, rather than the impressive output considered alone.

title: 42  Deciding With Data and AI
text:
Trust, valuation, and responsibility
Flint’s residents could be offered a better estimate while still disputing the decision made with it. The conflict asks us to separate confidence in a forecast from willingness to let a system determine what happens to one’s household. People’s willingness to accept algorithmic advice depends on what the advice is for. Bigman and Gray’s experiments found reluctance to let machines make morally consequential decisions, with less aversion when machines advised rather than decided. Other experiments found algorithm appreciation: people sometimes placed more weight on advice attributed to an algorithm than on advice attributed to a person (Bigman & Gray, 2018; Logg et al., 2019).
Distinguish between trust in a prediction, acceptance of a value trade-off, and recognition of legitimate authority. A resident can believe that a pipe-risk model is useful while still expecting public officials to justify whose street is excavated next.
This chapter’s recommendation is that valuation and consequential final choice remain human responsibilities. People and institutions should own the objectives, constraints, trade-offs, authorization, and remedies. AI can help articulate competing values, reveal inconsistencies, estimate consequences, or summarize affected people’s expressed preferences. Predicting what people are likely to approve is different from establishing what they ought to accept.
Human authority must also have substance. A reviewer who cannot inspect the relevant evidence, has no time to disagree, or is punished for overriding the system offers little protection. Responsibility belongs to those who design and control the process as well as those who use it. The previous chapter develops the danger of making the frontline operator a convenient bearer of blame without corresponding power (Elish, 2019).
For a consequential decision, retain a person or authorized body who can hear reasons, approve or refuse the action, explain exceptions, and arrange review. People can authorize bounded automated actions under an explicit policy, while retaining responsibility for the policy, monitoring, escalation, and withdrawal of that authority. The boundary should be chosen in advance and scaled to the consequences (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023).
In Flint, this would mean distinguishing a challenge to the risk estimate from a challenge to the allocation policy, and identifying who can respond to each. Accountability becomes meaningful when an objection has somewhere to go and can change the relevant decision.
crumbs: 42  Deciding With Data and AI

title: 42  Deciding With Data and AI
section: Test the whole decision, not just the model
text:
Test the whole decision, not just the model
Evaluation should match the analytical purpose. A descriptive report needs accurate definitions, denominators, and coverage. A diagnostic explanation must address competing accounts; a causal claim needs a defensible comparison. A prediction needs testing on relevant new cases. A prescription needs evaluation against the objective, constraints, costs, and consequences of the action. These checks build on the distinctions in Table 42.1.
Imagine receiving a report that a model is “95 percent accurate.” Before celebrating, ask what was predicted, which cases were included, and what comparison matters. If an event occurs in only 5 percent of cases, a rule that always predicts its absence is already 95 percent accurate. It may still be useless for finding the cases that require action.
Begin by testing the estimate on observations that did not determine the fitted model, keeping validation separate from final testing (James et al., 2023). Then follow the estimate into use: which errors change actions, what capacity limits those actions, and what consequences follow? The sections below separate these checks so a favorable model score cannot stand in for an evaluation of the decision.

Make the test resemble the task
Begin with the unit and moment of decision. Are we predicting a property, a customer session, a student term, or tomorrow’s demand? Use only information available at that moment. Data leakage occurs when information that should be unavailable to the prediction enters its development or evaluation. A variable recorded after the outcome can make a model look excellent by leaking the answer into its inputs.
Keep an untouched test set for the final comparison. Use the training and validation data to fit and tune the model. When future performance is the target, respect time order; when the same person or organization appears repeatedly, avoid treating their related observations as independent evidence of generalization. Apply preprocessing within the relevant training partitions. Document exclusions, missingness, source versions, and the exact model that produced the result.
Compare a complex model with a credible simple rule on the same cases and under the same information constraints. A base rate, a transparent regression, or the existing procedure may be hard to beat after operating costs are included. Better-looking performance on a more favorable test does not show improvement.


Evaluate probabilities and decisions separately
A city may use a risk cutoff to decide whether an inspection is worth its cost. A model can rank properties correctly while overstating their probabilities; the ranking then looks useful, but more properties may cross the action threshold than the evidence justifies. Evaluation needs to test both what the scores separate and what their numerical values mean. Discrimination concerns how well scores distinguish cases with different outcomes. Calibration concerns whether stated probabilities agree with observed frequencies across appropriate groups of predictions. Among many comparable cases assigned a 30 percent probability, roughly 30 percent should have the event.
Then evaluate the action rule. Count the important kinds of error, inspect subgroup performance, and apply the stated costs and capacity limits. A model with a slightly better ranking metric can still produce a worse decision if its probabilities are poorly calibrated around the action threshold. Conversely, an improvement far from any threshold may change almost no actions.
Record the number of cases underlying each result and the uncertainty in estimated performance. Chapter 15 develops the discipline of calibration and learning from samples.


Compare workflows before scaling
A practical pilot should compare the current process, a simple baseline, and the proposed AI-assisted process. A model-only comparison can be informative in a retrospective or otherwise safe evaluation even when it would not be an acceptable live policy. Measure verification time, error consequences, appropriate reliance, and outcomes—not only how quickly a draft appears.
Start with a mode that lets the system produce outputs without automatically changing consequential actions when that is feasible. Then use a limited, monitored deployment; randomize or use another credible evaluation design when the question is whether the new workflow causes improvement. Prespecify what would justify expansion, revision, or stopping.
The live system also changes its own evidence. A fraud review prevents some losses; outreach may prevent some departures; an excavation reveals a previously unknown pipe. Outcomes under the new policy are not a neutral test of what would have happened under the old one. Log the action as well as the prediction, and preserve the distinction between forecasting quality and policy effects.


Communicate enough uncertainty to support a choice
A useful display makes the relevant comparison visible. Show the same units and time horizon across alternatives, label the action threshold, and distinguish observations from predictions. If an interval is shown, say whether it concerns an average effect, an estimated parameter, or an individual future outcome; those are different uncertainties. Wilke’s treatment of uncertainty emphasizes that a visually precise mark can easily be mistaken for certainty (Wilke, 2019).
For the city, a map should make missing inspections visible. For the event organizer, the forecast should appear beside the consequences of moving or remaining. For the university, the display should distinguish baseline dropout risk from estimated benefit of outreach. A dashboard earns its place when updated information can trigger a useful decision.
crumbs: 42  Deciding With Data and AI

title: 42  Deciding With Data and AI
section: Why this is the final chapter
text:
Why this is the final chapter
The book began by asking how a decision should be made and how it actually takes shape. Data analysis brings those two questions together. Description makes the current process visible; diagnosis investigates its failures; prediction reduces uncertainty; and prescription compares possible actions. AI can assist this work, while the human discussion of what matters and who may act remains explicit. A city with better pipe estimates still needs to decide what its replacement program should accomplish.
Using that opportunity draws on the whole book:

Attention and interpretation: Chapter 3 asks what becomes evidence; Chapter 12 examines how its presentation changes a decision. These questions apply to the cases included in a dataset, the information supplied to an AI assistant, and the way a score or recommendation is displayed.
Prediction and evidence: Chapters 14 and 15 supply base rates, updating, and calibration. They help us judge whether an AI forecast deserves reliance and whether an apparent improvement survives an appropriate comparison.
Valuation and a better life: Chapter 6 examines how outcomes become worth pursuing; Chapter 22 asks what makes the resulting life better. Together they keep a convenient target—spending, clicks, or speed—from silently defining success.
Other minds and institutions: Chapter 28 examines authority and responsibility, while Chapter 35 treats negotiation as joint decision design. An AI-supported policy still needs a way to address conflicting interests, hear objections, and assign authority over the final choice.
Design and learning: Chapters 39 through 41 turn these distinctions into changes that can be implemented and tested. A forecast becomes useful when someone can act on it, record the result, and revise the process.

These connections give the chapter its practical test: identify the uncertainty a tool could reduce, decide what action would follow, and compare that arrangement with the existing process. A model’s score matters because of what it enables people to do.
crumbs: 42  Deciding With Data and AI

title: 42  Deciding With Data and AI
section: Practice Lab: improve a decision with data
text:
Practice Lab: improve a decision with data
Work with a recurring decision that is important enough to improve but small enough to test: scheduling staff, classifying incoming requests, prioritizing maintenance inspections, or preparing a document review. First state whether the missing contribution is descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, or prescriptive. A spreadsheet or simple comparison may be sufficient; add AI when it has a defined job. If using real records, use data authorized for this purpose and the chosen tool. The exercise can also use fictional cases. Working alone, record your assessment before seeing the analysis and preserve that version. You can study how the output changes your judgment, but you cannot use your own two assessments as evidence about disagreement between independent people.

The data and AI decision canvas
Use Table 42.5 to specify the decision, missing evidence, protected values, and review rule before selecting a product or writing a prompt. The separate fields make it possible to judge the tool by the contribution the decision actually needs.



Table 42.5: A decision canvas that keeps the analytical question, valuation, causal evidence, and responsibility distinct









Field
What to write before the pilot




Decision and owner
Who must choose what, by when, from which feasible alternatives?


Analytical question
Is the immediate task description, diagnosis, prediction, or prescription? What would its answer change?


Evidence or estimate
What information is needed? For a prediction, specify unit, target, horizon, and uncertainty.


Valuation
Whose benefits, burdens, rights, and error costs count? Which constraints are protected?


Causal link
Why would the proposed action improve the outcome? What evidence is still needed?


Tool and baseline
Which function should the tool perform? What simple rule or existing process must it improve upon?


Evidence and test
Which data are legitimate and available at decision time? What held-out or prospective comparison will be used?


Authority and exceptions
Who authorizes actions, checks uncertain cases, handles challenges, and can stop the system?


Learning rule
What is logged, when is it reviewed, and what result triggers continuation, revision, or withdrawal?






Round 1: preserve independent judgment. Give two people the same case. Each records the available actions, the missing information, any relevant forecast, the consequences that matter, and a provisional choice before seeing analytical output. This uses the independence principle from Chapter 41.
Round 2: assign the analysis a bounded job. Produce the summary, investigate the pattern, estimate the missing quantity, or compare feasible actions under stated criteria. Select a tool suited to that job and record the time and cost of obtaining and checking the result. If using AI, request a specific contribution. If the system cannot justify a probability from an appropriate model and validation, keep its suggestions qualitative rather than inventing precision.
For an LLM helping with a document-based decision, a useful instruction is:

Using only the supplied material, make a comparison table for these alternatives. Link each factual claim to its supporting passage. Separate stated facts, assumptions, and missing information. Show which additional evidence could change the comparison. Use our stated criteria; flag any value trade-off that we have not resolved.

This prompt structures a checkable output. Verify the supporting passages and important calculations before using the table.
Round 3: diagnose the disagreement. When individual assessments and analytical results differ, classify the reason. Do they disagree about evidence, probability, values, feasibility, or authority? A model cannot settle a disagreement about priorities merely by restating its forecast. A senior person cannot refute a well-validated forecast merely by disliking its implications.
Round 4: record a choice and a test. Use the canvas to authorize a limited action or decide that more evidence is needed. Preserve the initial forecasts, the advice received, what was checked, and why the advice changed—or did not change—the decision. Set a review date before the outcome can rewrite the story.
Debrief with one question: What became better because of the analysis, and what evidence would show that improvement? A useful answer identifies a changed part of the process and an observable consequence, taking the cost of analysis and implementation into account. “The output sounded professional” is not enough.

title: 42  Deciding With Data and AI
text:
Take it forward
Flint needed a replacement policy it could explain to anxious residents and evaluate against the removal of hazardous pipes. Better predictions made the search more informative; the dispute concerned how those predictions should guide action and who could set the priorities. A defensible process needs both useful evidence and accountable authority over the trade-offs.
More available data and cheaper computation make this discipline feasible for more recurring decisions. Choose one this week. State the question, identify the relevant records, and begin with a simple analysis. Use AI where it improves a defined contribution. Make the values behind the choice explicit, keep an identifiable owner, and preserve a record that later evidence can challenge.
Return finally to the hiring committee that opened the book. AI might help compare applications or estimate later performance. The committee still has to define which kinds of performance matter, examine how evidence was selected and presented, hear disagreement, and justify its choice. It then needs to check what happened without letting the outcome rewrite the original reasoning. Attention, prediction, valuation, influence, design, and learning meet in that one decision.
The decision map in Figure 1.1 gives us a common reference from the first chapter to the last. We can ask which part a tool improves, which judgment still needs attention, and what later evidence would justify a change. The more a machine can tell us about what may happen, the more clearly we need to decide what is worth making happen.

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
1. Feasible and consideration sets
Formal details supporting Chapters 1 and 2
Suppose one job offer pays more while another leaves more time and flexibility. A salary comparison favors the first; a comparison of daily life may favor the second. Then an employer offers to negotiate, changing the menu you thought you had to choose from. What looked like a simple ranking now depends on which terms can change and what the alternatives would mean for your life. Which assumptions determine the recommendation, and which further question is worth asking?
This appendix puts the reasoning from Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 into mathematical form. Use the equations to expose an assumption or test a recommendation. Start with feasible options, beliefs, and values; then use the information and sensitivity sections to find out what could change the answer. The final section asks when further analysis is worth its own cost.
Let \(\mathcal{A}\) denote the set of actions under discussion, including options whose feasibility has not yet been checked. An action is feasible only if it satisfies the relevant constraints. Suppose the decision contains inequality constraints \(g_j(a)\leq 0\) and equality constraints \(h_\ell(a)=0\). The feasible set is
\[
A
=
\left\{
a\in\mathcal{A}:
g_j(a)\leq 0\ \text{for all }j,
\quad
h_\ell(a)=0\ \text{for all }\ell
\right\}.
\]
The constraint functions determine which actions belong to \(A\). A job that requires a licence you cannot obtain in time, for example, may be imaginable without being feasible.
This formulation also explains why prescriptive analysis tests apparent constraints. If a deadline can be negotiated, a role redesigned, or a commitment staged, the relevant constraint changes and the feasible set may expand. The best imaginable action need not be feasible, and the current visible menu need not contain every feasible action.
The consideration set \(K\) contains the alternatives a person notices, recalls, generates, or takes seriously:
\[
K(z,m)\subseteq \mathcal{A},
\]
where \(z\) represents external context and \(m\) represents internal state. Considered options can include ones that later prove infeasible, while feasible options may be overlooked. After feasibility has been checked, the available considered options are \(K(z,m)\cap A\). Comparing that intersection coherently can still miss a better option elsewhere in \(A\), which is why generating alternatives matters.
crumbs: A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
2. Preferences and the choice correspondence
Let \(\succeq\) be a weak preference relation over the feasible alternatives. The statement
\[
a\succeq b
\]
means that alternative \(a\) is at least as good as alternative \(b\) for the purposes represented by the model.
For a finite, nonempty feasible set, completeness and transitivity are sufficient for a numerical value representation \(V\) such that
\[
a\succeq b
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
V(a)\geq V(b).
\]
With a finite, nonempty \(A\), a maximum exists.1 This benchmark has long organized decision research (Edwards, 1954).
The model’s choice correspondence returns all feasible maximizers:
\[
C(A)
=
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in A}V(a)
=
\left\{
a\in A:
V(a)\geq V(b)\ \text{for every }b\in A
\right\}.
\]
If several alternatives tie, \(C(A)\) contains several actions. Predicting a single observed choice then requires a tie-breaking rule. For the job offers, equal scores mean that the model has not yet selected one job over the other.






NoteValue scales



A value representation of a ranking is ordinal: any strictly increasing transformation represents the same preferences. Interpreting numerical gaps such as \(V(a)-V(b)\) requires a cardinal scale. Expected-utility indices are unique up to positive affine transformations, and multiattribute scores require explicit normalization.
crumbs: A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
3. Consequences, beliefs, and expected utility
Two advisers may recommend different jobs because they predict different promotion prospects, or because they value the same prospect differently. A single score can hide that distinction: evidence about promotion addresses the first disagreement, while the second requires a discussion of priorities. The reduced-form function \(V(a)\) can be unpacked into beliefs about consequences and values over those consequences.
If action \(a\) produces a known consequence \(x(a)\), and \(u(x)\) represents the value of consequence \(x\), then
\[
V(a)=u\bigl(x(a)\bigr).
\]
Under uncertainty, let \(O\) be a finite set of possible consequences. Let \(P(o\mid a)\) be the probability assigned to consequence \(o\) if action \(a\) is taken, and let \(u(o)\) represent preferences over consequences. A standard expected-utility evaluation is
\[
V(a)
=
EU(a)
=
\sum_{o\in O}P(o\mid a)u(o),
\]
so that
\[
C(A)
=
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in A}
\sum_{o\in O}P(o\mid a)u(o).
\]
This representation separates three objects:

\(A\): feasible alternatives;
\(P(o\mid a)\): beliefs or specified probabilities over consequences; and
\(u(o)\): values or preferences over consequences.

The probabilities describe the consequences of taking each action. Observed outcomes among people who chose an action need not supply that forecast: their circumstances may also explain their outcomes. Chapter 42 returns to this distinction when separating prediction from the benefit of an intervention. For lotteries with specified probabilities, the von Neumann–Morgenstern expected-utility representation relies on completeness, transitivity, continuity, and independence conditions (von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944). A subjective-probability interpretation adds assumptions connecting choices to beliefs. Chapter 16 develops expected value, expected utility, final consequences, curvature, and the independence axiom in the setting of risky choice.
A consequence may include effects on other people, fairness, identity, environmental outcomes, duties, or future generations. Some rights and obligations may instead be represented as constraints that remove impermissible actions from \(A\).

Decision trees make the sequence explicit
A decision tree represents choices, uncertain events, and their consequences in the order they can occur. Decision nodes branch into available actions; chance nodes branch into possible events, with probabilities conditional on reaching that point; terminal nodes record the resulting consequences. The distinction prevents an uncertain event from being treated as something the decision maker controls (Raiffa, 1968).
Under expected-utility analysis, work backward from the terminal consequences: average utility at a chance node using its probabilities, and select the feasible action with the greatest expected utility at a decision node. For the job choice, branches might distinguish accepting an offer now, negotiating first, or waiting, followed by the responses each action could receive. A useful tree states which information will be available before each choice; it must not let today’s decision use tomorrow’s knowledge.
crumbs: A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
4. Invariance, regularity, and omitted variables
If descriptions leave options, consequence distributions, and values unchanged, a coherent ranking should survive a change in wording. Observed choices can nevertheless shift with a frame, a decoy, or a default. To locate the source of that shift, we need to identify which part of the decision changed. A descriptive extension allows context and internal state to shape the consideration set, beliefs, and values:
\[
V(a\mid z,m)
=
\sum_{o\in O}
P(o\mid a,z,m)\,
u(o\mid z,m),
\qquad a\in K(z,m)\cap A.
\]
After feasibility checking, and assuming at least one considered option remains feasible, observed selection can then be written as
\[
a^{\mathrm{choice}}
\in
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in K(z,m)\cap A}
V(a\mid z,m).
\]
To test this representation, specify or measure \(K\), \(P\), \(u\), and their response to context independently of the observed choice. A model of implementation adds a mapping from chosen action to performed action and realized consequence.
Let \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) be two descriptions of a decision. If they leave the feasible set, consequence distributions, and values unchanged, then description invariance requires the same choice correspondence:
\[
C_{d_1}(A)=C_{d_2}(A).
\]
This condition does not require the same single action to be observed when the common correspondence contains several tied maximizers. An invariant point prediction requires either a unique maximizer or a tie-breaking rule that is itself held fixed.
The survival-versus-mortality result challenges description invariance: descriptions designed to express complementary versions of the same outcome information produced different preferences (McNeil et al., 1982).
In stochastic choice models satisfying regularity, adding a new alternative \(d\) cannot increase the probability of choosing an existing alternative \(a\):
\[
\Pr(a\mid A\cup\{d\})
\leq
\Pr(a\mid A).
\]
An attraction effect occurs when an asymmetrically dominated decoy raises the choice share of a target, violating regularity across otherwise comparable menus (Huber et al., 1982).
Defaults illustrate a different boundary. An opt-in and an opt-out design are not the same decision merely because both responses are physically available. A default may change effort, delay, perceived recommendation, responsibility, anticipated regret, or the consequence of inaction. If action costs matter, they should enter the consequences or a consistently defined net value; they should not appear as an extra primitive after \(V\) has already absorbed them. Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 use these distinctions to separate a challenge to an invariant benchmark from a variable omitted by a thin model.
crumbs: A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
5. Opportunity cost and decision margins
Suppose \(A\) contains at least two alternatives. For a contemplated action \(a\), define a best feasible alternative forgone as
\[
b^*(a)
\in
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{b\in A\setminus\{a\}}V(b).
\]
The alternative \(b^*(a)\)—or the set of tied alternatives that satisfy the expression—is the opportunity-cost benchmark. Discovering a better feasible option can change that benchmark even when the contemplated action itself has not changed.
When \(V\) has a declared cardinal scale, including an explicit origin and unit, the opportunity cost can be reported numerically as
\[
OC(a)
=
V\bigl(b^*(a)\bigr)
=
\max_{b\in A\setminus\{a\}}V(b).
\]
A corresponding decision margin is
\[
M(a)
=
V(a)-OC(a).
\]
If \(a\) is uniquely optimal, \(M(a)>0\). If the scale is merely ordinal, however, the meaningful statement is that \(a\) ranks above or below its best forgone alternative—not that the gap is “small.” Even on a normalized cardinal scale, fragility should be assessed by varying substantive beliefs, values, and constraints rather than interpreting an arbitrary score gap in isolation.
Opportunity costs are easy to neglect when the displaced alternative is not made explicit. Experimental evidence shows that prompting consumers to consider other uses of money can change purchase decisions (Frederick et al., 2009). Chapter 2 develops the practical question: what is the best feasible path this commitment would prevent?
crumbs: A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
6. Multiattribute value
The job offers differ on income, flexibility, and learning. Comparing each attribute separately makes the trade-offs visible but still leaves the choice unresolved. Combining them requires a statement of how much improvement on one attribute compensates for a loss on another. Suppose each alternative produces outcomes on \(J\) attributes, such as income, health, autonomy, learning, and security. Let \(x_j(a)\) be the performance of alternative \(a\) on attribute \(j\). A common additive model is
\[
V(a)
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}w_jv_j\bigl(x_j(a)\bigr),
\]
where each \(v_j(\cdot)\) maps performance on attribute \(j\) to a common normalized scale and the weights satisfy
\[
w_j\geq 0,
\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{J}w_j=1.
\]
A transparent normalization sets \(v_j=0\) at the least-preferred relevant level and \(v_j=1\) at the most-preferred relevant level for the decision. The resulting \(w_j\) are swing weights: they represent the importance of moving across the stated range of attribute \(j\), not a context-free claim that “health matters 30 percent.” Changing the range changes the meaning of the weight.
The additive form requires appropriate preferential-independence and scaling assumptions. If workload affects health, learning affects future income, or two attributes describe the same consequence, a simple sum can double-count value. Redefine overlapping attributes first, then model and elicit any substantively important interaction.
When consequences are uncertain, an additive multiattribute utility model can be nested inside expected utility:
\[
V(a)
=
\sum_{o\in O}P(o\mid a)
\left[
\sum_{j=1}^{J}
w_jv_j\bigl(x_j(a,o)\bigr)
\right].
\]
This expression keeps prediction and valuation separate. \(P(o\mid a)\) represents what is expected to happen; \(v_j\) and \(w_j\) represent how performance over defined attribute ranges is valued. An expected-utility interpretation requires cardinal von Neumann–Morgenstern utility components on compatible scales and additive independence over the relevant lotteries (Keeney & Raiffa, 1976).2
crumbs: A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
7. Value of information
You could spend another evening researching an employer and still choose the same job regardless of what you find. Meanwhile, one short question about flexible hours might reverse the decision. Information has instrumental value when its possible answers let you choose better. A question that cannot affect any relevant action has no instrumental value for that decision, even if the answer is interesting.
Let \(\theta\in\Theta\) denote an uncertain state of the world, where \(\Theta\) is finite or countable and the relevant expectations converge. Let \(p(\theta)\) be the prior probability and \(u(a,\theta)\) the value produced by action \(a\) in state \(\theta\). Without additional information, the best expected value is
\[
V_0
=
\max_{a\in A}
\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}
p(\theta)u(a,\theta).
\]
Perfect information reveals \(\theta\) before action is chosen. The expected value attainable with perfect information is
\[
V_{\mathrm{PI}}
=
\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}
p(\theta)
\max_{a\in A}u(a,\theta),
\]
and the expected value of perfect information is
\[
EVPI
=
V_{\mathrm{PI}}-V_0.
\]
With finite expectations, a fixed action set, and costless accurate revelation of the relevant state, \(EVPI\geq 0\). It is a gross upper bound on the value of any signal about that \(\theta\) for the same decision.
Now suppose a test, pilot, interview, or study produces a finite or countable signal \(Y\), with likelihood \(p(y\mid\theta)\). A coherent joint probability model implies
\[
p(y)
=
\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}
p(y\mid\theta)p(\theta),
\]
and, whenever \(p(y)>0\), Bayes’ rule gives
\[
p(\theta\mid y)
=
\frac{p(y\mid\theta)p(\theta)}
{p(y)}.
\]
The expected value of acting after the signal is
\[
V_Y
=
\sum_y p(y)
\max_{a\in A}
\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}
p(\theta\mid y)u(a,\theta).
\]
The expected value of sample information is
\[
EVSI(Y)=V_Y-V_0.
\]
Under the same action set and payoff model, costless observation, and finite expectations,
\[
0\leq EVSI(Y)\leq EVPI.
\]
If the total cost of obtaining and using the information is \(c(Y)\), expressed in the same cardinal units as \(V\), its net value is
\[
NVSI(Y)=EVSI(Y)-c(Y).
\]
False positives, false negatives, and other ordinary signal errors belong in the likelihood \(p(y\mid\theta)\). The cost term can include money, delay, attention, privacy loss, implementation effort, and strategic disclosure. Model misspecification—such as an incorrect likelihood or an omitted state—is a separate robustness problem rather than a cost that should be added after the fact.
If every possible signal leads to the same action and the signal changes no other payoff or future decision, then the information has zero instrumental value for this decision. This is the formal counterpart of Chapter 2’s branch test: state what action follows each plausible answer before gathering more information (Raiffa, 1968).
crumbs: A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
8. Sensitivity and robustness
A precise-looking ranking can conceal a fragile recommendation: a small revision to promotion prospects or the value of flexibility may put the other job first. Before committing, you need to know whether the recommendation survives the uncertainty you actually face. Sensitivity analysis asks how far those inputs would have to change before the recommendation changes. On a declared cardinal scale, the value difference between alternatives \(a\) and \(b\) is
\[
\Delta_{ab}=V(a)-V(b).
\]
The sign identifies the ranking: \(a\) is preferred when \(\Delta_{ab}>0\), the alternatives tie when \(\Delta_{ab}=0\), and \(b\) is preferred when \(\Delta_{ab}<0\). The magnitude has meaning only under the scale assumptions stated earlier.

Probability threshold
Suppose action \(a\) produces a high outcome \(H\) with probability \(p\) and a low outcome \(L\) otherwise, while action \(b\) produces certain outcome \(c\). Assume \(u(H)>u(L)\). Indifference requires
\[
p\,u(H)+(1-p)u(L)=u(c),
\]
which gives the threshold
\[
p^*
=
\frac{u(c)-u(L)}
{u(H)-u(L)}.
\]
An interior threshold requires \(0<p^*<1\), equivalently \(u(L)<u(c)<u(H)\). Weak inequalities allow boundary thresholds at zero or one. When \(p^*\in[0,1]\), \(a\) is preferred when \(p>p^*\). If the plausible range for \(p\) lies entirely on one side of the threshold, the ranking is robust to that uncertainty. If the range crosses the threshold, information about \(p\) may have decision value.


Weight threshold
With two normalized attributes, suppose
\[
V(a)=w\,v_1(a)+(1-w)v_2(a),
\qquad 0\leq w\leq 1.
\]
The weight at which \(a\) and \(b\) tie is
\[
w^*
=
\frac{v_2(b)-v_2(a)}
{\bigl[v_1(a)-v_1(b)\bigr]+\bigl[v_2(b)-v_2(a)\bigr]},
\]
provided the denominator is nonzero. The threshold is decision-relevant only if \(w^*\in[0,1]\); the signs of the attribute differences determine which alternative is preferred on each side. The useful question is whether reasonable stakeholders or elicitation ranges place \(w\) on different sides of the threshold, not whether an unsupported point weight equals \(0.63\) rather than \(0.61\).


Joint sensitivity
One-at-a-time sensitivity can mislead when inputs move together. A start-up’s survival, salary growth, workload, and future options may be correlated. Scenario analysis therefore varies coherent bundles of assumptions:
\[
V(a\mid s),
\qquad
s\in
\{\text{favorable},\text{central},\text{unfavorable}\}.
\]
A recommendation is robust over the declared scenario set when the same alternative remains preferred throughout it. When rankings change, report the conditions producing each recommendation.
crumbs: A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
section: 9. Sequential choice, reversibility, and the cost of analysis
text:
9. Sequential choice, reversibility, and the cost of analysis
Accepting a job lets you learn what working there is like. That knowledge may arrive only after leaving has become costly or another offer has expired. The value of learning therefore depends on which choices remain open. Let \(a\) be an action taken now, \(y\) information observed later, and \(B(a,y)\) the set of actions available after \(a\) and \(y\). Let \(V_0(a)\) be the immediate value of the initial action and \(V_1(b;a,y)\) the continuation value of later action \(b\). Their sum requires a common cardinal, additively separable intertemporal scale; \(V_1\) must be discounted to the decision time where necessary. Under those assumptions, a two-stage evaluation is
\[
V_{\mathrm{seq}}(a)
=
V_0(a)
+
\sum_y p(y\mid a)
\max_{b\in B(a,y)}
V_1(b;a,y).
\]
Switching costs, exit costs, and implementation burdens should enter \(V_1\) or restrict \(B(a,y)\). If one initial action preserves a superset of future actions while all immediate consequences, probabilities, and costs remain the same, its continuation value is weakly higher. In practice those “all else equal” conditions often fail: a pilot may preserve flexibility while delaying benefits or imposing a setup cost.
This formulation avoids adding a free-standing “reversibility bonus” to a value function that already includes every consequence. It also clarifies why information and reversibility interact. A future signal has more instrumental value when the decision-maker retains an action that can respond to it.
Analysis itself consumes scarce resources. Let \(r\) denote one additional analysis step that may produce result \(y\), and let \(A(r,y)\) be the feasible set remaining after the step and result. Express the direct resource cost \(c(r)\), plus any delay cost not already represented through \(A(r,y)\) or \(V(a\mid y,r)\), in the same cardinal units as \(V\). The net expected gain can then be written as
\[
G(r)
=
\sum_y p(y\mid r)
\max_{a\in A(r,y)}V(a\mid y,r)
-
\max_{a\in A}V(a)
-
c(r).
\]
Under this stylized metareasoning rule, conduct the step when \(G(r)>0\). The analysis-dependent action set represents options that expire, emerge, or become infeasible during deliberation; any other consequence of delay belongs in \(V(a\mid y,r)\) or \(c(r)\), but not both. This is a normative comparison of the expected benefit and cost of one more analysis step. It is not Simon’s satisficing model itself. Bounded rationality supplies the motivation—search, attention, time, memory, and computation are scarce—while satisficing describes a different stopping strategy based on aspiration levels (Simon, 1955, 1956).
This comparison helps decide how much structure to use. Familiar, reversible decisions with little at stake often justify a routine or simple rule. More analysis may be worthwhile when the stakes are high, commitment is difficult to reverse, outcomes depend on other people, or experience provides little useful feedback.

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
10. Put the analysis to work
Return to the job offers. The analysis is useful if it reveals an overlooked option, a forecast that deserves checking, or a trade-off hidden inside a single score. It can tell you which assumptions support the recommendation and what would change it.
Formal analysis makes the assumptions precise. Behavioral evidence, practical knowledge, and ethical reasoning help determine which assumptions to use and how to act on the result.
Chapter 16 develops risky choice further, while Chapter 19 examines how labels and mental accounts change the way consequences are compared.

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
text:
Tinbergen’s four questions about behavior
Why minds value what they do—and why origin is not obligation
A pastry can look irresistible before lunch and uninteresting afterward. The pastry has not changed, yet the same person now values it differently. Explaining this as hunger addresses the immediate shift. It leaves a deeper puzzle: why do some attractions develop so readily, and how can a familiar attraction pull against a person’s longer-term goals? The answer matters for deciding what to change—the immediate cue, a learned routine, or the surrounding environment.
To separate these questions, we first distinguish what produces a response now from how the capacity developed and evolved. We can then ask whether an account of its origin helps evaluate a present choice. This appendix extends Chapter 6 on valuation and Chapter 8 on useful shortcuts. Appendix A asks how a choice should relate to its stated objectives; here we ask how motives and decision processes came to take their current form.
Return to the pastry. Four questions help us separate explanations that are often compressed into the word cause.
Tinbergen (1963) distinguished these four questions to prevent one kind of explanation from displacing the others. Mechanism and ontogeny are commonly grouped as proximate explanations; function and phylogeny as ultimate or evolutionary explanations (Mayr, 1961; Scott-Phillips et al., 2011). Ultimate does not mean deepest, final, or morally superior. It identifies a kind of historical question.
The smell of the pastry, the person’s hunger, and memories of eating it contribute to an account of the present response. An evolutionary explanation asks a different question about the history of the capacities involved. Neither account replaces the other.
“Genes are the distant reason” is also too simple. Gene expression and gene–environment interaction operate during development, so genetic processes can be part of a proximate account. Evolutionary explanations concern changes in populations across generations, not a special gene located behind each behavior. Cultural transmission can recalibrate motives within a lifetime, preserve practices across generations, and alter the environments in which biological selection occurs. The useful distinction is among questions and evidence, not between genes and everything else. Modern accounts accordingly emphasize interaction among development, ecology, inheritance, and culture rather than a one-way chain from distant gene to present act (Laland et al., 2011; Richerson et al., 2010).
crumbs: B  Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
text:
Mechanism: Which bodily, perceptual, affective, learning, and neural processes produce the attraction now?
Ontogeny: How did the response develop through maturation, individual learning, family practices, and culture?
Function: Under which past conditions, if any, did similar mechanisms affect survival or reproduction relative to alternatives?
Phylogeny: Through what evolutionary history did the relevant capacities arise?
