title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
section: Distinguishing evolutionary fitness, preferences, and well-being
text:
Distinguishing evolutionary fitness, preferences, and well-being
Natural selection requires variation, some form of inheritance, and systematic differences in survival or reproduction among variants (Lewontin, 1970). It works through historical population change. It has no foresight, does not design from scratch, and cannot guarantee a globally optimal result (Gould & Lewontin, 1979).
Even “survival and reproduction” needs precision. Survival matters evolutionarily insofar as it affects genetic transmission; selection can favor reproductive benefits that carry survival costs. Fitness accounting can also include effects on relatives’ reproduction under the conditions specified by kin-selection theory (Hamilton, 1964). None of this implies that a person consciously computes genetic fitness or that reproductive success is the person’s experienced objective.
Before judging whether the attraction serves the person well, distinguish four questions. How much does the person want it, what experience follows, what evolutionary history is proposed, and what ought they to pursue? Table B.1 keeps these questions separate, so that an explanation of a preference is not mistaken for a reason to endorse it:



Table B.1: Fitness, preference, well-being, and moral worth are not interchangeable










Kind of assessment
Unit of analysis
The question it answers




Subjective decision value
A person choosing in a current state and context
How much weight does the option receive now?


Experienced value or well-being
A person’s experience and evaluation over a stated horizon
What pleasure, pain, satisfaction, connection, or meaning follows?


Evolutionary fitness consequence
Relative genetic representation in a specified population and environment
How did a variant affect transmission across generations?


Normative value
Persons and institutions under an ethical or prudential argument
What ought to be pursued, protected, permitted, or prohibited?






Sweetness illustrates the distinction. A preference can have a plausible evolutionary history while producing different consequences in a setting where concentrated sugar is readily available. Explaining its origin does not decide whether eating another pastry serves this person’s present goals.
The same distinction applies beyond food. A status motive may once have improved access to resources and allies while making a current career choice anxious or destructive. People may deliberately value contraception, celibacy, adoption, scholarship, art, spiritual practice, truth, or justice. Such commitments are not errors in a hidden reproductive utility function. They are products of human capacities for learning, language, reflection, culture, and institutional life.
Even a recurring response need not be an adaptation. Learning and cultural transmission may explain it; it may be a by-product of another capacity or an exaptation, a feature co-opted for a current role for which it was not originally shaped by selection. Developmental constraints, drift, pathology, or a mismatch with the present environment are further possibilities, and several explanations can contribute at once. Gould and Lewontin (1979) warned against treating a plausible adaptive story as sufficient evidence; Buss and colleagues (1998) later clarified distinctions among adaptations, by-products, and exaptations. The burden is to derive discriminating predictions, not merely to tell a coherent origin story.
crumbs: B  Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
section: Needs and motives: Maslow and Kenrick
text:
Needs and motives: Maslow and Kenrick
A person can want food, security, belonging, and recognition at the same time. Explaining a choice requires an account of which motive takes priority when those aims compete. Maslow (1943) proposed five broad classes of goal: physiological needs, safety, love and belonging, esteem, and self-actualization. He described them as a hierarchy of relative prepotency. On Maslow’s account, when several needs are seriously deprived, the relatively prepotent need is more likely to dominate attention. This is a claim about motivational priority, not a declaration that only one need can exist at a time.
The familiar pyramid makes the account look more rigid than Maslow’s text. Historical research found that Maslow did not create that diagram; later management writers turned the hierarchy into the now-standard stepped pyramid (Bridgman et al., 2019). Maslow explicitly allowed partial satisfaction, simultaneous motives, reversals, and exceptions. A meal can serve hunger, affiliation, identity, celebration, and status together.
Evidence supports the relevance of multiple needs more clearly than a universal staircase. Wahba and Bridwell’s (1976) review found limited support for the fixed ordering and little convincing support for the proposed sequence in which satisfying one level activates the next, while noting serious measurement problems. Tay and Diener (2011), using survey data from 123 countries, found that fulfillment of several kinds of need was associated with different aspects of subjective well-being. Those associations were largely independent of whether other needs had been fulfilled. This pattern weighs against the claim that social connection, respect, or autonomy matter only after material needs are complete.
Kenrick and colleagues (2010) renovated the hierarchy using evolutionary, developmental, and life-history reasoning. Their proposal retains immediate physiological needs, self-protection, affiliation, and status or esteem, then distinguishes mate acquisition, mate retention, and parenting. Later-developing systems overlap rather than replace earlier ones, and current cues can activate any system that has developed.



Table B.2: Three representations that should not be treated as equivalent










Maslow’s original proposal
Popular simplification
Kenrick et al.’s proposal




Several partly satisfied needs; relative priority, reversals, and multiple motivation
A fixed staircase completed one level at a time
Overlapping, cue-sensitive systems linked to development and proposed evolutionary problems


Physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, and self-actualization
The same labels presented as a universal ranked pyramid
Physiological, self-protection, affiliation, status, mate acquisition, mate retention, and parenting


Useful taxonomy with limited direct testing in the original paper
Memorable teaching icon
Integrative theory linking motives to development and evolutionary function






The comparison in Table B.2 shows why the popular pyramid cannot stand in for either theoretical proposal. Keep three questions separate when using these accounts: when a motive develops, what activates it now, and what historical function is proposed for it. Those are different claims even when they concern the same behavior.
Kenrick and colleagues also removed self-actualization as a separate fundamental motive; they proposed that activities commonly described as self-actualizing could be largely subsumed under status or esteem and mating-related motives. Commentators argued that this reduction underweights culture, meaning, and distinctively human symbolic goals, and that discarding self-actualization was premature (Kesebir et al., 2010; Peterson & Park, 2010).
Maslow offered a taxonomy of recurring needs; Kenrick and colleagues proposed an evolutionary reorganization. Both suggest questions about an active motive. The meal remains a useful reminder that hunger, belonging, and social meaning can matter at the same time.
crumbs: B  Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
section: Rationality has more than one benchmark
text:
Rationality has more than one benchmark
A quick choice of food might be consistent with a person’s preference, sensible given limited time, and unhelpful for a long-term health goal. The standards in Table B.3 can therefore produce different assessments of the same choice: consistency, feasible effort, and fit to the environment are distinct criteria. Appendix A develops the formal benchmark. Here the task is to keep its purpose distinct from ecological and evolutionary questions.



Table B.3: Different rationality standards can produce different assessments of one behavior










Rationality standard
Central question
A possible failure or limit




Coherence rationality
Do beliefs and preferences satisfy stated logical, probabilistic, and consistency relations?
Intransitive choice or a probability judgment that violates the named rule


Epistemic rationality
Are beliefs and confidence appropriately responsive to the available evidence?
Confidence can exceed what the evidence warrants.


Instrumental rationality
Given the person’s beliefs and endorsed ends, is the chosen means expected to advance those ends?
The chosen means may not be expected to advance the endorsed end. An instrumentally rational action can also fail because a reasonable belief was false or bad luck intervened.


Procedural rationality under bounds
Is the process appropriate to the stakes and the limits of information, time, attention, and computation?
A feasible process can still spend far too much or too little effort for the decision.


Ecological rationality
How well does this strategy exploit the structure of this environment?
A reliable cue in one ecology can become misleading in another.


Resource rationality
Does the procedure use limited computational resources efficiently for the modeled objective and costs?
The conclusion changes when the assumed resource, prior, objective, or cost changes.






An evolutionary explanation asks a different question: what historical fitness consequences could have favored this mechanism over alternatives? It is not an additional rationality standard. Historical success need not produce present coherence, welfare, or moral value.
Simon (1955, 1956) made limits and environmental structure central to theories of choice. The heuristics-and-biases program then documented systematic departures from specified benchmarks (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974), while the adaptive-toolbox program formalized simple procedures and asked when they succeed (Gigerenzer & Goldstein, 1996; Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier, 2011). These are not mutually exclusive questions. A judgment can violate a coherence rule, arise from an identifiable heuristic, and perform well under one environment but badly under another.
Ecological rationality is strategy–environment fit. Recognition, for example, can help when exposure genuinely covaries with the target, and mislead when publicity is manufactured (Goldstein & Gigerenzer, 2002). Resource-rational analysis goes further by modeling the value of improved performance against the costs of computation (Lieder & Griffiths, 2020). It can turn an apparent imperfection into an efficient approximation under stated constraints. Rahnev (2020) argues that the method’s usefulness should be distinguished from the empirical claim that people generally optimize computational resources.

Optimally irrational?
These different standards help frame Lionel Page’s Optimally Irrational (2023), which develops the thesis that some behavioral anomalies become intelligible when evolution, cognition, strategic interaction, and omitted constraints are brought into the analysis.
Before calling a behavior optimally irrational, specify:

The benchmark it violates. Logic, Bayesian updating, expected utility, consistency, or something else?
The objective being optimized. Accuracy, current payoff, time, computational cost, experienced welfare, strategic commitment, or fitness?
The information and constraints. What could the decision-maker actually know and compute?
The environment. Which cue–outcome relations and feedback conditions make the rule succeed?
The comparator. Better than which feasible alternative procedure?
The evidence. Does the model predict new variation, or merely rationalize an observed error after the fact?

A richer model may vindicate a simple rule or reveal why it no longer fits the setting. The original benchmark may also remain appropriate, with the observed choice representing a consequential error. “Evolution produced it” cannot decide among these possibilities.
crumbs: B  Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
section: Heuristics can be tools and sources of bias
text:
Heuristics can be tools and sources of bias
A familiar cue can make a good shortcut when it tracks the outcome we care about. If the relationship changes, the same shortcut can mislead. The recognition and availability examples in Table B.4 show why evaluation must specify which cues track the target and what could break that relationship.



Table B.4: Heuristics and the conditions that support or weaken them










Heuristic
Why it can work
When it can fail




Recognition
Exposure may covary with prominence, size, quality, or another target.
Advertising or unequal exposure breaks the relation.


Availability
Ease of retrieval can track frequency or recency in a representative sample of experience.
Vivid news, selective memory, and engineered exposure distort what is retrievable.






Skilled intuition is a broader capacity, rather than another heuristic in this comparison. Kahneman and Klein (2009) argue that intuitive expertise deserves trust when an environment contains learnable regularities and the decision-maker has substantial practice with sufficiently clear feedback. Rare, unstable, or strategically manipulated events and delayed feedback can prevent that learning. Confidence alone does not establish expertise.
Error-management theory makes the evolutionary logic precise in a different way. If the fitness costs of false negatives and false positives were systematically asymmetric, selection could favor a decision threshold that produces many errors of the cheaper kind (Haselton & Buss, 2000). Nesse’s (2005) smoke-detector model applies the same signal-detection logic to defensive responses. A sensitive threat threshold can therefore produce many cheap false alarms when missed dangers are much costlier. This specifies when to act given asymmetric error costs, whereas recognition and availability specify which cue guides a judgment. The model shows that apparently excessive alarms can be optimal under specified costs and base rates; changed cues, base rates, or costs can make the same threshold inappropriate.
Three empirical claims must remain separate:

A strategy can outperform an alternative in a modeled environment.
People actually use that strategy under the stated conditions.
The strategy or its selection mechanism evolved because of that performance.

Evidence for the first does not prove the second or third. This separation prevents ecological rationality from becoming an all-purpose defense of behavior.
crumbs: B  Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
text:
Testing an evolutionary mismatch hypothesis
A mechanism whose performance or fitness consequences depended on a recurrent cue–outcome relation can perform poorly when the distribution, intensity, or meaning of cues changes. This evolutionary mismatch is one bridge from adaptation to contemporary bias (Li et al., 2018). But “Stone Age mind in a modern world” is too vague to explain an observation.
A useful mismatch claim identifies four elements:

Cue: What feature does the mechanism detect?
Past relation: What outcome did that cue reliably predict in the relevant historical ecology?
Environmental change: How has the cue–outcome relation, intensity, or timing changed?
Predicted consequence: When and for whom should the response now become excessive, insufficient, or misdirected?

Sweetness offers a plausible structure: a cue related to energy availability can remain attractive when food production concentrates it beyond earlier ranges. A digital notification offers a more tentative hypothesis: cues of socially relevant information may capture attention even when platforms generate far more cues with weaker informational value. The second account needs direct evidence about the cue, mechanism, learning history, and comparison environment; “technology hijacks evolution” is not evidence.
Ancestral environments were diverse, and human learning and culture can change quickly. A response that looks mismatched may instead reflect current incentives, habit, social learning, measurement error, or deliberate choice. A good mismatch hypothesis predicts when the behavior should strengthen, weaken, or disappear as the cue–outcome structure changes.
crumbs: B  Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
section: How to evaluate an evolutionary explanation
text:
How to evaluate an evolutionary explanation
A coherent evolutionary story can make a puzzling preference seem explained. Yet learning, current incentives, or cultural transmission might fit the same observation. Accepting the first plausible story would leave us unable to predict when the preference should change. An evolutionary account earns confidence by predicting evidence that distinguishes it from those alternatives. Table B.5 separates what each source of evidence can establish from the historical claims it leaves open.



Table B.5: Different evidence answers different parts of an evolutionary claim










Evidence
What it can contribute
Persistent limitation




Formal model
Makes variants, objectives, constraints, and trade-offs explicit
A result follows only from its assumptions.


Comparative evidence
Tests whether variation across species or populations matches the proposed ecology
Similarity and difference can have several historical causes.


Developmental evidence
Reveals timing, plasticity, sensitive periods, and learning pathways
Early emergence alone does not prove genetic adaptation.


Cross-cultural evidence
Tests universality and predicted ecological variation
Sampling, translation, institutions, and shared history complicate inference.


Experiment or natural experiment
Tests cues, mechanisms, and environmental contingencies
Present causal effects do not by themselves identify evolutionary origin.


Genetic or historical evidence
Connects heritable variation or change across time to selection hypotheses
Complex behavior is polygenic, developmentally mediated, and culturally embedded.






Before accepting an adaptation claim, identify the mechanism, the proposed historical problem, and the alternative variants or explanations. Then ask what the account predicts across environments, development, cultures, or species. The strongest test is an observation that the proposed account and a plausible rival predict differently.
The optional population-model note below applies this approach to simulations by examining their update rules.
crumbs: B  Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
section: What the evolutionary lens changes in a decision
text:
What the evolutionary lens changes in a decision
Return to the invitation to give a prestigious talk from Chapter 6. Its prestige makes acceptance appealing, but accepting also commits time that could serve other priorities. Calling the attraction a status motive explains little about whether to accept. The useful question is what prestige predicts here and how those consequences fit the person’s commitments. The questions in Table B.6 unpack the attraction before asking whether to act on it:



Table B.6: Applying the evolutionary lens to a decision









Lens
Question for the invitation




Proximate mechanism
Which feelings, bodily states, memories, and anticipated rewards make the invitation attractive or aversive now?


Development and culture
How did professional identity, family obligations, institutional norms, and prior experience shape those signals?


Evolutionary hypothesis
Are status, affiliation, threat, or opportunity motives plausible parts of the explanation, and what evidence would distinguish them?


Ecological fit
Does prestige predict the outcomes the person cares about in this professional environment, or is it a noisy cue?


Resource fit
Would further analysis improve the choice enough to justify its time and attention costs?


Normative judgment
After forecasting consequences for self and others, which values and obligations does the person endorse?






For the invitation, the next useful step may be to investigate whether prestige brings the opportunities the person expects, or to reconsider the time those opportunities would cost. An evolutionary explanation can help us ask why status attracts attention. It leaves the present choice to be evaluated against the person’s commitments and the available alternatives.
crumbs: B  Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
text:
Optional research notes






NoteCauses across timescales





Sapolsky’s backward clock
Robert Sapolsky’s Behave (2017) starts with an action and works backward: from immediate neural activity to the preceding situation, bodily state, development, and evolutionary history. The method makes a useful demand on an explanation. Naming what happened in the brain just before a choice leaves open how that system came to respond as it did.
Determined (Sapolsky, 2023) opens with the old anecdote of a world resting on a turtle, which rests on another turtle, and so on. Sapolsky reverses the usual joke. A final turtle floating without support would resemble a choice with no antecedent cause. He uses the phrase “turtles all the way down” for the claim that intentions, neural events, development, social conditions, culture, and evolution form an unbroken causal history. He uses that history to argue that there is no causally independent chooser outside biology and environment, and then asks how punishment, praise, inequality, and compassion should change if free will is rejected.
Two distinctions matter for the argument. Showing that an event has antecedent causes does not by itself establish causal determinism. Determinism is not perfect prediction: even a causally deterministic system can remain practically unpredictable because it is complex, sensitive to initial conditions, or imperfectly observed. Randomness is not agency: an undetermined event would not, merely by being random, become an authored or controlled choice. These distinctions explain why Determined examines chaos, emergence, and quantum mechanics rather than treating unpredictability as evidence of free will.
The useful scientific lesson is narrower than Sapolsky’s conclusion about free will. Tinbergen’s framework distinguishes kinds of explanation; it does not by itself settle the metaphysics of agency or the ethics of responsibility. Current states, development, institutions, and culture interact through feedback, and causes at one level can alter conditions at another. This book therefore adopts Sapolsky’s demand for causal depth—do not stop at the reported reason or nearest mechanism—without presenting his rejection of free will as an empirical consensus. Compatibilism offers a live alternative: it holds that free will can be compatible with determinism, and some compatibilist accounts locate relevant control in causally realized capacities such as responsiveness to reasons rather than in an exception to causal history (McKenna & Coates, 2024).









NoteA proposed history of cognitive capacities





Bennett’s five proposed breakthroughs
Human choices draw on immediate attraction, learned rewards, imagined futures, and other people’s knowledge. Treating all of this as one capacity called intelligence hides the different ways a choice can form. How could capacities for learning from consequences, simulating possibilities, and interpreting other minds have arisen? Max Bennett works forward from simpler nervous systems to address that question. In A Brief History of Intelligence, drawing on an earlier hypothesis-and-theory article, Bennett proposes five cumulative “breakthroughs” in the lineage leading to humans (Bennett, 2021, 2023).



Table B.7: Bennett’s proposed five breakthroughs





Proposed breakthrough
Lineage used in Bennett’s model
Decision-relevant capacity
Connection in this book




Steering
Early bilaterians
Integrate internal state with external cues to approach or avoid
Valuation


Reinforcing
Early vertebrates
Learn action values from experienced consequences
Habits and reinforcement


Simulating
Early mammals
Represent possible actions and outcomes before acting
Internal models and goal-directed control


Mentalizing
Early primates
Represent one’s own and others’ knowledge, intentions, and future states
Strategic interdependence and communication


Speaking
Early humans
Use semantic, rhythmic communication, including language and music
Communication






The proposed sequence in Table B.7 suggests an expansion in the sources from which choice can learn: inherited valence, the consequences of one’s own actions, internally simulated futures, observed agents and inferred minds, and culturally communicated experience. Later capacities do not replace earlier ones. Human deliberation still depends on approach and avoidance, reinforcement, and embodied action; language and culture can redirect those systems rather than float above them.
Bennett presents this human-lineage account as a first approximation.1 It connects phylogeny to capacities for valuing, learning, imagining, understanding other agents, and sharing models.









NotePopulation and spatial models






Classical game theory asks what a deliberate player should choose against another strategy. Evolutionary game theory instead asks which strategies become more common under a declared process linking payoff to replication, survival, or imitation (Maynard Smith & Price, 1973). The vocabulary can describe genes, cultural transmission, or organizational routines only when the transmission mechanism is named. A frequency change is not evidence of natural selection merely because an evolutionary equation can reproduce it.
For two strategies, let \(x\) be the share using strategy 1. Let \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) be nonnegative reproductive or imitation weights derived from their payoffs, with \(xf_1+(1-x)f_2>0\). A discrete replicator-style rule is
\[
x' = \frac{xf_1}{xf_1+(1-x)f_2}.
\]
These restrictions keep the updated share between zero and one. Arbitrary game payoffs, especially negative ones, cannot be inserted without a stated mapping to admissible weights. An evolutionarily stable strategy is resistant to invasion by any sufficiently rare alternative strategy in the model’s strategy space. A stable population mixture is also different from each person deliberately randomizing.
Spatial models add another dependency: who interacts with whom. Cooperative clusters, conditional helping, or aggregate segregation can arise under particular neighborhoods and update rules. The record in Table B.8 makes these dependencies explicit, so another reader can reconstruct the result and assess how far it applies:



Table B.8: A minimum provenance record for population and spatial models









Aspect to document
Minimum provenance




Frequency update
Payoffs, initial shares, update rule, and horizon


Spatial interaction
Topology, neighborhood, timing, mobility, vacancies, and tie-breaking


Stochastic simulation
Pseudorandom generator, seed, replications, and outcome distribution—not only one attractive run


Transport claim
The real-world observation that could distinguish the modeled process from learning, imitation, institutional change, or selection






Figure B.1 applies that standard. In one seeded Schelling-style teaching run, agents move only when fewer than one-third of their occupied neighbours share their group and choose a vacancy satisfying that threshold. The average same-group-neighbour share rises from 0.48 to 0.68.






Figure B.1: Local moves produce more same-group clustering in one teaching simulation (seed 20260830). Agents seek at least one-third same-group occupied neighbors. A sweep visits agents once; neighbor shares exclude vacancies.



The retained generator, scripts/build_schelling_sequence.py, uses Python’s random.Random(20260830) on a bounded 18 × 14 grid, with 107 agents per group and 38 vacancies. Neighbors are the eight surrounding cells, excluding vacancies from the same-group share. An agent with no occupied neighbors is treated as satisfied and assigned a same-group share of one. Each sweep shuffles occupied cells; an unsatisfied agent moves uniformly among currently acceptable vacancies. The run stops after a sweep with no moves or after 25 sweeps. Here it stops after four sweeps and 44 moves.
Reproducible teaching implementations include Schelling-style segregation (Schelling, 1969; Wilensky, 1997), evolutionary prisoner’s-dilemma dynamics (Wilensky, 2002), and one specified ethnocentrism model (Hammond & Axelrod, 2006; Wilensky, 2003). Tournament success, repeated-game equilibrium, and evolutionary stability answer different questions: tit-for-tat’s success in one tournament and its vulnerability under another mutation–selection process are not contradictory findings (Axelrod, 1984; Imhof et al., 2007).

title: Appendix C — Conducting and Writing a Literature Review
text:
A topic becomes a review question
From a broad topic to a research question worth investigating
A student decides to review the advice to “think positively.” Its appeal is clear: expecting success may make a difficult goal worth pursuing. Yet someone can feel encouraged while leaving the hardest preparation for later. For a student facing an exam or a graduate seeking work, encouragement matters only if it supports the effort and judgment the goal requires. When does positive thinking help, and when might it get in the way?
Reading more papers will help only if the student learns how to compare them. A literature review develops an answer from the available research, showing what the evidence supports and where the answer remains uncertain. It can be a contribution in its own right. It can also establish why another study is needed and which comparison would make that study informative.
This appendix follows the work from choosing a question to writing a defensible synthesis, then connects the remaining uncertainty to the experimental study developed in Appendix D.
“Positive thinking” names a topic. A starting question is: Under what conditions do positive expectations help rather than hinder goal attainment? Its importance comes from a practical tension: people need enough confidence to attempt difficult goals, while also recognizing obstacles, preparing adequately, and knowing when to reconsider a goal.
Preliminary reading sharpens the question. Positive expectations are judgments that success is likely; positive fantasies are pleasant images of a desired future. Someone can enjoy imagining an excellent result without believing it likely or preparing for it. Studies distinguish these forms of thought and report different relationships with later effort and achievement (Oettingen & Mayer, 2002). If the review covers both, its question should become: Under what conditions do different forms of positive thinking support or hinder goal attainment? This revision changes the comparison, not just the wording.
Start with an uncertainty that matters to an explanation or a decision. Identify what is being compared, for whom, and over what period. Then do enough preliminary reading to find out whether the question can be answered within the time and evidence available. A broad question may need narrowing; a seemingly novel one may already have a substantial literature.
Each boundary should serve the argument. A term paper could focus on academic goals if it needs comparable measures of preparation and performance. Including job searches might help examine goals whose outcomes also depend on other people’s decisions. Adding a country or date merely to make the title narrower does not explain why that restriction matters.
Keep a short question record: the current question, why its answer matters, its boundaries, and what the preliminary search suggests. Revise the question when the reading exposes a better comparison, while recording why the scope changed. This makes exploration useful without quietly redefining the review around a preferred conclusion.
crumbs: C  Conducting and Writing a Literature Review

title: Appendix C — Conducting and Writing a Literature Review
section: Choose a review that fits the question
text:
Choose a review that fits the question
A focused term-paper review may aim to explain a debate or compare competing accounts. Its scope can be modest, provided the selection is transparent and the conclusion respects that scope. A systematic review takes on a more demanding task: use explicit, reproducible methods to identify and evaluate the evidence relevant to a specified question. A broad mapping question may instead call for a scoping review and its corresponding methods.
The choice affects the search, selection rules, appraisal, and form of synthesis. Decide what kind of answer the review promises before collecting a large folder of papers (Snyder, 2019). A meta-analysis is a statistical method for combining suitable estimates; a systematic review can proceed without one when pooling would not answer a meaningful common question.
For a systematic review, use reporting guidance appropriate to its type. PRISMA 2020 helps authors report how an intervention-effect review was conducted and what it found; it is not a substitute for the conduct of the review or an assessment of its methodological quality (Page et al., 2021).
For the positive-thinking question, the student first needs to distinguish studies that measure existing expectations from experiments that ask people to imagine success or consider obstacles. Combining them into one estimate of “positive thinking” could conceal the distinction the review needs to explain.
crumbs: C  Conducting and Writing a Literature Review

title: Appendix C — Conducting and Writing a Literature Review
section: Build a search you can explain
text:
Build a search you can explain
Turn the question into concept groups and identify alternative terms within each group. For this example, one group concerns thoughts about the future and another concerns action or achievement. An initial search might be:
("positive expectations" OR "positive fantasies" OR optimism OR "mental contrasting")
AND
(effort OR preparation OR persistence OR "goal attainment")
This is a starting query, not a complete search strategy. Adapt the syntax to the database and inspect what it retrieves. Requiring the exact phrase “goal attainment” might miss studies reporting grades, job offers, or task performance. Read promising abstracts to discover those terms, then refine the search. Search terms can bring related research into view without making its concepts interchangeable: a general optimistic outlook is not the same measure as an expectation about a particular exam.
Use bibliographic databases alongside the references and later citations of useful papers. A recent review can reveal terminology and important disagreements; the primary studies are still needed to assess the comparisons behind its conclusions. Search for results that could challenge the emerging answer as deliberately as those that support it (Pautasso, 2013).
Before selecting the main evidence, state the inclusion criteria. For example: which populations, goals, and forms of positive thought are relevant; whether both observational and experimental studies are included; which outcomes and follow-up periods count; and how the review will handle working papers, unavailable texts, languages, or publication dates. The criteria should follow the question. A rule that admits only statistically significant findings would instead select the answer.
Keep the record in Table C.1 as you work. It lets a reader understand the scope and lets you recover a decision you might otherwise forget.



Table C.1: A compact search and selection record









Record
What to preserve




Search
Database or source, search date, exact query, filters, and number of records returned


Citation trail
The paper whose references or later citations led to another record


Screening
Inclusion or exclusion decision and a reason tied to the criteria


Version
Publication details, DOI or stable link, and relationship to earlier versions


Remaining limits
Unavailable texts, coverage restrictions, and questions requiring another search






Check versions before counting studies. A working paper and its published article may report the same experiment; several articles may reuse one sample. Keep useful versions linked in the record and identify overlapping data so the synthesis does not treat them as independent confirmations. Check corrections and retractions on the publisher’s record, and return to the search before finalizing a review of an active topic.
Search tools and generated summaries can suggest terms or papers to inspect. They cannot establish that a citation exists, that it says what the summary claims, or that its evidence answers your question. When the full text is unavailable, record that limitation and restrict the claim to material you could examine.
crumbs: C  Conducting and Writing a Literature Review

title: Appendix C — Conducting and Writing a Literature Review
section: Read studies for the comparison they support
text:
Read studies for the comparison they support
Begin each paper with the question you need it to answer. Locate the design, comparison, outcome, and result before treating the authors’ interpretation as your own. If confident students later perform better, they may already have stronger skills or better preparation. That association does not establish what would happen if an intervention increased their confidence. Conversely, an experiment that changes feelings of energy does not by itself establish a lasting change in achievement.
The fields in Table C.2 keep the study’s design, result, and role in the review distinct. Use one row per study, adding separate rows for materially different experiments or outcomes and marking shared samples. Record enough detail to reconstruct a claim, without copying every result into the review.



Table C.2: An evidence matrix for comparing studies









Field
Question to answer while reading




Study and location
Which version is this, and where is the supporting passage, table, or figure?


Question and proposed explanation
What is being investigated, and what competing account would fit?


Design and comparison
What variation supports the claim? Was treatment assigned, chosen, or changed by a policy?


Population and setting
Who was studied, how were they recruited, and which conditions may matter?


Outcome and horizon
What was measured, in what units, and when?


Finding and uncertainty
What estimate or qualitative finding is reported, and how precise or well supported is it?


Limits and role in the review
What can this study establish, what remains open, and why is it included?






Keep three kinds of notes separate: what the study reports, how its authors interpret that finding, and your assessment of what follows. Mark copied language as a quotation immediately, with its location. This prevents a later paraphrase from inheriting either the wording or the confidence of the original without inspection.
Assess limitations by their consequences. “The sample was small” is incomplete criticism until you explain which effects the uncertainty leaves plausible. A convenience sample may limit generalization while still supporting a randomized comparison within that sample. As Appendix D explains, random sampling supports population generalization, whereas random assignment supports the internal validity of a causal comparison. Neither alone answers every question about the study.
crumbs: C  Conducting and Writing a Literature Review

title: Appendix C — Conducting and Writing a Literature Review
text:
Synthesize the evidence
The matrix becomes a review when the comparisons produce an answer. Organize sections around questions, explanations, or consequential differences in design. Explain a study’s essential design where it first matters, then recall only the detail needed for later comparisons. This is the difference between taking notes on a collection and developing an argument from it (Pautasso, 2013).
The selected studies in Table C.3 show why a synthesis needs more than a list of favorable and unfavorable results. Compare what each study measures or changes before deciding whether its finding answers the same question. These papers provide a starting comparison, not a complete review of the literature.



Table C.3: Distinguishing forms of positive thought and the evidence about them










Study
Design and comparison
What the finding supports—and leaves open




Oettingen and Mayer (2002), Study 3
Measured expectations and fantasies among 117 students, then followed preparation and course-grade improvement over six weeks
Expectations and fantasies had different relationships with later effort and performance; the observational design does not isolate the effect of increasing confidence


Kappes and Oettingen (2011), Study 3
Randomly assigned 49 students to ideal-positive imagery about the coming week or thoughts about it without an instructed emotional tone; 40 completed follow-up
Ideal-positive imagery reduced immediate reported energy and reported accomplishment one week later; self-reports and incomplete follow-up limit the conclusion


Oettingen et al. (2001)
Four experiments compared imagining a desired future and then present obstacles—mental contrasting—with other ways of thinking about the future or present
Contrasting made commitment more dependent on expectations of success; the studies did not establish that those expectations were accurate






A synthesis could begin:

Positive thinking does not describe one process. Oettingen and Mayer (2002) found that favorable expectations predicted better achievement, whereas positive fantasies predicted poorer achievement. Their observational comparisons do not establish what increasing confidence would cause. Kappes and Oettingen (2011) instead manipulated idealized imagery, finding lower reported energy and subsequent accomplishment in one student experiment. Oettingen and colleagues (2001) tested a further distinction: connecting a desired future with obstacles made commitment more dependent on perceived chances of success. Together, the findings suggest that a review should distinguish believing success is likely, enjoying an image of success, and considering what achieving it requires.

The paragraph links a claim, evidence, a comparison, and an implication. Chapter 39 develops the practical use of mental contrasting; the review’s job here is to establish what the comparisons justify.
When findings appear to conflict, compare what was actually estimated. Differences may concern treatment content, comparison group, population, measurement, follow-up, or research design. They may also reflect imprecision or selection in what reached publication. A significant finding in one paper and a nonsignificant finding in another do not establish that their effects differ; inspect the estimates and uncertainty rather than counting significant papers as votes. Appendix E examines how selective reporting can distort the body of evidence itself.
crumbs: C  Conducting and Writing a Literature Review

title: Appendix C — Conducting and Writing a Literature Review
text:
Identify a gap worth investigating
A useful gap emerges from what the comparison cannot yet settle. It could be an unresolved explanation, a result that may depend on a particular condition, a poorly measured outcome, or a mismatch between the available evidence and an important decision. Explain both the uncertainty and the consequence of resolving it.
For the positive-thinking example, the distinction between expectations and fantasies is already established in the cited literature. Rediscovering that distinction is not a new research gap. A review can still contribute by explaining how definitions, study designs, and outcome measures affect the advice the evidence supports. For instance, do studies assess whether expectations are accurate, and do they follow actual preparation as well as reported energy or commitment?
Before claiming that gap, search specifically for studies that might already address it. Check mechanism experiments, later follow-ups, relevant reviews, and research using different terminology. State the scope of a gap claim: “In the studies covered by this search…” is more defensible than “No research has examined…” when the search cannot support that universal statement.
Writing a gap statement requires four connected decisions:

State what the strongest relevant evidence establishes.
Identify what remains unresolved and why the existing designs cannot settle it.
Explain what an answer would change in theory, practice, or the interpretation of an earlier finding.
Describe the comparison or evidence that could reduce the uncertainty.

A new country or population may matter when institutions, incentives, or other conditions could change the result. Their novelty alone is not enough. Conversely, a careful replication, better measurement, or a more precise estimate can make a valuable contribution even when the topic is familiar. The review should explain the gain in understanding rather than manufacture a claim of being first.
crumbs: C  Conducting and Writing a Literature Review

title: Appendix C — Conducting and Writing a Literature Review
section: Write the review as an argument
text:
Write the review as an argument
Draft from the question and evidence matrix. Use Table C.4 to give each section a job in answering the question, then write paragraphs that make an interpretable claim, examine its support, and explain what the comparison adds. Revise the introduction once you know the answer so that it promises the review you actually deliver.



Table C.4: A writing structure in which each section advances the answer









Section
Its job for the reader




Introduction
Establish the problem, its importance, the review question, scope, and principal answer


Background or theory
Explain the concepts and competing accounts needed to compare the evidence


Search and selection
Show how the relevant evidence was found and which limits remain


Thematic synthesis
Develop the answer through explicit comparisons among studies


Conclusion
Answer the question at the strength the evidence allows, explain the implications, and identify useful next research






The introduction can move from common ground (And) to a consequential difficulty (But) and then to the review’s response (Therefore). The difficulty must explain why the reader needs an answer; the response must say what the review will clarify. In this example, advice that encourages confidence may leave preparation and realistic assessment unspecified. Comparing forms of positive thought can clarify what that advice should ask people to do. Use this progression when it clarifies the argument, without forcing every paragraph into a fixed template.
Theory belongs where it changes a comparison. If expectations, fantasies, and attention to obstacles imply different routes to action, explain those differences before evaluating studies that try to separate them. A long background catalogue that the analysis never uses delays the question instead of preparing the reader for it.
Make a limitation do explanatory work. Rather than end every paragraph with “more research is needed,” state what the design leaves unresolved and whether that uncertainty changes the review’s answer. Likewise, a conclusion should first say what can now be concluded. The remaining gaps make sense once the reader knows what the review has established.
Before submitting, reverse-outline the draft: write one sentence naming the job of every paragraph. Two adjacent paragraphs doing the same job may be combined; a paragraph whose purpose cannot be named may need moving or removal. Check whether the transitions express the actual relationship between claims and whether the conclusion answers the original question.
Finally, audit citations against the text. A citation should support the sentence it accompanies. Read the original source when making a claim about its design or result, and identify secondary citation honestly when that is all you could access. Use your own sentence structure when paraphrasing, preserve the author’s meaning, and mark direct quotations with a locator. Reconcile in-text citations with an alphabetized reference list and verify names, years, titles, and identifiers. A reference manager can assist with formatting; it cannot determine whether a source supports your claim.
crumbs: C  Conducting and Writing a Literature Review

title: Appendix C — Conducting and Writing a Literature Review
text:
From review to study
The review’s final research proposal should follow from its comparison of evidence. Record what is known, the unresolved question, why it matters, and the observation that could distinguish the remaining explanations. Carry forward the closest studies’ treatments, measures, populations, and weaknesses so that the next design builds on them deliberately.
For the clinic introduced in Appendix D, this means reviewing existing reminder evidence before proposing another trial. If a focused review leaves uncertainty about whether understandable wording adds value beyond a reminder’s timing, a useful comparison would vary wording while holding timing fixed. If the uncertainty concerns what causes the effect, attendance alone will not settle it; the design needs evidence that distinguishes the proposed pathways. These are illustrations of how a documented gap can guide design, not claims that the reminder literature currently lacks those studies.
A clear review may also show that another experiment is premature or unnecessary. An existing answer may already support the decision; a measurement problem may need resolving first; access or ethics may prevent the proposed comparison. The transition to research design is therefore a reasoned choice about what evidence is needed next.
crumbs: C  Conducting and Writing a Literature Review

title: Appendix C — Conducting and Writing a Literature Review
text:
Practice: build a review plan
Begin with the proposal below. It gives the review a practical reason to exist while leaving the answer open.
1. Working title
Positive Thinking: When It Helps—and When It Backfires
2. Problem statement

AND: Expecting success can encourage people to pursue opportunities, invest effort, and persist after setbacks.
BUT: People can also feel confident while underestimating obstacles and preparing too little. Advice to “think positively” does not explain when encouragement supports useful persistence and when it leaves someone underprepared or pursuing an unrealistic goal. Understanding that difference matters for students and job seekers deciding how to prepare and when to change course.
THEREFORE: This review will distinguish positive expectations from idealized fantasies and compare how each relates to effort, preparation, and goal attainment. It aims to clarify how to encourage confidence without sacrificing realistic assessment or preparation.

3. Starting research question
Under what conditions do positive expectations help rather than hinder goal attainment?
This first question still needs refining to match the proposed comparison of expectations and fantasies. The contribution is an explanation of the conditions under which encouragement supports effective action. “Positive thinking” works as an accessible title, but the review needs to define and distinguish the forms it examines.
Develop the proposal in four steps:

Refine the question. Decide whether to focus on expectations alone or compare forms of positive thinking, and revise the question accordingly. Choose a population and goal for reasons that affect the comparison. Define how you will recognize adequate preparation, goal attainment, and useful reconsideration of a goal.
Build the evidence. Draft a search strategy and inclusion criteria, then use the evidence matrix above for an initial set of relevant studies. Include evidence that could challenge your first answer. Distinguish measured confidence from experimentally assigned exercises, and feelings of readiness from observed behavior or performance.
Write a synthesis. Compare the studies in one paragraph, give a provisional answer, and explain what a student or job seeker could reasonably take from it. Make clear where advice would go beyond the evidence.
Justify the next question. Write a gap statement that names what remains uncertain, why resolving it matters, and what comparison could help. Search for work that might already answer it before calling it a research gap. If it survives that check, use Appendix D to develop the design.

You can then apply the same structure to another question from the book. The plan should show how the evidence changed the question, not simply how many papers you collected.






NoteA second example: retirement-saving defaults





Automatic enrollment creates a different tension: the tendency to accept a preset option can bring employees into a pension plan while also keeping their contributions at its default rate. In Madrian and Shea’s (2001) employer study, participation increased and many employees retained the default settings. Designers therefore need to consider both how defaults encourage entry and how the chosen contribution rate influences what happens afterward.
A review titled Beyond Enrollment: How Pension Defaults Shape Saving could ask: How do default contribution settings affect participation, contribution levels, and additional total saving? Its contribution would be to connect outcomes often evaluated separately, clarifying what enrollment figures can and cannot tell a policymaker about saving. A review restricted to U.S. 401(k) contribution choices would need a narrower evidence set than this broader question.
The three studies in Table C.5 demonstrate the broader comparison. They are a selected teaching set, not an exhaustive or current review.



Table C.5: Three studies with different roles in a savings review










Study
Design and setting
What it helps the reviewer distinguish




Madrian and Shea (2001)
An employer’s introduction of automatic enrollment and comparisons across employee cohorts in a U.S. 401(k) plan
Participation and persistence at default settings; a policy change, rather than individual random assignment


Chetty et al. (2014)
Danish administrative data and quasi-experimental variation in saving incentives and pension contributions
Retirement-account contributions versus additional total saving; movement between accounts can change the interpretation


Blumenstock et al. (2018)
Randomized contribution defaults and matching incentives among employees of a telecom firm in Afghanistan
Causal effects of default contribution settings in the study; all employees had accounts, so account access was not the randomized contrast






Chetty et al. (2014) found that automatic pension contributions generated additional saving, while tax subsidies largely shifted saving between accounts. Blumenstock et al. (2018) showed that contribution defaults changed participation among employees who already had accounts, but their follow-up measures were too imprecise to establish displacement of other savings. Additional total saving is therefore a separate outcome to investigate, rather than a conclusion to infer from enrollment alone.
The same caution applies to explanations. Remaining at a default could reflect inattention, an inferred recommendation, or the effort of changing a setting. Blumenstock and colleagues already use additional experiments to investigate why defaults matter. A new review or study must explain what remains unresolved after that work, rather than present those explanations as an untouched gap.

title: Appendix D — Running an Experimental Study: From Question to Credible Evidence
text:
The experimental workflow
A practical workflow for designing, implementing, analyzing, and reporting behavioral experiments
A clinic introduces a shorter appointment reminder, and attendance rises. The staff would like to keep it and expand its use. Yet attendance might also have risen because the season changed or a different group of patients received appointments. Acting on the wrong explanation could direct time and money toward a reminder that made no difference. What comparison would let the clinic decide whether the change deserves credit?
Before planning that comparison, the clinic needs to establish what earlier reminder research has already answered. Appendix C explains how a literature review can identify the remaining uncertainty and show why a new study would matter.
This appendix follows an imagined study from that question to a report another researcher could examine. The final worked example uses generated data so you can reproduce its calculations. Read the appendix as a methods chapter or return to the relevant phase while planning your own study.
The five phases in Table D.1 turn the clinic’s question into a study whose decisions and results can be examined. Each leaves a record needed to interpret the next: the question determines the comparison, the design determines what must be recorded, and those records determine which conclusion the analysis can support.
The design card collects the decisions to make before data collection. In the sections below, return to the clinic whenever a technical distinction becomes difficult to follow: what would it change about the reminder comparison?

title: Appendix D — Running an Experimental Study: From Question to Credible Evidence
text:
Table D.1: Running an experimental study from definition to preservation










Phase
What you do
What you preserve




1. Define
Turn the topic into a testable question; define the construct, outcome, comparison, population, and estimand
Research question, theory, hypotheses, construct definitions


2. Design
Choose the experimental design; create treatments and measures; plan assignment, power, exclusions, and analysis
Protocol, materials, code, design calculation, preregistration, ethics approval


3. Implement
Recruit, assign, deliver, measure, and monitor without steering the study toward a preferred result
Recruitment and assignment logs, timestamps, deviations, attrition, treatment fidelity


4. Analyze
Freeze the data, execute the planned analysis, check robustness, and label exploration
Immutable raw data, cleaning scripts, analysis code, output log, deviation record


5. Report and preserve
Report estimates and uncertainty, match the claim to the design, share what can be shared, and archive what must be protected
Manuscript, tables and figures, reproducibility package, access conditions, correction path
