title: Appendix E — When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity
section: Distinguishing error, questionable practices, and misconduct
text:
Distinguishing error, questionable practices, and misconduct
Scientific records can contain serious mistakes: a mislabeled cell, a merge that duplicates rows, a reverse-coded item left unchanged, or a misunderstood software default. Researchers remain responsible for checking and correcting these errors. Establishing what went wrong, however, is a different task from establishing misconduct.
The United States Office of Research Integrity defines research misconduct as fabrication, falsification, or plagiarism in proposing, performing, reviewing, or reporting research, and explicitly excludes honest error and differences of opinion from the definition (Office of Research Integrity, n.d.). Its terms are useful beyond one jurisdiction:

Fabrication: inventing observations or findings and presenting them as research.
Falsification: altering, suppressing, or manipulating research inputs or outputs so that the record becomes misleading.
Plagiarism: using someone else’s intellectual work without proper attribution.

Formal findings also require standards of evidence and mental state defined by the applicable institution and law. Suspicion, an unusual distribution, or a failed replication is not by itself proof.
Between honest error and formally established misconduct sits a wide range of questionable research practices: undisclosed outcome switching, opportunistic exclusions, misleading rounding, inadequate recordkeeping, selective citation, ghost variables, or presenting exploratory results as confirmatory. Some acts may be reckless or prohibited; others reflect weak training or ambiguous norms. The label does not remove the need to identify the exact action, evidence, intent standard, and policy.
Survey evidence suggests that fabrication and falsification occur, but prevalence estimates are difficult because the behavior is sensitive and definitions vary. Fanelli’s (2009) meta-analysis of survey studies found that 1.97% of scientists admitted at least one instance of fabricating, falsifying, or modifying data or results, while substantially larger shares admitted other questionable practices.1
An impossible value or duplicated observation warrants investigation, but the immediate task is to reproduce the discrepancy and check its provenance. Coding, versioning, and transcription errors can produce alarming patterns without fabrication. The correction procedure below keeps that distinction visible.
crumbs: E  When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity

title: Appendix E — When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity
section: Why incentives matter without removing responsibility
text:
Why incentives matter without removing responsibility
The one hundred teams in the opening example work within institutions that reward some contributions more visibly than others. Individual responsibility remains, but the incentives affect which findings readers eventually see.
Novel, clean, and positive results are easier to tell as stories. Hiring, promotion, funding, journal space, and media attention can reward speed and surprise more visibly than careful null results, replications, data curation, or corrections. When many career decisions depend on a small number of papers, researchers and institutions may optimize for publication rather than cumulative information.
The design task is therefore two-level:

Researcher level: make choices traceable, distinguish planned from discovered analysis, preserve data provenance, and correct errors.
Institutional level: reward credible process, replication, data stewardship, team contributions, and correction—not merely the count and novelty of positive findings.

A useful reform therefore asks both what would make the evidence easier to check and what would make careful work worth doing.
crumbs: E  When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity

title: Appendix E — When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity
text:
Safeguards and complementary checks
Choose among the safeguards in Table E.2 according to the problem each can address. Recording an analysis plan makes later changes visible; sharing code makes calculations inspectable. Neither alone establishes that the outcome measures what the researcher intended.



Table E.2: Safeguards solve different credibility problems










Safeguard
What it strengthens
Complementary check




Design analysis and adequate precision
Reduces exaggerated selected estimates; makes informative nulls more likely
Valid measurement, unbiased implementation, or generalizability


Preregistration
Time-stamps planned hypotheses, outcomes, and analyses; reveals deviations
Theory, measurement, compliance, and execution


Registered Reports
Reviews question and method before results; offers in-principle acceptance independent of outcome
Implementation and interpretation


Open materials and code
Enables inspection, reuse, and computational reproduction
Ethical release of confidential data or validity of the design


Governed data access
Balances verification with consent, privacy, and legal constraints
Access burden and re-identification risk


Multi-analyst or multiverse analysis
Shows sensitivity to defensible analytical choices
Credibility of each included model


Direct and multi-site replication
Estimates stability and heterogeneity under declared protocols
Transport to the target context


Corrections and retractions
Updates the visible record when evidence changes
Earlier citations, publicity, and downstream use






Registered Reports move part of peer review before outcomes are known: journals evaluate the question and proposed method and can offer in-principle acceptance based on that plan rather than the direction of the findings (Chambers, 2013). The format weakens publication bias at the journal stage.
The Transparency and Openness Promotion guidelines encourage journals to state standards for citation, data, materials, code, design transparency, preregistration, and replication (Nosek et al., 2015). Credibility depends on interacting practices, incentives, and checks (Munafò et al., 2017; Nosek et al., 2018).
crumbs: E  When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity

title: Appendix E — When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity
text:
How to interpret a replication
When an original and a replication appear to disagree, first establish what each study estimated. Work through the following checks, recording any information that is unavailable rather than treating it as verified.

Reproduce each result. Do the reported data and code generate the claims?
Compare the estimands. Did both studies estimate the same effect for the same treatment, outcome, population, and horizon?
Inspect protocol fidelity. Which materials, incentives, timing, exclusions, and implementation details changed?
Compare estimates and intervals. Ignore the temptation to reduce the pair to significant versus nonsignificant.
Examine precision and selection. Was the original small and selected? Was the replication powered for a plausible effect rather than the original point estimate alone?
Test moderators cautiously. A post hoc explanation is a new hypothesis until tested with new variation.
Update cumulatively. Combine the new evidence with prior studies under a transparent synthesis model; report heterogeneity and uncertainty.
Narrow the claim. If the effect depends on a population, material, institution, or period, make that condition part of the theory.

A failed replication can reveal that the effect was absent, smaller than thought, badly measured, analytically fragile, or conditional on an unrecognized feature. A successful replication can increase confidence under that protocol while leaving external validity open. Both outcomes are information.
crumbs: E  When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity

title: Appendix E — When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity
text:
Before you repeat a finding
Use the short audit in How to Read Evidence, then look up the study in the evidence-status map. Record the original comparison, the later update, and the sentence you would now be willing to teach. This last step forces the evidence review to change the claim.
crumbs: E  When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity

title: Appendix E — When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity
section: What to do when you find a serious problem
text:
What to do when you find a serious problem
The first obligation is to the accuracy of the record, not to winning an argument.

Preserve the original files, metadata, logs, outputs, and correspondence. Do not alter source data.
Reproduce the discrepancy with a written, versioned procedure.
Check benign explanations: versions, filters, merges, coding, duplicated exports, unit conventions, and undocumented but legitimate decisions.
Describe the observable problem precisely. Separate what is known from what is inferred.
Use the relevant journal correction process or institutional research-integrity officer when misconduct may be involved. Requirements differ by jurisdiction and institution.
Protect confidential data and good-faith reporters. Do not circulate identifiable allegations beyond those who need to assess them.
Correct the public claim proportionately: erratum, corrected analysis, expression of concern, retraction, or a documented explanation that resolves the discrepancy.

A system that can reveal, investigate, and correct error strengthens the scientific record.
crumbs: E  When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity

title: Appendix E — When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity
text:
Study and practice
Return to the one hundred teams. Suppose you can change only one feature of their research system: study precision, prospective registration, results-independent publication, or data and code preservation. Explain which problem your choice addresses and which would remain. Then compare a significant original estimate with a smaller nonsignificant replication: what information would you need before deciding whether they conflict?






TipActivity: audit the evidence pipeline



A small original study reports a large intervention effect on one of six measured outcomes. The article discusses only that outcome and does not disclose its stopping rule. A larger preregistered replication estimates a much smaller effect with an interval spanning zero. The raw data and analysis code for the original are unavailable.
Do not vote “true” or “false.” Map the case onto Figure E.1. Identify the uncertainty introduced at design, data, analysis, publication, and replication. Then propose: (a) the next study, (b) the cumulative claim that is warranted now, and (c) one institutional change that would have made the evidence easier to interpret.
Submit the completed pipeline, two distinct threats stated without alleging intent, the next test, the revised cumulative claim, and the institutional safeguard.
crumbs: E  When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity

title: Appendix E — When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity
section: Famous findings after replication: an evidence-status map
text:
Famous findings after replication: an evidence-status map
A list of “studies that failed to replicate” can mix events that have different implications. A direct replication may estimate almost no effect, while a multilab project or meta-analysis may reveal a smaller average or substantial variation. Better controls can weaken a predictive association without repeating the original study, and a reanalysis can expose a statistical artifact. A retraction concerns the reliability of the research record. Read each update for what changed and what that change allows us to conclude.
This map covers influential cases used in or closely related to the book. Each entry connects the memorable claim to a later test or correction. The FORRT Replication Database provides a broader, evolving index of replication studies (Röseler et al., 2024).






ImportantInterpreting the evidence-status labels




Not reproduced means that a strong direct or coordinated test did not recover the focal effect under the tested protocol.
Attenuated or conditional means that the cumulative estimate is smaller, more heterogeneous, or more dependent on moderators than the famous version implies.
Reinterpreted means that later controls or analysis changed what the evidence can identify; it is not necessarily a direct replication failure.
Retracted or integrity-qualified records a problem with the original research record. Nonreplication alone is not evidence of misconduct.




Direct tests, coordinated replications, and integrity updates
Read Table E.3 across each row, from the original claim to the later test or integrity update. A result that was not reproduced and a retraction change confidence for different reasons; the table keeps the tested procedure and the broader interpretation distinct.



Table E.3: Prominent direct and coordinated replication cases, updated 10 September 2026





Famous finding
Key update and defensible conclusion




Elderly-word priming slows walking. Bargh, Chen, and Burrows (1996) reported that exposure to words associated with old age made participants walk more slowly.
Not reproduced under automated timing. Doyen et al. (2012) did not recover the effect in a larger replication with automated measurement. A second experiment produced slowing only when experimenters expected it. Expectancy and implementation are plausible moderators.


Professor priming improves trivia performance. Dijksterhuis and van Knippenberg (1998) reported that activating the professor stereotype increased general-knowledge performance.
Not reproduced in a registered multilab project. Twenty-three eligible replications involving 4,493 participants produced no reliable professor-priming advantage (O’Donnell et al., 2018).


Holding something warm produces interpersonal warmth. Williams and Bargh (2008) reported warmer personality judgments and more prosocial choices after brief physical warmth.
Not reproduced in two blinded replications. Chabris et al. (2019) obtained near-zero estimates in two larger samples.


Moral threat increases interest in cleansing—the “Macbeth effect.” In Study 2, Zhong and Liljenquist (2006) reported greater interest in cleansing products after copying an unethical rather than an ethical first-person story.
Not reproduced in three direct attempts at Study 2. Earp et al. (2014) did not recover the predicted preference for cleansing products.2


Expansive “power poses” change hormones and risk taking. Carney, Cuddy, and Yap (2010) reported higher testosterone, lower cortisol, and greater risk tolerance after brief expansive poses.
Focal physiological and risk effects not reproduced. Ranehill et al. (2015) found no effects on hormones or risk tolerance in a substantially larger sample, although self-reported feelings of power increased.


A first act of self-control depletes a general resource. Baumeister et al. (1998) launched the sequential-task account of ego depletion.
Effects were near zero or small in coordinated tests. A preregistered 23-laboratory replication of a later sequential-task protocol estimated a near-zero effect whose interval included zero (Hagger et al., 2016). A 36-site paradigmatic test also found a very small, nonsignificant effect (Vohs et al., 2021), while another multilab project found a small significant effect (Dang et al., 2021). The protocols leave room for explanations involving motivation, fatigue, and task design (Ch. 39).


Mortality salience increases worldview defense. Greenberg et al. (1994) reported more favorable evaluation of a pro-American author, relative to an anti-American author, after participants wrote about death.
Not reproduced in Many Labs 4. Seventeen laboratories and 1,550 participants found little evidence for the focal effect using both in-house and original-author-advised protocols (Klein et al., 2022).


Distraction produces better complex decisions than conscious thought. Dijksterhuis et al. (2006) reported an “unconscious-thought advantage” for multiattribute choices.
Not reproduced in a large replication and unsupported by the small-study pattern. Nieuwenstein et al. (2015) found no advantage in a sample of 399 and concluded that the meta-analytic pattern was concentrated in small studies.


Ill-fated disease–birth-year combinations shorten Chinese-American lives. Phillips, Ruth, and Wagner (1993) reported that Chinese-American decedents with combinations considered unfavorable in Chinese astrology and traditional medicine died 1.3–4.9 years earlier than expected.
Not reproduced in independent years; the original specification was also challenged. Smith (2006) found that a more direct and inclusive analysis of the 1969–1990 data provided little support for the claim, and California mortality records from 1960–1968 and 1991–2002 did not reproduce it. The reanalysis and independent years challenge both the original specification and its out-of-sample stability.


Images of watching eyes increase generosity. Bateson et al. (2006) reported higher coffee-room honesty-box contributions under eye images than under flower images.
No reliable overall effect in two meta-analyses. Northover et al. (2017) found that artificial surveillance cues did not reliably increase generosity. See the worked case above.


Recalling moral rules reduces cheating. Mazar, Amir, and Ariely (2008) reported that recalling the Ten Commandments reduced dishonest reporting.
Not reproduced; original article carries an expression of concern. Twenty-five preregistered direct replications involving 5,786 participants found a small difference in the opposite direction (Verschuere et al., 2018). A 2024 journal notice separately identified reporting and data-provenance concerns. The notice records concerns about the article’s evidence.3 The moral-reminder result is unsupported by the direct replications (Ch. 7).


Signing an honesty statement first reduces cheating. Shu et al. (2012) reported less dishonest reporting when people signed at the beginning rather than the end of a form.
Not reproduced; original article retracted. Five conceptual replications and a preregistered direct replication found no signing-first effect (Kristal et al., 2020). The original article was later retracted. The replication result updates the intervention claim; the retraction separately updates confidence in the original record.


Evenly spaced external deadlines reduce procrastination and improve performance. Ariely and Wertenbroch (2002) reported that imposed, evenly spaced deadlines outperformed self-set or end deadlines.
Not reproduced; original article retracted on 2 September 2026. Hyndman and Bisin’s (2026) replication of Study 2 found negligible deadline effects and no advantage of evenly spaced deadlines. The journal retracted the original article because it could no longer attest to the findings’ reliability; both authors agreed (Psychological Science, 2026). The replication challenges the spacing prescription (Ch. 20).


Holding a pen in the teeth makes cartoons funnier. Strack, Martin, and Stepper (1988) used the pen-in-mouth task as evidence for facial feedback.
Specific procedure not reproduced; broader mechanism has qualified support. A 17-laboratory registered replication found essentially no pen-condition difference (Wagenmakers et al., 2016). A later 19-country multilab study found effects on reported happiness for voluntary smiles and facial mimicry, while evidence from the pen-in-mouth task was less conclusive (Coles et al., 2022).








Famous conclusions that became smaller, conditional, or different
The cases in Table E.4 belong in the same teaching map because they are often described casually as “debunked.” That label discards the most useful information: what changed and what remains.



Table E.4: Famous findings revised by later evidence and analysis





Famous conclusion
Key update and defensible conclusion




More choice demotivates—the jam-study story. Iyengar and Lepper (2000) reported that a larger display attracted more attention but a smaller display produced more purchases.
Attenuated and moderator-dependent. Scheibehenne, Greifeneder, and Todd’s (2010) meta-analysis found a near-zero mean effect with substantial heterogeneity; Chernev, Böckenholt, and Goodman (2015) identified conditions involving task difficulty, preference uncertainty, and decision goals. The cumulative evidence favors a conditional account of overload (Chs. 2 and 40).


The marshmallow test reveals a stable trait that predicts life success. Shoda, Mischel, and Peake (1990) reported associations between preschool delay and later competencies.
Reinterpreted and attenuated. Watts, Duncan, and Quan (2018) used a larger, more diverse sample. Among children whose mothers had not completed college, the association between waiting and adolescent achievement was smaller than in the original studies and fell by about two thirds after controls for family background, early cognitive ability, and home environment. Experiences of an experimenter’s reliability can also change waiting (Kidd et al., 2013; Ch. 20).


Stereotype threat explains performance gaps. Classic experiments showed that identity-relevant cues can impair performance (Steele & Aronson, 1995; Spencer, Steele, & Quinn, 1999).
Conditional and smaller in operationally realistic settings. Meta-analytic estimates vary with domain, design, setting, and publication selection; effects in settings resembling real high-stakes testing are negligible to small (Flore & Wicherts, 2015; Shewach et al., 2019). The operational setting is central to interpreting the effect (Ch. 5).


Reminders of money make people self-sufficient and less prosocial. Vohs, Mead, and Goode (2006) reported a broad package of effects across nine experiments.
Heterogeneous and sensitive to study selection. Lodder et al.’s (2019) meta-analysis found a positive overall average with indications of publication bias. The 47 preregistered experiments, most of which tested system justification, averaged near zero. Evaluate the evidence for each cue and outcome.


Explicitly naming a forgone use of money reduces purchasing. Frederick et al. (2009) reported that adding “keep the money for other purchases” shifted some participants away from buying.
Replicated on average, but smaller than the original impression. A meta-analysis of 39 experiments found a reliable but modest effect, mainly in hypothetical decisions (Maguire et al., 2023). Making opportunity cost visible can change reported choice (Ch. 2).


People falsely believe in the hot hand. Gilovich, Vallone, and Tversky (1985) treated basketball streak beliefs as a cognitive illusion.
Reinterpreted by statistical correction, not a failed replication. Miller and Sanjurjo (2018) showed that the conventional within-sequence comparison was biased against detecting positive dependence and found evidence consistent with hot-hand performance. The statistical correction changes the interpretation of the original result.


Choosing a chance outcome makes people believe they control it. Langer (1975) linked choice and other skill-like features to responses in chance tasks.
The choice-to-belief mechanism is challenged. Across 17 experiments, Klusowski et al. (2021) found that choosing rarely increased success beliefs beyond pre-existing misunderstandings of the options. Valuing choice is not sufficient evidence of believing that it changes the odds (Ch. 15).






A changed conclusion can come from new data, a better comparison, or a correction to the record. The distinction matters: Smith (2006), for example, both reanalyzed the original Chinese-American mortality period and tested independent years. The first operation assessed robustness; the second assessed replication.

title: Appendix F — Portable Tools
text:
Choose a tool
You can recognize a bias after a decision and still repeat it next time. When the next deadline arrives, the missing forecast, unasked question, or unexamined trade-off may be just as easy to overlook. These worksheets put the chapter ideas into a record you can use while the decision is still open. Choose one tool for the difficulty you face. Its value lies in what it helps you produce: a forecast you can check, a question you can ask, or a change you can try and review.
If the outcome is still unknown, the One-Page Decision Journal helps preserve your reasoning. If you are reviewing a completed decision, the Decision Audit Studio helps separate the process from the result. Use Table F.1 to match the depth of the tool to the stakes and the record you need. Add another tool only when the first reveals a question it cannot answer. Each box is labelled by its role below; a quick check can start a discussion, but consequential decisions may require a fuller record.

title: Appendix F — Portable Tools
text:
Individual judgment and decision process
Preserve a decision before its outcome with the journal, or examine an earlier decision with the audit. The shorter tools below focus on evidence, disagreement, and intuitive judgment.








NoteOne-Page Decision Journal



Core tool
Use one entry for a consequential, uncertain, repeated, contested, or difficult-to-reverse decision. Complete Before choosing before the result is knowable. At the review trigger, append After the outcome without rewriting the original. Definitions and evidence are in Chapter 41.
Use the same seven labels in Table F.3 at both moments. Read across each row: the entry after the outcome must answer the question recorded before choosing, so hindsight cannot silently replace the original reasoning.



Table F.3: A decision journal that compares the original reasoning with the later outcome.










Learning loop
Before choosing — freeze
After the outcome — append; do not overwrite




1. Decision and execution
Entry ID, time stamp, owner, deadline, scope, and exact decision.
What was implemented, when, and with what deviations or delayed effects?


2. Alternatives and opportunity cost
Serious options, best feasible alternative forgone, and excluded options.
Was an important option missing? What is known—and still unknowable—about the forgone paths?


3. Evidence and reference class
Sources, base rate or comparable cases, missing evidence, and fact–estimate–assumption labels.
Which evidence proved diagnostic, weak, misleading, missing, or unresolved? What new evidence arrived?


4. Predictions and assumptions
Resolvable forecasts with horizons, probabilities or ranges, and load-bearing assumptions and causal rationale.
Resolve the same forecasts. Which assumptions were supported, failed, or remain untested? Score calibration across comparable entries where useful.


5. Values and stakeholders
Criteria, priorities, affected people, protected constraints, and trade-offs.
Evaluate the same criteria and people. What was misweighted, neglected, or legitimately changed?


6. Context, incentives, dissent, and tools
Affect, pressure, incentives, roles, conflicts, strongest contrary view, and model or AI advice with follow-or-override reasons.
Which influence, dissenting concern, or tool output mattered? Was reliance or override calibrated to demonstrated value?


7. Choice, thresholds, and learning rule
Choice and reason, implementation owner, review trigger, evidence to collect, and continue–stop–scale–revise thresholds.
Were the process and thresholds followed? Rate process and outcome separately. State what should change, what should not, and the next test or review.






Remember the rhythm: freeze → compare → update. A concern noticed only afterward is useful evidence, but label it “not anticipated” rather than rewriting the original reasoning.
Keep access and retention proportionate to the stakes. Keep any required minutes, approvals, and professional records alongside the journal.









NoteDecision Audit Studio



Core tool
Part 1 — capture the story. In five sentences, state the decision, choice, why it seemed right at the time, what happened, and how good the decision now seems on a 1–7 scale.
Part 2 — expose the process. Reconstruct alternatives, predictions, valuation, opportunity cost, context or state, and intended feedback. Identify the weakest link. Rate process quality and outcome quality separately. Finish: “The weakest link was ___ because . Process quality: /7. Outcome quality: /7. Next time I will improve it by .”
Use the difference between your two ratings to identify what the outcome alone would have hidden. A good result may conceal a weak process, while a disappointing result may follow a reasonable choice.









NoteAttention Audit



Core tool
Write down what received attention and what was overlooked. Identify a feature of the situation that could explain the difference—for example, a vivid story, the order of information, or time pressure. Propose one change that would make the missing evidence easier to notice.









NotePrediction–Valuation Split



Core tool
Write the disputed claim twice. Under Prediction, state what each person believes will happen, with probability or range and the evidence that could change it. Under Valuation, state what matters, to whom, the consequence if the prediction is wrong, and the trade-off each person is willing to accept. Finish with one sentence: “We disagree mainly about , so the next useful step is .”








NoteExpectation Loop Map



Specialized extension
Choose one expectation and draw a possible path through which it could help change an outcome. The links might involve attention, interpretation, action, another person’s response, or physiology where relevant. Mark which links are observed and which are conjectures. Identify one comparison that could distinguish an expectation’s causal influence from an accurate forecast.








NoteBias Redesign Studio



Specialized extension
Choose one process—hiring, investing, exam preparation, project planning, purchasing, or negotiation. Name a likely trigger such as an early anchor, vivid anecdote, identity threat, global impression, or time pressure. Redesign the process before the trigger appears: specify who does what, when, using which independent evidence. Prefer a changed environment to a promise of willpower.









NoteHeuristic Detector



Core tool

What question needs an answer?
Which cue or rule appears to guide the judgment? If an easier question was substituted, name it.
When would that cue or rule give a useful answer?
What comparison or missing evidence could reveal a mistake here?

Finish with one change to the judgment process that addresses the identified weakness.

title: Appendix F — Portable Tools
text:
Probability, risk, time, and well-being
Start with the Probability Judgment Audit for a forecast or the Risky-Choice Audit for a choice among uncertain outcomes. The remaining tools address the specific problems named in their titles.







NoteProbability Judgment Audit



Core tool
Define the event, population, time horizon, and the condition on which the probability depends. Translate percentages into counts within a shared population, keeping clear which subgroup each conditional rate refers to. For a conjunction, check that it is no more likely than either component; when adding probabilities, account for overlap.
Record the forecast and a rule for deciding whether the event occurred. After resolution, score that same event. For a binary outcome, the Brier score is the squared difference between the forecast probability and the outcome, coded as one if the event occurred and zero otherwise. Lower scores indicate better forecasts. The mathematical analysis in Chapter 15 gives the formula and a worked example; the chapter explains how to learn from a series of forecasts.









NoteRisky-Choice Audit



Core tool
List each option’s possible outcomes and what is known about their probabilities. For monetary outcomes with specified probabilities, calculate expected monetary value. Evaluate other consequences in terms appropriate to the decision. Consider what the gains and losses would mean for the chooser, including the maximum affordable loss. Ask what certain outcome the chooser considers equivalent to the risky option before naming a risk attitude. State the reference point and whether the same prospect was described as a gain or a loss. Ask how insurance or diversification changes the possible payoffs. Separately, ask whether new information would change the probability estimates or the chosen action enough to justify its cost. Finish by naming what expected utility explains, what prospect theory describes, and what neither model identifies from one choice.








NoteExperience-Sample Audit



Specialized extension
What outcomes were encountered, how many times, and through which sampling policy? Which rare outcomes could easily be absent? What caused sampling to stop? Are recent, vivid, or similar cases overrepresented? Did earlier choices remove opportunities for corrective learning? Add the best available description—base rates, denominators, time horizon, and uncertainty—then explain why description and experience agree or conflict.








NoteIntertemporal MOST Audit



Specialized extension
Write the full stream of outcomes for each option. Use MOST to check magnitude, opportunity cost (including hidden zeros), sign, and time frame. Then ask whether cash needs, trust in future payment, inflation, or transaction costs explain the choice before attributing it to impatience. If you propose a commitment, specify the goal it protects and what happens after a missed step.








NoteMental-Accounting Audit



Specialized extension
Identify the mental account being used: its label, budget, reference point, opening and closing dates, and the connection between payment and consumption. Separate whether what you obtain is worth its total cost from how attractive the deal feels, and distinguish payments that cannot be recovered from consequences that can still change. Reconstruct the choice once within that account and once across the full balance sheet or portfolio. Chapter 19 develops these distinctions. Preserve a boundary when it protects a valued goal; relax it when the label, rather than future value, drives the decision.








NoteMarket Claim Audit



Specialized extension
State the information set and expected-return model behind an efficiency claim. For an anomaly, ask about risk, mispricing, data mining, transaction costs, financing, short-sale constraints, and post-publication decay. For a bubble claim, separate uncertain fundamental value from evidence of feedback, resale motives, leverage, liquidity, and arbitrage limits.








NoteWell-Being Measurement Audit



Specialized extension
Specify whether the claim concerns experienced affect, remembered experience, life evaluation, meaning, or behavior. State the question wording, time window, scale, sample, comparison, and uncertainty. Separate income level from changes and adaptation; correlation from intervention; average effects from distribution and subgroup differences. Use forecasts from comparable lives or episodes before trusting a focusing intuition about what will make life go well.

title: Appendix F — Portable Tools
text:
Social and strategic decisions







NoteStrategic Interdependence Map



Core tool
Identify the players, their available actions, and how each person’s outcome depends on the combination of choices. Record what they know and when they move. Find best responses under the stated beliefs, then ask how repetition, social preferences, norms, or enforcement could change the prediction. Mark the assumptions you would need to check before applying the game to a real situation.

title: Appendix F — Portable Tools
text:
Behavior and self-regulation
Use the Behavior Redesign Canvas to change a repeated action. The short urge-observation exercise is useful when a noticeable impulse is part of the episode.







NoteBehavior Redesign Canvas



Core tool
Choose one mild, repeated behavior. Reconstruct cue → impulse → action → outcome, using impulse to mean readiness to act even when it was not consciously noticed. Record what the action accomplished in the moment.
Specify one feasible replacement and one change to the setting that would help it occur. Decide what you will record for a week, when you will review it, and how you will resume after a lapse. The output is the old routine, the proposed change, and a measure of whether it helped the person’s own goal.








NoteOne-Minute Urge Observation



Quick check
Choose a mild everyday impulse. Pause, breathe, and notice what the urge feels like without requiring it to disappear. After about a minute, record what changed and choose the next action.1

title: Appendix F — Portable Tools
text:
Persuasion, communication, and connection
Use the Verified Understanding Loop when people may be interpreting the same words differently. The message and listening tools help you prepare what to say or ask.






NoteModel-Updating Message



Specialized extension
Before drafting, state who the audience is, what they currently believe, what concerns them, and what evidence could reasonably change their view. Name the desired response and the strongest objection to it.
For a short message, use AND–BUT–THEREFORE: establish the audience’s reasonable expectation, show the obstacle or observation that disrupts it, and make clear what is at stake. Let the resulting question lead to the proposed response. The logic should read naturally; the message need not display the labels. For a fuller message, STORY means Shared reality, Trouble, Opportunity, Reasons to believe, and Yes to a specific decision. Make the action feasible and the uncertainty visible.








NoteLayered Listening



Quick check
Begin with what happened, then ask what it meant to the speaker. Explore feelings, history, or relationships when they are relevant and the person welcomes the question. Check what is wanted from the conversation: understanding, advice, a decision, repair, or a commitment.









NoteVerified Understanding Loop



Core tool
Ask, listen, and restate the meaning in your own words. Invite the speaker to correct what you missed, then check again. The aim is an account the speaker recognizes as accurate. You can understand a position while continuing to disagree with it.

title: Appendix F — Portable Tools
text:
Negotiation
Begin with Negotiation Preparation to establish what would make an agreement worth accepting. Use the Package and Contingency Worksheet to explore differences that could create value. The other tools help when a tactic, dispute, or implementation problem needs closer attention.







NoteNegotiation Preparation



Core tool

State your best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA) and how you could improve it. Use it to determine the least acceptable agreement, allowing for risk and implementation costs.
List the issues, priorities, target, proposed opening, and supporting standards.
Record what you know about the other side’s interests and alternatives, and what you need to ask.
Prepare possible packages, a concession plan, and terms for implementation and review.









NoteTactic Diagnostic



Specialized extension
Use Table F.4 to separate what a bargaining move may be trying to signal from the evidence you need before responding. A flinch or deadline is a reason to investigate a constraint, not proof that the constraint is binding.



Table F.4: A diagnostic response to common bargaining tactics.










Move
What it may be trying to signal or produce
Disciplined response




Flinch or visible shock
Your proposal is unreasonable
Return to standards and ask for the basis of the reaction.


Nibble
A late, small request will be conceded because both sides want closure
Reopen the package and link any addition to a reciprocal change.


Limited authority
An absent approver prevents movement
Verify the mandate and make any proposal conditional on approval of the whole package.


Good cop / bad cop
Pressure followed by relief should accelerate concession
Treat the roles as one process; slow down and ask for constraints and proposals in writing.


Exploding offer or deadline
Delay will destroy the opportunity
Verify what changes at the deadline, compare the BATNA, and request enough time for informed review.


Take it or leave it
The stated term is final
Test credibility without bargaining against yourself; compare the complete offer with the BATNA.


Bogey—falsely presenting a low-priority issue as crucial—false scarcity, or a fake bottom line
A priority or constraint is more important or fixed than it is
Ask for evidence, use conditional packages, and verify claims where possible. Deliberate deception remains unethical even when tactically common.














NoteMediation and Arbitration Are Different Choices



Specialized extension
A mediator helps parties seek a voluntary agreement and ordinarily does not impose the result. An arbitrator hears the dispute and issues a decision under the applicable procedure. In final-offer arbitration, the arbitrator chooses between submitted final offers; whether that choice concerns a whole package or individual issues depends on the rules. Before choosing a process, establish the neutral’s authority, costs, confidentiality, and whether the decision is binding or reviewable.








NotePackage and Contingency Worksheet



Specialized extension
List the negotiable issues and estimate what matters to each side. Prepare several packages of approximately equal value to you that trade differently across issues; these are multiple equivalent simultaneous offers (MESOs). Use the response to learn about priorities.
If the disagreement concerns a future event, consider a contingent term with a clear measure and verification process. Check whether either side could manipulate the measure or bear a risk it cannot manage. A signed agreement can remain the fallback while the parties voluntarily search for an improvement.

title: Appendix F — Portable Tools
text:
Organizational choice and decision systems
Use the Structured Judgment Pipeline to organize a group decision. Add the choice-architecture audit or AI-use record when the design involves those features. For a new AI-supported workflow, use the AI Decision Canvas; use the ethical audit to examine who is affected.






NoteChoice-Architecture Audit



Specialized extension
Trace one real path: objective → menu → understanding → action → feedback. Mark the options, order, categories, default, mapping, friction, timing, social information, and exit. Write the mechanism as a testable sentence: “Changing ___ should affect ___ because ___.” Compare a nudge with a boost, incentive, mandate, or structural change. Check purpose, welfare, evidence, transparency, exit, and distribution of burden.









NoteStructured Judgment Pipeline



Core tool
Define the decision, its owner, and the people affected. Break the judgment into relevant criteria and establish a comparison or reference class. Have members record estimates independently before hearing the group or an AI recommendation.
Compare estimates and the reasons behind them, then examine the strongest objection. Record the decision, trade-offs, implementation responsibility, and conditions for reconsidering it. Set a review date and an outcome that can be checked. Use fewer steps when the stakes and complexity are low.









NoteMinimum AI-Use Record



Specialized extension
Use this extension when a model materially informs a consequential decision:

Task and tool: task delegated; tool, model, or rule; version or access date; and reason for use.
Inputs and boundaries: material inputs and sources, missing information, and privacy, consent, or use restrictions.
Output and reliance: material output; what was followed, modified, or rejected; and why.
Independent checks: fact and source verification, baseline or independent human comparison, uncertainty and subgroup checks where relevant, and strongest contrary evidence.
Authority and correction: decision owner, affected people, exception or appeal, monitoring signal, review date, and who can pause or reverse the use.

Scale the record and validation with consequence, repetition, irreversibility, unequal power, and automation. Do not place sensitive data in an unauthorized record. Chapter 41 explains the distinction between prediction, valuation, intervention, and responsibility.









NoteAI Decision Canvas



Specialized extension
Complete the decision canvas in Chapter 42 before introducing AI into a recurring decision. It connects the decision and prediction target to values, intervention evidence, human authority, validation, and review. The output is an inspectable proposal for a limited test.









NoteEthical Audit



Quick check
Answer six questions before implementation and again at review:

Whose objective is being optimized?
Who receives the benefit, and who bears the cost or tail risk?
Would affected people understand and endorse the mechanism under informed reflection?
Is refusal, correction, appeal, or exit genuinely available?
Does unequal power change the meaning of apparent consent?
What evidence will reveal harm or failure after implementation?

Add the domain-specific risk—deception, stigma, distribution, coercion, privacy, automation, or another foreseeable harm—and name who has authority to pause, correct, compensate, or end the intervention.

title: Appendix F — Portable Tools
text:
Classroom extensions
Assign an activity that serves the learning objective.






NoteCase, Video, and Conversation Practice



Specialized extension
Case or video debrief. Before viewing or reading, predict the central difficulty. During the case, record observable behavior rather than inferred motive. Afterward, identify the proposed mechanism, a plausible alternative explanation, information learned or lost, economic or relational cost, one boundary condition, and one better action to test. Linked videos remain with their rights holders.
Message production. Create a 3–5 minute message for a real audience and attach a design note of no more than 200 words. State what the audience currently believes, what observation or problem gives it a reason to reconsider, and what you want it to understand or do. Identify the strongest evidence, a value or identity concern to respect, the remaining uncertainty, and an ethical safeguard. Peer feedback should address how the message works rather than judge the presenter.
Connection prediction. Before a four-minute paired conversation, privately predict enjoyment, awkwardness, and connection. Compare forecast with experience. Participation and depth must be voluntary.
Depth and responsiveness. Begin naturally, then ask permission to follow one answer a level deeper—from fact to experience, meaning, emotion, or value. Debrief the difference between curiosity and intrusion.
Warm honesty. In triads, practice care + observable behavior + owned impact + invitation to the other person’s view + one testable request. Unsafe or high-power conflicts may require documentation, representation, or formal support rather than a classroom script.
