title: Index of Concepts
text:
A
Start with a concept’s main explanation, then follow the selected applications to see how it works in another setting. See also links connect related ideas; Appendix G indexes cases and demonstrations. A chapter link covers the wider discussion, while a section link takes you to a specific treatment.
Ability. B=MAP component: Ch. 39, Diagnose the moment with B=MAP. Here ability means momentary feasibility, not a fixed trait. See also: B=MAP; Motivation; Prompt.
Accessibility. Main treatment: Ch. 13. Opening causal-inference case: Ch. 1, Mars publicity. Related: attention in Ch. 3 and availability in Ch. 9. See also: Cognitive ease; Familiarity; Priming.
Acquisition utility. Main treatment: Ch. 19. See also: Transaction utility; Mental accounting.
Action affordance. Opening interface case: Ch. 1, Advertising arrow. Main design application: Ch. 40. See also: Attention; Choice architecture; Friction.
Active choice. Main treatment: Ch. 40. See also: Defaults; Choice architecture.
Active inference. Theory and evidence: Ch. 4. See also: Predictive processing; Prediction error; Precision weighting.
Adaptation. Definition, alternatives, and claim test: Appendix B, Distinguishing evolutionary fitness, preferences, and well-being. See also: Evolutionary explanation; Evolutionary mismatch.
Affect heuristic. Main treatment: Ch. 9. Valuation foundation: Ch. 6. See also: Availability heuristic; Risk as feelings; Valuation.
Affective forecasting. Predicting future feelings: Ch. 22. Future-self connection: Ch. 20. See also: Focalism; Impact bias; Projection bias.
Aggregation of judgments. Main treatment: Ch. 41. Related: independence before social discussion in Ch. 26. See also: Noise; Independent judgment.
Agreement design. Main treatment: Ch. 38. See also: Contingent contract; MESO (multiple equivalent simultaneous offers); Negotiation process; Staged disclosure.
AI Decision Canvas. A design aid for specifying the target, values, intervention evidence, authority, validation, and review: Ch. 42. Portable-tool entry: Appendix F. See also: Artificial intelligence in judgment; Decision journal.
Algorithm appreciation. When algorithm-attributed advice receives greater weight, contrasted with aversion and authority. Ch. 42.
Allostasis. Anticipatory regulation of bodily needs and its proposed relation to value. Ch. 6.
Altruism. Concern for another person’s welfare, distinguished from inequality and strategic motives. Ch. 25.
Ambiguity. Main treatment: Ch. 16. Related: incomplete experiential information in Ch. 18. See also: Risk; Uncertainty.
Ambiguity aversion. Main treatment, including the Ellsberg pattern: Ch. 16. See also: Ambiguity; Expected utility.
Analytical flexibility. Main treatment: Appendix E, Flexible analysis creates many paths to a result. Design safeguard: Appendix D. See also: Preregistration; Publication bias; Questionable research practices.
Anchoring. Main treatment: Ch. 11. Negotiation application: Ch. 36. Design application: Ch. 40. See also: First offers; Contextual comparison.
Apology. Main treatment: Ch. 34. See also: Repair; Validation; Warm honesty.
Arbitration. Main treatment and contrast with mediation: Ch. 38, When direct negotiation needs a third party. Portable comparison tool: Appendix F. See also: Mediation; Negotiation process.
Arithmetic mean return. Contrast with compounded growth and expected terminal wealth: Ch. 16, A positive arithmetic average can conceal multiplicative collapse. See also: Compounding; Geometric mean return; Probability of ruin.
Artificial intelligence in judgment. Prediction–valuation–intervention–responsibility distinction and accountable use: Ch. 41, AI and accountable judgment. Distinction between predictive processing and predictive judgment: Ch. 4. Extended practical treatment: Ch. 42, Deciding With Data and AI. See also: Prediction; Valuation; Structured judgment.
Artificial surveillance cues. Robot-image example and its limits: Ch. 25. Cumulative-evidence case: Appendix E. See also: Replication; Watching-eyes effect.
Aspiration point. Main treatment: Ch. 36. See also: BATNA; Reservation value; ZOPA (zone of possible agreement).
Asset bubbles. Main treatment: Ch. 27. Strategic and social foundations: Chs. 23 and 26. See also: Information cascade; Limits to arbitrage; Strategic resale.
Attention. Main treatment: Ch. 3. Valuation link: Ch. 6. Design applications: Chs. 39 and 40. See also: Accessibility; Bottom-up capture; Top-down attention.
Attention architecture. Main treatment: Ch. 3. Organizational application: Ch. 41. See also: Choice architecture; Salience.
Attention networks. Default, control, salience, and attention networks; boundaries of brain-to-function inference. Ch. 3.
Attribution. Main treatment: Ch. 10. Communication link: Ch. 33. See also: Self-serving explanation; Mind-reading.
Attrition. Main treatment: Appendix D, Attrition and missing outcomes. See also: Noncompliance; Treatment fidelity.
Audience model. Main persuasion diagnosis: Ch. 30. Story and message applications: Chs. 31 and 32. See also: Model updating; Motive–message fit; Persuasion.
Authority. Main treatment: Ch. 28. Persuasion-cue audit: Ch. 30. Process safeguard: Ch. 41. See also: Groupthink; Influence cues; Responsibility; Pluralistic ignorance.
Automaticity. Main treatment: Ch. 21. Skill-practice connection: Ch. 8. Redesign: Ch. 39. See also: Habit; System 1.
Autonomy. Persuasion treatment: Ch. 30, Resistance and reactance. Choice-design safeguard: Ch. 40. See also: Reactance; Transparency.
Availability heuristic. Main treatment: Ch. 9. Sampling extension: Ch. 18. Market application: Ch. 27. See also: Accessibility; Affect heuristic; Hidden denominator.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
B
Bargaining power. Main treatment: Ch. 36, BATNA, aspiration, and bargaining power. See also: BATNA; Reservation value; ZOPA (zone of possible agreement).
Bargaining range. Main treatment: Ch. 36, Map the bargaining zone. See also: Reservation value; ZOPA (zone of possible agreement).
Base rates. Main treatment: Ch. 14. Related: representativeness in Ch. 9 and outside-view forecasting in Ch. 41. See also: Bayesian updating; Reference class.
BATNA. Main treatment: Ch. 36. Orientation: Ch. 35. See also: Bargaining power; Reservation value; ZOPA (zone of possible agreement).
Bayesian updating. Main treatment: Ch. 14. See also: Base rates; Conditional probability; Natural frequencies.
Behavioral finance. Main treatment: Ch. 27. See also: Asset bubbles; Efficient-market hypothesis; Limits to arbitrage.
Behavioral game theory. Strategic reasoning and learning: Ch. 23. Coordination evidence: Ch. 24. See also: Cognitive hierarchy; Level-k reasoning.
Behavior design. Main treatment: Ch. 39. Behavioral diagnosis: Ch. 21. See also: B=MAP; Choice architecture; COM-B.
Ben Franklin effect. When a direct request for help can increase liking, with the study’s relational limits. Ch. 34.
Best response. Definition and worked meeting matrix: Ch. 24. Coordination under uncertainty: Ch. 24. See also: Nash equilibrium; Strategic interdependence.
Between-subjects designs. Different people in different conditions, contrasted with within-person comparisons. Appendix D.
Bias. Mechanism-focused treatment: Ch. 10. Distinction from noise: Ch. 41. See also: Decision hygiene; Noise.
Big Five. Personality dimensions, separated from culture, identity, and fixed types. Ch. 29.
B=MAP. Main behavior-diagnosis framework: Ch. 39. See also: Ability; Motivation; Prompt; COM-B.
Boost. Taxonomy and contrast with nudges: Ch. 40. See also: Choice architecture; Nudge.
Bottom-up capture. Main treatment: Ch. 3. See also: Attention; Salience; Top-down attention.
Bounded rationality. Main treatment: Ch. 2. Heuristic application: Ch. 8. Strategic application: Ch. 23. See also: Rationality; Satisficing.
Bracketing. Main treatment: Ch. 19, Four operations: label, bracket, couple, and close. See also: Fungibility; Mental accounting.
Brain evolution. Bennett’s five-breakthrough first-approximation model and its limits: Appendix B, Bennett’s five proposed breakthroughs. Distinction between sensory prediction and model-based simulation: Ch. 4. See also: Evolutionary explanation; Mentalizing; Valuation.
Brier score. Main treatment: Ch. 15. See also: Calibration; Forecast scoring.
Bright spots. Successful exceptions as clues for a change to test: Ch. 39.
Bystander effect. Main treatment: Ch. 28. See also: Diffusion of responsibility; Pluralistic ignorance.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
C
Calibration. Main treatment: Ch. 15. Predictive foundation: Ch. 4. Organizational application: Ch. 41. AI workflow evaluation: Ch. 42. See also: Brier score; Overconfidence; Prediction.
Cardinal value. Scale requirements and limits: Appendix A, Preferences and the choice correspondence. See also: Ordinal utility; Multiattribute value; Valuation.
Causal inference. Distinction from prediction in decision systems: Ch. 41, AI and accountable judgment. Experimental treatment: Appendix D. Risk versus treatment benefit: Ch. 42. See also: Counterfactual; Identification; Prediction.
Central executive network. Control-network terminology and coordination with other networks. Ch. 3.
Certainty effect. Main treatment: Ch. 17. Related Allais pattern: Ch. 16. See also: Probability weighting; Prospect theory.
Certainty equivalent. Main treatment: Ch. 16. See also: Expected utility; Risk premium.
Change blindness. Main treatment: Ch. 3. See also: Attention; Inattentional blindness.
Choice. Conceptual distinction from judgment: Ch. 1. Normative structure: Ch. 2. See also: Commitment; Decision loop; Opportunity cost.
Choice architecture. Main treatment: Ch. 40. Ethical and learning safeguards: Ch. 41. See also: Behavior design; Defaults; Friction; Sludge.
Choice blindness. Main treatment: Ch. 7. See also: Confabulation; Introspection; Narrator.
Choice correspondence. Formal treatment of maximizers and ties: Appendix A, Preferences and the choice correspondence. See also: Choice; Rationality.
Choice overload. Option construction: Ch. 2. Menu-design evidence and application: Ch. 40. See also: Option construction.
Cognitive dissonance. Main treatment: Ch. 7. See also: Post-choice rationalization; Self-perception.
Cognitive ease. Main treatment: Ch. 13, Familiarity and cognitive ease. Message-design application: Ch. 32. See also: Familiarity; Fluency; Illusory truth effect.
Cognitive hierarchy. Main treatment: Ch. 23. See also: Behavioral game theory; Level-k reasoning.
Collectivism. Cultural emphasis on group obligations and shared goals, distinguished from individual self-construal. Ch. 29.
COM-B. Comparative behavior-diagnosis framework: Research Lens in Ch. 39. See also: B=MAP; Behavior design.
Commitment. Choice-as-sacrifice treatment: Ch. 1. Strategic use: Ch. 24. Persuasion-cue audit: Ch. 30. See also: Choice; Influence cues; Opportunity cost.
Commitment device. Main treatment: Ch. 20. Self-control application: Ch. 21. Design application: Ch. 39. See also: Present bias; Preference reversal.
Common currency. The hypothesis that unlike rewards can be compared on a shared subjective scale. Ch. 6.
Common ingroup identity. A more inclusive group boundary, distinguished from common knowledge and from erasing subgroup differences: Ch. 25. See also: Group identity; Ingroup favoritism; Superordinate goals.
Common knowledge. Private knowledge, mutual knowledge, and higher-order beliefs: Ch. 24. Distinction from credible commitment: Ch. 24. See also: Coordination; Focal point; Communication.
Communication. Main treatment: Ch. 33. Relationship extension: Ch. 34. Negotiation application: Ch. 35. See also: Grounding; Verified understanding.
Compensatory rivalry. The John Henry effect as a possible response to assignment and group status. Appendix D.
Compounding. Multiplicative-risk treatment: Ch. 16. Market application: Ch. 27. See also: Arithmetic mean return; Geometric mean return; Probability of ruin.
Concessions. Main treatment: Ch. 36, Make concessions carry information. See also: First offers; Reciprocity.
Conditional cooperation. Main treatment: Ch. 25. See also: Cooperation; Reciprocity; Social norms.
Conditional probability. Main treatment: Ch. 14. See also: Bayesian updating; Conjunction; Natural frequencies.
Confabulation. Main treatment: Ch. 7. See also: Choice blindness; Introspection; Narrator.
Confirmation bias. Main treatment: Ch. 10, Confirmation and myside bias. Process safeguard: Ch. 41. See also: Disconfirmation; Motivated reasoning; Myside bias. Distinction from expectations changing actual outcomes: Ch. 10.
Conformity. How informational and normative influence shape beliefs and behavior: Ch. 26. Cultural context: Ch. 29. See also: Informational influence; Normative influence; Social proof.
Confounding. Main treatment: Appendix D, Make the counterfactual and confounding visible. See also: Causal inference; Counterfactual.
Conjunction. Main treatment: Ch. 14, Research Lens: conjunction, disjunction, and dilution. See also: Conditional probability; Probability.
Consideration set. Practical distinction from the full feasible set: Ch. 2. Formal treatment: Appendix A. See also: Feasible set; Option construction.
Construct validity. Main treatment: Appendix D. Reader orientation: How to Read the Evidence. See also: Measurement; Identification.
Context cue. Habit treatment: Ch. 21, What is a habit?. See also: Habit; Habitual control.
Context-dependent memory. Environmental retrieval cues, with limits and links to reconstructive memory. Ch. 13.
Contextual comparison. Main synthesis: Ch. 11, Three forms of contextual comparison. See also: Anchoring; Decoy effect; Halo effect.
Contingent contract. Main treatment: Ch. 38. See also: Differing forecasts; MESO (multiple equivalent simultaneous offers); Agreement design.
Cooperation. Main treatment: Ch. 25. Strategic foundation: Ch. 23. See also: Conditional cooperation; Reputation; Social preferences.
Coordination. Main treatment: Ch. 24. Introductory meeting problem: Ch. 23. Communication application: Ch. 33. See also: Focal point; Nash equilibrium; Strategic interdependence.
Counterfactual. Main treatment: Appendix D. See also: Causal inference; Confounding; Experimental design.
Craving. Main treatment: Ch. 21. Response practice: Ch. 21. See also: Self-control; Wanting.
Cultural differences in negotiation. Main treatment: Ch. 38, Culture changes the meaning of a move. Orientation: Ch. 35. Meaning-audit foundation: Ch. 29. See also: Culture; Face; Identity; Negotiation.
Cultural transmission. Main treatment: Ch. 26. See also: Cumulative culture; Social learning.
Culture. Main treatment: Ch. 29. Social-learning foundation: Ch. 26. See also: Cultural differences in negotiation; Identity; Meaning audit.
Cumulative culture. Main treatment: Ch. 26. See also: Cultural transmission; Social learning.
Curiosity. Information gaps and evidence in a message: Ch. 32, optional research note.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
D
Data-driven decision making. Cheaper prediction, explicit valuation, and practical human–AI workflows: Ch. 42. See also: Artificial intelligence in judgment; Machine learning; Valuation.
Data fabrication. Research-integrity treatment: Appendix E. See also: Misconduct; Replication crisis.
Data leakage. Information that should be unavailable enters model development or evaluation. Ch. 42.
Deception. Main negotiation treatment: Ch. 38, Replace lie detection with claim verification. Orientation: Ch. 35. See also: Information verification; Lie detection; Staged disclosure.
Decision audit. Main treatment: Ch. 41. Portable tool: Appendix F. See also: Decision hygiene; Decision record.
Decision hygiene. Main treatment: Ch. 41. Foundations: Ch. 1. See also: Noise; Structured judgment; Process–outcome distinction.
Decision journal. Definition, theoretical basis, evidence, and elements: Ch. 41. Psychological mechanism: Ch. 7. Portable template: Appendix F. See also: Decision record; Hindsight bias; Process–outcome distinction.
Decision loop. Main treatment: Ch. 1. Process integration: Ch. 41. AI-supported extension: Ch. 42. See also: Judgment; Learning; Model management.
Decision record. One time-stamped snapshot of what was known, expected, valued, and chosen; a decision journal links such a record to a later review without overwriting it. Psychological mechanism: Ch. 7. Definition and process application: Ch. 41. Experiential-learning application: Ch. 18. See also: Decision journal; Outcome bias.
Decision science, descriptive. Foundational distinction: Ch. 1, Three questions of decision science. Context-sensitive applications: Ch. 1. See also: Decision science, normative; Decision science, prescriptive.
Decision science, normative. Main treatment: Ch. 1, Three questions of decision science. Benchmark application: Ch. 1. See also: Decision science, descriptive; Decision science, prescriptive.
Decision science, prescriptive. Foundational distinction: Ch. 1, Three questions of decision science. Decision-repair tools: Ch. 2. System-level application: Ch. 41. See also: Decision science, descriptive; Decision science, normative.
Decisions from experience. Main treatment: Ch. 18. See also: Description–experience gap; Rare events; Sampling policy.
Decision trees. Decision, chance, and terminal nodes; expected-utility analysis backward through a sequence. Appendix A.
Decision utility. Main treatment: Ch. 22. Related: preference representation in Ch. 2. See also: Experienced utility; Remembered utility.
Decision weight. Main treatment: Ch. 17. See also: Probability weighting; Prospect theory.
Decomposition. Structured-judgment treatment: Ch. 41, Define and decompose before evaluating. See also: Aggregation of judgments; Structured judgment.
Decoy effect. Benchmark challenge: Ch. 1, Subscription menu. Main treatment: Ch. 11. Choice-architecture application: Ch. 40. See also: Contextual comparison; Regularity principle.
Default mode network. Internally directed cognition and coordination with control networks. Ch. 3.
Defaults. Opening organ-donation case: Ch. 1. Main treatment: Ch. 40. Competing-mechanism audit: Ch. 17. See also: Active choice; Status quo bias; Switching costs.
Deliberation. Main treatment: Ch. 8, The benefits and costs of deliberate thought. See also: Intuition; System 2.
Demand characteristics. Participants infer the study’s purpose and may adapt their behavior. Appendix D.
Description–experience gap. Main treatment: Ch. 18. Risk foundation: Ch. 16. See also: Decisions from experience; Rare events.
Description invariance. Opening survival–mortality test: Ch. 1. Full framing treatment: Ch. 12. See also: Framing; Rationality.
Descriptive decision science. See Decision science, descriptive.
Descriptive norm. Perceived prevalence within a relevant group: Ch. 26, Social norms require a reference group. See also: Dynamic norm; Empirical expectation; Injunctive norm; Social norms.
Determinism and free will. Sapolsky’s “turtles all the way down” argument and its boundary from multilevel causal explanation: Appendix B. Separate discussion of retrospective reasons: Ch. 7. See also: Evolutionary explanation; Introspection; Responsibility.
Dictator game. Main treatment: Ch. 25. See also: Social preferences; Ultimatum game.
Differing forecasts. Agreement-design treatment: Ch. 38, Use contingent terms when forecasts differ. See also: Contingent contract; Prediction.
Diffusion of responsibility. Main treatment: Ch. 28. See also: Bystander effect; Pluralistic ignorance.
Dilution effect. Nondiagnostic detail can weaken the implications of diagnostic information. Ch. 9.
Diminishing sensitivity. Main treatment: Ch. 17. See also: Value function, prospect theory; Reference dependence.
Disconfirmation. Main protocol: Ch. 10. Organizational application: Ch. 41. See also: Confirmation bias; Premortem.
Discounted utility. Main treatment: Ch. 20. See also: Intertemporal choice; Present bias.
Distributive negotiation. Preparing and claiming value: Ch. 36. Orientation: Ch. 35. See also: Anchoring; BATNA; Integrative negotiation.
Diversification bias. Variety seeking in combined versus sequential choices, distinguished from risk diversification. Ch. 19.
Door-in-the-face. A larger refused request followed by a smaller request; concessions and compliance. Ch. 30.
Dopamine. Reward anticipation, learning, and effort: Ch. 21. Measurement limits in gambling studies: Research Lens. Reward-related activity versus dopamine release in cooperation: Ch. 25. See also: Dopamine and reward prediction error; Wanting.
Dopamine and reward prediction error. Predictive cues, unexpected rewards, and omissions: Ch. 21. See also: Learning; Wanting.
Dynamic norm. A verified direction of change rather than current majority status: Ch. 26. Design application: Ch. 40. See also: Descriptive norm; Social norms.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
E
Ecological rationality. Main treatment through cue–environment fit: Ch. 8. Comparison with coherence, epistemic, procedural, and resource standards—and their distinction from evolutionary explanation: Appendix B. See also: Heuristic; Expert intuition; Resource rationality.
Efficient-market hypothesis. Main treatment, separating three efficiency claims: Ch. 27. See also: Event study; Joint-hypothesis problem; Limits to arbitrage.
Effort and reward. Dopamine and the allocation of effort to obtain a reward, distinguished from pleasure: Ch. 21. See also: Dopamine; Wanting.
Effort justification. Boundary treatment in the IKEA-effect discussion: Ch. 17. See also: Cognitive dissonance; IKEA effect.
Emotion. Valuation foundation: Ch. 6. Fast-thinking role: Ch. 8. Narrative application: Ch. 31. See also: Affect heuristic; Risk as feelings.
Empirical expectation. Belief about what relevant others do: Ch. 26. Norm-evidence distinction: Ch. 25. See also: Descriptive norm; Normative expectation; Social norms.
Encoding specificity. A retrieval cue’s usefulness depends on how the event was encoded. Ch. 13.
Endowment effect. Valuation introduction: Ch. 6. Mechanisms and evidence: Ch. 17. See also: Loss aversion; Ownership; Reference dependence.
Equilibrium. Intuitive introduction: Ch. 23. Matrix analysis: Ch. 24. See also: Best response; Nash equilibrium.
Escalation of commitment. Main mechanism and forward-looking correction: Ch. 19. Strategic application: Ch. 23, the €50 auction. See also: Sunk-cost effect.
Ethical audit. Questions about objectives, affected people, informed endorsement, refusal, power, and evidence after implementation: How to Use This Book and Appendix F. See also: Choice architecture; Informed consent; Power; Responsibility.
Ethnocentrism. Ingroup favoritism as selective cooperation and its evolutionary-model counterpart: Ch. 25. Local interaction, inheritance, and model limits: research notes. See also: Ingroup favoritism; Evolutionary explanation; Common ingroup identity.
Ethos. Persuasion treatment: Ch. 30. See also: Logos; Pathos; Source credibility.
Evaluability. Why some attributes become more informative when alternatives are compared together. Ch. 11.
Evaluation modes. Joint and separate evaluation, distinguished from changing the elicitation task. Ch. 11.
Event study. Main treatment: Ch. 27. See also: Efficient-market hypothesis; Joint-hypothesis problem.
Evidence-aligned message. Main construction treatment: Ch. 32. See also: Narrative persuasion; Source credibility; Story–evidence braid.
Evidence boundary. Reading a claim alongside its limits, alternatives, and possible updates: How to Read the Evidence. Research companions: Appendix D and Appendix E. See also: Identification; Replication; Transportability.
Evolutionary explanation. Proximate–ultimate distinction, Bennett’s proposed phylogeny of decision capacities, adaptation alternatives, and evidence audit: Appendix B. Valuation introduction: Ch. 6. See also: Adaptation; Brain evolution; Evolutionary mismatch; Proximate and ultimate explanations.
Evolutionary mismatch. Conditional cue–environment account and four-part test: Appendix B. See also: Adaptation; Ecological rationality.
Expectations. Main treatment: Ch. 5. Predictive foundation: Ch. 4. See also: Self-defeating process; Self-fulfilling process. Distinction from selective evidence and interpretation: Ch. 10.
Expected utility. Main treatment: Ch. 16. Formal representation and assumptions: Appendix A. Prospect-theory contrast: Ch. 17. See also: Certainty equivalent; Risk aversion.
Expected value. Main treatment: Ch. 16. See also: Expected utility; Probability; Valuation.
Experienced utility. Main treatment: Ch. 22. See also: Decision utility; Remembered utility; Subjective well-being.
Experimental design. Full treatment: Appendix D. Research-integrity extension: Appendix E. See also: Counterfactual; Power and statistical precision; Random assignment.
Expert intuition. Mechanism and boundary test: Ch. 8. See also: Ecological rationality; Intuition; Recognition-primed decision model.
Exploration–exploitation trade-off. Main treatment: Ch. 18. Organizational learning extension: Ch. 41. See also: Feedback; Sampling policy.
External validity. Generalizing beyond the people, settings, treatments, or outcomes studied. Sampling foundation: Appendix D, Random sampling and external validity. Broader limits: Transport the result only as far as the evidence travels. See also: Internal validity; Random sampling; Transportability.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
F
Face. Cultural-meaning treatment: Ch. 29. Negotiation application: Ch. 35. See also: Culture; Identity.
Factorial designs. Crossing factors to estimate their effects and interactions. Appendix D.
Fairness. Social-preference treatment: Ch. 25, Ultimatum-game fairness. Negotiation application: Ch. 35. See also: Inequality aversion; Reciprocity; Social preferences.
Familiarity. Main treatment: Ch. 13, Familiarity and cognitive ease. See also: Cognitive ease; Fluency; Mere exposure.
Feasible set. Main treatment: Ch. 2, Construct the feasible set. Formal treatment: Appendix A. See also: Consideration set; Opportunity cost; Option construction.
Feedback. Decision-loop foundation: Ch. 1. Experience and sampling: Ch. 18. System design: Ch. 41. See also: Learning; Outcome bias.
First offers. Main treatment: Ch. 36. See also: Anchoring; Concessions; Distributive negotiation.
Fitness consequence. Distinction from subjective value, well-being, and moral worth: Ch. 6 and Appendix B. See also: Evolutionary explanation; Valuation.
Fluency. Main treatment: Ch. 13, Make accurate information fluent. Message-design application: Ch. 32. See also: Cognitive ease; Familiarity; Illusory truth effect.
Focalism. Main treatment: Ch. 22. See also: Affective forecasting; Focusing illusion; Impact bias.
Focal point. Shared expectations, salience, and evidence: Ch. 24. See also: Coordination; Strategic interdependence.
Focusing illusion. Main treatment: Ch. 22, Social comparison and the focusing illusion. See also: Affective forecasting; Focalism; Social comparison.
Foot-in-the-door. A small initial commitment followed by a larger request. Ch. 30.
Forecast. Statistical prediction and calibration: Ch. 15. Boundary with perceptual prediction: Ch. 4, Two meanings of prediction. Structured use: Ch. 41. See also: Prediction; Predictive judgment.
Forecast scoring. Main treatment: Ch. 15, Calibration makes confidence answerable. See also: Brier score; Calibration; Prediction.
Forgiveness. Forgiveness, reconciliation, trust, and REACH: Ch. 34, optional research note.
Framing. Opening invariance test: Ch. 1, Survival versus mortality. Main treatment: Ch. 12. Prospect-theory bridge: Ch. 17. Design application: Ch. 40. See also: Description invariance; Reference dependence; Reframing.
Free-energy principle. Optional explanation of technical free-energy quantities and their limits: Ch. 4. See also: Active inference; Predictive processing.
Friction. Behavior-design treatment: Ch. 39. Choice-architecture treatment: Ch. 40. See also: Simplification; Sludge.
Fungibility. Normative benchmark and psychological qualification: Ch. 19. See also: Bracketing; Mental accounting.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
G
Game theory. Strategic interdependence through examples: Ch. 23. Models and payoff matrices: Ch. 24. See also: Best response; Nash equilibrium; Strategic interdependence.
Geometric mean return. Compounded-growth distinction: Ch. 16, A positive arithmetic average can conceal multiplicative collapse. See also: Arithmetic mean return; Compounding; Probability of ruin.
Goal-directed control. Main treatment and contrast with habit: Ch. 21. See also: Automaticity; Habitual control.
Grounding. Main treatment: Ch. 33. See also: Communication; Joint inference; Verified understanding.
Group identity. Ingroup favoritism, shared goals, and cooperation: Ch. 25. Cultural treatment: Ch. 29. See also: Identity; Social norms.
Groupthink. Treatment as a contested umbrella for observable group-process failures: Ch. 28. Process safeguards: Ch. 41. See also: Authority; Hidden profile; Pluralistic ignorance; Shared-information bias.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
H
Habit. Main treatment: Ch. 21. Redesign: Ch. 39. See also: Automaticity; Context cue; Goal-directed control.
Habitual control. Main treatment: Ch. 21. See also: Goal-directed control; Habit.
Habituation. Reduced responding to repeated stimulation, distinguished from habit formation and reward prediction: Ch. 21. See also: Habit; Dopamine and reward prediction error.
Halo effect. Main treatment: Ch. 11. Structured-judgment safeguard: Ch. 41. See also: Horn effect; Contextual comparison.
Happiness. Main treatment: Ch. 22. See also: Experienced utility; Life evaluation; Subjective well-being.
HARKing. Presenting a hypothesis suggested by the results as an advance prediction. Appendix E.
Hawthorne effect. Behavioral responses to participation or observation, with heterogeneous evidence. Appendix D.
Hedonic editing. Main treatment: Ch. 19. See also: Bracketing; Mental accounting.
Heuristic. Main treatment: Ch. 8. Specific probability shortcuts: Ch. 9. See also: Ecological rationality; Substitution.
Hidden denominator. Main treatment: Ch. 9. Statistical correction: Ch. 14. See also: Availability heuristic; Base rates.
Hidden profile. Group task in which the collectively best option depends on pooling uniquely held information: Ch. 28. See also: Groupthink; Independent judgment; Shared-information bias.
Hindsight bias. Process distinction: Ch. 1. Narrative mechanism: Ch. 7. Safeguard: Ch. 41. See also: Decision record; Outcome bias.
Hook Model. Trigger, action, variable reward, and investment in a recurring product experience: Ch. 39.
Horn effect. Main treatment: Ch. 11. See also: Halo effect.
Hot-stove effect. Main treatment: Ch. 18. See also: Decisions from experience; Sampling policy.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
I
Identification. Establishing which explanation or causal effect the evidence can distinguish: Appendix D. Model-testing limits: Ch. 4; risk-elicitation limits: Ch. 16. See also: Causal inference; Construct validity.
Identification with a character. Taking a character’s perspective, distinct from liking the character: Ch. 31. See also: Narrative persuasion; Self-reference; Transportation.
Identity. Valuation foundation: Ch. 6. Cultural treatment: Ch. 29. Persuasion application: Chs. 30–32. See also: Group identity; Self-reference.
Identity protection. Belief-protection treatment: Ch. 10. Message-design application: Ch. 32. See also: Motivated reasoning; Myside bias.
Identity-safe teaching. Application and evidence boundary: Ch. 29. See also: Identity; Psychological safety.
IKEA effect. Evidence-boundary treatment: Ch. 17. See also: Endowment effect; Effort justification; Loss aversion.
Illusion of control. Control beliefs about chance outcomes, separated from merely valuing choice. Ch. 15.
Illusory truth effect. Main treatment: Ch. 13. Message-design safeguard: Ch. 32. See also: Familiarity; Fluency; Repetition.
Impact bias. Main treatment: Ch. 22. See also: Affective forecasting; Focalism; Projection bias.
Inattentional blindness. Main treatment: Ch. 3. See also: Attention; Change blindness.
Incentive salience. Motivational attraction of reward-associated cues, distinguished from pleasure. Ch. 21.
Independent judgment. Main process treatment: Ch. 41. Social-learning application: Ch. 26. See also: Aggregation of judgments; Conformity; Noise.
Individualism. Cultural emphasis on autonomy and personal goals, distinguished from individual self-construal. Ch. 29.
Inequality aversion. Main treatment: Ch. 25. Negotiation application: Ch. 37. See also: Fairness; Social preferences.
Inequity aversion. Distributional preferences; the main text separates altruism, inequality, and intentions. Ch. 25.
Influence cues. Signal, counterfeit, and agency audit: Ch. 30. See also: Authority; Commitment; Reason-giving; Reciprocity; Scarcity; Social proof.
Informational influence. Main treatment and contrast with normative influence: Ch. 26. See also: Conformity; Normative influence; Social learning.
Information cascade. Main treatment: Ch. 26. Market application: Ch. 27. See also: Conformity; Social learning.
Information verification. Negotiation treatment: Chs. 35 and 38. See also: Deception; Lie detection; Staged disclosure.

Injunctive norm. Perceived approval or disapproval within a relevant group: Ch. 26. See also: Descriptive norm; Normative expectation; Social norms.
Integrative negotiation. Main treatment: Ch. 37. Advanced agreement design: Ch. 38. See also: Interests; Logrolling; MESO (multiple equivalent simultaneous offers).
Interests. Main treatment: Ch. 37, Interests behind positions. See also: Integrative negotiation; Priorities; Value creation.
Interference and spillovers. Experimental treatment: Appendix D. See also: Experimental design; Treatment fidelity.
Internal and external triggers. Feelings and environmental cues that can direct action toward or away from an intention: Ch. 39.
Internal validity. Whether a study supports the causal conclusion claimed within the study: Appendix D, Random assignment and internal validity. See also: Causal inference; Confounding; External validity; Random assignment.
Interoception. Sensing bodily states and their relevance to valuation. Ch. 6.
Intertemporal choice. Main treatment: Ch. 20. Self-control extension: Ch. 21. See also: Discounted utility; Present bias; Preference reversal.
Introspection. Limits and uses: Ch. 7. See also: Confabulation; Reasons versus causes.
Intuition. Main treatment and boundary conditions: Ch. 8. See also: Deliberation; Expert intuition; Recognition-primed decision model; System 1.

title: Index of Concepts
text:

Joint-hypothesis problem. Main treatment: Ch. 27. See also: Efficient-market hypothesis; Event study.
Joint inference. Main treatment: Ch. 33. See also: Communication; Grounding; Mind-reading.
Judgment. Foundational prediction–valuation distinction: Ch. 1, A functional decision loop. Structured organizational treatment and distinction among prediction, valuation, intervention, and responsibility: Ch. 41. See also: Choice; Prediction; Predictive judgment; Valuation.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
L
Large language models. Next-token generation, prompts, and the bounded analogy with predictive processing: Ch. 4, optional Research Lens. Decision-support uses, verification, and evaluation of assisted work: Ch. 42. See also: Artificial intelligence in judgment; Machine learning.
Learning. Decision-loop foundation: Ch. 1. Post-choice distortion and records: Ch. 7. Experiential sampling: Ch. 18. System design: Ch. 41. See also: Feedback; Prediction error.
Level-k reasoning. Main treatment: Ch. 23. See also: Behavioral game theory; Cognitive hierarchy.
Lie detection. Main treatment, including the limits of unaided demeanor judgments and the shift toward verifiable claims: Ch. 38, Replace lie detection with claim verification. Related inferential limits: Chs. 10 and 33. See also: Attribution; Confirmation bias; Deception; Information verification.
Life evaluation. Main treatment: Ch. 22. See also: Experienced utility; Meaning and purpose; Subjective well-being.
Life satisfaction. Evaluative component of subjective well-being: Ch. 22. See also: Experienced utility; Life evaluation; Subjective well-being.
Liking. Distinction from wanting: Ch. 21. Familiarity application: Ch. 13. Persuasion-cue audit: Ch. 30. See also: Liking gap; Mere exposure; Wanting.
Liking gap. Social-forecast treatment: Ch. 34, Test the social forecast. See also: Social connection; Social forecasts.
Limits to arbitrage. Main treatment: Ch. 27. See also: Asset bubbles; Efficient-market hypothesis; Mispricing.
Literature review. A reasoned synthesis of what research establishes, where studies disagree, and what remains unresolved. Full workflow: Appendix C. Search and selection: Build a search you can explain. Comparison across studies: Synthesize the evidence. See also: Research gap; Publication bias.
Logos. Persuasion treatment: Ch. 30. See also: Ethos; Pathos; Evidence-aligned message.
Logrolling. Main treatment: Ch. 37. See also: Integrative negotiation; Priorities; Trade-offs.
Loneliness. Perceived gap between desired and experienced connection: Ch. 22, How choices affect relationships and social support. See also: Social connection; Subjective well-being.
Loss aversion. Main treatment and boundary conditions: Ch. 17. Applications: mental accounting in Ch. 19 and markets in Ch. 27. See also: Reference dependence; Status quo bias.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
M
Machine learning. How different tools contribute to decisions: Ch. 42. Pipe-material prediction in Flint: Ch. 42. See also: Prediction; Large language models; Target-variable problem.
Market anomaly. Bounded comparison of historical patterns and rival diagnoses: Ch. 27. See also: Efficient-market hypothesis; Joint-hypothesis problem; Mispricing.
Market efficiency. See Efficient-market hypothesis.
Masked priming. Experiments on concealed cues: Ch. 13. See also: Accessibility; Priming.
Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. Flexible needs proposal and later developmental reinterpretation: Ch. 6 and Appendix B. See also: Motivation; Evolutionary explanation.
Meaning and purpose. Well-being treatment: Ch. 22, Across a life. See also: Life evaluation; Subjective well-being.
Meaning audit. Main tool: Ch. 29, The culture-and-identity meaning audit. Negotiation application: Ch. 38. See also: Culture; Cultural differences in negotiation.
Measurement. Reader guide: How to Read the Evidence. Construct and instrument treatment: Appendix D. See also: Construct validity; Identification.
Mediation. Main treatment and contrast with arbitration: Ch. 38, When direct negotiation needs a third party. Portable comparison tool: Appendix F. See also: Arbitration; Negotiation process.
Mental accounting. Main treatment: Ch. 19. Finance application: Ch. 27. See also: Bracketing; Fungibility; Sunk-cost effect.
Mentalizing. Bennett’s proposed evolutionary stage for representing one’s own and others’ minds: Appendix B. Decision applications: Ch. 23 and Ch. 33. See also: Brain evolution; Mind-reading; Strategic interdependence.
Mere exposure. Main treatment: Ch. 13. See also: Familiarity; Liking; Repetition.
MESO (multiple equivalent simultaneous offers). Main treatment: Ch. 38. Priorities foundation: Ch. 37. See also: Contingent contract; Integrative negotiation.
Mimicry. Research Lens: Ch. 26. Communication connection: Ch. 33. See also: Synchrony; Social learning.

Misconduct. Research-integrity treatment: Appendix E. See also: Data fabrication; Questionable research practices.
Mispricing. Main treatment: Ch. 27. See also: Asset bubbles; Limits to arbitrage; Market efficiency.

Motivated reasoning. Main treatment: Ch. 10. Persuasion application: Ch. 30. See also: Confirmation bias; Identity protection; Myside bias.
Motivation. Valuation and motive systems: Ch. 6. Evolutionary and developmental comparison: Appendix B. B=MAP component: Ch. 39. See also: Ability; Maslow’s hierarchy of needs; Prompt.
Motive–message fit. Opening museum-message case: Ch. 1. Valuation treatment: Ch. 6, Motives change the decision landscape. See also: Audience model; Persuasion; Valuation.
Multiattribute value. Practical use: Ch. 2, Make values and trade-offs inspectable. Formal treatment: Appendix A. See also: Cardinal value; Trade-offs; Valuation.
Myside bias. Main treatment: Ch. 10. See also: Confirmation bias; Motivated reasoning.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
N

Narrative persuasion. Main treatment: Ch. 31. Message construction: Ch. 32. See also: Identification with a character; Transportation; Story–evidence braid.
Narrator. Main treatment: Ch. 7. See also: Confabulation; Post-choice rationalization; Reasons versus causes.
Nash equilibrium. Introduction and guessing-game example: Ch. 23. Formal analysis and selection: Ch. 24. See also: Best response; Equilibrium.
Natural frequencies. Main treatment: Ch. 14. See also: Bayesian updating; Conditional probability.

Negative reinforcement. A response becomes more likely when it removes an aversive condition; distinguished from punishment. Ch. 21.
Negotiation. Process map: Ch. 35. Claiming value: Ch. 36. Creating value: Ch. 37. Agreement design: Ch. 38. See also: Arbitration; Mediation.
Negotiation process. Main treatment: Chs. 35 and 38. See also: Arbitration; Mediation; Process agreement.
Noise. Main treatment: Ch. 41. See also: Bias; Independent judgment; Noise audit.
Noise audit. Main method: Ch. 41. Portable tool: Appendix F. See also: Noise; Structured judgment.
Noncompliance. Experimental treatment: Appendix D. See also: Attrition; Treatment fidelity.
Normalcy bias. Normalization of warning risk after surviving earlier danger; observational evidence and alternatives. Ch. 18.
Normative decision science. See Decision science, normative.
Normative expectation. Belief about what relevant others think one ought to do: Ch. 26. Norm-evidence distinction: Ch. 25. See also: Empirical expectation; Injunctive norm; Social norms.
Normative influence. Main treatment and contrast with informational influence: Ch. 26. See also: Conformity; Social norms.
Nudge. Taxonomy and ethical treatment: Ch. 40. See also: Boost; Choice architecture; Transparency.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
O
Open science. Main treatment: Appendix D. Reform context: Appendix E. See also: Preregistration; Replication; Reproducibility.
Opportunity cost. Introduced in Ch. 1; main treatment in Ch. 2; formal treatment in Appendix A. Applications: Chs. 19 and 40. See also: Choice; Feasible set; Sacrifice.
Optimally irrational. Conditional interpretation and six-part test: Appendix B. See also: Ecological rationality; Rationality; Resource rationality.
Optimism bias. Unrealistically favorable forecasts require a defensible accuracy benchmark. Ch. 10.
Option construction. Main treatment: Chs. 1 and 2. Negotiation application: Ch. 37. See also: Choice overload; Feasible set.
Ordinal utility. Preference representation and the limits of numerical gaps: Appendix A, Preferences and the choice correspondence. See also: Cardinal value; Rationality; Valuation.
Outcome bias. Process distinction: Ch. 1. Risk application: Ch. 16. Experience application: Ch. 18. Safeguard: Ch. 41. See also: Hindsight bias; Process–outcome distinction.
Outside view. Main treatment: Ch. 41. Statistical foundation: Ch. 15. See also: Planning fallacy; Reference class.
Overconfidence. Overestimation, overplacement, and overprecision: Ch. 15. Applications: markets in Ch. 27 and negotiation in Ch. 36. See also: Calibration.
Overestimation. Overestimating absolute performance or a quantity. Ch. 15.
Overplacement. Overestimating relative standing in a defined comparison group. Ch. 15.
Overprecision. Excessively narrow uncertainty judgments, with an interval-coverage exercise. Ch. 15.
Ownership. Prospect theory and an ownership diagnostic: Ch. 17. See also: Endowment effect; Reference dependence.

title: Index of Concepts
text:
P
Pareto efficiency. Main treatment: Ch. 37. See also: Integrative negotiation; Value creation.
Pathos. Persuasion treatment: Ch. 30. See also: Emotion; Ethos; Logos.
Perceived support. Belief that practical help, understanding, or care would be available: Ch. 22, How choices affect relationships and social support. See also: Loneliness; Relationship quality; Social connection.
Personality traits. Patterns across observations, distinguished from identity and group averages. Ch. 29.
Persuasion. Main treatment: Ch. 30. Narrative mechanisms: Ch. 31. Message design: Ch. 32. See also: Influence cues; Model updating; Reactance.
Planning fallacy. Definition and reference-class correction: Ch. 15. Process safeguard: Ch. 41. See also: Outside view; Reference class.
Pluralistic ignorance. Social-norm mechanism: Ch. 26. Authority and bystander application: Ch. 28. See also: Bystander effect; Conformity; Social norms.
Positive assortment. Cooperators meet cooperators more often than random mixing predicts. Ch. 25.
Positive illusions. Motivation, accuracy, and the evidence debate: Ch. 10, optional research note.
Positive reinforcement. A response becomes more likely when it produces a reinforcing outcome. Ch. 21.
Post-choice rationalization. Main treatment: Ch. 7. See also: Cognitive dissonance; Decision record; Narrator.
Power. Capacity to shape another person’s options, incentives, information, or ability to refuse. Negotiation foundations: Chs. 35–36. Persuasion boundary: Ch. 30, Ethical persuasion. Recurring audit: Appendix F. See also: Authority; Bargaining power; Ethical audit; Informed consent.
Power and statistical precision. Main treatment: Appendix D. Failure consequences: Appendix E. See also: Underpowered study; Uncertainty.
Precision weighting. Main treatment: Ch. 4. See also: Attention; Prediction error; Predictive processing.
Prediction. Foundational distinction from valuation: Ch. 1, A functional decision loop. Boundary between perceptual prediction and predictive judgment: Ch. 4, Two meanings of prediction. Statistical discipline: Chs. 14 and 15. Accountable AI use: Ch. 41. Cheaper machine prediction and decision redesign: Ch. 42. See also: Forecast; Predictive judgment; Predictive processing; Valuation.
Prediction error. Main treatment: Ch. 4. Reward-learning application: Ch. 21. See also: Learning; Predictive processing.
Predictive judgment. Main conceptual treatment as judgment about what is true or likely: Ch. 1, A functional decision loop. Distinction from predictive processing: Ch. 4, Two meanings of prediction. Probability discipline: Chs. 14 and 15. Structured application: Ch. 41. See also: Judgment; Prediction; Predictive processing; Valuation.
Predictive processing. Theory and evidence: Ch. 4. Distinction from predictive judgment: Ch. 4, Two meanings of prediction. See also: Active inference; Precision weighting; Prediction error; Predictive judgment.
Preference reversal. Task-induced reversals between choice and valuation: Ch. 11. Reversals as a delayed outcome becomes immediate: Ch. 20.
Premortem. Process application: Ch. 41. See also: Disconfirmation; Planning fallacy.
Preregistration. Design safeguard: Appendix D. Research-integrity context: Appendix E. See also: Analytical flexibility; Open science.
Prescriptive decision science. See Decision science, prescriptive.
Present bias. Main treatment: Ch. 20. Self-control application: Ch. 21. Redesign: Ch. 39. See also: Commitment device; Preference reversal.
Price as a cue. Price as both monetary sacrifice and information about quality, demand, scarcity, exclusivity, or status: Ch. 6, Price as a cost and a signal of quality. See also: Scarcity; Subjective value; Valuation.
Priming. Main treatment and evidence hierarchy: Ch. 13. Persuasion application: Ch. 30. See also: Accessibility; Masked priming.
Principled negotiation. Interests, options, criteria, and the separation of people from problems. Ch. 35.
Priorities. Main treatment: Ch. 37, Discover priorities rather than guessing them. See also: Interests; Logrolling; Trade-offs.
Probability. Foundational treatment: Ch. 14, Probability begins with a model. See also: Conditional probability; Probability judgment.
Probability judgment. Intuitive mechanisms: Ch. 9. Rules and Bayesian updating: Ch. 14. Sampling and calibration: Ch. 15. See also: Predictive judgment; Risk.
Probability of ruin. Threshold-dependent distinction from expected wealth and average return: Ch. 16. See also: Arithmetic mean return; Compounding; Risk.
Probability weighting. Main treatment: Ch. 17. Contrast with experienced samples: Ch. 18. See also: Decision weight; Prospect theory.
Process agreement. Negotiation treatment: Ch. 38, Negotiate the process. See also: Agreement design; Negotiation process.
Process–outcome distinction. Main treatment: Ch. 1. Applications: Chs. 7, 16, and 41. See also: Hindsight bias; Outcome bias.
Projection bias. Main treatment: Ch. 22. Intertemporal link: Ch. 20. See also: Affective forecasting; Impact bias.

Prompt. B=MAP component: Ch. 39, Diagnose the moment with B=MAP. See also: Ability; B=MAP; Motivation.
Prospect theory. Main treatment: Ch. 17. Contrast with experience: Ch. 18. Applications: Chs. 19 and 27. See also: Loss aversion; Probability weighting; Reference dependence.

Publication bias. Main treatment: Appendix E. Reader orientation: How to Read the Evidence. See also: Replication crisis; Selective reporting.
Punishment. Consequences that reduce responding; distinguished from negative reinforcement. Ch. 21.

title: Index of Concepts
text:

Questionable research practices. Main treatment: Appendix E. See also: Analytical flexibility; Misconduct; Publication bias.

title: Index of Concepts
text:

Random sampling. Selecting units from a population by chance to support inference about that population: Appendix D, Random sampling and external validity. See also: External validity; Random assignment.
Random variation. Main treatment: Ch. 15. See also: Regression to the mean; Small samples; Streaks.
Rare events. Main treatment under description and experience: Ch. 18. Probability foundation: Chs. 14 and 15. See also: Description–experience gap; Sampling policy.
Rationality. Foundational benchmark and context-sensitive tests: Ch. 1. Prescriptive repair: Ch. 2. Formal foundation: Appendix A. Comparison of coherence, epistemic, instrumental, procedural, ecological, and resource standards—and their distinction from evolutionary explanation: Appendix B. Risk benchmark: Ch. 16. Strategic benchmark: Ch. 23. See also: Bounded rationality; Ecological rationality; Resource rationality.
Reactance. Main treatment: Ch. 30. Choice-design safeguard: Ch. 40. See also: Autonomy; Persuasion.
Reason-giving. Conditional persuasion-cue treatment: Ch. 30. See also: Influence cues; Logos.
Reasons versus causes. Main distinction: Ch. 7. See also: Confabulation; Introspection; Narrator.
Reciprocity. Main treatment: Ch. 25, Outcomes and intentions are different. Persuasion-cue audit: Ch. 30. Negotiation application: Ch. 37. See also: Conditional cooperation; Fairness; Influence cues; Repeated interaction.
Recognition-primed decision model. Expert-intuition mechanism: Ch. 8. See also: Expert intuition; Intuition; Satisficing.
Reference class. Main probability treatment: Ch. 14. Experience link: Ch. 18. Forecasting application: Ch. 41. See also: Base rates; Outside view.
Reference dependence. Main treatment: Ch. 17. Applications: Chs. 19 and 27. See also: Framing; Loss aversion.
Reframing. Main treatment: Ch. 12, Reframing as a decision skill. See also: Framing.
Regression to the mean. Main treatment: Ch. 15. See also: Random variation; Small samples.

Relationship quality. Responsiveness, trust, affection, conflict, strain, safety, and repair within important ties: Ch. 22, How choices affect relationships and social support. Communication and repair: Ch. 34. See also: Perceived support; Social connection; Verified understanding.
Relative position. Well-being treatment: Ch. 22. Valuation foundation: Ch. 6. See also: Social comparison; Subjective value.
Remembered utility. Main treatment: Ch. 22. See also: Decision utility; Experienced utility.
Repair. Main treatment: Ch. 34. Communication foundation: Ch. 33. See also: Apology; Verified understanding; Warm honesty.
Repeated interaction. Main treatment: Ch. 25, Repetition gives current behavior a future. See also: Cooperation; Reciprocity; Reputation.
Repetition. Familiarity and truth treatment: Ch. 13. Strategic distinction: Ch. 25. See also: Familiarity; Illusory truth effect; Repeated interaction.
Replication. Reader orientation: How to Read the Evidence. Protocol treatment: Appendix D. Interpretation, integrity, and the evidence-status map of famous findings: Appendix E. See also: Reproducibility; Replication crisis.
Replication crisis. Main treatment and catalogue of famous cases: Appendix E. See also: Publication bias; Replication; Underpowered study.
Representativeness heuristic. Main treatment: Ch. 9. Statistical correction: Ch. 14. See also: Base rates; Probability judgment.

Reputation. Cooperation treatment: Ch. 25. Negotiation application: Ch. 35. See also: Repeated interaction; Social preferences.

Reservation value. Main treatment: Ch. 36. See also: Aspiration point; BATNA; ZOPA (zone of possible agreement).
Resource rationality. Modeling efficient use of limited computation under an explicit objective and cost structure: Appendix B. See also: Bounded rationality; Ecological rationality; Optimally irrational.

text:

Sacrifice. Main treatment: Ch. 2, Name the opportunity cost. See also: Choice; Opportunity cost.

Salience network. A proposed coordination role, rather than a single center that commands attention. Ch. 3.

Satisficing. Main treatment: Ch. 2. Expert-intuition mechanism: Ch. 8. See also: Bounded rationality; Feasible set; Recognition-primed decision model.

Self-defeating process. Main treatment and contrast with self-fulfilling processes: Ch. 5. See also: Expectations; Feedback.
Self-disclosure. Bounded, reciprocal disclosure and responsiveness: Ch. 34. See also: Social connection; Verified understanding.
Self-fulfilling process. Main treatment and causal pathways: Ch. 5. Market feedback application: Ch. 27. See also: Expectations; Self-defeating process.
Self-perception. Main treatment: Ch. 7, When behavior becomes evidence about the self. See also: Cognitive dissonance; Narrator.
Self-persuasion. Generating and examining one’s own reasons for a change. Ch. 30.
Self-reference. Narrative treatment: Ch. 31. Identity foundation: Ch. 29. See also: Identification with a character; Narrative persuasion.
Self-serving explanation. Main treatment: Ch. 10. Post-choice extension: Ch. 7. See also: Attribution; Motivated reasoning.

Small samples. Main treatment: Ch. 15. Intuitive-probability connection: Ch. 9. See also: Regression to the mean; Streaks.
Social comparison. Main treatment in well-being: Ch. 22. Valuation foundation: Ch. 6. See also: Focusing illusion; Relative position.
Social connection. Relational outcome and measurement distinctions: Ch. 22, How choices affect relationships and social support. Communication and repair: Chs. 33–34. See also: Loneliness; Subjective well-being; Verified understanding.

Social identity. See Group identity and Identity.
Social integration. Structural roles, groups, contacts, and participation connecting a person to others: Ch. 22, How choices affect relationships and social support. See also: Loneliness; Perceived support; Social connection.
Social learning. Main treatment: Ch. 26. Market application: Ch. 27. See also: Conformity; Cumulative culture; Information cascade.

Subjective value. Main treatment: Ch. 6. See also: Valuation.

Sunk-cost effect. Main treatment: Ch. 19. Organizational rationalization: Ch. 7. See also: Escalation of commitment; Mental accounting.

Synchronization risk. Market treatment: Ch. 27. See also: Asset bubbles; Limits to arbitrage; Strategic resale.

Top-down attention. Main treatment: Ch. 3. See also: Attention; Bottom-up capture.

title: About This Book
text:
About the Author
This book grew from courses in Behavioral Economics and Decision, Persuasion, and Negotiation taught and refined over several years. Its central question is practical: how can people make better decisions when attention is limited, the future is uncertain, and other people have goals of their own? The chapters follow that question from individual judgment to conversations, agreements, and institutions.
The book applies a recurring ethical test to messages, choice environments, conversations, agreements, and decision systems. Could we justify the arrangement to the people affected by explaining how it works, whose objective it serves, and what evidence supports it? That justification must also address their ability to refuse, correct, or revise it.

title: About This Book
text:
Huanren Warren Zhang.




Huanren Warren Zhang is Associate Professor at Aalborg University Business School and in the Department of Economics at University of Southern Denmark.
He is a behavioral economist who uses experiments, game theory, computational models, and empirical analysis to understand human and organizational behavior. His research examines strategic and risky decision-making, social norms, social preferences, social dilemmas, coordination, and human and organizational learning.
